event_description: A Śreṣṭha family that claims ownership of the Phalcā replaced its traditional tile roof with corrugated metal sheets.

Bhavānīśaṅkara, son of Bhavānīdāsa Bhāro, from Kirtipur built the temple together with other individuals from local groups named Duvāra and Deśa. Bhavānīdāsa Bhāro, on the other hand, installed the sculptures of the deities and donated land parcels to set religious trusts to oversee daily and periodic rituals at the temple.

event_name: Installation of gilded flag and brass finial
event_description: Bhavānīdāsa offered a gilded flag to the temple while also installing a brass finial together with Jayarāma, Śivadāsa, and others.

The deities enshrined in the temple received an offering of gilded finials from Phojasi Mahata, Mildārāma, Daśanārāyaṇa, Siddhisiha, Dharmanātha, Maheśvara, Śrīkṛṣṇa, and the chief of a local religious trust.
Rāmacandra of Kipulcā, together with his wife Māyācā, his younger brother Jogalāla and his wife Nanda laid the temple premises with black stone slabs.
The temple underwent renovation with government funding and local community involvement.

Following damage sustained in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple was reconstructed in 2023 CE (VS 2079) with financial support from the Department of Archaeology and Chandragiri Municipality, alongside the active participation of the Gaṇeśa Bhagavatī Kālikā Rājaguthi, a religious trust associated with the temple.
In front of the temple stands the bell, donated by Durgādāsa’s family. However, the inscription on the bell does not confirm the temple’s exact construction date.

An stele inscribed in Nāgarī script is installed on the right side of the temple's door.Bishwo Pokharel recently published the following reading of the inscription (Pokharel 2011):1. oṁ maṇi padme huṁ2. ālokastimire vipaddibamaṇiḥ pāte ka3. rālambanaṁ yācñākalpatarurjagajjayaratheḥ4. pātheyamanne(nnaṁ)pathi | duḥkhavyādhimahaubadhirbha5. vabhayod vedāntaprayāṇāsanaṃ tāpe  candanakā6. nanaṃ sthirasuhadbhargstatāṃ bāndhavaḥ ||...||7. narakapatitāssatvāṃḥ sukhāvatiṃ modatu || a8. nena puṇyakuśalena | jaisiṃdhena vinirmitāyam9. śrīśāke 1277

The Phalcā, damaged in the 2015 earthquake, was dismantled and reconstructed by the metropolitan city in 2020 CE. For the reconstruction, original carved wooden materials seem to have been reused.पछिल्लो महाभूकम्पमा क्षति भएको फल्चालाई भत्काई महानगरपालिकाले विसं २०७७ सालमा यसको पुनर्निर्माणकार्य सम्पन्न गरेको थियो । यस पुनर्निर्मानका दौरान पुरानै बुट्टेदार काष्ठसामग्रीलाई पुनः प्रयोगमा ल्याइएको देखिन्छ ।
One inscriptions in this Phalcā makes reference to the construction year. However, the inscription is mostly illegible and thus, the date is unreadable.
Pinchẽ Phalcā was renovated by Lalitpur Metropolitan City and the local community.

The letters of this inscription are illegible. The symbol of a sword can be seen above the inscription, whilst two kneeling devotees or donors have been carved into the lower part. They are shown performing a gesture of greeting.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust reconstructed the Sataḥ as it was in a poor state of repair.

A local club by the name the Jayabāgeśvarī Yūvā Klaba began operating from theSataḥin 2007 CE (VS 2064). As the club has obtained permission from the PADT to stay, the club does not pay any rent for using the rooms on both floors.
The Bāhāḥ was founded by and named after Kuladīpa Vajrācārya, a resident of Lagan Ṭola, Kathmandu.

event_name: Handover of the Bāhāḥ to the Sarvahita Guṭhī
event_description: The donor's family handed over the monastery to the Sarvahita Guṭhī since they could not properly run the monastery.
By collecting donations from the Guṭhī members, thekvāḥpāḥdegaḥand boundary walls of the monastery were repaired. An iron gate was also installed during the renovation process.
Bama Bahādura Kũvara, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, built thisśivālaya.
As the 2015 earthquakes caused damage to the temple, the Pashupati Area Development Trust initiated restoration efforts.

Individuals such as Govindarāma Bhāvo and Darasiṃha Bhāvo, among others, collectively restored and re-established the well in Dathulāchi ṭola. The group involved in the restoration also arranged to visit Jawalakhel every year on the day of theBhoṭō Jātrā (Jāhvalā Jātrā) of Buṅgadyaḥ, to perform worship and partake in a feast.

The phalcā where Gaṇeśa was installed, located inthathvatvāla(upper ṭola) of Harisiddhi, was restored. After a month-longGuṃlā Dharmacelebration in Harisiddhi, the residents of the ṭola, under the leadership ofThakāliCandrarāma Bhāvo, collectively restored the phalcā housing Gaṇeśa. The responsibility for its upkeep was assigned to Śiva, Siddhirāma, and Darasiṃha.

event_name: Paving the temple courtyard with stones
event_description: Budhbir Kālu, a resident of Thathukvākva ṭola in Harisiddhi, together with his wife Śaṃlakṣmi and his sons Purnalāl, Śaṅkhalāl, Bekhalāl, and Jītlāl, had paved the stone slabs in front of the Gaṇeśa temple.
A bell was installed for Gaṇeśa, but the name of the person who donated the bell is not mentioned in the inscription.
In memory of the late Birabahadura (Bīr Bahādura), Dabala, Bāsū, Chīrīkājī, Daśarāma, and Sīntalī together built a small temple of Nārāyaṇa.

The area behind thisphalcāis calledbāhāḥ,where one can see several Buddhist statues and Hindu shrines. The organisation managing thephalcāis named Laganakhela Bhajana Maṇḍala. It has organisedbhajanain thisbāhāḥfor the last 40 years and is also responsible for renting shop space.

In the 1970s the Lagankhel area was reconstructed and a public bus station was built. At that time homeless people from the area started using thephalcāas their shelter. To prevent this, the residents of Lagankhel, Thati and Taṃgaḥ decided to rent thephalcāout to shops. According to an elderly man living in Thati Ṭola, the rent collected from thephalcāwas used to install street lights in the area.
Due to the continuous rainfall of the monsoon season, the roof was damaged and began to leak water under thephalcā. The roof was repaired once the monsoon ended.

On the occasion of Kājīlāla Avāle'sjaṃkva(thejaṃkvacelebration takes place when a man is 77 years, 7 months and 7 days old), he donated paintings of five Buddhas and of other auspicious signs such as parrots, the eyes of the Buddha, andkalaśasto be placed around the donor statues.
Bhindyaḥlāchi Phalcā was reconstructed in 2019.

Under the collective initiative of Gopāla Bhāvo (Jyāpu/agricultural community) and other members of the Bhāvo community, a stonetoraṇawas established in the name of Conideva Bhaṭṭāraka. In addition to thistoraṇa, certain stone base structures were also constructed; however, due to the erosion of some letters in the inscription, the precise nature of these structures cannot be clearly ascertained.गोपाल भाव (ज्यापु/कृषक) सहित यस समुदायका अन्य व्यक्तिहरूको सामुहिक प्रयासबाट चोनिदेव भट्टारकको नाममा ढुङ्गाको तोरण स्थापना गरे । यस तोरणका अलावा ढुङ्गाकै केही आधार संरचना निर्माण गरिएको कुरा पनि परेको छ तर केही अक्षर खिइएकाले बनेको वस्तु के हो भन्ने तथ्य स्पष्ट छैन ।

Under the leadership of Kina Bhāvo (Kṛṣṇa Bhāvo), a group from the Bhāvo community constructed small temples on either side of the central stone revered as Cunadevi.किन भावो (कृष्ण भावो) को प्रमुखत्वमा भावो समुदायका व्यक्तिहरूको समुहले यस देवस्थलमा साना मन्दिरहरू (चुनदेवी मानिने शिलाको दायाँ-बायाँ) निर्माण गरे ।

Under the leadership of the contemporary Vaiṣṇava activist Kaviprasāda, a week-long spiritual chanting (kīrtana) program was conducted in the Cunadevi precinct, culminating in the erection of adharmastambha.तात्कालिक वैष्णव अभियन्ता कविप्रसादको नेतृत्वमा चुनदेवी परिसरमा एक सप्ताहव्यापि कीर्तन कार्यक्रम सम्पन्न गरी धर्मस्तम्भ खडा गरियो ।

A concrete structure was constructed directly in front of Cundevi and named the “Cunīdevī Bhāgavata Bhavana.” Its inauguration was carried out by the Mayor of Lalitpur Metropolitan City, Ciribābu Maharjana.चुनदेवीको ठिक सामुन्ने एक कंक्रिड संरचना निर्मान गरियो । यस भवनलाई चुनदेवी भागवत भवन नाम दिइएको छ । यसको उत्घाटन ललितपुर महानगरका मयेर चिरिबाबु महर्जनले गरे ।
The Department of Archaeology renovated thehitiin early 2022 CE. During the renovation, the worn-out spouts of thehitiwere replaced by a new one.

As the Phalcā was on the verge of collapse, it was dismantled and rebuilt at the initiation of local residents. Using brick and cement, it was rebuilt as a two-bay concrete shed, making the Phalcā lose its traditional look.

After the Phalcā was reconstructed as a modern into a concrete shed of two rooms, they were rented out to local residents. The Suntvāḥ Ṭola Sudhara Samiti, a local committee for the conservation of the area, collects the rent from the shops.
The 2015 earthquakes damaged the roof of the Phalcā, which was renovated by The Suntvāḥ Ṭola Sudhara Samiti, a local committee for the conservation of the area.

Both the Phalcā andhitiwere constructed by a person named Viśvanātha Bhaṭṭa in 1863 CE (see the description above for more information). He had also endowed tworopanīsof land and established aguthifor the maintenance of these monuments. However, neither theguthinor land exists for decades.

event_name: Installation of the inscription by recording the construction of Temple and land endowment
event_description: The stone inscription (see description above) erected by Udaya Bahādura Pā̃ḍe and his wife Lalitā Devī mentions the installation of the inscription by recording the construction of the Temple by his grandparents, parents and uncles on their private land and land endowment by them for the maintenance of the Temple. However, it does not mention the date of the Temple’s construction.
In memory of her husband Ḍambara Jaṅga Pā̃ḍe and son Śiva Jaṅga Pā̃ḍe, Ratna Kumārī Pā̃de renovated the Temple in 2007 CE.
The Dhaḥmā Phalcā was restored with funding from the Lalitpur Municipality.
The Bahī was caught on fire.

In 1328 CE (NS 448) the Khaśīyā king Āditya Malla invaded the Kathmandu Valley. He occupied the Pulavahīrī in Patan and laid seige on the town for 22 days. Mentioned Pulavahīrī most possibly is this Bahī. He set fire to all the three cities.
Padmoparijinālaṅkṛta Caitya was constructed near the Bahī.
Narahari Bhāro and his wife Pūrṇā donated thetoraṇawhich is fixed on top of the sanctum door of the Bahī.
Sugarāma set up a stone post used to tie up the sacrificial beast beside the shrine of the lineage deity of Malekus (LAL0640-005).

In the reigning period of Indra Malla, in the memory of diseased Mahāsiṃha Bhāro, fire ritual worship was performed for a whole day and a gilded statue of Akṣobhya was enshrined in the sanctum of the Bahī.
In the reigning period of king Ṛddhinarasiṃha, Bhaneśvara Maī renovated the Caitya in the memory of her father Kutisiṃha. She had also established aguṭhīfor the anniversary and other worships of it.

Some of the inspired youth from Lalitpur planned to reconstruct the Bahī. They requested the king for help. King Vīrendra Vīravikrama Śāha released a fund and the youths collected donations from the locals. The reconstruction process was started in 1980 and was completed in 1988. The king inaugurated the new Bahī complex.
Hemarāja Śākya donated the statue of Akṣobhya that is placed in the sanctum of the Bahī.

event_name: The earliest mention of Pūco Cvaya Bahī
event_description: Athyāsaphū, dated NS 373, preserved in the collection of Dhīrjamuni Śākya, a resident of Kvāthā Bāhāḥ (LAL0660), contains an old map of this Bahī. This is the oldest record of the monument.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Mandira (reconstructed in 2000 CE in its present look)
event_description: The bell, established on the southeast corner of the temple with a cement pillar, was offered by a local Mānandhara family.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Mandira (reconstructed in 2000 CE in its present look)
event_description: The temple had become dilapidated and was replaced around the 1970s with a small modern rectangular building with a cement slab. By the late 1990s, the concrete building had also fallen into disrepair and was eventually demolished.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Mandira (reconstructed in 2000 CE in its present look)
event_description: In the beginning of the 2000s, the rebuilding of the temple in its original form was carried out in consultation with the Department of Archaeology (DoA). The DoA covered half of the expenses and the other half was raised from the local residents, who also provided free labour.

Two large inscriptions in Sanskrit and Newari record the construction of Kavīndrapura by King Pratāpa Malla. The inscriptions state that Narasiṃha, the fourth incarnation of Lord Viṣṇu, got infuriated when the king danced in the guise of the deity. To appease Narasiṃha, Pratāpa Malla built Kavīndrapura and enshrined a statue of Narasiṃha along with various other deities.

King Pratapa Malla recorded the endowment of many plots of land in the name of the deities enshrined in Kavīndrapura in this inscription. He also outlined various rituals and traditions to be carried out from the income of the lands.

Siddhi Tāmrākāra and others from Garakuta, the courtyard in front (west) of Kavīndrapura now known as Gaḥkuti, endowed land to set up a trust (guthi) in the name of Dvibhujasamvara, their lineage deity.

This inscription from the Rāṇā period is currently (April 2023) placed here in Kavīndrapura but is not related to the monument. It records the establishment of the Vaikuṇṭheśvara temple and other structures in a village named Sipāduyā (?) by Vīradhvaja Kārkī and his wife Bhaktakumārī. It also records the couple endowing 31ropanīs of land to set up a trust for observing the anniversary and other periodic rituals. The inscription appears to be from some village on the foothill of the Kathmandu valley and was probably placed here on the ground floor of Kavīndrapura.

event_name: Collapse of the top two roofs
event_description: The upper two roofs collapsed in the 1934 earthquakes.
Recent encroachments have eliminated the arcade and the balcony in the back. A repair scheme undertaken by the Department of Archaeology renewed the roofing and the walls of the side wings in 1986.

After a person named Abhimānasiṃha Khatrī intentionally destroyed the inscription installed by Vīradhvaja Kārkī in 1827 CE (VS 1883), his youngest wife Mahāmāyā petitioned Jagat Śamśera and Raṇa Uddīpa Siṃha in the Rāṇā administration and got the content of the broken inscription reinstalled on this inscription. However, the year of the installation of this inscription is erroneously given as VS 190. Therefore, the year is unclear.

The Hanumandhoka Durbar Square Conservation Program of the Kathmandu Metropolis renovated Kavīndrapura at a cost of NRs. 1.76 million (J. Sāha VS 2068,online). The shops on the ground floor were vacated and thephalcāwas closed with wooden enclosures designed like latticed windows.

A four line inscription indevanāgarīscript is inserted above the temple's door. It is inscribed on stone. Yogi Naraharinath first mentioned it in 1956 (Naraharinath 1956 (VS 2013), 168-169, cited inShrestha 2009, 80).The inscription records the construction of the temple under the auspices of Pratāpa Śāhī and his nephew Māna Śāhī, in ŚS 1504 (1582 CE). It was consecrated by Ātmanātha and Laṁgarnātha, two Nātha yogis. Interestingly, the inscription was written by a certain Rāma Kṛṣṇa from Benares (Shrestha 2009, 280).
The inscription is incised in the cement covering the pilaster at the southern corner of the monument. It records the renovation of the temple in VS 2040 (1984 CE).
An inscription of four lines runs on the northeastern, northwestern and southwestern sides of the base of the Nandī stone sculpture. It records the installation of the sculpture in VS 2042 (1986 CE).

event_name: Damage suffered from the earthquakes and renovation
event_description: The monument was damaged in the 1934 earthquakes and renovated after 1934.
Paramahaṃsa Mahanta Rāma Girī, an ascetic, offered a bell to Śaṅkarācārya. The donation took place before the Śaṅkarācārya Mandira was built.
Mahanta Rāma Girī constructed the temple dedicated to Śaṅkarācārya.
During the Nepal visit of Jagadguru Śaṅkarācārya from the Śṛṅgerī Maṭha, the temple underwent renovation.
During the 2015 earthquakes, a portion of the temple crumbled, and the remaining part that still stood sustained numerous cracks.

Following the damage sustained in the 2015 earthquakes, the temple was reconstructed. The rebuilt temple was inaugurated by Jagadguru Śaṅkarācārya Svāmī Niścalānanda Sarasvatī, the head of the Govardhana Maṭha.
Two stone lions were offered to the temple. Their donors cannot be identified from the inscription.

event_name: Donation of a stone pillar with a golden lion
event_description: King Srīnivāsa Malla erected a pillar with a golden statue of a lion atop it. This pillar is no longer in the temple complex.
Someone called Bhīmabahādura donated a metal flag in VS 1987 (1930 CE). His grandson Kājiratna and grand grandson Suvarṇa Tāmrākāra repaired it.
The legible portion of the inscription mentions that a group of artisans from Jombāhāḥ offered something to Mahālakṣmī.
Govindamāna Śreṣṭha from Bholākhela Bālakumārī plastered the plinth around the temple.

In Nepal, many people believe that when there is a big problem in the country, tears leak from the eyes of gods or sweat comes out of their bodies. When tears flowed from the eyes of Rāto Matsyendranātha in Taḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0050), thePañcarakṣātext was recited for eight days and a special worship followed by sacrifices was performed in this temple, the Vaiṣṇavī temple of Yappā and the Bālakumārī temple of Kvāṭhachẽ. This event took place before the Mahālakṣmī temple was reconstructed in its current style.
Govindamāna Śreṣṭha from Bholākhela Bālakumārī paved the southern street of the temple in stone.

event_name: Construction of a shrine for Mahālakṣmī
event_description: The Mahālakṣmīpīṭhawas located in an open space until this date (NS 821). Vīranārāyaṇa Siṃha, a trader from Mūlacoka, commissioned the construction of the present temple structure and made an offering of a golden pinnacle. Aguṭhīwas also established to perform the anniversary worship in the temple on the day of Śrīpañcamī.
Nāike Niramāna Siṃha and his family erected a stone pillar with a metal lion atop it.
King Viṣṇu Malla endowed land to sponsor theśirāhūtiyajña(a kind of fire ritual) and made arrangements for a regular worship of Mahālakṣmī to take place on the full moon day of every Jyeṣṭha.

event_name: Donation of flags to the main deity
event_description: Bhīmabāhādura Tamoṭa from Naḥ Bāhāḥ offered two metal flags.
Govindamana Śreṣṭha of Bholākhela Bālakumārī repaired and plastered the south-west side of the temple.

Nhurche (an artisan from Jombāhāḥ by profession) and his family offered two stone statues of goddesses riding on lions (Simbāhā) in front of Mahālakṣmī. The anniversary worship of these statues takes place every year on the full-moon day of Āśvina.

event_name: Replacing jhiṅgaṭī-tiled roof with copper sheets
event_description: Sundaralāla Khaḍgī replaced thejhĩgaṭī-tiles on the roof with copper sheets and gilded the top roof.
Govindamana Śreṣṭha of Bholākhela Bālakumārī repaired the temple plinth and commissioned for it to be clad in marble.
An organisation called Buddhi Vikāsa Maṇḍala constructed an artistic brick gate at the entrance of the the temple.
Sudīparatna Tāmrākara repaired the flags donated by Kājīratna Tamoṭa in VS 1987.

event_name: Donation of a pair of lions
event_description: Someone donated the two stone lions which now flank the entrance of the sanctum. The name of the donor could not be deciphered from the inscription.
An artisan from Jombaha clad thetoraṇain brass. This object is fixed above the Mahālakṣmī statue in the sanctum.
Led by artist Ambaradeva of Sātigla (Saugala) Ṭola, Dhanmurta Singh and five other people renovated the roof of the temple. Apāṭīwas also built to the east of the temple on this occasion.
Mahālakṣmīsthāna Vyavasthāpana Samiti (a committee established for the management of the local area) paved the temple courtyard in stone.
During the reign of King Tribhuvan, Jotīrāja, Sidhīrāja, Lakṣmīvīra and others offered the two brass flags which flank the entrance to the sanctum.

Kṛṣṇa Bahādura, a resident of Cāku Bāhāḥ and son of Bhīma Kṛṣṇa, and his wife Pārvatī offered a bell to Mahālakṣmī. It was repaired by their daughters Lakṣmī Kumārī Śilākāra and Viṣṇukumārī in NS 1097 and NS 1100 (VS 2036).
Cinimāyā and others donated a bell in memory of Candra Jālopi.

event_name: Donation of a metal stand, cladding the pillar
event_description: Govindamana Śreṣṭha of Bholākhela Bālakumārī donated a stand for oil lamp inside the sanctum. He also had the pillar clad in brass and offered a bell garland.

event_name: Installation of a Buddha Statue and Construction of a Caitya
event_description: Hākuju and his other family members jointly installed a statue of Śākyamuni Buddha in the sanctum. Moreover, he added acaityato the centre of the Bāhāḥ courtyard.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (KIR0011-006) and Covering Its Top with a Brass Plate
event_description: Jayadatta Siṃha Vajrācārya (son of Karṇa Jyoti) and his other family members jointly constructed the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (KIR0011-006) and covered its top with a brass plate. This inscription refers to Cvay Bāhāḥ as Harṣakīrti Mahāvihāra.
The monument was severely damaged during the 1934 CE earthquakes.
It was renovated after the 1934 CE earthquakes by Bhīmavajra Vajrācārya.
The façade of the Bāhāḥ cracked during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
Rājendra Vajrācārya who performs the daily rituals in the Bahāḥ, repaired the façade of thedyaḥchẽafter the 2015 CE earthquakes.

event_name: Pavement of the Courtyard with Teliyā Bricks
event_description: The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ was paved withteliyābricks in 2017 CE with the financial support of the local government.

The Phalcā, which had remained in an endangered state for a long time after the 2015 earthquakes, was reconstructed by Godāvarī Municipality in 2024 CE (VS 2081). The municipality invested 6 million NR in the reconstruction, making the Phalcā grander compared to its earlier form (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69).भूकम्प पश्चात् लामो समय जोखिमावस्थामा रहेको फल्चा विसं २०८१ सालमा गोदावरी नगरपालिकाद्वारा पुनर्निर्माण भएको हो । नगरपालिकाबाट कूल ६० लाख खर्च गरी विगतको तुलनामा फल्चालाई भव्य तुल्याइएको छ (local resident, Śreṣṭha, male, age 69) ।
The inscription is severely damaged and can be deciphered partially. According toŚākya(VS 2035, 30), it records that aguṭhīwas formed to carry out the worship of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥof the Bāhāḥ.
The inscription on the wooden top rail of the main door records that the doorway was repaired by an individual named Trailokya (text: Terokraju) from Ituṃ Bāhāḥ.
Cikidhi Lakṣmī (text: Lachimi) and her family members jointly constructed the Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya in the Bāhāḥ's courtyard.

event_name: Repair of a Seat of Kvāpāḥdyaḥ
event_description: The seat of thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥwas repaired.

event_name: Construction of a concrete structure over the pīṭha
event_description: This shrine used to be under an open sky. The present concrete structure with four pillars was built in 2001 CE by collecting funds from local residents. At the same time, a brass statue of Basundharā (see object number KIR0046-001 above) was also installed next to the aniconic stone.

event_name: Planned conversion of the present concrete structure into a traditional phalcā-like strcuture
event_description: In November 2021, the Kirtipur Municipality has disbursed NRs. 14,40,000 to convert the present concrete structure of the Pīṭha into a traditionalphalcā-like structure, and the works will commence shortly (2021-11-20).

event_name: Arrival of Vajrācārya Jīvacandra in Bhaktapur
event_description: At the invitation of King Rāya Malla of Bhaktapur, Vajrācārya Jivacandra of Tache Bāhāḥ, Kathmandu had arrived in Bhaktapur.
This inscription on the strut records its installation. However, the full name of the donor from the Vajrācārya caste is not visible.
During the reign of king Jagatprakāśa Malla, Vajrācārya Jayadeva and his son Jayaratna offered a bell to Padmapāni Lokeśvara.
Vajrācāryya Jayadeva offered a strut to the east of the bāhāḥ courtyard.

event_name: Consecration of guardian lions at the main entrane
event_description: Vajrācārjya Jayavidyānanda with his wife and daughter established a pair of stone lions at the main entrance to the bāhāḥ.
Ānandarāja offered a strut to the south of the bāhāḥ courtyard.
Vajrācāryya Jayamuni and his family offered a wooden toraṇa. King Raṇajita Malla was present at the ceremony.

During the reign of King Raṇajita Malla, Kumārīs were sought from outside the Śākya-Vajrācārya family and appointed as Kumārī. In doing so, the virgins died unlucky. After that, a rule was made that a Kumārī should be appointed only from the Śākya-Vajrācārya family and the Kumārī was also given special rights. The king framed the following regulations: anyone including the king and the gods who observed the Ihi, Cuḍākarma and piercing of the ears without a permission of Kumārī would be fined of Rs. 100.

Jujuharṣa, Mohanamāyā, Mayalānī and other people had observed Aṣṭamī Vrata at the bāhāḥ. On the day after the vrata, all of them performed yajña together and offered a silver hegā to Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara.

The temple was levelled during the earthquake of 1934 (Rāṇā1992, 115). TheDevmalavaṃśāvalīstates that all the three stories of the temple collapsed and the image of the main deity was covered in rubble (Yogī2013, 55).

Prime minister Juddha Śamśera reconstructed the temple and consecrated the deity in 1938 (VS 1995 Jestha 11). He was honoured withsindurajātrāand welcomed with many decorated gates in Patan. Gambling was also allowed from 9.00 pm on that day.

event_name: Construction of five storied temple for Degutale
event_description: Śivasiṃha Malla established the temple. However, we do not know whether he only installed the deity or if he really constructed the temple. King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla is credited for changing the structure of the Degutale; he turned it into a five-storey temple and made an offering of a golden pinnacle and a flag. Various historical records disagree on the dates that these events took place. TheDevmalāvaṃśāvalīmentions that this occured on NS 787 Jestha 2 (see inYogī2013, 55), whileBhaṣāvaṃśāvalīstates that it was NS 767, on the second of the dark half of Jestha (see inLamsāl2023, 62). The inscription, however, provides NS 761 as the date when this event happened. The inscription appears to be the most authentic source.

Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.152) states that King Śrīnivāsa Malla rebuilt the three-tiered Degutale temple in NS 783. Aṭhyāsaphūrecording the historical events mentions that there was a huge fire on the sixth day of the bright half of Vaiśākha NS 783 (Regmi1966, part 3, page 100, Thyasaphu). A colophon ofKubjikāpaddhatimanuscript notes that Degutale was completely destroyed by the fire of NS 783 (Regmi1966, part 2, 76). Although the event year is similar, only one document provides the full date.
King Śrīnivāsa Malla offered the four pinnacles for the four corners of the Degutale.

The year of construction of the reservoir is known from the inscription engraved on the door lintel. As for most inscriptions of the time, the main body of text is written in a Nāgarī script, preceeded by the mantra of Avalokiteśvara (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ) written in the Rañjana script. The same is observed on the two-sided inscription of the Kīrtikhambā (DLK0260-001).The text of the inscription, published by Giuseppe Tucci (1956, p. 45), is as follow:Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ(Rañjana script)1.oṃ svasti śrīśāke 1276 pauṣe vadi 2 śukravāśare mahārājādhirājaparameśvaraparamabhaṭṭārakaparamadhārmi[ka]2.paramakalpadrumāvatāraśrīmatpṛthvīmalladevavijayarājye|mahāmatyaśrīyaśovarmadevānāṃ samaye||3.naṣṭā śrīr bhi(sic)marājasya dhararājasya dhīmataḥ|cchatyālavaṃśatilakaḥ sūnur graṃthadvavarmaṇaḥ||nāvalladevyā saṃjāto||4.devavarmā mahāmatiḥ|tenāpūrvatarā vāpī nirmitā amaravallabhā||caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā vasati[r]buddhasaṃtateḥ|vi5.śrāmabhūmi śrāntānāṃ jīvitaṃ sarvadehināṃ mahāmatya śrīmaddevavarmadevaiḥ sarvasattvopakārārthaṃ svakīyokta6.budhyā(sic)nūtanarītyā | devānām api vallabhā | vāpī viracitā likhita dharmadāsena | iti subham astuThe translation published by Mahes Raj Pant (2009, p. 301-302), goes as follows:śrīśāke 1276 pauṣe vadi 2 śukravāśare mahārājādhirājaparameśvaraparamabhaṭṭārakaparamadhārmikaparamakalpadrumāvatāraśrīmatpṛthvīmalladevavijayarājye |mahāmatyaśrīmatyaśovarmadevānāṃ samaye ||naptā śrīr bhimarājasya dhararājasya dhīmataḥ |chatyālavaṃśatilakaḥ sūnur graṃthadvavarmaṇaḥ ||nāvalladevyāḥ saṃjāto || devavarmā mahāmatiḥ |tenāpūrvatarā vāpī nirmitā amaravallabhā ||caityapaṃcakasaṃyuktā vasati buddhasaṃtateḥ |viśrāmabhūmi śrāntānāṃ jīvitaṃ sarvadehināṃ mahāmatyaśrīmaddevavarmadevaiḥ sarvasattvopakārārātha svakīyāktabudhyā nūtanarītyā | devānām api vallabhā | vāpī viracitā ||Translation:In the glorious [year of] Sake 1276, in Pauṣa, in the waning moon, on the 2nd, on Friday; in the realm of victory of the illustrious Pṛthvīmalladeva, who is the supreme king of great kings, the supreme lord, the supreme king and a supremely pious [man] (paramadhārmika), the supreme incarnation of the Wishing Tree; during the time of the great minister (mahāmātya) the illustriousYasovarmadeva-he who is the great-minded (mahāmati) Devavarmā, the ornament (tilaka) of the Chatyāla family, the grandson of glorious Bhīmarāja [and] the wise Dhanarāja, the son of the Varmā named Grantha, and born of Navalladevī, built an unprecedented water reservoir (vāpī) which is dear to the gods, is endowed with fivecaitya-s and is a residence for the progeny of the Buddha, a place (bhumī) to rest for those who are weary, and life to all living creatures. •The Great Minister the illustrious Devavarmadeva built a water reservoir, dear even to the gods, for the benefit of all beings in accordance with his own intention, as stated [above], using a new method.

This inscription is placed in the inside of a wall of the Sāḥgaḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā, but does not belong, or directly refer, to it. Instead, it relates to the nearby Mandaḥ Phalcā (KIR4056). This inscription was probably relocated for security reasons after the Mandaḥ Phalcā collapsed. It clearly mentions the initial construction of the Phalcā with ajaḥdhuṃand formation of aguṭhīby Bhāgīsiṃha Bhāro (Amātya) and his younger brother Siddhisiṃha from the Dathu Ṭola (text: Dathu Tvāra) in the memory of their father Manoharasiṃha. The inscription also records the installation of statues of Trivikrama and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa. While the statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is still placed in the Sāḥgaḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā, the Trivikrama statue is no longer available at the site.

event_name: Offering of a gilt Ganeśa statue
event_description: Amṛta Nārāyaṇa (text: nārāṃ) and five other lineage brothers together commissioned a golden repousse of Gaṇeśa.
The Śivaśaktiśvara temple was renovated by the Pashupati Area Development Trust after it was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
Thebahīwas reconstructed in its present form around 1993.
Rāmadeva, Nandarāja Bhālo and others carried out certain act that is unclear due to illegibility of the inscription.
The gate was dismantled and rebuilt with financial contribution from the Local Governance and Community Development Program, Madhyapur Thimi Municipality, and locals.
Nosiṃ Mulmī, Kṛṣṇarāma Mulmī, Śivahari Mulmī and others from Devanani Bungmati engaged in the renovation of the Phalcā.
The Phalcā collapsed as a result of the Great Earthquake of 1934.
Ratnakumārī and her family funded the reconstruction of the Phalcā.
The monument was renovated with the joint efforts of UNESCO, Buṅgamatī VDC, Buṅgamatī OLC and local residents.

The door to this shrine is clad in finely carved gilt metal. An equally fine gilttoraṇadepicting Mahiṣāsuramardinī at its center has been placed above the door. This gilttoraṇawas offered to Taleju by King Ṛiddhinarasiṁha Malla.

event_name: Restoration of the Golden Door ensemble
event_description: The golden door, the statues of Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and thetoranawere restored with support from the University of Applied Arts, Vienna, Austria.
Restoration of Taleju Mandira South by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) with funds provided by the American Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.

The temple was restored following the collapse of the top tier of Taleju Daśaĩghara in the 2015 earthquake. The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) was in charge of the project and used funds provided by the American Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.
Installation of the pillar at a date that remains difficult to ascertain since the second line of the inscription bears the figures 1(?)3112.
A bell was installed at the temple dedicated to the deceased Prime Minister Candra Śamśera Rāṇā. It is unclear from the bell inscription who was responsible for the offering of the bell.
The monument was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.

Lāykū Phalcā was established at the time of King Jitāmitramalla by his younger brother Ugra Malla and son Bhūpatindra along with his chief minister Dukhi Bhāgirāma (Gutschow2011, 645). The inscription also records rules and regulations about distributing water to farmers by an irrigation system. This inscription is a very important source of information with respect to the traditional irrigation system of the valley and the state's role in it.
The monument was badly damaged in the Great Earthquake of 1934. The upper tower(pura) of the shivaliṅga shrine was destroyed and has since then not been rebuilt.
Lāykū Phalcā was renovated after the 1934 Earthquakes (with a few details missing, like the upper tower).
The southern wing of Lāykū Phalcā was rebuilt by the DOA.
The Kathmandu Municipality's Ward No. 8 office reconstructed the gate.
The metal arch on top of the gate was added during another reconstruction funded by the Kathmandu Municipality's Ward No. 8 office.

This is an inscription indicating its installation by Ajasiṃha during the reign of Mahāsāmanta Jaitarāmajīva under King Bhīmadeva in 1260 CE (NS 381). The inscription does not mention a dharmaśāla or the phalcā itself, suggesting that the jaḥdhuṃ was installed first, with the phalcā being added centuries later.नेसं ३८१ (सन् १२६०) उक्त अभिलेख अनुसार भीमदेव राज्यकालमा फर्फिङ्गका महासामन्त जैतरामजीवको पालामा स्थानीय अजसिंहले जःधुं स्थापना गरेका थिए । अभिलेखमा धर्मशाला अर्थात् फल्चाको कुरा नपरेकाले यहाँ शुरुमा फल्चा नभई जःधुंमात्र स्थापना गरिएको देखिन्छ ।

Puruṣaratna, a member of the bāhāḥ, and his family, which included his elder brother Sudharatna, established thedharmadhātujinālayacaityawithin thebāhāḥcourtyard. They also undertook the renovation of the Aśoka Caitya besides laying traditional floor tiles in the courtyard.
Following damage from the 2015 earthquakes, thebāhāḥunderwent reconstruction funded by the Kathmandu Metropolis. The restored structure was inaugurated by then Mayor Vidyāsundar Shākya.
The two-storey Sataḥ was dismantled and replaced by a five-storey concrete building.
A statue of Tanasiṃ was established at the Bhīmasena shrine premises.
Locals formed a separate committee and collected donations to organize the annual palanquin procession of Bhīmasena. There was no tradition of this Bhīmasena’s procession previously.

event_name: Installation of brass plate in front of Bhīmasena
event_description: Śekharalāla Palikhela installed a brass plate on the area in front of Bhīmasena in memory of his deceased parents Īśvarīprasāda and Keśarīmaiyā Palikhela.
A statue of a lady was established at the Bhīmasena shrine. Details of this event are unclear due to erosion of text of the inscription.
Rudravīra, Rādhākṛṣṇa, Harinārāṃ, and others offered a brasstoraṇaon top of the entrance to the shrine premises in the name of deceased couple Cakravīra Kājī and Kṛṣṇamāyā.
The 2015 earthquakes incurred severe damage to the Phalcā.

A family of the Siṃha caste living near the Phalcā is known to be a descendant of its sponsor. After the Phalcā was badly damaged during the 2015 earthquakes, the Siṃha family sponsored its restoration. The inscription posted on the interior wall of the Phalcā records that Miśrī Devī Siṃha and her family members sponsored its restoration in memory of her husband, Cakramāna Siṃha.

The temple met a tragic fate during the devastating earthquakes of 1934. Its original appearance, however, has been preserved in a photograph captured by Kurt Boeck in 1898 CE and subsequently published by Gutschow (2011, p.460). The photograph serves as a glimpse into the past, showcasing the temple in its full glory before the destructive forces of nature took their toll.
Following its collapse in the 1934 earthquake, the temple was restored in reduced height.

Some regulations for the proper maintanance of the Agnimaṭha were established through discussions held by the Pāñcālī group whilst Maṇikādeva of Maṇichẽ and Agnihotrī jūjū of Svaniṃha were the head.The inscription has been effaced, and is no longer readable. The portion that showed the date is broken. Sharma (1984, 25) identifies the last number as 2 and Pruscha (1975, 137) dates it to 1572 CE. On the basis of these vague readings, it is generally assumed that the date read NS 692 (1572 CE).

During the time of Prince Dharma Malla and Dvijavara Mūrtyaṅga Ācharya Jayaprakaku, thekūpa(agnikuṇḍa) of the Agnimaṭha was restored.Readings of D.R. Regmi (1966), Sharma (1984) and D. Vajrācārya (2068) could not clarify what was restored and who was the ruler at that time. However, Yogeśa Rāja (2057) has answered these questions. This inscription is no longer available on site.
A stone inscription with a hymn (śloka) dedicated to Bhairava is located inside the temple. It is attached to the wall above the main deity.
Golden vessel and flags were offered to the god by Daivajñamanyarāja Bhāro (the son of Siddhirāja Bhāro).
Reconstruction of Ṭīkābhairava temple and offering ofsalipauto Śvetabhairava Koṭarākṣanātha by Kājī Ratna Bahādura Jośī and his wife Ramā Kumārī Jośī.

event_name: Construction and Maintenance of a Hiti and Phalcā at Thimi
event_description: The earliest inscription found at the site is a stone inscription dated to CE 1732 (NS 852). It is not related to the construction of the Sataḥ but instead pertains to Thimi. This is evident from the depiction of Bālakumārī and the inscriptional reference to “Śrī Śrī Śrī Bārakumāli (the venerable goddess Bālakumārī).” The text records that residents of Codo ṭola in Thimi collectively built ahiti(stone water spout) and aphalcānear the pond where Kvarakhu Bālakumārīdevī is enshrined, assigning maintenance responsibilities to local inhabitants under threat ofpañcamahāpātaka(the five grievous sins) for neglect.

event_name: Installation of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa by a Bhaktapur Householder
event_description: Cakravira, a resident of Tulāchẽ ṭola in Bhaktapur, together with his wives, Cidhi Thakuṃ and Hari Thakuṃ, installed a statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (object no. BKT0770-002) on the ground-floor wall of the building. To ensure the daily worship of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and the performance of the annual ritual, the donor endowed land for the founding of aguṭhi.

In memory of his late father Sanaksiṃha Buḍhāthokī and late mother Bhagavatī Buḍhāthokī, Haribhakta Buḍhāthokī offered a bell (ghaṇṭā) to the temple.वंगत बुबा सनकसिंह बुढाथोकी र आमा भगवती बुढाथोकीको स्मृतिमा हरिभक्त बुढाथोकीले मन्दिरमा घण्टा चढाएका थिए ।

As the Dhanvantari Vārāhī temple had become old and dilapidated, it was reconstructed through the active initiative of the Hāḍīgāũ Sampadā Samāja, in collaboration with local residents and the Kathmandu Metropolitan City.धनवन्तरी वाराहीको मन्दिर पुरानो भएर जीर्ण भएकोले हाँडीगाउँ सम्पदा समाजको सक्रियतामा स्थानीबासी, काठमाडौं महानगरपालिकाले मिलेर मन्दिरको पुनर्निर्मान गरेको थियो ।

The eastern side of the pillar is inscribed with 7 lines written in a Nāgarī script. The date of 1231 can be read. If referring to the Śāka era, this date would correspond to 1339 CE.It is possible that the inscription was executed years after the installation, as it goes past the square space usually used for it and ends below it.

The inscription reveals that the Aṣṭamī Sevā Samiti, a group of devotees from the Svayambhū area in Kathmandu, built the Phalcā that lies on the way to the Cobhāra hillock where the temple of Ānandādi Lokeśvara is situated. The inscription also instructs the concerned persons to perform the Phalcā’s anniversary ritual.

The artworks preserved at this site appear to date to the Rāṇā period. During that time, Buddharatna Śākya installed the image of Akṣobhya here asKvāḥpāḥdyaḥand placed a brasstoraṇaabove the entrance doorway. He carried out this installation on the occasion of the marriage of his son Bhairavkara. This information was provided by Rājendra Kumāra, a member of the Śākyasaṃgha associated with thisbāhāḥ.यहाँका कलाकृति सबै राणाकालीन देखिन्छन् । राणाकालमा बुद्धरत्न शाक्यले यहाँ अक्षोभ्य मूर्ति क्वाःपाःद्यःका रूपमा स्थापना गरी ढोकामाथि पित्तलको तोरण चढाएका थिए । बुद्धरत्नले आफ्ना छोरा भैरवकरको विवाहको अवसरमा यो कार्य गरेका थिए । यसै बाहाःका संघसदस्य राजेन्द्र कुमारबाट यो जानकारी प्राप्त भएको हो ।

Ratna Śākya, a resident of Naka Bāhāḥ, together with his wife Vetimāyā and other members of their family, carried out the restoration of thecaityalocated in the courtyard. It is likely that the present dome-shapeddevalawas constructed during this phase of renovation.नक बाहाः निवासी रत्न शाक्य, उनकी पत्नी वेतिमाया र अन्य परिवार सदस्य मिली ननिमा भएको चैत्यको जीर्णोद्धार गरे । सम्भवतः यही जीर्णोद्धारको चरणमा वर्तमानमा भएको गुम्बजाकार देवल बनाइएको थियो ।

Subbā Pṛyavarta, Priyalakṣmī, and Ratnabahādura Thāpā built a rest house (sataḥ) and water spout (hiti). The inscription recording the construction of thehitiandsataḥmandates trust land’s income used for feeding brahmins and distributing sherbet on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha. The pond’s construction date is unclear, but it presumably predates thehitiandsataḥ.

Over time, thesataḥcollapsed, thehitidried up, and the pond nearly vanished. Changunarayan Municipality restored the structures, adding a Śiva statue, along with his vehicular mount Nandī, and a Hanumān statue donated by Kedārabahādura Thāpā’s family.

An inscription in Gāthādyaḥ Phalcā records that the monument was constructed by someone from the Harisiddhi Jyāpu community in 1780 CE. It also mentions the presence of a Gaṇeśa statue from an earlier period. The inscription further mentions the construction of a three-bayed phalcā during the renovation of the Gaṇeśa temple. Additionally, it references the establishment of the Yosiṃ guṭhī (Indradhvaja guṭhī). It is likely that the same community, which also celebrates Indrajātrā in Harisiddhi, was responsible for building the arcaded platform.यस फल्चामा प्राप्त अभिलेख अनुसार नेसं ९०१ मा हिरिसिद्धि निवासी कुनै ज्यापु समुदायका व्यक्तिले यस फल्चाको निर्माण गरेका थिए । यहाँ गणेशको मन्दिर पहिले नै भएको कुरा पनि यस अभिलेखबाट ज्ञात हुन्छ । अभिलेखमा “गणेश मन्दिरलाई जीर्णोद्धार गर्दै तीन कवलको फल्चा बनाइयो’’ भनिएको छ । योसिं गुथि (इन्द्रध्वज गुठी) पनि गठन भएको प्रसंग परेको छ । यसले हरिसिद्धिमा इनद्रजात्रा मनाउन एक समूहबाट यो फल्चा बनेको देखिन्छ ।
The phalcā was reconstructed by Lalitpur Metropolis in 2023 CE (VS 2080).फल्चाको पुनर्निर्माण ललितपुर महानगरपालिकाले विसं २०८०(सन् २०२३) मा गरेको थियो ।
A balustrade, supporting small oil recepticals, was installed around the temple. The supporting structure is made of steel angles and rectangular tubing.

event_name: Gaṇeśa Statue Turning into White Color and the Death of the Son of King Rājya Prakāśa Malla
event_description: According toKāyastha(NS 1117, 19), the Gaṇeśa statue consecrated in the sanctum of this temple turned into white. Such an incident is considered inauspicious among Newars. Soon after this incident, the son of King Rājya Prakāśa Malla (1745-1758 CE) died.
The temple was renovated in 2017 CE (VS 2074) with the financial support of thirty lakhs rupees from the Lalitpur Metropolitan City.

event_name: Unknown Event (not related to the temple)
event_description: This inscription was issued before the construction of the Ālko Gaṇeśa Temple. Since it is severely damaged, its content remains obscure.

event_name: Initial Construction of the Temple and Establishment of a Guṭhī
event_description: The temple was built by Yaśovanta Siṃha Raghuvaṃśa in 1704 CE (NS 824). On its completion, he had offered a feast to Brahmins and Jośīs, and also established aguṭhīfor its regular operation.

This inscription, kept inside the Ālko Gaṇeśa Temple, is not related to the temple itself. It records the initial construction of aphalcāby Bhavanīśaṅkara. Thephalcārecorded in the inscription is not yet identified.
A group of eight people offered twenty silver coins namedmahendra mallīto the temple to sponsor regular worship of Gaṇeśa and light up oil lamps on every first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra.
Bhavānī Rāotta (Rāuta) Raghuvaṃśa and his wife offered a gold pinnacle to the temple in 1864 CE (NS 984).
Devarāja Śākya, a resident of the Ikhāchẽ Ṭola, offered this banner wishing for the salvation of his deceased parents (his father and mother died on 26-05-VS 2054 and 12-08-VS 2075, respectively).
सन् १९३४ को महाभूकम्पमा क्षति भएको बाहाःको द्यःछेँ लामो समय यथास्थितिमै रह्यो । सन् १९७० को दशकतिर सो क्षतिपूर्ण द्यःछेँ भत्किएकाले हाल देखिने स्वरूप (जनवरी २०२६) मा पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको थियो ।
Two stone lions flanking the entrance were installed by Guṇa Siṃha Bhāro and the Saṇkrānti Guthi, respectively.

event_name: Establishment of the Caturdaśi Sevā and installation of a stone toraṇa above the main door to the sanctum
event_description: The inscription records about the establishment of a certain Caturdaśi Sevā (probably aguthi) and installation of the stonetoraṇaabove the main door to the sanctum on which Aṣṭamātrikās with Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Mahālakṣmī are depicted. Note that theguthidoes not exist at present.

event_name: Offering statue in front of Mahālakṣmī Devī
event_description: The inscription records that Candra Bhāro, Siddeśvarī Mayi and Maheśvarī Mayī from Balambu jointly offered a statue to the Mahālakṣmī Devī. However, the mentioned statue could not be identified on the site.
Since the upper part of the inscription has badly eroded, what is recorded there remains unclear, but its date is still readable.

event_name: Offering stone statue and performing pūjā
event_description: Siva Narasiṃha Bhāro, Teja Narasiṇ, Vinalasiṇ and Viṣṇusiṇ jointly offered a stone statue to Mahālakṣmī Devī and performed a ritual worship at the Temple. However, the mentioned stone statue could not be identified on the site.
A certain Jivalachimi, the wife of Bhiṃṣvāla offered some ritual objects to the Temple.
Āśālāla Śreṣṭha and Harṣa Māyā Śreṣṭha, both residents of Balambu offered the brass bell to the Temple (note that the bell is in the sanctum).
Thepatāḥwas offered in memory of Bulāla Maharjana, Hari Māyā Maharjana, Hari Vahādura Maharjana, Āśā Māyā Maharjana, Kul Vahādira maharjana, Teja Lakṣmī Maharjana and others.
The bell was offered in memory of Bhāju and Kānchī Maharjana, both residents of Dhalko.
A resident of Dhalko offered the bell.
Prakāśa Śreṣṭha (together with his family members) offered theIlā̃in memory of his father Badrimāna Śreṣṭha.
According to Pruscha (1975, 266), the temple was renovated by His Majesty's Government in 1949 CE.

event_name: Suffered damages by the 2015 earthquakes and renovation
event_description: The Temple suffered damages by the 2015 earthquakes. Local residents rebuilt it with the help of the Department of Archaeology. The renovation was completed in 2021 CE.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: A pair of lion statues was placed, one on each side of the steps leading up to the Gaṇeśa shrine by Gopāla Rājakarṇikāra, his wife Tuyumatī, Punavī, Ghālāla, Akṣilāla and Āśālāla.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: The Phalcāwas renovated by Rājakarṇikāra Jīvanarasĩha.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: Atoraṇawas offered to the the shrine of Gaṇeśa by Mādhava Dhãguri, Viśva Sĩha, Hidaya Bhāva, Viṣṇu Bhāva, Manirāma Bhāva, Bayana Sĩ Bhāva, Rugu Sĩ Bhāva, birāma Bhāva, Āpãlhāma Bhāva (among others).

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: A bell was placed at the left corner of the Phalcā,donated by Dhana Jyāpu, Bilanādã, Jyāpu, Devakṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa Jyāpu.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: The Phalcāwas renovated and the ground floor was paved with stone. A fund for the renovation work was collected by Haugaḥ Bhajana Khalaḥ and Viddhyālāla Rājakarṇikāra. The inscription mentions the Phalcāas adegala(temple).

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: The Phalcāwas renovated during the reign of King Birendra with the help of Department of Archaeology, Nepal and the German Government.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: A copperpatāḥ,a metal banner hanging from the pinnacle of a temple,was offered to the Gaṇeśa shrine by Sattu Maharjan, Rāmalāla Maharjan and their families.

monument_name: Haugaḥ Ganedyaḥ Phalcā (ca. mid-17th century CE)
event_description: A stonejarũhitihas beenattached to the western wall of the Phalcā byDãju Bhāro and Rājakarṇikāra Cikidhikala Bhāro. Land had also been donated for its annual function. The inscription also mentions about the necessity of giving certain amount of paddy (45 Pāthis) to a person who fills up water in thejarũhitieveryday. According toFurukawa/Shrestha/Bajracharya and Ogasawara 2010(p. 121) the water tank was built in the Malla period.

A newtoraṇawas fixed on top of the entrance to the sanctum sanctorum after the old one was stolen. The name of the donor could not be deciphered, but according to the locals it was donated by Cakrarāja Śākya.

There are no historical records regarding the foundation of the Aśoka Caitya. However, a damaged inscription records that the Caitya was renovated in NS 777. The name of the person responsible for this is not legible, as the letters are broken in many places.
Viśvavajra Vajrācārya established this Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala together with his two sons Pañcavajra Vajrācārya and Hevajra Vajrācārya and daughters Nanda Kumārī, Dhana Kumārī and Rīti Kumārī.

The name of the donor is not recorded, but according to the locals Viśvavajra Vajrācārya established the Mañjuśrī Pādukā. The donor has arranged for the anniversary worship of this Pādukā to take place on the 8th day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, on the day of death of his mother Gyana Thakuṃ.
The Bāhāḥ collapsed in the earthquake of 1934 and was rebuilt by the descendants of the founder.

event_name: Replacing jhiṅgati roof with zinc sheet
event_description: The family of Viśvavajra Vajrācārya replaced the oldjhĩgaṭī-tiled roof with zinc sheets.
Bekhādeva Vajrācārya built Āana Bāhāḥ and enshrined the statue of Akṣobhya. He bestowed land worth fourropanisand fourānāsto fund religious activities related to the Bāhāḥ.
The religious trust associated with thedyaḥchẽrenovated the building.
After thedyaḥchẽsuffered minor damage during the 2015 earthquakes, it was renovated through the collective efforts of the local government and community members.
Puṇyarāja Śākya's wife bore three sons after her husband established thisbāhāḥand performed the ritual worship at the Dvādaśa Tīrtha and Aṣṭavaitarāga Tīrtha.
Pūṇyarāja Śākya, his wife Vyatimāyā, and their three daughters Buramāya, Kṛnsamāya (Kṛṣṇamāyā) and Nandamāyā constructed thisdharmadhātu maṇḍalatogether with thebāhāḥ.
Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha had granted land parcels with an annual produce of 40murīs of crop in Nepālavyāsī to set up a religious trust for the Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple.

Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā retained the 40murī-land trust that Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha had granted for the Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple. He issued a royal decree (lālamohara) in the names of Colonel Gajarāja Siṃha Thāpā, Lieutenant Dalabhajana Thāpā, and Major Captain Keśara Siṃha Thāpā to retain the trust. Among the three persons mentioned in thelālamohara, Gajarāja Siṃha Thāpā seems to have familial ties with Jaṅga Bahādura. One of Jaṅga Bahādura’s daughters, Badana Kumārī (Magarnī Maiyā̃), was married to Gajarāja, who started tea cultivation in Ilam. Since it is mentioned as “62sāla” in thelālamohāra, it is possible that the land of Śyāmapāṭī Śiva temple was also confiscated by Raṇa Bahādura Śāha in 1805 CE (VS 1862), and Jaṅga Bahādura may have returned the same land to retain the trust.

event_name: Reconstruction of Śiva Mandira and pāṭī
event_description: The Department of Archeology reconstructed the Śiva temple (NMB0010-009) located southeast of the mainśivālayaand the rest house.

event_name: Consecration of Amoghasiddhi statue and beautifying it by offering various decorative ritual objects
event_description: Two local groups named ‘Bhagavāna Buddha Palisthā Samiti’ and ‘Sāymi Dabū’ installed a statue of Amoghasiddhi to the southwest of the Temple. Meanwhile, Jñānaratna Sāymi offered anilāṃover the statue in memory of his father Jñānabahādura Sāymi. Likewise, Hari Sāymi and Buddhalakṣmī Sāymi got a balustrade of 108dalūlamps installed here in memory of their parents Pūrṇabahādura and Jñānamāyā. Buddhalakṣmī also offered a bell.

In 1968 CE (VS 2024), the tall and open Phalcā was used as 'Motī Library', with its columns covered for this purpose. However, over time, the library became inactive and unused, after which the Phalcā remained closed for decades.खुला र अग्लो फल्चालाई सदुपयो गर्दै विसं २०२४ (सन् १९६७) मा “मोती पुस्तकालय” नाम दिई यहाँ किताबहरू राख्न थालिएको थियो । सो साल पुस्तकालय संचानका लागि चौतर्फीका कवल बन्द गरिएको थिए । कालान्तरमा पुस्तकालय निस्कृय भई लोप भए पश्चात् दशकौंसम्म फल्चा बन्द अवस्थामै रह्यो ।

In 2023 CE (VS 2079), two thefts occurred, and three statues were stolen from a nearby Caitya (CHG0070). After this, the previously vacant and closed phalcā became a police station.नजिकैको चैत्य (CHG0070) बाट विसं २०७९ (सन् २०२३)  सालमा दुई पटक गरी तीनवटा मूर्ति चोरी भएको थियो । यस घटना पश्चात् खाली र बन्द अवस्थामा रहेको चैत्य समीपैको यस फल्चामा चौबीसै घण्टा प्रहरी बस्ने व्यवस्था मिलाइएको छ ।

This inscription is attached to the eastern wall of the Nāsaḥ Chẽ. Unfortunately, it cannot be deciphered because it is badly eroded. It might be the same inscription that is mentioned by D. Śākya (VS 2030, p. 582). He writes that almost all letters (akṣaras) of the inscription, except the part where its date is mentioned, have deteriorated. The date reads as follows: ‘saṃbat 454 jyeśṭhakṛiṣṇadivā 6’. Thus, it could be said that the inscription was issued during the reign of King Vasantadeva (r. 506 - 532 CE).

event_name: Formation of Dāphā (a traditional musical group)
event_description: The inscription records that Punasiṃha Bhāro and his wife Śyāmā formed the Dāphā (a traditional musical group) and appointed gurus who were trained to play the traditional musical instruments.

event_name: Formation of team to produce a play
event_description: A group of people formed a team to perform a play titled “Santa’s Story of Balambu”. The play was written by Dhananaṇda Gopari.
This inscription is related to the Mahālakṣmī temple. It records a stone pavement of the plinth of the temple etc. This task was completed in 1939 CE (VS 1996).

The water tap for drinking water is attached to the eastern wall of the Nāsaḥ Chẽ. An inscription issued during the reign of King Mahendra (r. 1955-1972) is attached above the tap. It mentions that the monarch commissioned this project.
Twotoraṇas(placed atop the main door of the Nāsaḥ Chẽ and Hiphaḥdyaḥ shrine)were stolen sometime around 2006 CE (VS 2063).

event_name: Dhana Bāhāḥ, construction of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala
event_description: Harṣajyoti and Śrīramāyā constructed this Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala.

event_name: Dhana Bāhāḥ, consecration of the Śikharakūṭa Caitya
event_description: Dhanajyoti Śākyavaṃśa constructed this Śikharakūṭa Caitya.
Pañcajoti, his wife Ghanalakṣmī, and their son Candramāna donated funds for a new bell stand.

event_name: Dhana Bāhāḥ, construction of the main shrine
event_description: Vratarāja Śākya and his family members (Indramāyā, Vyatimāyā, Cinimāyā, Viṣṇu Kumāri and Harṣa Kumāri) constructed a small shrine for the Akṣobhya Buddha

event_name: Stone inscription of NS 1059 on the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala

event_description: Pruscha (1975, p. 241) suggests the lion statues at the Siddhivināyaka temple were established in 1603 CE. He probably referred to the lion statues that flank the Gaṇeśa statue, as the lion statues by the main entrance appear to be considerably later addition.
Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera and his wife Padmakumārī Devī installed a water spout to address the severe water shortage in Tokha.
Established by Joganārāṃ from Kathmandu’s Thãhiti, acaityawithin the complex was renovated by Jogaratna, along with his wife Surjamāyā, younger brother Dharmaratna, and son Rattabahādura.

The renovation of this temple, including the repair of the northern door, inner seat, door leaves, windows, etc., was completed under the coordination of Tokha Construction Workers Union and M.D.S. Cement Design. The inauguration after the completion of the work was performed by the comedy duo Madan Krishna Shrestha and Hari Bansha Acharya.
Indrarāja Jośī, Prakāśa Maharjana, and Ravi Daṃgola from Tokha jointly installed a brass statue of shrew, the animal mount of Gaṇeśa, here at the temple in memory of their deceased family members.
Since the inscription is no longer in readable condition, the details mentioned in it are unknown.

The statue was established by Śakhalāla, his wife Āsāmāyā and their two daughters.
In 2003 CE, it was reconstructed with the financial assistance of the Kathmandu Metropolis and donations from the locals. Theā̃ypātiles on the roof were replaced by copper sheets on that occasion.

The inscription is on the base of the Pañca Buddha statues, beneath theesoteric deity(kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ). It is fragmented, and so the date and event is not clearly readable. The inscription mentions that Viso Siṃ was a caretaker. It also mentions that everyone must respect the wishes of the donors. It states that any act contrary to their wishes would be sinful and equivalent to killing a Brāhmaṇa.
Land was endowed by Kamarāma Prajāpati to perform ritual activities.

The reconstruction of both Kalaśa Pukhūs was carried out with a fund of NRs. 6 million from the Shankharapur Municipality and NRs. 4 million from the Kathmandu Valley Development Authority. Local residents and businessmen had also contributed financially to the reconstruction, which cost around NRs. 17.5 million.See also the historical events of the Bhagavatī Kalaśa Pukhū 1 (SKH0242).

event_name: A Licchavi Royal Edict of tax exemption and local jurisdiction establishment
event_description: Although the inscription associated with this event is unrelated to the Mañjuśrī and Nāsaḥdyaḥ Dyaḥchẽ, it substantiates the Licchavi settlement status of the area. Aṃśuvarman (r. 605-621 CE) erected this inscription, featuring a royal edict on behalf of the Vatu ṭola populace. In the proclamation, he granted a tax exemption for sheep and pig farming, previously levied on the Vatu ṭola community. Additionally, he empowered the local chief administrator (pāñcālī) to oversee cases involving the five major crimes (pañcāparādha).
As the Dyaḥchẽ was on the verge of collapse, it was renovated with a sum of NRs. 10,000 received from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and NRs. 55,000 collected from the members.
The Dyaḥchẽ was renovated at a cost of NRs. 254,000 by collecting donations from the members and an assistance of NRs. 45,000 received from King Gyanendra Shah.

event_name: Listing the religious and social activities
event_description: A marble inscription was installed to inform the members of the Nāsaḥdyaḥ Guthi about the activities that need to be carried out over the period of a year.
The Dyaḥchẽ was reconstructed with the fund received from the Kathmandu Metropolis. The two-storied Dyaḥchẽ was rebuilt into a concrete structure of three floors with a balconied tower on top.
After the reconstruction of the Dyaḥchẽ, the Sikhrākāras of Te Bāhāḥ offered a wooden ornamented arch (toraṇa) on top of the entrance to the Mañjuśrī sanctum.

The temple was commissioned by a certain Harisiṃha, who endowed it with several plots of land to ensure the performance ofnitya(daily) andvārsika(annual) rituals. This information is recorded in an inscription preserved inside thegarbhagṛha(sanctum) of the temple. However, the section of the inscription bearing the date has been eroded. Pruscha (1975, p. 77) dated the inscription to 1637 CE (NS 757–758).

In memory of his deceased ancestors, the son installed within the temple a stone slab bearing the image of Umāmaheśvara. At the center of this slab appears the divine couple Umā and Maheśvara, while on either side and along the lower section are carved the figures and names of the donor’s family members.
Vīrabhadra, Caṃpādevī, and Ratnadevī dedicated a bell (KAT2290-009) to the deity Gaṇeśa.
Through the joint initiative of Ward No. 20 of the Kathmandu Metropolitan City and the Cikamugaḥ Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, an iron fence and gate were installed around the temple premises.
The previous Gaṇeśa Phalcā 1  was dismantled and a new RCC building was built. Political parties helped to collect the funding for this.
The Phalcā was heavily damaged in the 2015 earthquake.

The Government of Nepal provided two million rupees for the reconstruction of the Phalcā.Dinesh Maharjan, a member of the parliament, has helped with this. However, the current installment of funds has almost been entirely used up, meaning that the reconstruction work has been put on hold.

यस मन्दिरको निर्माणबारे केही तथ्य प्रकाश पार्न सकिने अभिलेख संगैको यन्त्र वत्सला मन्दिरभित्र प्राप्त छ । उक्त अभिलेखमा नेसं ८१६ (सन् १६९६) मा राजा जितामित्र मल्लले सो मन्दिरमा वत्सला देवीको स्थापना गर्नुका साथै यस मन्दिरमा सिद्धिलक्ष्मी स्थापना गरेको उल्लेख छ (B. Pauḍela VS 2022, p.50)। सिद्धिलक्ष्मीको यस मन्दिर बनाउने कार्यको थलानी नेसं ८१३ (सन् १६९३) बाटै सुरु भैसकेको तथ्य भक्तपुरस्थित वासुकी खोला किनारमा भएको ढुङ्गामा कुँदिएको अभिलेखबाट खुल्दछ ।
यस मन्दिरमा भूपतिन्द्र मल्लले पछि एक घण्ट ठपेको कुरा सोही घण्टमा भएको नेसं ८३५ (सन् १७१५) को अभिलेखबाट थाहा हुन्छ (P. Śreṣṭha VS 2078, online newspaper) ।

Ratnadeva Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāryya Ratnadeva) and Bramha Thakura, a local functionary (pātra), endowed land and garden in the name of Akṣobhya, the main deity of the Bāhāḥ. The construction of the Bāhāḥ was probably coming to an end at that time.

event_name: Establishment of Akṣobhya, Aśoka Caitya and Āgama Devatā
event_description: After the construction of the Bāhāḥ came to an end with the establishment of Akṣobhya, a Caitya, and the esoteric deity (āgaṃdyaḥ), it was formally handed over to Amṛtapāra Vajrācārya and Amṛtacandra Vajrācārya.

event_name: Offering a flag (dhvajārohaṇa) to a golden caitya and pavement with telia bricks
event_description: Pūrṇadeva (text: Punnadeva) installed a banner (dhvaja) on the golden caitya installed as the Bāhāḥ’s finial and laid floor tiles (cikaṃaḥpā) at the premises during the reign of King Nṛpendra Malla.

event_name: Repair of the sanctum of Akṣobhya
event_description: Jinadeva Vajrācārya renovated the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ during the reign of King Bhūpālendra Malla.

event_name: Renovation of temple of Aśoka Caitya
event_description: Twenty persons including Kūlaratna Śākya (text: Śākyabhikṣu Kularatna) and Dānaratna of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ renovated the temple where the Aśoka Caitya is established.
Kūlaratna Śākya (text: Sākebhīchu Kularatna) of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ established adharmadhātujinālayacaityatogether with his family.
Mānakāji, together with his wife, son, and daughter-in-law, established adharmadhātujinālayacaityain the name of his grandparents Kularatna and Lakṣmīnānī.
A pair of guarding lions were installed in front of the Bāhāḥ’s sanctum. The inscription does not mention the name of the donor.
After the old toraṇa was stolen, Pūrṇaprabhā Vajrācārya offered a new toraṇa in the name of her deceased husband Padmaśrī Vajra Vajrācārya.

The main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) of the Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with funds from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office and donations from the locals. A local organization named ‘Vajracharya Club’ played a crucial role in the collection of donations.
The 2015 earthquakes left cracks in the temple that houses the Aśoka Caitya.

event_name: Reconstruction of the temple of Aśoka Caitya
event_description: The temple that houses the Aśoka Caitya was reconstructed after it was damaged by the earthquakes. A person from the area currently residing in the US provided financial assistance for the reconstruction.
Durgālakṣmī Vajrācārya and her family members established acaturvyūhacaityaat the Bāhāḥ premises in memory of the deceased members of their family.

event_name: Donation of an embossed brass toraṇa
event_description: An embossed brasstoraṇawas added in front of the main deity.
A pūjāwith fasting was perfomed together with a pilgrimage to allbāhāḥs, bahisanddharmadhātus.

event_name: Consecration of the image of the main deity in the sanctum of the Vihāra
event_description: Śākyamuni Buddha's image was constructed inside the courtyard of the Jñānakīrti Vihāra in memory of Jñānavīra Bhāvo's late wives Asala and Guṃchimī (Guṇalakṣmī). A life-giving ritual (prāṇapratiṣthā) was performed for the image withdaśakarmas.

event_name: Construction of the Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya
event_description: Jñānavīra Bhāvo and his family constructed the Caitya and performed itsahorātrapūjā(worship for one whole day and night).
This Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala was constructed after a pilgrimage (tīrthayatrā). Aprāṇapratiṣṭhā(life-giving ritual) was performed.

monument_name: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ (built around seventeenth and eighteenth century)
event_description: The temple was renovated by Jaifal in 1803 CE.

monument_name: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ (built around seventeenth and eighteenth century)
event_description: This inscription is embedded into the southern wall of the Temple and is not directly related to the Temple. It records the construction of aphalcāaround the place of Yamaleśvara. Moreover, this inscription also records the regulations laid down for organising the anniversary celebration of thephalcā.

monument_name: Mahādyaḥ Degaḥ (built around seventeenth and eighteenth century)
event_name: Rebuilding the Temple in its Original Style
event_description: The temple was in ruins with entirely damaged roofs by the time Oldfield visited Kirtipur in 1855 CE. His sketch shows that it was originally a tiered temple. Its upper had been completely rebuilt with a dome on top in the Rāṇā Period. It was reconstructed in its original style in 1999 CE by the Kirtipur Municipality.

According to this inscription, asuvarṇamukha(gilded face) was fixed to the previously existing statue of Gaṇeśa. Fifteen people from the Bhāvo or Bhāro (Jyāpu) and Śākya communities were involved in this task. The chief of the group was an individual named Devarāja. The group also formedpunhī sevā,performing certain activities to honour Gaṇeśa. The inscription also records the offering of a gilt "mudaya"to the temple. The exact meaning "mudaya"is not clear.
An individual named Gaṅgārāja paved the sanctum (garbhagṛha) with the imported tiles of different colours.
The Gaṇeśā Guṭhī paved the ground floor of the temple and plastered its walls in the memory of late Gaṇeśa Māna Amātya.

event_name: Offering of an oil lamp balustrade
event_description: Amīramāna Amātya and his wife Rohiṇī (text: Rohinī) Amātya offered the oil lamp balustrade to the temple.

In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Bamabahādura Kũvara built the Tina Devala temple along the Vāgamatī riverbanks, showcasing a distinctive architectural style.The historical record of the temple, preserved in atāmrapatra, offers evidence of the simultaneous construction ofsataḥs, particularly highlighting the Tīna Devala Sataḥ.

A signboard is positioned against the wall in the west wing, detailing the establishment of Bambeer Bikateshwar Shiavalaya Guthi by Bamabahādura Kũvara Rāṇā, the builder of the Tīna Devala temple,sataḥs, and other surrounding monuments.

After the earthquakes in 2015 CE (2072 VS), both the Tīnadevala temple and the adjacentsataḥsincurred significant damage. The restoration of thesataḥwas initiated by the Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee, operating under the Ministry of Urban Development, with financial support from a loan provided by the Asian Development Bank. The reconstruction of the temple andsataḥswas successfully concluded on October 23, 2022 CE.

The construction of the Phalcā started by digging the foundation as per the treatise on architecture. Khaḍgīkāra Gvārā from the Iti Ṭola, along with Tulasimāyā and the family constructed the Phalcā wishing his deceased grandfather Lāju and father Kuberasīṃ the heavenly abode of Sukhāvatī Bhuvana.

event_name: Construction of a metal fence around Matsyendranātha Mandira (LAL0060)
event_description: A committee named Śrī Macchindranātha Mandira Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti was formed. The Samiti installed metal railings to surround the temple to protect the statues and other historic items from theft.

event_name: Formation of Macchindra Bahāla Sudhāra Samiti
event_description: Community members formed a committee named Macchindra Bahāla Sudhāra Samiti for the conservation of Matsyendranātha Mandira and other monuments in the area.

event_name: Installation of metal grills and door
event_description: Motilāla Śilpakāra sponsored the installation of metal grills and a door in thephalcā.
The Phalcā was renovated

event_name: Construction of a new water spout
event_description: The Shankharapur Municipality renovated the Pukhūlāchi Pukhū (SKH0342) and installed a new water spout which is attached to the southern plinth of the Temple.
विसं १९६४ बाट निर्माण कार्य थालिएको आयोजना समापन भई विसं १९६८ (सन् १९११) जेष्ठ ९ गते सोमवारका दिन तत्कालीन राजाको उपस्थितिमा टुँडिखेलमा बत्ती बाली उद्‌घाटन गरियो ।
Marshall Plan को सहायता स्वरूप सन् १९५० को दशकमा यहाँ थप नयाँ मेशिनहरू जडान भए ।
विसं २०३८ सालदेखि विद्युत प्रणालीका पाइपबाट निस्केको पानीलाई खानेपानी कार्यालयले पाटनमा वितरण गर्न थाल्यो । हालसम्म पनि खानेपानीले यहाँको पानी पाटनक्षेत्रमा वितरण जारी राखेको छ ।
जलविद्युत निर्माणको शतवार्षिकीको अवसरमा विद्युतगृह नजिकै नेपाल सरकारले एक स्मारक पार्कको नर्माण गरे ।
The temple was levelled in the 1934 earthquake.
As of November 2019 the temple is under reconstruction. The project is managed by the Department of Archaology, Nepal with funding from the Embassy of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.

event_name: A week-long event of reciting the texts and hymns
event_description: Guru Kavi Prasada organisedsaptāhakīrtana(a one-week long religious event) in Bungmati.

event_name: Formation of a guṭhī in 1662 CE
event_description: In 1662, King Śrīnivāsa Malla set up aguṭhīto run theāratī pūjāin the temple.

event_name: Installation of an inscription containing the regulations to govern the cultural events and activities
event_description: Śrīnivāsa Malla installed a long inscription at the temple at Taḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0050), which provides regulations to govern the cultural events and activities of Karuṇāmaya. The King of Patan must take personal responsibility for the arrangements for the bathing ceremony, the chariot procession and Karuṇāmaya's journey to Patan (Locke1980, 309).

event_name: Installation of an inscription regulating the Kārttika fesitval
event_description: Śrīnivāsa Malla installed an inscription at the temple to regulate the Kārttika festival. The inscription states that women of the Dhobi (washermen), Jogī (Kusle) and Kasāi (butcher) caste are not allowed to take the vow (vrata) to participate in the festival. Only those who come on the full moon day (24 hours) of Āśvina are allowed to take thevrata. The king had also endowed land to feed the devotees at the end of the festival.

event_name: Formation of a guṭhī by King Śrīnivāsa Malla in 1672 CE
event_description: King Śrīnivāsa Malla set up aguṭhīforāratī pūjāin the Karuṇāmaya temple at Bungmati.Nepālako Itihāsa Rājabhogamālā(inAncient Nepal10, p. 5) mentions that this took place in NS 702.

event_name: Pavement of the courtyard with black stone
event_description: The temple courtyard was paved with black stone.

event_name: Offering of golden toraṇa by a minister of King Jayasthiti Malla
event_description: An inscription from Ituṃ Bahāla mentions that a minister of King Jayasthiti Malla, Madanarāmavarddhana (brother of Jayasiṃharāmavarddhana) and his wife Jaitralakṣmī offered a goldentoraṇato Buṅgmalokeśvara.

event_name: Offering of a crown to Bugmalokeśvara by King Bālārjunadeva
event_description: King Bālārjunadeva offered his crown to Bugmalokeśvara. TheGopālarājavaṃśāvalī(fol. 23a) mentions this event.
Gopālarājavaṃśāvalī(fol. 43a) mentions that King Ripu Malla, the King of Khasāna, anointed the Buṅga deity and donated treasures.

event_name: Participation of king Jayasthiti Malla in Buṅgadyaḥ's procession
event_description: King Jayasthiti Malla went to Bugma Jātrā with his three sons.

event_name: Offering of a silver chain by King Mukunda Sen
event_description: King Mukunda Sen from Palpa came to the chariot procession of Buṅgadyaḥ and offered a silver chain to the deity.

event_name: A land endowment to establish a guṭhī for the bathing ceremony of Buṅgadyaḥ and Ādinātha (of Chobhar)
event_description: A copper-plate inscription preserved in the National Archives and dated NS 678 states that Melvagha Varma, Hṛdayasiṃha Varma, Jñānasiṃha Varma and Keśavasiṃha Varma from Jyeṣṭhavarṇa Vihāra Patan granted land to establish aguṭhīfor the bathing ceremony of Buṅgadyaḥ and Ādinātha (of Chobhar).

event_name: Establishment of a guṭhī for organising hāthuhāyukegu (see below)
event_description: King Jayanarasiṃha established aguṭhīto organisehāthuhāyukeguduring the chariot procession of Karuṇāmaya.Hāthuhāyekeguis a tradition of placing a mud vessel filled with local liquor (chyāṅ) behind the mask of Bhairava and connecting a pipe to his mouth from which the liquor comes. People drink the liquor during the chariot procession.

event_name: Offering of a water vessel by King Viṣṇu Malla
event_description: After thenhvã(bathing) of Buṅgadyaḥ in the sanctum of the temple, a water vessel called Brahmakvã is placed in the sanctum of the temple for one week. King Viṣṇu Malla offered a Brahmakvã to the deity.

event_name: Offering of a parasol and four banners by King Rājyaprakāśa Malla
event_description: King Rājyaprakāśa Malla offered akhatajalā(?), a parasol and four banners to the deity.

event_name: Donation of gold by a king of Sikkim
event_description: Paṇḍita Jīvarāja and Jayamuni from Gāḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0510) went to Sikkim and offered a full plateprasāda(gift) to the King of Sikkim. In gratitude, the King filled the plate with gold. When Jayamuni returned with the gold, he called a meeting of the members of thesaṅghato decide what to do with it. They decided to make fixtures (side panels for the four sides, thetoraṇas, and the decorations above thetoraṇasfor the chariot) for the Red Matsyendranātha. The fixtures were placed on the chariot for the first time in NS 774 after the chariot arrived at Gāḥ Bāhāḥ. Aguṭhīknown as theLusa Guṭhīwas then set up to ensure the safekeeping and maintenance of the fixtures.

event_name: Coins minted under the name of Buṅgadyaḥ
event_description: The following kings issued coins with the names of the deity on these dates:Śrīnivāsa Malla                     —   Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 781Yoganarendra Malla              —  Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 805Lokaprakāśa Malla               —  Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 826Indra Malla                            —  Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 826Vīra Narasiṁha Malla           —  Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 829Vīra Mahindrasiṁha  Malla   —  Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 829Ṛddhinarasiṁha Malla          — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 835Mahindrasṁha Malla            — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 837Yogaprakāśa  Malla              — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 842Viṣṇu Malla                           — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 849Rājyaprakāśa Malla              — Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 865Viśvajita  Malla                       — Śrī Lokanātha     — NS 878Jayaprakāśa  Malla                — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 880Raṇajita Malla                        — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 882Dalamarddan Śāha                — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 884Tejanarasiṁha Malla              — Śrī Karuṇāmaya — NS 885Prithivinārāyaṇa Śāha           — Śrī Lokanātha     — ŚS 1685

event_name: Pavement of steps in front of the outer entrance of the temple
event_description: The steps in front of the outer entrance of the temple were paved with stones. The steps around the stone lions were also paved.

event_name: References to Bugmalokeśvara (Buṅgadyaḥ) in the palm-leaf manuscripts
event_description: Slusser(1982, vol. 2, plate no. 594 and 595) gives photos of two Nepalese manuscripts with depictions of Bugmalokeśvara. She dates the first manuscript to 1071 CE and the second to 1679 CE. However, she does not provide any further details regarding the manuscripts and does not mention anything about how she dated them. Paleographically, the first manuscript cannot be from such an early date. It is more likely that it comes from the 17th-18th century.Locke(1980, 300) also mentions one such manuscript containing a miniture painting of Bugama Lokeśvara preserved in Paris and vaguely dates it to 120-220 NS.
A stone pillar with a statue of Vajrasatva was erected in front of the Karuṇāmaya temple.
The monument was seriously damaged in the 1834 earthquakes.
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Kũvara Rāṇā offered a bell to Buṅgadyaḥ.
The Maṇḍala was made in 1964 CE. The inscription does not mention the name of its founder. However, according to locals, the monument was commissioned by Harṣamuni Śākya.
Reconstruction of the Phalcā by the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City and the local community.

event_name: Renovation, Donation and Offering of a roof
event_description: Renovation of the Phalcā and offering of the roof by a group led by a person named Devisaṃṣa. The stone inscription (28 cm high, 16.5 cm wide) is attached to the centre of the back wall.The stone inscription of Dhaubaji phalcā is attached to the eastern wall. On the top of the inscription Lord Bhimsen's attribute, a club, is carved.
The former Chvāsa Phalcā was dismantled. It was reconstructed in a single-bay form and incorporated into the ground floor of a five-storey concrete building.
Rudramatī, the daughter of King Śrīnivāsa Malla and elder sister of Yoganarendra Malla, built a three-storied temple to the south of Narasiṃha Temple.

Aside from its plinths, the temple was completely destroyed by the earthquake of 2015. Almost all identifiable columns, windows, doors, carnes, tympanum, door wings, struts etc. were inventoried and are being reused in the present restoration of the temple. As the foundation of the temple remained intact and was found by the archaeological investigation to be strong enough to be reused, the temple is being reconstructed upon its original foundation. The restoration work of the temple is currently ongoing (2019).
