The monument was seriously damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
As of February 2022, the Phalca is being reconstructed with the fund provided by the Department of Archaeology.

event_name: Consecration of a new statue of Khaḍgayoginī
event_description: After the original statue of Khaḍgayoginī was stolen in 1979 CE, a newly built deity's statue was consecrated in 1980 CE. The consecration ritual performed by 12 Vajrācārya tantric priests lasted for 14 days (from the 3rd to 27th of Āṣāḍha in VS 2037). The closing ceremony of this ritual took place on the 28th of Āṣāḍha.
The inscription records that Bijasiṃ, Jayatarasiṃ and Jayanarasiṃ renovated this Caitya.

event_name: Theft of the original statue of Khaḍgayoginī
event_description: The original statue of Khaḍayoginī got stolen in 1979 CE.

event_name: Formation of a committee to make and enshrine a new statue of Khaḍgayoginī
event_description: After the original statue of Khaḍgayoginī got stolen in 1979 CE, a committee (named Śrīkhaḍgajoginī Uddhāra Samiti) headed by Śyāma Malekū, a resident of Pulchok) was formed in 1980 to make and enshrine a new statue of hers.
Dharmarāja malekū and his wife Gaṇeśamāyā, both residents of Pulchok offered a crest jewel to Khaḍgayoginī.

event_name: Construction of a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (monument object LAL0630-005)
event_description: The inscription records that Ciribābu and his wife Nhucche Māyā established a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya in the temple premises in the memory of his deceased father Dhanakṛṣṇa and mother Cirīmaiyā.

It is recorded in the inscription that Jahalasiṃ Vajrācārya, his wife Dhantalakṣmī and sons Pūrṇajoti, Ratnajoti and Bhīmajoti offered a gilt canopy (ilā̃) of 11dhārnī(2.393 kg) and 11 metal lamps to Khaḍagayoginī.
The temple was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.

event_name: Renovation of the temple after the 2015 earthquakes
event_description: The temple, severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes, is recently renovated with the financial support of the local residents.
Lokapati and Herāmāyā Vajrācārya, both residents of Yaśodhara Vihāra offered the bell to Khaḍgayoginī in the memory of their deceased parents.
Gaṇeśa Bahādura Śreṣṭha (the grandson of Māna Bahādura son of Lāla Bahādura) and his wife Sāvitrī, both residents of Māgādeurālī, Dolakha offered the bell to Khaḍgayoginī.

Ḍirakumārīdevī, the wife of Dhīra Śamśera, erected Dīrabhakteśvara as an expression of her reverence to Lord Śiva. Additionally, she pledged to provide land parcels to generate income for the temple, covering the costs of daily and occasional rituals, as well as compensating the priest, cleaners, and musicians for their contributions to the temple.
Ḍirakumārīdevī, the wife of Dhīra Śamśera, installed a bell at the temple four years after its inception.

During the reign of King Raṇabahādura Śāha, aśikharakūṭa caityawas established to the west of the monastic building. On this occasion, a golden necklace (hṛdayaphola) and a silverpiṇḍapātra(a bowl forpiṇḍa) decorated with lotus petals were also offered to thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.
The old structure was demolished and reconstructed.
The roof'sjhĩgaṭītiles were replaced with copper plates.
In the course of the widening of the road thepāṭīwas demolished. No historic materials are known to have survived.

A group of donors led by Manoharasiṃha Bhāro established the statue of Buḍābhīmasena. According to the inscription recording this event, the donors hailed from Bhaktapur, Banepa, and Sanga, suggesting that traders from various settlements under the Bhaktapur kingdom settled in Dāpcā for trade purposes. Their collective efforts led to the establishment of the Bhīmasena statue.

Thirty-seven years after the establishment of the Bhīmasena statue, Dhanasiṃ and his wife Māneśvarī of Tekhāco, Bhaktapur, expanded the temple. They enclosed the sanctum by building a temple on it and added aphalcādirectly in front, dedicated to Bhīmasena. To ensure the temple's continued maintenance, they endowed a four-ropanīplot of land in Banepa.
The eroded inscription on the Gaṇeśa statue (DPC0020-7) records some locals establishing the statue. The donor names are unclear due to the erosion of text.
Pūrṇe Kāmī offered a bell to the temple.
Haridāsa and Nānīmāyā Śreṣṭha offered a brasstoraṇainstalled on top of the temple entrance.
Thephalcā(DPC0020-9) in front of the temple was renovated by the Department of Archaeology.

Amarakānteśvarī is credited for the construction of the temple in 1856 CE (VS 1913) (M. Thapā VS 2077, p.205). There used to be a bell installed south of the temple in 1856 CE (NS 976). While the year mentioned on the bell may have prompted them to believe that the temple was built in 1856 CE, a later document from 1915 CE (VS 1972) relating to the settlement of a dispute regarding the operation of the temple cites alālamoharaissued in 1852 CE (VS 1909) in connection with Sureśakānteśvara Mandira (K_0131_0001). This suggests that the temple was already in existence in 1852 CE. The exact year of its construction is unclear, as currently (August 2023), there is no other historical source that sheds light on its initial construction.

The inscription on a bell installed south of the temple states that Princess Amarakānteśvarī offered the bell through Captain Juddhamānasiṃha Rājabhaṇḍārī. Michaels and Tandon (2017, p.70), however, mention that she offered the bell through Siddhimānasiṃha Rājbhaṇḍārī. The bell is no longer at the site. Therefore, it could not be ascertained if it was Juddhamānasiṃha or Siddhimānasiṃha, who assisted Amarakānteśvarī in offering the bell. Usually, the donor of the bell is also the person to commission the construction of the temple the bell was donated to.
The temple was reconstructed by the Pashupati Area Development Trust after it was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
Devajyoti Vajrācārya established thisbāhāḥas well as acaityaand adharmadhātu maṇḍala.
Mānakumārī and Thakũmatī endowed land to establish aguṭhīfor the management of the Bāhāḥ.
As mentioned in the description above, the Hiti suffered heavy damages in the 2015 earthquakes.
The Gāyatrī Fund, a local NGO, raised 19,59,828/- Nepali rupees and restored the Hiti in 2017.
The house was already in disrepair before the 2015 earthquake, which exacerbated the damage, rendering it unsuitable for residence.

During the reign of King Jayajaga (Jagajjaya Malla), acaityawas established. Dvāre Dhanasiṃha, a resident of Dhugāma Ṭola in Gokarṇa, together with his wife Rachamani and their children Kṛsnanasiha (Kṛṣṇanarasiṃha), Sumati, and Dhanakṛṣṇa, constructed the caitya. Thiscaityais located along the route from the Kāntibhairava Dyaḥchẽ to the Pakanāvatī Gaṇeśa temple.
Dhanasiṃha and his wife Rachamani together constructed aphalcāto the west of the Pakanāvatī temple.

Inscription on the eastern side of pillar MUG0050-005. The text is eroded. It contains 9 lines.A date of 1326 (ŚS) can potentially be read in the third line. This tentative reading would give a date 1404 CE.
Candrajyoti and Lakṣmīmāyā constructed this Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in the courtyard of the monastery.
Saṅgha-members of the Bāhāḥ and the Lalitpur Metropolitan City repaired the façadeof the monastery. The Metropolitan City office provided 80,000 RS for this reconstruction work.

This inscription predates the temple by many centuries. It is said to belong to the Mānadeva period back in the 5th century. As most of the text of the inscription has been damaged, its content is unclear. The inscription was installed after aśivaliṅgawas established in the name of a person’s son who died in his childhood.
King Surendra offered a bell to the Surendreśvara Mandira (PPK0610-001).
King Surendra’s second wife Surarājyalakṣmī offered a bell to the Sūryarājyeśvara Mandira (PPK0610-004).
King Surendra’s third wife Devarājyalakṣmī established the Devarājyeśvara Mandira (PPK0610-006) and offered a bell to the main deity.

Prince Trailokya, King Surendra’s son, established the Trailokyeśvara Mahādeva (PPK0610-007) in the name of his mother Trailokyarājyalakṣmī and also offered a bell to the temple. Born in 1847 CE, Prince Trailokya died in 1878 CE while his father was still the king.

Surendra’s father King Rājendra Vikrama offered a bell (PPK0610-010) to the Rājendreśvara Mandira (PPK0610-009) that produced a ‘beautiful sound’. He was in prison when he made the offering. With the intent to retake the throne, the dethroned King Rājendra and his army moved to the capital in 1847 CE but were defeated by Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura’s army in the Battle of Alau. He was imprisoned in Bhaktapur since then and passed away in incarceration in 1881 CE.
The upper platform was repaved and the plinths of the five temples were renewed.

The 2015 earthquakes damaged all five temples that were already in a poor state of repair. Cracks have appeared on the walls of these temples with the finial of the Trailokyeśvara Mandira (PPK0610-007) on the verge of collapse.
Tulsī Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha of Kobāhāla Tola offered a bell (LAL2940-004) to Dhūmāvatī.
Tulsī Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha, Sānumaiyā̃ Śreṣṭha, and others collectively paved the Dhūmāvatī shrine with stone and tiles.
Nārāyaṇamaṅgala and Beṇī Jośī donated a bell (LAL2940-010) in the names of their late father Dvijarāja Maṅgala, mother Premakumārī, brother Vaikuṇṭhamaṅgala, and sister Ambikā.

In memory of his late father Madanaprasāda Śreṣṭha, Bindeśaprasāda Śreṣṭha, together with his wife Sajanā Śreṣṭha and daughter Biyaṃkā Rānī Śreṣṭha, paved the floor and stairs inside the Dhūmāvatī shrine with tiles. As the previously laid tiles had deteriorated, he had them repaved with new tiles.
The Dhūmāvatī shrine was reconstructed with financial assistance from Lalitpur Metropolitan City and donations collected from devotees.
Residents of the Dhũllā Ṭola jointly commissioned the construction of this Shrine.

event_name: Devastation and restoration after the 1933 earthquakes
event_description: The inscription (BKT0250_I_002) bears witness to a significant chapter in the history of the Brahmāyāṇī Pīṭha. It narrates the tale of destruction and resilience that unfolded after the earthquake of 1933 CE (1990 VS). The seismic upheaval had taken a toll on thephalcā, rendering it in ruins. However, the spirit of the local community shone bright in the aftermath of this catastrophe. The inscription details how, in the year 1940 CE (1997 VS), the community united to undertake the restoration of thephalcā.
Juktamāna Śreṣṭha from Asvabārī offered the bell to the temple.

Following the 2015 CE earthquakes, the Department of Archaeology undertook the reconstruction of the Śobhābhagavatī temple, along with other temples like the Sarasvatī, Ratkavināyaka, and Buḍhībhairavī temples in Nuwakot in similar architecture.
It is was offered by a certain Rājavīra Jośī (text: Rājavira Josi).

event_name: Damage caused by the 1934 CE earthquake and rebuilding
event_description: Following the devastating earthquakes of 1934 CE, the Vaṃśeśvara Mahādeva temple suffered a collapse. Prior to this unfortunate event, the temple stood as a grand three-tiered structure. However, in the process of reconstruction that ensued after the earthquakes, the temple was restored with its upper tiers replaced by a domed top (see 'description' and 'historical photos' above).

Thākusiṅ and Toyuṣvā Thakunī a couple from nearby Valā Ṭola financed the restoration of the Phalcā. Oneropanīland of Jhurabu was donated to theguṭhī. The inscription directs theguṭhīto light three oil lamps on the day when the chariot of the deity stops in Gāḥbāhāḥ. It also encourages them to save some money every year to fund its potential reconstruction.
Nāsu Haribhakta, a resident from Kvālkhu Ṭola, supplied funding for the renovation of the Phlacā in the name of his daughter Hasinānānī.
The Phalcā was in poor condition and filled with rubbish. The Lalitpur Metropolitan City (Mahānagarapālikā) dismantled it in 2019 and rebuilt it in its traditional form.

"Before the coronation of the current king in 1975 and as part of the renovation of the adjacent Mani Ganesa Temple, the building's length was shortened approximately 6'-2" in the front and in the rear 6'-4"." (HSR Ayuguthi, p. 7)

Renovation under KVPT and DOA (see extensive reports from the KVPT). The HSR stated that funding came from the Andy Warhol Foundation, GTZ/UDLE, KVPT, and Mr Pandey and Mr Dickerman. Thi s was also part of the nationalisation process as the site was taken away from its occupants. The cost estimate mentioned in the HSR was US-$ 38,877.62 (KVPT Report HSR p A22)
An ascetic named Buddha Girī Bābā installed a door along with door leaves in the temple.

King Jayasthiti Malla restored this temple, appointed a Southern Bhaṭṭa to conduct worship, and established an endowment. From that time until now, the worship has been continually performed by the Southern Bhaṭṭa Brāhmaṇas.
During the reign of Śivasiṃhadeva and Raṇajitasiṃha, an individual named Gopirāma Bhāro offered a golden pinnacle to this temple.
Threeropanīsof land were set aside for the restoration of the śivālaya and for applying lime annually.

During the reign of Raṇabahādura Śāha, Dharmanārāyaṇa, with the desire to facilitate the salvation of ancestors, constructed a rest house on the south side of Gokarna on the new moon day of Śrāvaṇa and established a land endowment for the performance of śrāddha.
A phalcā containing six bays was constructed to the east of Gokarṇeśvara Mahādeva and to the west of Cyāsiṃkhya: Bhairava.

Numerous inscriptions are affixed to the wall at the north-eastern corner of the temple. Among these, one inscription is dated 1804 CE (SS 1725). On the upper part of the inscription, figures of the Trident, the Moon, and the Sun can be seen, while the lower part features the carved image of a donor couple. As the inscription has faded, the details contained within it are not clear.
The bell located on the southern platform of the temple was offered to Gokarṇeśvara Mahādeva by Lalitatripurāsundarī, the younger Queen of Raṇabahādura Śāha.

The topmost roof of the temple consists of gold-gilded brass plates and a cast metal pinnacle. This roof was installed during the reign of Raṇabahādura Śāha in 1830 CE (SS 1751). This detail is found in the inscription located on the roof.

The eastern entrance door of this temple was constructed with gold-gilded copper plates by Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe, together with his wives Viṣṇu Kumārī and Umā Devī, his daughter Khaḍga Kumārī, and the entire family.

event_name: Establishment of Hem Nārāyaṇa and endowment of land
event_description: Hemakarna Thapa Godar established agricultural land endowments in various locations for Hemnārāyaṇa, located east of Gokarṇeśvara Mahādeva on the banks of the Bāgmatī, and for Hema Bhakteśvara Mahādeva, located in the northeast direction.

event_name: Establishment of Śivaliṅga and endowment of land
event_description: Mahemanisiṃha Bhaṇḍārī, along with his wife Bālakumārī, his sons Navabahādura and Sthiti Bahādura, and three daughters, established Śrī Śiva Meheravāla Bhakteśvara near this temple on the banks of the Bāgmatī. They established agricultural land endowments in various places, and arrangements were made so that the income from that land would cover the expenses for the entire year's activities.
Kaviprasād Gautama came here on the new moon day of Bhādra (Father's Day), performed śrāddha, engaged in bhajana-kīrtana (devotional singing), and additionally arranged a feast for 108 priests.

The roofs were reconstructed, and gold-gilded brass roofs were installed on all the temple's roofs. Furthermore, the Savaṅgīṇa Vikāsa Samanvaya Samiti successfully concluded the Śrīmad Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa Historical Religious Grand Fair.

This inscription is also located on the wall at the north-eastern corner of the temple. Due to the lack of clarity in the letters, it is difficult to fully comprehend the inscription's details. The date mentioned on it is also erased and cannot be ascertained. Upon a careful reading of the inscription, it can be understood that there are mentions of offering pañcāmṛta to Mahādeva on the new moon day of Śrāvaṇa, that Kāśīrāma established endowments in various locations in the temple's name, and that various worship methods are described.
As the inscription is heavily faded and many of the letters have become illegible, the details mentioned in the inscription are not in a readable condition.

The gilt cover, adorned with the faces of Śiva, is utilized to envelop the stoneśivalingaduring the annual ritual of Rājarājeśvara Temple. The inscription on this metal cover records the donation of this artifact by a certain Harṣamāna from Jyābāhāḥ, Kathmandu.a.
जितविर (जीतवीर) शाक्य, उनकी पत्नी र परिवारका अन्य सदस्यको धर्मचित्त उत्पत्ति भई जधुंछेँ (जोग बाहाःको चोक)मा तेलीया इँट विच्छाउनुका साथै धर्मधातु जिनालय चैत्य (KAT2410-002) स्थापना गरे ।
Together with her three sons, Gomatī commissioned this Pāṭī in memory of her husband.

Kumārī Pāṭī was reconstructed with the help of the Rotary Club Lalitpur and the local residents, who together donated a sum of 550,000 NRS. The inauguration day was the 31st of Jyeṣṭha 2060 VS. Before the reconstruction, the building was severely dilapidated and had collapsed in places. A concrete structure which imitates traditional carving forms was selected as the replacement. 16 years later, some of the local residents have expressed a wish that the building included more traditional elements (such as wood carvings) so as to give it more traditional look.
Abhajanachanting committee was formed by the local senior citizens.

event_name: Licchavi King Aṃśu Varman issued a decree
event_description: This Licchavi inscription echoes a decree issued by King Aṃśu Varman. It stands at the south-eastern corner of the Pāṭī, though there is no historical relationship between the inscription and the Pāṭī. D.Vajrācārya(VS 2030, 290) mentions that he once saw this inscription somewhere far away from this site, at the banks of a pond in Bungmati. He notes that it later disappeared from there.
During the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla, something was offered to Bāghabhairava. Since the part of the inscription recording of this event is rubbed off, what exactly offered remains obscure.
Bijaya Bhāva from Thāna Bāhāla and his grandsons Bhāginātha Bhāva, Dharmanātha Bhāva, Dhanadeva Bhāva, and Siddhinātha Bhāva paved the temple premises with stones.

event_name: Offering of a Toraṇa and Other Metal Objects
event_description: During the reign of King Prithvī Vīra Vikrama, Jamadāra Bhīma Narasiṃha Bhāvo and his other family members offered a gilttoraṇaand other brass objects to Bāghabhairava.
Ratnabahādura Śāhī offered a brasspatāḥto the temple.

During the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla, Viṣvasiṃha Rāutta, Rāma Rāutta, Nalasiṃha Bhāro, and Nalasiṃha Bhāvo jointly built the stone plinth in the façade of the Nāsaḥdyaḥ shrine (see the object number KIR0004-009 above).

event_name: Thievery of the Gilt Toraṇa Offered in 1897 CE and Installation of a New One
event_description: Since the gilttoraṇa,which was offered in 1897 CE, was stolen in around 1994 CE, the Kirtipur United Club installed a newtoraṇato its place with the financial support of Śaṅkara Maharjana.
Tulārāma and his family members renovated the temple.

event_name: Land Grant and Offering of Silver Jewellery
event_description: Kvāthanāyaka Duṇḍirāja Bhāro and his wife Cikuṭi offered some silver jewelry. They also granted some plots of land from four different areas to aguṭhīto maintain lighting the lamp which refer to asmahādīpa(great light) in the inscription.
Maṅgala Dāsa and Putali Nāni from Kutujvaḥ Ṭola, Kirtipur wrapped in brass the lions, flanking the main entrance of the temple.

event_name: Inscription Issued by King Rājyaprakāśa of Kāntipura (Kathmandu)
event_description: The inscription issued by King Rājyaprakāśa of Kathmandu is not related to this temple. It records that only the king has the right to cut trees in the Kirtipur forts and if someone violates this regulation, he shall be fined twelve rupees.

event_name: Construction of a Stone Pillar and Beam
event_description: Jahara Siṃ Mānandhara constructed a stone pillar and beam to mount a bell.

Amoharamālā(jewellery made with coins) was offered to Bāghabhairava by a family living in Kirtipur. The family members, whose names can be deciphered from the readable part of the inscription, are: Tiyogī, Lumayi, Helamayi, Yogā, Mālasiṃha and Harṣavī.
Jahara Siṃ Mānandhara offered the bell which is installed in front of the temple.

event_name: Offering of a Gilt Window and a Flag
event_description: Karavani Kotavāla offered a gilt window and a flag to Bāghabhairava.

event_name: Installation of a Gilt Pinnacle and a Flag
event_description: During the reign of Purandarasiṃha, a certain Kvāthanāyaka (an officer of a fort) offered a gilt pinnacle and a flag to the temple.
A donation box (made of iron) was installed to collect cash donations. The box was offered by Mathurāma Maharjana.

event_name: Adornment of the Main Entrance and the Toraṇa
event_description: The main entrance of the temple and thetoraṇacrowning it were wrapped in brass plate by Bramhavatī Śreṣṭha and Tulavī Śreṣṭha.
Tavodhika Bhāro and his wife Lakṣmīśvarī offered a bell to Bāghabhairava.

event_name: Land Grant by King Viṣṇu Malla and Establishment of Regulations
event_description: The inscription is hard to decipher. The last numerical figure of the date is not clearly readable. It appears to be number 2.The legible part of the inscription records the land grant by King Viṣṇu Malla to organize the annual worship (which takes place on the first solar day of Bhādrā, also calledsiṃhasaṃkrānti). It also records various regulations regarding the organization of the annual worship.

event_name: Visit of the President of Republic Nepal
event_description: The first president of the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal, Rāmavaraṇa Yādava, visited this temple and worshipped Bāghabhairava.
Gaṃgārāma and other Bhāros jointly offered a woodentoraṇa, crowning the Hiphaḥdyaḥ shrine (see object number KIR0004-005).
This is the earliest historical record related to this temple. The legible part of the inscription records a certain renovation of the temple carried out by Jagatapāla Varmā, a Mahāpātra of Pātan.
Kvāthanāyaka Viśvanātha Bhāro, probably an officer of a fort, offered a gilttoraṇa,khāpā(door),windowandguṃgvāka(?) to the Bāghabhairava Mandira.
Kvāthanāyaka Viśvanātha Bhāro offered something to Bāghavairava. Since the part of the inscription where this event is recorded is hard to decipher, what he actually offered remains unknown.

Māhilā from Samala Ṭola, Janakalāla from Kvācva Ṭola, Dhanabahādura from Lāykū Ṭola, Bhuyū from Thambāhāḥ Ṭola, and Herālāla from Kutujhvaḥ Ṭola jointly offered a brassṭoranawhich crowns the main entrance of the temple.
Satajīva Jñānī, her son Kāku, and other family members jointly offered a pair of brass flags which are flank the main entrance of the temple.
Two flags, flanking the main entrance of the temple, were restored by Lāla and his wife Māna Kumārī.
A group of Bhāvo community from Thaṃbāhāḥ Ṭola, Kirtipur offered the bell which is also installed in front of the temple.
One of the Phalcā's bays is used by the owner of a plot of land behind it.  The owner provided 2 feet of their land so that the Phalcā could be reconstructed with a wider breadth.

Homeless people or other strangers used to sleep in the Phalcā at night and allegedly took part in prohibited activities here. The Taṅgaḥ Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti is now renting out nine of the Phalcā's bays. These have been converted into cabins and take the form of nine shops, whilst one bay is kept open for transit.
Phalcā was dismantled and reconstructed.

event_name: Offering a stone statue of a goddess

event_description: Govaladhana Puli (Govardhana Purī) appointed Tapodhana Viśvanātha as the priest.
Kāśirāma Bhāro, Virāja Bhāro, and Gayārāma Bhāro of Sakva got a temple constructed for the Śivaliṅga representing Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mahādeva and also offered a goldenkalaśa.
A statue of Jalaśayananārāyaṇa was installed at the Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mandira complex. The donor's name cannot be deciphered in the inscription.
Gopirimayi and her Śivahari Bhāro had established a statue of Māheśvarī.

event_name: Establishment of statues of Viśṇu (SKH0010-024) and Annapurṇa (SKH0010-025)
event_description: Vaṃśīdharadeva established a statue of Mādhavadeva (Viṣṇu) while his mother Lachamanidevī installed a statue of Annapūrṇa. A statue of Yichyādevī was also established on the same occasion in the name of the deceased daughter Rājyeśvarī.
Pāhāna Bhāro, along with his son Haliśaṃkara (Hariśaṅkara) Bhāro and grandson Śunandahali, established Pāspati (Paśupati) Mahādeva to the west of the Temple.

event_name: Repair of golden pinnacle and offering struts
event_description: During the reign of King Jagajjaya Malla, Devarāma Bhāro, a resident of  the Yapāta Ṭola in Sankhu, along with his three sons Latneśvara Bhāro, Dhaneśvara Bhāro and Vireśvara Bhāro, repaired the golden finial of the Temple. On the same occasion, they also offered struts to the Temple.

During the reign of King Surendra Śāha, aśivaliṅgawas established by Vira Bhāro, his wife Dhaṃcā Thakuṃ and other members of the family. The Śivaliṅga has been stolen. At present, a fragment of a pinnacle of a shrine has been installed at the place theśivaliṅgaused to be.

event_name: Repair of monuments at the Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mandira complex
event_description: The Jyotirliṅgeśvara Mandira, along with the water tank,aṣṭamātṛkā pīṭha(Ghorarūpā Yoginī), and other monuments around the area were renovated with the financial assistance provided by organizations from the Netherlands and Vajrayogini Village Development Committee. An local organization named Friends of Sankhu had coordinated the renovation works.

event_name: Paving the Temple complex with telia bricks
event_description: Cikaṃaḥpā (bricks) were laid on the ground around the Temple with the financial assistance from various organizations from the Netherlands collected at the initiation of Bālagopāla Śreṣṭha and Bert van dek Hoek.
The 2015 earthquakes resulted in multiple cracks in the Temple.

The Department of Archaeology in cooperation with the Shankharapur Municipality completely dismantled the temple and rebuilt it at a total cost of a little over NRs. 4.5 million. There used to be atoraṇaon top of each entrance of the temple. They were not installed after the reconstruction.

event_name: Theft of metal cover of Jyotirliṅgeśvara
event_description: Thepañcamukhīśivaliṅga, a ceremonial hollow cover made of gilt copper in the shape of aśivaliṅgawith five figures of Lord Śiva’s face embossed on it, was stolen from the priest’s own house. The cover that is taken around the town on a palanquin has not been recovered so far. A replacement has been made for the procession now.

Cakrasiṃha Bābu (a son of Bhīmālakṣmī who married the daughter of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla) and his four sons Pratāpasiṃha Bābu, Narasiṃha Bābu, Jayabhadrasiṃha Bābu and Ānandasiṃha Bābu commissioned this Sataḥ and established the statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa. They also performed a fire ritual, established aguṭhi,and had a golden pinnacle fixed upon the Sataḥ. King Yoganarendra Malla was present at the inaugural ceremony.
Punārāṃ Citrakārī, Gvapāla Citrakārī and other members of Henu Bāhāḥ established aguṭhīto organisebhajanachanting in the Satah.

The first floor's façade contains struts depicting Harihara, Lakṣmīnarasiṃha, Bhairava together with his consort. These struts also show the name of King Yoganarendra Malla. Nowadays, however, this is hidden behind electricity and telephone cables.

event_name: Offering of a brass palanquin to Kṛṣṇa
event_description: Dilabahādura, Gaṇeśabahādura and others offered a brass cot to lord Kṛṣṇa.

event_name: Donation of silver nāgas to Kṛṣṇa
event_description: Jagatamāna from Bālakumārī donated the silver serpents that are fixed behind the Kṛṣṇa statue.
Nārāyaṇabahādura Śreṣṭha and Lakṣmīkumārī Śreṣṭha repaired the cot of lord Kṛṣṇa.
Harṣabahādura Nāpita covered Kṛṣṇa’s cot with bronze plates.
Lalitpur Metropolitan City and GTZ/UDLE renovated the Sataḥ with the help of Āśābahādura Śreṣṭha, Bhīmahari Jośī, Amira Sinyā and others.
Donation by Śaṅkha Dhar Avāḥ. A stone inscription is available on the wall of the main monastic building.
The 2015 earthquakes damaged Bhajanachẽ, leaving multiple cracks on the building.
The Department of Archaeology reconstructed it in cooperation with the Shankharapur Municipality.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_description: Hirālāla, his wife Canda Kumārī, and other family members covered the walls of the sanctum with brass plate. They also gilded the brassilāṃ.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_description: Devarāja, Bekhārāja, and others offered a pair of metal flags to the temple which adorne the entrance to the sanctum.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Replacement of the Jhĩgaṭī Tiled Roof with Brass Plates
event_description: During the premiership of Juddhaśamaśera, Bhājumuni Mānandhara (a local resident) replaced the temple's roof (which was tiled withjhĩgaṭībricks) with brass plates in the memory of his deceased son Pānavīra.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Offering of Two Pillars Cladded with Brass
event_description: Rāma Gīri erected two wooden pillars cladded with brass plates on both sides of the sanctum's entrance.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_description: The temple's surrounding was paved with marble by an individual in the memory of his deceased parents, Buddhinātha Māske and Kīrtivāsinī Māske.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Offering of a Metal Toraṇa to Gaṇeśa (LAL2840-005)
event_description: Bhājunarasiṃha (text: Bhāju Narasī), Viṣṇumāyā (text: Visnumayā), Devanarasiṃha offered a metaltoraṇato the Gaṇeśa (LAL2840-005).

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Repair of the Statue of Gaṇeśa (see object number LAL2840-004)
event_description: Rāma Kumārī repaired the statue of Gaṇeśa.

monument_name: Baṭuka Bhairava (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Repair of the Statue of Gaṇeśa (see object number LAL2840-004)
event_description: Rāma Kumārī and her son Kṛṣottama repaired the statue of Gaṇeśa.
The inscription records that Devīdāsa Bhāro constructed thephalcāin NS 784 (1664 CE) with the intention of liberating the soul of his late uncle Viśva Bhāro.
The inscription documents the date of thephalcā's original construction and notes that Devīdāsa Bhāro installed a statue of Mañjuśrī. However, as of August 2020, there is no record of this statue.

Harinasī and his family from Thaiba built a temple for the Sthānagaṇeśa. They also set up a religious trust by donating land parcels to fund expenses for various rituals at the temple and for its timely renovations.

event_name: Laying of gilded sheets on upper roof
event_description: Jagotahamāna Siṃha Bhāro (Mulmī), his wife Rānimani, and his son Kṛṣṇamānasiṃha Bhāro overlaid the top roof with gilded sheets.

An inscription was installed, recording the offering of a gilded finial, parasol, and roof after the construction of the temple. The new inscription quoted the events from earlier inscriptions recording the construction of the temple in 1877 CE (NS 997) and laying of gilded sheet on the roof in 1881 CE (NS 1001).

Mānakṛṣṇa Bhāro and his family from the Jalacapāḥkva Ṭola offered a set of five musical instruments to the temple. The inscription mandates the performance of these instruments during the morning and evening rituals daily. The Badyakāra andjogicommunities were required to repair the instruments in case they were damaged. Thejogis who performed these instruments were allowed to till fiveropanīs of land.

The Śrīdharanārāyaṇa temple in Thaiba was renovated and nineropanīs of land were donated to set up a religious trust to arrange an income for the temple. Two priests, Mādhavarāja Upādhyāya and Candreśvarānanda Upādhyāya, were given the responsibility of performing daily and periodic worships at the temple and offer the gifts (prasāda) from the deity to the donor family and local administration office. Out of the annual income, twomoharas were to be saved to fund the timely renovations of the temple. The trust members were required to worship Buṅgadyaḥ on the first day of the solar month, and worship Gaṇeśa from this temple and Bhūteśvara of Thaiba on the 14th of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
Sirimāyā Śreṣṭha of Thaiba offered a bell to the temple.
Bābukājī Śreṣṭha and Pārvatī Śreṣṭha offered a bell to the temple.
The reconstruction committee led by Īśvaralāla Śreṣṭha of Thaiba reconstructed the temple under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology.

event_name: Establishment of a śivaliṅga and bell
event_description: The Śubheśvara temple was built by establishing aśivaliṅga(KAT2820-009), wishing for eternal peace of Śubhakumārī, one of Jaṅga Bahadura’s queens. A bell (KAT2820-005) was also installed on the occasion.
In the course of constructing the Jaṅgehiraṇyahema Nārāyaṇa Mandira (KAT2800) in 1875 CE (VS 1931), Jaṅga Bahādura also built the Vairāgī Maṭha.
Marble slabs were laid around the Hanumān temple (KAT2820-010) premises inside theakhaḍā.
This inscription recounts Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera restoring the temple damaged in the 1934 earthquakes without clearly mentioning if it was a renovation or a reconstruction.

The temple was reconstructed under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology following the damages sustained by the temple in the 2015 earthquakes. In the course of dismantling the temple for reconstruction, bricks with the inscription ‘Śrī3 Candra’ were recovered from the temple’s foundation. This suggests that the temple was built during the reign of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera (1901-1929 CE).

As the Phalcā was in a poor state of repair, it was dismantled and rebuilt. Old columns, capitals, windows, and other usable components of the Phalcā were reused. Therefore, the traditional architecture of the Phalcā is retained.

The inscription mentions that the founder of the Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya constructed anothercaityaand adharmadhātu maṇḍala. The inscription does not mention the name of its founder, but locals claim that Harṣamuni Śākya was the one who commissioned it.

Pruscha (1975, p.33) mentions, without citing a source, that the statue of Garuḍa in front of the Temple was erected in 1641 CE. The statue (KAT0830-010) no longer has an inscription. So it's unclear whether the current statue had an inscription when he assessed the site or if the older one was stolen at some point and then replaced with the current one.

event_name: Construction of a sataḥ next to the Temple
event_description: There are seven inscriptions embedded on a wall east of the Temple, as discussed in the 'description' above. The first, from 1697 CE (NS 817), records the construction of asataḥnext to the Temple by Vāsudeva Bhāro and Racherāma Bhāro. This demonstrates that the Temple itself existed prior to 1697 CE.

event_name: Offering of a stone oil lamp 'dalūpāḥ' (object number KAT0830-009)
event_description: Punasiṅa (Pūrṇasiṃha) offered it in order to please Nārāyaṇa.

Malinānī Yala constructed aphalcānext to the Temple and endowed tworopanīsof land in Tokhā for  commemoratingphalcā'sanniversary and feeding Brahmins on the occasion  However, there is nophalcāon the site (as of November 2022 CE).
The inscription commemorating this event has deteriorated. It mentions that something was built here at the Temple, but it is unclear what was built and who funded it.

The inscription recording the construction of thesataḥis eroded. As a result, the identity of the donor who commissioned the execution cannot be determined. It is most likely the samesataḥas seen in Pruscha's photograph (Pruscha 1975, p.33). A school building now stands where thesataḥonce stood.

event_name: Construction of a dharmaśālā and endowment of land
event_description: Dhaṃtanāya Jyeṣṭha Maharjana of the Dalāchi (text: Darāchi) Ṭola constructed the dharmaśālā and endowed oneropanīof land to perform the anniversary ritual (varṣavarddhana) of thedharmaśālāand offer balls of rice (piṇḍa) in memory of Dhaṃtanāya’s deceased mother.

event_name: Construction of a dabū (elevated public platform)
event_description: Lohokāra …, his wife Malakṣmī, daughters Bhimalakṣmī and Daśalaksṃī, and other family members constructed thedabūin memory of the main donor’s deceased father Lakṣmīdhara (text: Lachimidhara) and mother. The name of the donor is illegible due to surface chipping. He was, however, clearly a stone sculptor (lohokāra). He also established a fund of 101 mohararupaīyā̃ from which to perform the anniversary ritual of thedabū.
Following the earthquakes of 1934 CE, the Temple was renovated.

event_name: Installation of a stone pillar (object number KAT0830-011)
event_description: The stone pillar (dharmastambha) in front of the Temple was inaugurated by Guru Kaviprasāda and Komalaprasāda Gautama as part of their larger campaign of flourishing Krisnaism in Nepal and beyond. Inscriptions can be found on the pillar's eastern, western, and southern faces.
Only a portion of the inscription remains today. As a result, the event it records remains unidentified.
The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust renovated theāgamawith funding from the Prince Claus Fund and other contributors.

A stone inscription is attached to the eastern wall of the Bhailaḥ Phalcā which provides information about its construction in 1871 CE (NS 991). According to the inscription, thephalcāwas built by Rāma Prajāpati Thakura and his family in the name of his late parents. Aguṭhīwas established at the same time, and land was donated to fund the organisation of annual rituals. As of 2018, theguṭhīno longer exists. Some of the rituals have therefore also come to an end.One can find images of the donors at the bottom of the inscription and a Bhairava flanked by two deities above it. Bhairava is shown standing in theālīḍhaposture with four arms; holding akhaḍgaand akhaṭvāṁka in his upper two hands.

monument_name: Ī Bahī Vãtā Vihāra (ca. 17th cent. CE)

event_name: Installation of stone lions flanking the main entrance of the Pīṭha
event_description: The earliest inscription from the Pīṭha premises records the installation of two guardian stone lions by theguthis of Bhāro and Bhābos of Balambu. Due to the poor condition of the inscription, the date cannot be ascertained although the first digit can be read as '8'. As the inscription mentions the name of the king as Mahīndra Malla, it is certain that the event took place in between his reigning years NS 829 (1709 CE) and NS 835 (1715 CE) (Burleigh 1976, 56).

event_name: Construction of the present Pīṭhe structure
event_description: The Pīgaṃdyaḥ Pīṭha was under an open sky with a pair of lions guarding it before Kumāra Śreṣṭha, a resident of Balambu, constructed the present structure.
The resident of Hāmanani Ṭola of Balambu, Bhadra Siṃ Bhāro, and his family jointly commissioned this Phalcā.

According to local residents, the Phalcā had been renovated by the Pradhāna Pañca, Māndāsa Śreṣṭha in 1973. At that time, the Phalcā had not been in its "traditional" form. The floor and the wall were built using cement and bricks. This way, the Phalcā could not retain its previous appearance.

King Pratapa Malla initiated the erection of the Hanumān statue upon the pillar. An accompanying inscription commemorated the occasion, emphasizing the statue's role in granting victory in battles and protecting homes. This inscription is edited in G. Vajrācārya (VS 2033, pp. 224-225). Vajrācārya noted that the inscription was engraved on the statue's pedestal during his site documentation. As of February 2023, the pedestal has been painted over, obscuring all traces of the inscription.
Theśikharakūṭa caityawas built by Lakṣmidhara(?) Vajrācārya and his family.
In NS 999, Gajarāja Vajrācarya, together with other members of his family, offered a bell to the Śākyamuni Buddha enshrined in the Triratna Joga Mahāvihāra.
Establishment of aguṭhīfor thevarṣabandhana pūjāand daily worship of the Triratna (Śākyasiṃha) shrine by a Vajrācārya family.

Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Kũvara erected the Śivālaya in 1863 CE (1920 VS). He built nine Śivalayas, four in Gaurīghāṭa and five in Gorakhanātha premises, collectively known as Nau Śivālaya..कृष्ण बहादुर कुँवर राणाले विसं १९२० (सन् १८६३) मा यो शिवालयहरुको निर्माण गरेका थिए । उनले यस्तै प्रकारका गौरीघाटमा ४ वटा र गोरखनाथ क्षेत्रमा ५ वटा गरी जम्मा ९ वटा शिवालयहरू बनाइका थिए जसलाई नौ शिवालय भनेर चिनिन्छ ।
The Paśupatī Area Development Trust has undertaken the reconstruction of the Śivālaya in 2019 CE (2076 VS).पशुपति क्षेत्र विकाष कोषले विसं २०७६ (सन् २०१९) मा यसको पुनर्निर्माण गरेको थियो ।

Jītajaṅga Rāṇā built the temple by establishing Jītajaṅgaprakāśeśvara, aśivaliṅganamed after himself, in the sanctum. He also established two additionalśivaliṅgas with the name Suprakāśeśvara. These twośivaliṅgas are probably the ones established as Suprakāśeśvarathat flank Jītajaṅgaprakāśeśvara from the north and south. Besides the main threeśivaliṅgas, there are 12 otherśivaliṅgas inside the temple. He also donated 306ropanīs of land to set up a trust for the management of daily and periodic worship at the temple. Jītajaṅga also built a rest house (sataḥ) west of the temple. In the inscription that records these events, Jītajaṅga eulogizes his ancestors while also inscribing their names starting from Abhirāma Kũvara to his father Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
Northern Commanding General Jītajaṅga offered a bell weighing over 400 kgs (176dhārnī) to Jītajaṅgaprakāśeśvara.
The 2015 earthquakes left the temple walls cracked all around.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust reconstructed the temple.

As mentioned above in the ‘description, the inscription installed on the Phalcā is not clearly readable due to the oil coating. It ascribes the family of certain Kṛṣṇanārā Bhābo (living at Kothunani of the Cīthū Ṭola, Kirtipur) for the construction (or rebuilding?) of the Phalcā.

The 2015 earthquakes damaged several monuments in the Cilancva Caitya complex including the Caitya itself. The Department of Archaeology and Jagatapāla Mahāvihāra Conservation Committee signed an agreement in 2017 CE for the renovation of the damaged monuments including the Phalcā and concluded the renovations in 2019 CE.
Siddhirāja Śilvakāra (Śilpakāra), his wife Tuyunānī and their sons founded thisvihārain the Talāchẽ courtyard.
Tuyunānī Sikrīkāra, Siddhirāja Sikrīkāra, Khaḍgarāja Sikrīkāra and Rāju Sikrīkāra constructed thisdharmadhātu jinālaya caitya.

As of January 2023 CE, the once-standingphalcāhas given way to a two-story concrete building, marking a contemporary shift in the landscape. The transition commenced around 1988 CE (2045 VS), when thephalcāunderwent a conversion into the modern edifice that stands today. An archival photograph from Shokoohy's work (1994, p.186) offers a glimpse of the originalphalcāin its traditional configuration, boasting four bays, before succumbing to eventual demolition.
An inscription dating back to the year 2008 CE (2065 VS) stands testament to the renovation of the building.

राजा नृपेन्द्र मल्लको मृत्यु भएपछि उनको नाममा त्रैलोक्यमोहन नारायणको मूर्ति स्थापना गरी नेसं ८०१ (सन् १६८०) मा मन्दिर निर्माण गरिएको थियो । मन्दिरको स्थापना गर्ने बेला नृपेन्द्र मल्लका भाइ पार्थिवेन्द्र मल्ल राजा थिए ।

event_name: Installation of a statue of Garuḍa
event_description: मन्दिर अगाडिको गरुड मूर्ति विसं १७४६ (सन् १६९०) मा भएको थियो । त्यस बेलासम्म राजा पार्थिवेन्द्र मल्लको पनि मृत्यु भइसकेको हुँदा उनकी रानी ऋद्धिलक्ष्मीले बालक राजा भूपाेलेन्द्रलाई काखमा राखेर प्रधानमन्त्री लक्ष्मीनारायणको सल्लाहबमोजिम राज्य चलाइकी थिइन् ।
लामो समयसम्म जीर्णोद्धार नभएकोले कमजोर भइसकेको यस मन्दिरले विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्पमा पूर्ण रूपमा भत्किएको थियो ।
पुरातत्व विभार र हनुमानढोका संरक्षण समितिको समन्वयमा विसं २०७४ (सन् २०१७) देखि सुरु गरिएको पुनर्निर्माण कार्य विसं २०७७ (सन् २०२०) मा सम्पन्न भएको थियो ।

During the reconstruction in 2024 CE (VS 2081), an inscription from the Licchavi period was discovered (Source: Ward President, Śreṣṭha, male, age 41). As the stone is completely worn away, the specific date and purpose of the inscription remain unknown. Nevertheless, this record confirms the fact that Tusāla and its surrounding areas were already settled during the Licchavi era.

Budhanilkantha Municipality aimed for the reconstruction of the shrine on a grand scale. In accordance with this goal, construction was completed in 2024 CE (VS 2081), and the new temple was inaugurated by former President Bidya Devī Bhaṇḍarī. The previous structure, simply built of brick, has been entirely transformed into a stone temple ofśikharastyle. In the new temple, an attempt has been made to replicate the architectural design of the Siddhikālī temple (BKT0110) in Bhaktapur.
Following the completion of the temple in 2024 CE (VS 2082), a local couple, Jagat Bahādur Śreṣṭha and Sānumāyā Śreṣṭha, along with their family, installed a bell on the plinth at the temple facade.
Consecration of thecaityain the reign of King Jaya Mahīndra Siṃha Deva (Bhāskara Malla) by Dhani Joti.Locke(1985, 66) mistakenly recorded the date of the inscription as NS 930.

event_name: Reconstruction after the Great Earthquake of 1934 CE
event_description: Caṇḍeśvarī Dharmaśālā, formerly aphalcā, was reconstructed with beams and pillars of the old building reused during the reconstruction process.

The surviving threecaityas of Nyāgaḥmaṇi were renovated with donations collected from the devotees. A statue of Amoghasiddhi was also established south of thecaityas. The statue was jointly inaugurated by Ven. Bhaddiya Mahāsthavira, Sri Lankan Ambassador W. M. Senevirathna, and Puṇya Śākya (President of Jñānamālā Bhajana Khalaḥ, Svayambhū).
Dānapati, Devajyoti (text: Devajotī), Harṣajyoti (text: Harṣajotī) and their family members from Amṛtavarṇa Vihāra installed this statue in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.

Local residents reconstructed thekvāḥpāḥchẽin the early 1980s. A photo by Ganeshman Chitrakar, circa 1972/73 CE, shows the building in ruins. A photo by Hugh Downs, circa 1980-82, shows the reconstructedkvāḥpāḥchẽ.Many historic elements including the wall paintings weret lost in the reconstruction work.

event_name: Renovation of Hiti and pond next to it and prohibition of soap at Hiti
event_description: Lack of care and renovations for a long period had left both the Hiti and pond next to it shrouded in bushes. In 2021 CE, the Kirtipur Municipality reconstructed both monuments. At the same time, Icchā Maharjana, a local resident, sponsored the statue of Viṣṇu to fill up the empty niche in memory of his deceased mother. As there are fishes farmed in the water pond, the use of soap for doing laundry or bathing at the Hiti is now prohibited.

Viśvarāma Bhāro, Viśvanātha Bhāro, Viśveśvara Bhāro and Dhana Bhāro constructed the Caitya in the Bāhāḥ's courtyard during the reign of King Mahendra Malla. The donors offered land and established aguṭhīfor the Caitya's maintenance and regular worship.
Rudranārāyaṇa, Harṣavīra, Harṣarārā̃ and others repaired the Caitya.
Krisnarāja (Kṛṣṇarāja) constructed it in memory of his father Maṇirāja Śilpakāra.
Bhājuvīr, Mānavīr, Siddhimāna and other members of their families constructed the Phalcā.
In 2014, the old structure was demolished and this three-storey building was erected.

As the pond constructed for Sarveśvara Mahādeva had fallen into disrepair, during the reign of King Gīrvāṇayuddhavikrama Śāha, four brothers Amatya Hanumanta Siṁha Bhāro, Bhājudhana Siṁha, Sadāśiva Siṁha, and Lakṣmīnarasiṁha, residing in Dhaugala Ṭola, Lalitpur, jointly undertook its restoration. The responsibility of overseeing this work was entrusted to Daivajña Sadāśiva and other residents of Calakhu Ṭola. They also installed a goldenhitiand a golden statue of Umāmaheśvara. It is likely that they adorned thehiti’sspout and the Umāmaheśvara statue with sheets of gilded copper.

event_name: Initial construction of the present-day temple structure
event_description: Kvāṭhanāyaka (Kvāthanāyaka) Lakṣmīsiṃha Bhāro renovated the existing statue of Sarasvatī (see object number KIR0049-001 above) and constructed a stone temple to enshrine her. The renovation work suggests that there must have been a small shrine or temple on the site preceding the present-day stone temple.
The temple was renovated and a retaining wall was built by the Lāyekū Gāũ Pañcāyata (Lāyekū Village Council) with funding from the Kathmandu Jillā Pañcāyata (Kathmandu District Council).
Since this stone inscription, placed to the right of the main statue in the sanctum, is covered by a thick layer of ghee (clarified butter), it cannot be deciphered.

event_name: Construction of a Śikharakūṭa caitya and the renovation of shrines
event_description: A Śikharakūṭacaityawas constructed and the shrines of Gandhuridevatāand Bārāhi were renovated.

event_name: Installation of a statue of Gaṇeśa
event_description: The inscription records the installation of a Gaṇeśa statue in the Bahī. The inscription has been lost.
Silver ornaments were offered to Śākyamuni and Vajravārāhī.
The copper portion of the statue of the main deity was gilded.
Religious instruments were offered to theguṭhīto perform the daily rituals of Śākyamuni Buddha and Vajravārāhī.

The inscription informs about the installation ofteliyātiles in the Cikã Bahī courtyard. The inscription is inscribed on the stone surface of the upper part of aCaityain Taḥdhã Bahī (LAL1960).(VajrācāryaVS 2068: 37)

event_name: Renovation and beautification of the main deity
event_description: Renovation work on the main deity was completed and the copper part of the statue was gilded.
Thebahīcomplex was renovated. A photograph inLocke(1985, 211) shows that construction work was carried out in theBahīcourtyard.
The main shrine(gandhurīdeva-degaḥ) was renovated.
The Ministry of Local Development (Sthānīya Vikāsa Mantrālaya) provided funding for the renovatio of the Bahī.
A newly made statue of Mahākāla was installed.

event_name: Buddha Jayanti: Sponsoring of festivals and processions
event_description: On the occasion of Buddha Jayanti, Jagatmān Vaidya (also known as Dharmāditya Dharmācārya) sponsored a procession, acūḍākarmaceremony and a feast for thesaṅgha. In addition to this he donated Rs. 100 and a piece of land as an endowment. This seems to be the first attempt to revive the ancient observance of Buddha Jayanti which has somewhat lapsed amongst the Buddhists in Nepal (Locke1985, 212).
The plinth was paved with stone.
The inscription reads 'suvarṇakoṣa dayaku thvate' but the meaning is unclear.
Chatrārohaṇa(a parasol was offered to the main deity).Locke(1985: 212) mentions the offering of a golden finial in reference to the inscription of NS 758 (1638 CE).

The Bahī was renovated. After the performance of ayajña,acaitya-shaped pinnacle was installed on top of thepura(phucā). 9tolāof gold, 15dhārniof copper and wages of 30 [Rupees] was spent on this work.
Various ornaments were offered to Śākyamuni and Vajravārāhi.
The metaltoraṇaover the door of the shrine was donated.
Two lion statues were installed in front of the entrance.
A donation of 5mohars(Rs.2.50) was given by each of the families of thesaṅghato repair the Bahī.
The courtyard was paved withteliyābricks and two lion statues were placed at the entrance of thenani. Pariṣadeva, Jñānadeva and others donated funds for this.
Śaṅkharāja Śākya and his family constructed adharmadhātu maṇḍalain front of thevajradhātu caitya.
Śaṅkharāja Śākya established the Akṣobhya shrine. This structure faces west.
Bekhā, Hākudeva and others renovated thecaitya. A plinth was also added.
Due to significant erosion, the inscription's content is unclear, but it appears to belong to the later-medieval period.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust renovated thehitiin 2002 CE (VS 2059).

The large marble inscription placed next to the entrance to thehitidocuments an organization named Paśupati Sevā Samāja renovating the Vanagaṇeśa Mandira that stands in front of thehitiin 2009 CE (VS 2065).
Minā Mahārānī Kṛṣṇakumārī, one of the spouses of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, built thisśivālayaand she named it Kṛṣṇabhogeśvara in her honor.

The inscription dating back to 1613 CE (NS 733), located to the northeast of the temple, is unrelated to the temple itself. It precedes the temple's construction by a minimum of two centuries, likely originating from another structure but later placed at this site. Due to significant erosion, the complete understanding of its content remains elusive. The inscription makes reference to the establishment of an oil-related trust, indicating that a benefactor likely erected a statue or temple and instituted a trust for the purpose of illuminating oil lamps at the site.
An undated inscription on the pedestal of the Jayavāgīśvarī statue is believed to be from the Aṃśuvarman(r. 605-621 CE) period.
Vaidya Śirāna Bhāro and his wife Durggāmayī established a pair of lions flanking the steps leading to the sanctum.

Special rituals for auspiciousness were performed by sacrificing two he-goats after blood was seen on the Jayavāgīśvarī statue. The sacrifices were probably made at the Navadurgā shrine, as Jayavāgīśvarī does not accept animal sacrifices. A few days later, blood was seen on the statue again on the 2nd of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa. A fire oblation was performed to remove the defilement caused by the blood this time.

event_name: Wound on the chin of the deity
event_description: A cut was seen on the chin of the Jayavāgīśvarī statue. It is unclear if any ritual for auspiciousness was performed after the incident.

event_name: Covering door wings with gilded plates
event_description: Vaidya Nityānanda Bhāro and others installed a gilded cover on the door and door leaves of the sanctum.
Sivānanda Vaidya, Vidyānanda Vaidya, and Muktānanda Vaidya offered a bell to Jayavāgīśvarī.
A previously installed bell was renovated but the name of the donor is not mentioned in the inscription.
Vaidya Rudranārāyaṇa offered an ornamented arch of metal on top of the entrance to the sanctum in the name of his parents Rājavaidya Siṃghanārāyaṇa and Vaṃśalakṣmī.
Bhīmasiṃha and his wife Bhiṣvā Thakuṃ erected a stone pillar with a statue of a lion on top.
An oblong narrow banner (patāḥ) was offered to the temple. The name of the donor is not mentioned.
A previously installed narrow oblong banner (patāḥ) was renovated and reinstalled. The name of the donor is not mentioned.

The uppermost tier was dislocated and the walls were cracked in the 2015 earthquakes. The dislocated tier was later removed and the finial was stored inside thesataḥsouth of the temple. Cracks were visible all around the temple including the corners of the Bhairava painting on the northern wall.

The Pashupati Area Development Trust rebuilt the temple at a cost of NRs. 31.4 million. Some of the locals protested against the use of lime and brick-powder mortar during the reconstruction. Later, only clay mortar was used.
"Jayakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, and Dharmamuni together established the idol of Bhavānīśaṅkara and his wife Pundhrikā."

event_name: Repair of the bahī and offering a toraṇa
event_description: शाहको राज्यकालमा लक्ष्मि थकुंले छोराहरू पूर्ण्णपति, भीमपति लगायत परिवारका सदस्यहरूसँग मिलेर बही जीर्णोद्धार गरी गन्धकुटीभित्र प्रवेश गर्ने ढोकामाथि काष्ठतोरण चढाएकी थिइन् ।"During the reign of King Pṛthivīvirvikram Śāha, Lakṣmī Thakuṁle, along with her sons Pūrṇṇapati, Bhīmapati, and other family members, repaired the old ledger and placed a woodentoraṇaabove the entrance door to the Gandhakuṭī."
It is not mentioned in the inscription what work was done. Since this inscription is kept in thebahī dyaḥchēṁko peṭī,it may have the record of the plint's repair.
There is a Nāmasaṅgīti shrine to the west of the Maṇḍapa. Amararāja Tulādhara facilitated the construction of this shrine in 2013.
Dhvākhāpine Maṇḍapa was initially constructed to monitor security in the locality. Locals collected donations and worked together on its construction.
The Maṇḍapa was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.

event_name: Reconstruction of the Phalcā in the form of a Maṇḍapa
event_description: The LUMANTI Support Group for Shelter reconstructed the site with the help of UN Habitat and CIUD. The project cost NRs 2.500,000.

The inscription dating back to 1825 CE (NS 945) documents the restoration of a structure, likely aśivaliṅga, undertaken by Tejanarasiṃha, a resident of Phasikeba. This monument was originally erected by Tejanarasiṃha's forebears.

event_name: Installation of a pillar with inscribed hyms of Rāmabhajana
event_description: During the full moon day of Kārtika in 1955 CE (VS 2012), Gopāla Bahādura led an overnight religious chanting event (Harirāma Kīrtana) organized by Kaviprasāda Gautama at the Hanumāna statue site. Following the event's conclusion, directives were issued to erect a stone stele and conduct religious hymns annually on this auspicious day.हुनुमान् मूर्ति भएको स्थानमा कविप्रसाद गौतमको अभियान अन्तर्गत डिल्लीबजार निवासी गोपाल बहादुरको अगुवाइमा विसं २०१२ (सन् १९५५) सालको कार्तिक पूर्णिमाका दिन अहोरात्र हरिराम कीर्तनकार्य भएको थियो । यस कार्यको समापन पछि धर्मस्तम्भ स्थापना गरी प्रतिवर्ष यही दिन कीर्तन गर्नुपर्ने निर्देश पनि गरिएको थियो ।
The locals dismantled the old Phalcā withjhĩgaṭītile roof in the mid-1980s and rebuilt it into a two-storied concrete structure.
One more floor was added to the Phalcā with financial support from the Kirtipur Municipality Office.
It was reconstructed with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality. Also, the local community members volunteered for the reconstruction.
The bell was offered in the memory of a deceased person by his/her family member(s).
A monk called Īndrajyoti established this statue.
नरसिंह भारोले भीमसेनको लागि ढुङ्गाको गदा चढाएका थिए ।
धत्त आचार्य र मयन भारो दुईजनाले मिलेर भीमसेनलाई ढुङ्गाको तोरण चढाएका थिए । प्रत्येक वर्ष एउटा हाँस बलिको बलि सहित पूजा गरेर तोरणको वर्षवर्द्धनपूजा गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था पनि गरिएको थियो ।
भाजुकुतुले श्रीमती मति थकुं र छोरा साहेब सिंहसँग मिलेर भीमसेन देवस्थलमा तोरणसहितको ढुङ्गाको प्रवेशद्वार बनाएर चढाएका थिए ।
Jñānavajra Vajrācārya commissioned the renovation of the Temple and its gate.

event_name: Construction of a new entrance gate
event_description: The son of Jñānavajra Vajrācārya commissioned the construction of a new gate.

There is a large stone inscription set on the rear wall of the Pañcagaṇeśa Mandira, situated north of Vatsaleśvarī. This inscription, dating back to the Licchavi period, is now considerably eroded but is believed to be associated with the Vatsalā Mandira.

An extensive area of over 45ropanīs of land was endowed to set up a trust (guthi) responsible for conducting various rituals at the temple. The trust included Mānandhara (text: Manaṃdhra) Puna, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛdayasiṃha, Viṣṇusiṃha, and Harisiṃ as members. The income from the land was to be used for sacrificing a buffalo a day ahead ofPiśācaCaturdaśī, the 14th of the dark fortnight of Caitra, and lighting five sets of lamps at the Kvāthachẽ Āgaṃ. Additionally, the funds were utilized for the worship of Vatsalā on the new moon day of Caitra. Likewise, the trust was also responsible for sending the set of five nectars (pañcāmṛta) to Buṅgadyaḥ on the day of the deity’s ritual bathing (nhavaṃ), the 1st of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha. The original donation deed was damaged in a fire and was copied into a new donation deed.

event_name: Offering horn of wild water buffalo
event_description: King Raṇabahādura Śāha offered three horns of wildarnābuffaloes for fermented beer (thvã) to be poured from it on to the stoneyantrarevered as Goddess Vatsalā on the new moon day of Caitra. Gold sheets were wrapped around the horns back then.

event_name: Lālamohara by Raṇabahādura Śāha for Sindūra Guṭhī
event_description: King Raṇabahādura Śāha, through a royal decree with a red seal (lālamohara), granted authorization to a trust named the Sindūra Guthi, allowing it to operate in accordance with the established tradition. King Jayaprakāśa Malla had endowed 120ropanīs of land for the trust of Goddess Vatsalā. Thelālamoharainstructed the trust members to perform thepañcopacāraworship, which involved offering a buffalo sacrifice to Vatsalā onPiśācaCaturdaśī, the 14th of the dark fortnight of Caitra. Additionally, during the same occasion, the horns of the wildarnābuffaloes were to be blown. Furthermore, the royal decree made the trust responsible for organizing thesindūrajātrāof Vatsalā on the new moon day of Caitra. Sixdhārnīs (1dhārnī= 2.39 kgs) of vermillion powder (sindūra) were required for the procession. Devotees participated the procession by throwing thesindūrapowder in the air and at each other, creating a vibrant atmosphere.
Ṭhākuraprasāda Ṭaṇḍana Lāhurī Kṣetrī and his wife offered a bell and 54 pieces of lamps to Vatsalā.

भतकुनि टोल (भकुंटोल) बस्ने कजि विष्णुदेवी र काजीमान दंगुले वत्सला मन्दिरमा सुनको मोलम्बा लगाइएको पता: चढाएका थिए । काजीमान, तुलसीमान लगायतका व्यक्तिहरूले मिलेर अरु पनि केही वस्तु चढाएका थिए । अभिलेख स्पष्ट नभएकोले को भाव बुझ्न गार्‍हो छ ।
The Chaudhary Foundation in cooperation with the Pashupati Area Development Trust renovated the temple and furbished it with colors.

event_name: Replacing the roof with brass plates?
event_description: The content of the inscription embossed on the temple's eaves board poses some challenges. It involves the names of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā and his wife Siddhigajendralakṣmī, who happened to be the younger sister of his first wife. Following the passing of his first wife, Jaṅga Bahādura proposed marriage to Siddhigajendralakṣmī, but her father declined the proposal and instead married her to another man. After Jaṅga Bahādura took the office of the prime minister, he took Siddhigajendralakṣmī as his wife forcibly but paid her husband the compensation (P. Rāja VS 2073, p.57).

A family from the Dhaṃgu caste offered a narrow oblong banner (patāḥ) to the temple. The name of the donor and the year of the donation are not clearly visible. Only the name of the donor’s wife, Pāravati, can be read.

‘[Nepāla samvat]797’ (i.e., 1677 CE) is inscribed on a stone which is in the northern side of the Dabū. However, it cannot be ascertained whether this date refers to the construction of the Dabū or some other event.
According to the stone inscription embedded to the northern façade of the Dabū, the Sālkhā Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti renovated it in 2009 CE.
The temple collapsed in the earthquake of 1934. The debris of the temple scattered on the ground for many years.
The descendants of its founders and locals reconstructed the temple with the help of local governmental authorities in 1988.

The temple was constructed and aguṭhīwas also established for its management. The name of the founder could not be traced from the damaged inscription. According to locals, the temple was made by Bārāhīs.
Jñānajoti, his son Candrajoti and some more of his family members made thisdharmadhātu maṇḍala.It is situated to the east of theAśokaCaitya.
The monastic building was completely dismantled and rebuilt by Laitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, the District Development Committee and local people.
Rām Bhāro of Nāyalakhu constructed thisaśokacaityaand endowed land so that the daily and anniversary ritual worships could be performed.

event_name: Covering the niches of the Aśoka Caitya with copper plates
event_description: Herāmāyā, in the memory of deceased Mānakājī Śākyavaṃśa, covered the niches of the Aśoka Caitya with copper plates.

The presence of an inscription rendered unreadable by a thick layer of ghee is most likely associated with the construction of both the Sataḥ and the Rājarājeśvarī temple located in front of it. The reference to Ratnavīra as the builder of the Sataḥ in the 1983 CE (2039 VS) inventory, is probably derived from this inscription (Inventory VS 2039, p.162).बाक्लो घ्यूको लेपका कारण केही पढ्न नसकिएको यो अभिलेख यस सतः र अगाडिको राजराजेश्वर मन्दिर निर्माणसंग सम्बन्धित हुन सक्ने बढी सम्भावना छ । विसं २०३९ सालमा प्रकाशित काठमाडौं उपत्यका नगर विकास योजनाद्वारा प्रकाशित इन्भेनटोरीमा यो सतःका निर्माता रत्नवीर नामक व्यक्ति भनी टोकिएको छ जुन यसै अभिलेखलाई आधार मानी भनिएको अनुमान गर्न सकिन्छ (Inventory VS 2039, p.162) ।

Purandara Siṃha Deva, a Mahāpātra of Lalitpur, built this temple in memory of his father Viṣṇu Siṃha. The inscription states that Purandara Siṃha Deva declared his son Purushottama as the prince and was preparing to make him king.
Guṭhi Saṃsthāna repaired the temple

The temple was completely destroyed by the earthquake. However, the main deity is safe and is still in its original place. Many of the struts have been stored safely inside the Patan Museum. KVPT is rebuilding the temple.

This inscription is heavily eroded, making it undecipherable. Thus, its contents remain obscure. However, with the carvings of a jagged-edged knife (kartṛ) and a skull cup (kapālapātra), the implements of Bhairava, on its topmost part, the inscription appears to belong to the late-medieval period. The inscription was already in an unreadable shape in 1975 CE when D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha documented the inscriptions from Nuwakot (VS 2032, first part, p. 7).
Together with his wife, Ratnamānasiṃha (text: Ratnamānsī) of the Sahara Ṭola in Nuwakot donated the bell to thepīṭha.

Wooden pillars and rafters recovered from the ruins of the buildings that collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes were piled up at the Hiti. The Hiti’s spout was broken after coming under the load of the timbers. The broken spout is kept to the northern wall of the Hiti.
The Shankharapur Municipality has already allocated the budget for the renovation of the Hiti. However, the renovation process is yet to be started (as of March 2022).

The copper-plate inscription mentioned above records that a person named Devasiṃha renovated/repaired the Kāḥpāḥdyaḥ (Devāvatāra/Maitreya) statue consecrated in the sanctum (see 'description' above for more information).

event_name: Donation of land to a Vajrācārya
event_description: Sudra Dhrijanārāyana, Muninārāyana, and Bhavāni, three brothers, donated a plot of land to house Vajrācāryya Caṃdrapati. These brothers most likely donated the land so that some of the Vajrācāryas from Musuṃ Bāhāḥ could be permanently relocated to Lhugaḥ Bāhāḥ and serve as 'priests' there.

event_name: Construction of a caitya (object number KAT0840-004)
event_description: During the reign of King Surendra Vikrama Śāha, Nāpita Haridāśa built the caitya at the Bāhāḥ premises in memory of his father Narasiṃ, and younger brothers Devidāsa and Rāmadāsa.
Thejhĩgaṭītiled roof of the Bāhāḥ was replaced with corrugated metal sheets.

Aṃśuvarmā allotted financial assistance to Māneśvara, along with various temples and monasteries. He classified popular temples of his time into three categories and made arrangements for financial grants from the state. Paśupatinātha, Cā̃gunārāyaṇa, Guṃ Vihāra, Māna Vihāra, and Rāja Vihāra were placed in the first category, and an arrangement was made to grant 6purāṇas 2paṇas. In the second category, Rāmeśvara, Haṃsagṛhadeva, and Māneśvara were also included, and an arrangement was made to grant 3purāṇas 1paṇa.

A strut with a carving of Bhairava trampling on Vetāla was installed at thedyaḥchẽ. The name of the strut's donor is not inscribed, but it was possibly King Bhāṣkara Malla himself who established the Bhagavatī statue on the same date.

event_name: Exempting revenue of Manamāneśvari Guṭhī land
event_description: Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa Śāha exempted 104ropanīs of land dedicated to Manamāneśvarī frompotātaxes.
King Gīrvāṇayuddha granted land with an annual produce of 420murīs to set up a trust to ensure the smooth conduct of worship at Manamāneśvarī.

event_name: Excavation in front of the dyaḥchẽ
event_description: To investigate the antiquity of the Manamāneśvarī site, the Department of Archaeology, led by S.B. Deo, conducted excavations in the vacant area north of thedyaḥchẽin 1965 CE. The excavations yielded artifacts such as Paśupati coins, stone seals with the imprint of a cow and calf from the Aṃśuvarmā period, and earthenware from the pre-Lichhavi period. These findings confirm that the Manamāneśvarī site existed as early as the Lichhavi period.
The Kathmandu Metropolis carried out the renovation of the Manamāneśvarī Dyaḥchẽ.

A well was dug up southwest of thedyaḥchẽto provide drinking water for devotees visiting Manamāneśvarī for worship. This well was constructed in memory ofSaradāraKājilāla Pradhāna, a resident of Dhālāchẽ, Patan, by his descendants.
Renovation of the Umāmaheśvara Temple by the Ṭola Sevā Samiti
The temple was constructed by Vaṁsidhara Bhāro in the name of his elder brother Gauriśankara Bhāro.
Metal roof was fixed to the Nhāgaleśvara temple. Stone tiles were fixed on the floor of the shrine and small bell was hung up.

Kamalākānta Upādhyāye of Patan Svatha Ṭola made a request to the authorities (most probably to the Prime minister Candra Śamśera) to retain his priestly duties in this temple. Sahadatta Miśra from Patan's Mahāpāla Ṭola, and Kṛṣṇacandra Jhā from Cīkaṃmugala Ṭola also claim be the legitimate priest of the temple.
Temple was renovated

event_name: Initial construction of the Temple and land endowment
event_description: As stated in the 'description' above, Ḍiṭṭhā Dharma Siṃha and his younger brother Premanārāyaṇa Siṃha from the Jaisīdevala Ṭola constructed the Temple, along with rest houses (caugharā sataḥ) on all four sides (surrounding the Temple in the centre), a garden, and a pond. Over 121ropanīsof land were endowed for Temple's annual and periodic rituals, as well as other cultural activities.

Dharma Siṃha and Premanārāyaṇa Siṃha presented Rāma with a bell fifteen years before the Temple was built. This implies that a Rāma shrine existed before the Siṃha brothers built the current Temple for the deity.
Anitā Śreṣṭha and Agnikumārī Śreṣṭha established a new statue of Viṣṇu. The previous statue had been stolen, and only its jalaharī remained.
Devotees placed white marble on the Temple's plinth. The names of the donors are listed on the inscription, but the date is not.

The temple built by establishing Cakramukteśvara Mahādeva in memory of Lieutenant Cakra Śamśera, the third son of Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera and the first from his second wife Topakumārīdevī. The individual responsible for its construction is, however, unclear from the bell inscription.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust carried out renovations of the temple, as it was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
Vāsaḥ Hiti Phalcā was repaired through the initiative of Jayarāja Śreṣṭha.
The rebuilding of thephalcāwas managed by Lalitpur Metropolitan City with funding from the World Bank.
Tīrtha Rāja Śreṣṭha of Paṭko Ṭola initiated the construction of thisphalcā. It is said that he also granted a plot of land to the east of thephalcāto be used for revenue for thephalcā's maintenance.

In April 2021 construction of a new library buiding was started. The project is managed and financed by the INGO Read Nepal.While installing the heavy concrete foundations, it was discovered that the drawings did not specify the exact location and elevation of the building.Community members became aware that ground floor windows would be located below ground. Concerns were also raised regarding the building's disproportional size and lack of a sensitive design fitting the historic setting.The project was stopped and is currently under review. Communiy representatives requested the donor to develop a more traditional design.

The east side of the pillar is inscribed. The inscription contains 5 lines in Nāgarī script. According toPokharel(2011; p. 67) another side contains an inscription bearing the date ŚS 124.... This could not be verified in situ. If true, it would situate the pillar between 1318 and 1327 CE.

The west and north sides of the pillar are inscribed. The inscription to the west contains 6 lines in Nāgarī script. It mentions the date Śake 1256 (1334 CE). The inscription to the north contains 5 lines, no date but bears the name Thāpā and the mention of a son (putra).

The west and north sides of the pillar are inscribed. The inscription to the west contains 5 lines in Nāgarī script. It mentions the date Śake 1256 (1334 CE). The inscription to the north contains 5 lines and no date.D. R.Sharma(2012: p. 101) reads the inscription as follow:Oṁ swosti śri sāke 1256 ghi a putra Bāmu Khadgā ko bira khaṃtranslated as:Hail, saka 1256 (1334 A.D.) this is the memorial pillar of Bāmu Khadgā
The east side of the pillar is inscribed. The inscription contains 6 lines in Nāgarī script. It mentions the date Śake 1264 (1342 CE) as well as the patronym Thāpā.
The north side of the pillar contains 4-5 lines of an unreadable Nāgarī inscription.

event_name: Converting the traditional Phalcā into a modern concrete building
event_description: The local youngsters transformed the traditional Phalcā into a two-story concrete structure in the late 1980s.

Local youths, with permission from the local ward office, added one more floor to the Phalcā, making it a three-story structure. The funding for this came from local residents, and the youth helped with the construction.

The recent beatification of the Phalcā was carried out by the Kirtipur Municipality. The Municipality desired to give the Phalcā a traditional appearance by using animation sketches. However, the plan did not materialize, and only veneer bricks were used to cover the concrete wall.
Jayananda Vajrācārya and Vidyānanda Vajrācārya established a pair of lion statues in front of the Pīṭha.
Keśavalāla Ñācā Śreṣṭha and Hari Śreṇīlāla Ñācā Śreṣṭha laid the Pīṭha premises with marble stones in memory of their deceased father Viṣnulāla Ñācā.
Belabhakta Jośī, Śāntā Bhuvaneśvarī Jośī, and the family installed a roof of metal sheets along with a finial in memory of their deceased parents Lakṣmībhakta and Campādevī.

event_name: Stone paving and territorial wall construction at the Pīṭha premises
event_description: The community united in a collective effort to embellish the Pīṭha premises by laying stones for paving. Simultaneously, they undertook the task of erecting a protective boundary wall encircling the area.

event_name: Phalcā construction in honor of deceased parents
event_description: Lakṣmī Jośī from the Taumaḍhī Ṭola erected aphalcā, a rest house, in memory of her departed parents, Śivacaraṇa and Padmakumārī Jośī.
Rāmaprasāda Dyolā and his family constructed the Phalcā just south of the Pīṭha, as a tribute to his parentsf, Kānchā Dyolā and Sānu Dyolā.
Sānu Dyolā and the family from the Bhelukhela Ṭolabuilt the Rādhākṛṣṇa shrine just east of the Pīṭha.
Of the two stone inscriptions in the temple’s sanctum sanctorum, the inscription on the right (south) side of the Gaṇeśa idol records the paving of the stone pathway beside thephalcā.
Jogānārāyaṇa Dhānju established Gaṇeśa and Nṛtyanātha and constructed the temple.
Haribhakta Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha carried out the renovation of this temple.
The temple was renovated by the Takhāchẽ Khalaka with the support of Vadrinātha Śreṣṭha, and the builder was Harka Bahādura Silaupakāra (Śilpakāra) of Bhaktapur.
Haridevī, Durgādevī, and their family of Takhāchẽ Tola offered the bells to Siddhi Gaṇeśa.
The text of the inscription is as follows:1.oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ’2.maṃgalaṃ bhavatu śrī pṛthvīmalladevaḥ | likhitamidaṃ puṇyaṃ jagatisiṃdasyā
The date when the nameplate was installed is not mentioned in the inscription.
The Lalitpur Metropolitan City rebuilt thephalcāin 2017 CE with the financial support from the World Bank.

event_name: Installation of the Statue of Bhavānīśaṅkāra and Endowment of Land
event_description: Bhavānīśaṅkara Bābu of Dvaka installed this statue inside the Buĩcā Hiti Phalcā. He also endowed some plots of land for painting lime and further repair of thephalcā.
Thephalcāhad completely collapsed. A resident by the name of Bhavānīśaṅkara Bābu of Dvaka initiated its reconstruction.

monument_name: Yanāmugaḥ Phalcā (first third of 17th cent. CE)
event_description: The Phalcā was renovated by Pūrṇeśvarī Mayī in the memory of her late husband Maheśvara.

monument_name: Yanāmugaḥ Phalcā (first third of 17th cent. CE)
event_description: The Phalcā was rebuilt with the financial support of the local ward office and donations by local residents.

The presentyaḥsipole was brought from Nālā in 1979 on March 27th. One member from each family of Sunāguthi went to collect theyaḥsi. The event took place because the formeryaḥsibroke. It was said to be have been installed in the year 1946 CE. The pole was carried for three days in 1979, from Sunday March 25th to Tuesday March 27th.Informant: Mr. Ram Sundar Maharjan (participant of the event Yaḥsi kā vanegu in 1979)

According to the inscription on the bell installed on the plinth on the northern side of the temple, it was offered to the Goddess in 1946 CE (VS 2003). However, as half of the inscription is illegible, the name of the donor cannot be identified.

Herākāji and Herāmāṅkāji, sons of Herā Bahādura Tāmrakāra, who himself was the son of the late Gvārā Tāmrakāra and Nhucchē Kumārī, offered anilāṃplated with gilded gold, which also bears an idol of Caṇḍeśvarī, in the name of the Goddess.

In the names of Gaurīnārāyaṇa, Raghunārāyaṇa, and Tulsīnārāyaṇa, the sons of Raghunātha from his eldest wife Hirāmāyā, Raghunātha’s youngest wife Māyā and his other wife Herāmāyā Tāmrakāra jointly paved the temple with tiles.
Kula Kṛṣṇa Māka contributed NPR 1,002, and together with all the residents of theṭola, offered a bell to the Goddess.
All threejhiṅgaṭī-tiled roofs of the temple were renovated and replaced with copper roofing, completing the temple’s reconstruction.

As the temple had become extremely dilapidated, it was reconstructed under the chairmanship of Kedāraprasāda Tvānābāsu, with the support of Khvapa Municipality and the Department of Archaeology, during which thejhiṅgaṭīroofs were once again replaced with copper sheets.

Kāśī Bahādura Tvānābāsu offered the peacock on the northern side of the temple premises to the Goddess, in memory of hisguruof theŚrīCaṇḍeśvarī Dāphā Bhajana, as well as his elder brother Ratna Bahādura Tvānābāsu and his sister-in-law Mohana Lakṣmī Tvānābāsu.
Tulsī Nārāyaṇa Ḍhukuchu, Ranta Keśarī Ḍhukuchu, and the entire Ḍhukuchu family offered a peacock to Caṇḍeśvarī on the southern side of the temple premises.

event_name: Establishment of the statue of Durgā (PPK1001-001)
event_description: The stone toraṇa that adorns the Durgā statue contains an inscription from 1682 CE (NS 802) suggesting that it was established in that year. The art of the statues of Durgā and Bālakumārī, the main deity, are similar. Therefore, the statue of Bālakumārī may also have been established around that time in the 17th century.
The Phalcāwas dismantled and replaced by a concrete structure with a slab roof. People from the Śākyaguṭhīof Haḥkhā were involved in the event.

Harṣaratna Vajrācārya established thebāhāḥin 1876 CE (VS 1933) together with his son, Tejaratna Vajrācārya, and with contributions from his wife, Harṣalakṣmī, and other family members. It was constructed on two adjacent plots of land. One plot had been used by Harṣaratna's ancestor, Samaju Āḥju.
