The other, granted to Bhājuvīra Prajāpatī of Jyāthā Ṭola, Khyāḥ Bāhāḥ in Kathmandu bylālamohara(royal decree), was purchased by Harṣaratna. Combining these two plots, Harṣaratna built thebāhāḥ. Following its construction, he installed thetriratna(Akṣobhya, Prajñāpāramitā, and Lokeśvara), acaitya, and images of Meṣasamvara, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmañjuśrī, and Bhīmasena. Harṣaratna and Harṣalakṣmī also celebrated theirbhīmarathārohaṇa(jaṃko), an old-age ritual, at this time. Land was endowed to thebāhāḥas a religious trust to support its annual rituals.

Jyotiratna Vajrācārya reinstated daily worship and other religious practices after thebāhāḥ,built by his grandfather Harṣaratna and father Tejaratna Vajrācārya, as the rituals at the monastery were not regularly performed. He also installed a commemorative stone inscription. Because of his systematic organization and management, thebāhāḥbecame known as Jyotiyā Bāhāḥ (Jyoti'sbāhāḥ), after him.
The three-storied temple collapsed in the 1934 CE earthquakes and is now reduced to a one-storied structure.

The reconstruction of the temple is underway after the 2015 CE earthquakes further damaged the temple which was already in poor condition. A private trust operated by the descendants of Upendra Vikrama is carrying out the reconstruction of the temple together with the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna.

By December 2022 CE, a significant portion of the rest houses, approximately 80%, had been disassembled due to the effects of the earthquakes. The Department of Archaeology has undertaken plans for the eventual restoration of these structures.

The Jaḥdhuṃ near the Sataḥ was constructed by Mahāpātra Purandarasiṃhadeva, a powerful local functionary of Patan during the late Malla period. He also formed a community-based trust with the responsibility of filling water in the Jaḥdhuṃ. The members of the trust were required to keep the Jaḥdhuṃ full as long as the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ remained in the temple at Taḥ Bāhāḥ. Every year on the 1stsolar day of Māgha, the Jaḥdhuṃ was worshipped and whitewashed. The trust distributed puffed rice (syāḥbaji), fermented rice beer (thvã), meat, etc. to the locals on the occasion.
The Jaḥdhuṃ was renovated.

The Sataḥ collapsed due to the lack of timely renovations and remained in ruins for a long time. With funds from the Indian Embassy, its reconstruction began but the Lalitpur Metropolitan City also contributed financially, as the fund from the embassy was not sufficient for the reconstruction. Donations were also collected from the locals to meet the total expense of NRs. 5.6 million for the reconstruction.
Jayant Prasad, Indian ambassador to Nepal, inaugurated the reconstructed Sataḥ.
The Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya was constructed by Jagata Bahādura and the family.
As the Phalcā was in a dilapidated condition, it was dismantled and rebuilt using concrete. The Phalcā’s traditional architecture was lost in the reconstruction.

The Phalcā was rebuilt again in traditional architecture with some modifications to its original form. A floor was added on top for the elderly people to rest while a room below the ground level was also constructed.

An inscription on the plinth of thejalaharyoparijinālaṅkṛtacaityareveals that it was established in memory of the deceased Lāmā Maharjana of Kilāgaḥ Ṭola by his family members in 1911 CE (NS 1031).धर्मधातुजिनालय चैत्यको आधारशिलामा रहेको अभिलेख अनुसार उक्त चैत्य नेसं १०३१ (सन् १९११) मा किलागः टोल निवासी दिवंगत लामा महर्जनको सम्झनामा उनका परिवारका सदस्यहरूले स्थापना गरेको थियो ।

After the temple was on the verge of collapse, the Ward no. 26 office of the then Kathmandu Municipality rebuilt it.जीर्ण भई भत्कने अवस्थामा पुगेपछि विसं २०५३ (सन् १९९७) मा काठमाड‍ौं नगरपालिकाको वडा नं २६ को पहलमा यसको पुनर्निर्माण कार्य सम्पन्न गरिएको थियो ।
An inscription from the temple that is no longer present at the site confirms that Māthavarasiṃha Thāpā established Goddess Bhagavatī here in 1837 CE (VS 1894).

After the establishment of Goddess Bhagavatī, Māthavarasiṃha Thāpā constructed a temple for the deity in 1844 CE (VS 1901). He also installed a golden finial on the temple after the completion of its construction and endowed 75ropanīs of land to form aguṭhīfor carrying out various rituals at the temple.

As mentioned above in 'description', the inscription from 1849 CE (VS 1906) at the site records that a person named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha of Kulāṃbhulu made some offering to the Temple which was built by General Mathavarasiṃha Thāpā.

Sankhu Primary School was established in 1964 CE (VS 2021) in this Sataḥ. The school has run for more than 40 years. Because of insufficient space for growing classes, the school has meanwhile been shifted to Mahādevasthāna.

event_name: Installation of the statue of Kṛṣṇa and Gītāmātā
event_description: The family of Cakramān Siṃha of Sankhu has installed the statue of Kṛṣṇa and Gītāmātā in the Sataḥ in 2007 CE.
The Sataḥ was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
The collapsed building was rebuilt in 2020 CE. The Department of Archaeology has funded the budget for rebuilding. It has taken 4 years to complete.

Jāiphala Adhikārī, a government officer (subbā), commissioned the temple's construction in 1815 CE (VS 1871). In the accompanying inscription, he traces his genealogy back to his ancestor Bhāradvāja. The inscription also documents the construction of the Gaurīghāṭa bridge, the establishment of a path near the cremation site, the construction of a rest house, and other infrastructure projects, along with the provision of food for a thousand brahmins. Additionally, he endowed 48ropanīs of land to establish a trust responsible for temple rituals and maintenance.
The Department of Archaeology reconstructed the shrine (object no. NWK0640-006) in front of thepīṭha.

This inscription from 1721 CE (NS 841) documents the establishment of thedāphābhajana, a group of devotional singers led by Mānadeva of the Suraṃki dynasty. It also records the construction of the rectangular stone structure at thepīṭha. The contributors proudly trace their lineage to the Suraṃki dynasty.
This inscription from 1724 CE (NS 844) mentions Jayakṛṣṇa Bhāro as the leader of the initiative to erect a wall around the premises of the Mahālakṣmī shrine.
The temple was rebuilt from ground up by the Department of Archaeology.

A statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara is established on the wall of the house situated on the western side of thisbāhāḥ. An inscription containing details of the statue's installation is carved on its pedestal. Although the remaining text is unreadable due to the letters having worn away, the installation date "Samvat 901" is clearly visible.

event_name: Renovation of Mañjuśrī Vihāra (Viśvakarmā Bāhāḥ KAT2190)
event_description: This inscription is affixed to the wall of the house situated on the western side of thisbāhāḥ. According to the details mentioned within, it does not pertain to thisbāhāḥbut rather concerns the renovation of the nearby Viśvakarmā Bāhāḥ, located to its west. Motikāji, the son of Caitavarasiṃ of Kathmandu, carried out the renovation of Viśvakarmā Bāhāḥ.

From the inscription located at the base of the main door, it is known that Caityavara Siṃha, the son of Harṣamāna and grandson of Rudramāna Śākya, along with his family, offered the woodentoraṇa. Locke (1985, p. 358) has mentioned the date of this inscription as NS 1024, whereas it is actually inscribed as 1905 CE (NS 1026)

An inscription is carved on acaitya(KAT2170-002) located in the courtyard of thebāhāḥ; however, because the letters have worn away and become illegible, the specific details contained within are unknown. Since inscriptions of this type primarily document the establishment of thecaitya, it can be assumed that this inscription also contains details regarding thecaitya's installation.

event_name: Restoration of Mūla Coka and establishment of the Yantāju shrine
event_description: King Śrīnivāsa Malla restored the courtyard and established the Yantāju shrine at its centre.
A bell was offered to Taleju by Yoganarasiṁha Malla.

event_name: Treaty between Patan, Kantipur and Bhaktapur
event_description: An agreement was reached between the kings of Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and Kantipur that Mahādeva Ojha and his descendents should not be allowed to enter the Valley. This agreement took the form of a treaty. The document further mentions that whoever permits them to enter in the Valley, talks to Mahādeva Ojha or gives him fire, water, money or clothes will be cursed by Taleju Māju and other gods of the Valley.
Mūla Coka was restored

Thislālamoharaof King Gīrvāṇa appropriates 336murīof land for the rituals of Śrī Talejyu of Lalitapatan (Patan). People involved in the donation process were: Saṃkalpavākyavaktā purohita Śrī Daivajña Kesarī Paṃḍita, the 5 ministers of King Gīrvāṇa, namely, Pāḍe Śrī Raṇajit, Pāḍe Śrī Dāmodara, Śrī Tribhuvana, Śri Narasiṃha and Śrī Kīrtimānasiṃha; and Mahākośādhyakṣya: Pāḍe Śrī Bhoṭu and Kośādhyakṣya: Śrī Śyāmalāla Upādhyāya.
King Rājendra Śāha issued alālamoharatransferring the power of theguṭhīholder of Talejuguṭhīfrom Padmanābha Bhattarāī to Mitra Śarmā.
Mūla Coka was restored and received a new enlarged main gate and a window above it.
The palace building was restored from the ground up by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust. The project was funded by the American Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.
The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) restored the Yentāju shrine in cooperation with the Department of Archaeology.The project was generously funded by Yogeśvara Amātya.
Dhanamayju from Shankhamul organised apīṭhapūjāin which he wished for the salvation of all creatures.
Kājilāla Maharjana, Kailāsa Maharjana and Kṛsa Ḍaṅgola erected the statue of Manakāmanā.

During the reign of King Yoganrendra Malla, a donor from Kobāhāḥ, Gāḥ Hiti Ṭola built a temple for Cāmuṇḍā and offered a golden lion throne to the deity. The name of the donor cannot be deciphered from the broken inscription. However, in NS 821 and NS 823, Bhavānī Śaṅkara Bhāro renovated the temple and bestowed land for the management of aguṭhī. It is likely that he also commissioned the initial construction of this temple.

Milamha from Dhumbāhāḥ, Lalitpur commissioned thekuṇḍaat the south-west corner of the temple. The inscription also mentions that his predecessors funded the construction of a pond in the Sika Bahī premises. The pond was later filled in and the temple was constructed on top of it. Milamha made this smallkuṇḍato record the work of his ancestors.
Lachimi Nakrami (Lakṣmī Nakarmī) offered two brass flags to the deity.

Herāmāyā Maharjana, a resident of Bijulibazar, Kathmandu, donated threemandaḥpāḥsmade of brass plates in memory of Gyānalāla Maharjana. These have been placed on the plinth of the Śveta Gaṇeśa shrine (LAL0153-009).

event_name: Donation of brass torana to Sveta Gaṇeśa
event_description: Raju Deula and other members of his family donated a brasstoraṇain memory of Mīnā Deulā. This has been fixed above the statue of Śveta Gaṇeśa (LAL0153-009).

Kisalāla Maharjana and his family commissioned four artistic brick entrance gates, one for each of the cardinal directions. They donated these gates in memory of their parents. The Minister of Culture Gopāla Kirātī inaugurated the doors.
Chiribābu Maharjana, Tirthalāla and others donated brasspatāḥin the temple.

Bhavānī Śaṅkara Bhāro commissioned the renovation of the temple. This began after the performance of a fire ritual in front of the Patan Palace, at which King Yoganrendra Malla was the guest of honour.
Bhavānī Śaṅkara Bhāro bestowed land for the management of aguṭhīrelated to the temple.
Mādhavalāla Pātravaṃśa Rāvata set up four lions, one for each of the four directions of the temple.

As previously mentioned, the inscription dated 1583 CE (NS 703) found on the pedestal of the Garuḍa statue (refer to the 'description' section above) documents a land donation by Uddhava Bābu from Maṃgalā̃chẽ, Bhaktapur. This act took place during the joint reign of King Śivasiṃha and Raṇajitasiṃha. While the inscription signifies the dedication of the land, it remains unclear whether the construction of the temple corresponded with the establishment of the Garuḍa statue positioned in front of it.
The Śreṣṭha family, residing in close proximity to the temple, contributed a coppertoraṇaabove the entrance door.

event_name: Establishment of Vijyādhari and Gatirāja statues
event_description: Statues of Vijyādhari (Vidyādhari) and Gatirāja, devotees of Viṣṇu, were installed. The male and female figures above the spout are probably the statues that were installed on this occasion.

event_name: Installation of pillar BTD0020-003 in ca. late 14th century
event_description: The southern side of the pillar contains adevanāgarīinscription of seven lines. It remains difficult to read the inscription. Owing to the stylistical ressemblance between this pillar and the others from the site that are dated of ŚS 1309 (1387 CE), it may be suggested that this pillar was installed around the same time period, i.e., the late 14th century,The inscription is less well executed than on the other pillars.

event_name: Installation of pillar BTD0020-004 in 1387 CE
event_description: Pillar BTD0020-004 contains an inscription of three lines indevanāgarīscript. According to D. R. Sharma the reading of the inscription is as follows:Śri sāke 1309 bāghi kot vadā likhitam...gutahatranslated as: "In saka [śaka] 1309 this... is written by Vadā from Bāghikot" (Sharma 2012: 350).

event_name: Installation of pillar BTD0020-005 in 1387 CE
event_description: Pillar BTD0020-005 contains an inscription of three lines indevanāgarīscript. According to D. R. Sharma, one may only read the date ofśaka1309 (1387 CE). This reading makes the pillar contemporaneous to BTD0020-004 (Sharma 2012: 351).

Rāmajī Sāpakoṭā, the grandson of Janārdana, details that his grandfather Janārdana belonged to the same generation as Pṛthvīvilāsa, that is, to the late Rāṇā-period generation (oral testimony at age of 76, in 2025).जनार्दनकै नाति रामजि सापकोटा आफ्ना बाजेबारे जानकारी राख्छन् र यी तथ्य सुनाउछन् । जनार्दन पृथ्वीविलासकै समकालीन अर्थात् राणाकालको उत्तरार्धतिरका पुस्ता थिए (one of the descendants of the initial constructor, male, age 76) ।
The Phalcā was renovated: It was plastered with cement and its roof was replaced with corrugated metal sheets.

Although the Phalcā was not in a very bad condition, it was dismantled and rebuilt in a style seen as 'more traditional'. The reconstruction work began in September 2019. Lalitpur Metropolitan, Ward no. 16 provided Rs. 1.4 million rupees for its reconstruction. The inauguration of the Phalcā was held on the 10thday of the dark fortnight of Phālguna. This was also the day that the spirits of the serpents were returned to their vessels during Itilhane Samyak.
A group of people including Viṣṇurāma Bhāro, Bhāgīrāma Bhāro and Viśvarāma Bhāro offered the pair of lions to this Temple.

During the reign of King Siddhinarsimha Malla, Hari Bhāro undertook the renovation of thecapāḥ.This marks the earliest reference to the Bhīmasena Mandira, originally built as acapāḥ, before being transformed into a temple in 1681.
A bell was donated to Bhīmasena Bhaṭṭāraka by Sunādevaju.
The ground floor was paved withteliyābricks by Vajrācārya Cintāmaṇi and Laghunātha Bhāro. In this inscription, Bhīmasena is referred to asMahābhīma Māṇeśvara.

The stone stele inscription confirms that in 1681 CE (NS 801), King Śrīnivāsa Malla reconstructed the single floorcapāḥinto its present temple form by adding two additional stories. (Regmi1960, 287).The inscription refers to Śrīnivāsa Malla as Nepaleswara and mentions that the temple was built following the recommendations of Bhagīratha Bhaiyā. An offering of two pinnacles was made.
Viseśvara Bhāro donated a strut.
The inscription notes that Yoganarendra Malla assumed the title of Saṅgītārṇṇva Pāragata.Dogs start howling when the bell is rung (Jośī2065, 25).
The ancient clay statue of Bhīmasena was substituted with a new bronze statue, followed by a ceremonial installation ritual.
The inaugural Bhīmasenajātrāwas orchestrated in Lalitpur by Yoganarendra Malla. Buffaloes, goats, and ducks were offered as sacrifices during the event.

In NS 827, a group ofguṭhīmembers contributed to the donation of the stone pillar.The inscription on the brass collar also indicates that originally, in NS 777 during the rule of King Indra Malla, a wooden pillar was donated by Bhīmasena, Sunādevaju, Hākuju, Maṅgaladevaju, and others.The stone pillar replaced the wooden pillar.The inscription etched into the stone lists the names of the donors.
Bhīma Bhāro of Nakapasala donated the two stone lions flanking the main entrance.
Offering of the giltpatāḥby Tīrtharāja Śreṣṭha, residing in Patan, to please Bhīmasena.
The earthquake on April 26, 2015, resulted in the collapse of the stone pillar. The upper half of the shaft fractured into two pieces upon impact with the brick pavement.
Following the damage suffered from the 2015 earthquake, the temple was braced on all four sides.

event_name: Restoration of the stone stambha and lion statue
event_description: The stone pillar, which supported a gilt metal lion, crumbled in the 2015 CE earthquakes, and the upper stone shaft fractured into two pieces. In the period spanning 2015-2016, a team from the University of Applied Arts, Vienna, meticulously carried out the restoration of the pillar and the lion statue.
Offering of the patāḥ by Lakṣmīmāyā and her family members in memory of Nāyacā Maharjana, a resident of Lilitpur, Baliphal, to please Bhīmasena.

The restoration of the temple was executed by the Lalitpur Chamber of Commerce and the Mangal Tole Sudhar Sangh with technical support from KVPT.The inscription lists various donors to the restoration project.

monument_name: Vajradhātu Caitya (known as Khāsti Caitya, built in  17th cent.)
event_description: A Bhāro family formed theguṭhīto sponsor the annual rituals including a fire sacrifice in the Caitya on the Kojāgrata Pūrṇimā day.

monument_name: Vajradhātu Caitya (known as Khāsti Caitya, built in  17th cent.)
event_description: Viśvanātha Bhāro and others made themuṣanaand offered it to the Caitya.

monument_name: Vajradhātu Caitya (known as Khāsti Caitya, built in  17th cent.)
event_description: A Bhāro family offered the stone oil lamp to the Caitya which is erected in front of the Akṣobya Buddha statue.
The monument was renovated by the Department of Archeology.

An inscription on the inner wall of the phalcā reveals that Rakṣakumārīdevī Rāṇā, wife of Bālanarasiṃha Kũvara Varmā Rāṇā, granted 50 ropanīs of land for a three-day donation event to visitors on the day of Śivarātrī in Mṛgasthalī in 1854 CE (VS 1911). Additionally, 46 ropanīs of land were dedicated for the rituals and donations to Rakṣeśvara and Raṇabāleśvaradevī, along with an extra 22 ropanīs of guthī land for Gorakhnātha’s anniversary ritual and the donation to visitors.फल्चाको भित्री भित्ताको केन्द्रभागमा आकारमा ठुलो शिलापत्र गाभिएको छ । उक्त शिलापत्रमा विसं १९११ (सन् १८५४) मा बालनरसिंह कुँवर वर्मा राणाकी पत्नी रक्षाकुमारीदेवी राणाले मृगस्थलीमा शिवरात्रीदेखि तीनदिनसम्म निरन्नतर आगन्तुकहरूलाई दान गर्न ५० रोपनी खेत चढाएको कुरा उल्लेख छ । यसका साथै रक्षेश्वर र रणबालेश्वरदेवीको पूजा एवं दानका खातिर ४६ रोपनी र गोरखनाथको वर्षवर्धन एवं आगन्तुकलाई दानको खातिर थप २२ रोपनी खेत गुठी राखेको कुरा उल्लेख छ ।

Six members of Hāthu Guthi including Jīvanarāma Mānandhara (text: Mānāndhala Jevaṇarāma), Bābudeva Mānandhara (text: Mānāndhala Bābudeva), and Viṣṇusiṃha Mānandhara (text: Mānāndhala Viṣṇusiṃha) renovated the Phalcā in the name of their deceased younger brother Dhana.
The Phalcā was reconstructed into a concrete structure after its condition deteriorated.

event_name: Reconstruction and addition of another floor
event_description: The previous concrete structure was dismantled and rebuilt into a two-storied concrete Phalcā.
Theaśoka caityawas established at the courtyard.

Someone called Viṣṇurāma and his brother Rāghavasiṃha established an image of Śākyamuni Buddha and offered a golden pinnacle for theāgamadeity. This took place during the reign of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla and his sons Śrīnivāsa Malla and Jyotinarasiṃha Malla.

event_name: Consecration of the statue of Lokeśvara with Vasundharā
event_description: Someone called Viṣṇurāma and his wife Damana consecrated the image of Lokeśvara with Vasundharā.

event_name: Donation of a golden door to Vidyāpīṭha
event_description: Two people named Ratneśvara and Jīvanarasiṃha donated a golden door to Vidyāpīṭha (āgamadeity).

event_name: Establishment of the statue of Sūryanārāyaṇa with Lakṣmī
event_description: Individuals called Sujarāmaju and Manadhariju established a statue of Sūryanārāyaṇa with Lakṣmī.
An individual named Ratneśvara and his younger brother Jīvanarasiṃha renovated thebāhāḥ. Twenty-one people and their names have been carved upon the lower part of the inscription.
An individual called Gajarāja Rājakarṇikāra (born into the Kāśyapa clan) and his family gilded the copper roof of thephucā.

Rājakarṇikāra Nara, his son Jotirāja, his grandson Badrinātha and some of his other family members made a donation so that a stone-made and gold-clad aura (prabhamaṇḍala) could be fixed on the Akṣobhya image in the sanctum.

event_name: Donation of a seat for the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ
event_description: Rājakarṇikāra Nara, his son Jotirāja and grandson Badrinātha donated a seat for thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ(Akṣobhya).

event_name: Donation of a pair of metal flag
event_description: A person named Kulavi[ra] and his wife Rājamati donated a pair of metal flags. These have been erected on either side of the sanctum.
Thebāhāḥwas renovated after the 1934 earthquake.

event_name: Construction of the Relaxing Buddha Shrine
event_description: A person named Kṛṣṇa Bahādur Rājakarṇikāra constructed the Relaxing Buddha Shrine.
Individuals called Kṛṣṇa Giri, Rāma Kṛṣṇa Lāla, Kṛṣṇamāyā, Rāmakṛṣṇa, Madanakṛṣṇa and Premalāla repaired the steps leading to the sanctum.

event_name: Face reparation of the Akṣobhya image and donation of a crown
event_description: An individual called Harṣa Bhādur Rājakarṇikāra and his wife Pūrṇamāyā Rājakarṇikāra repaired the face of the Akṣobhya image and donated a crown to it.
Someone named Indralakṣmī and her family donated a vajra. This has been fixed above thedharmadhātu maṇḍala.
The esoteric shrine of thebāhāḥwas slightly damaged by the 2015 earthquake. It was later retrofitted .

The inscription states that Śivarāma Māhāna Bhāva, a resident of Mikhabāhāḥ (LAL0810), constructed the phalcā in 1712 CE (NS 832) in memory of his parents. It also mentions a Triratna statue that was installed at the same time.

event_name: Demolition of the phalcā and construction of a commercial building
event_description: The phalcā was dismantled in 2013 and replaced with a four-storey brick and concrete structure named Bahichẽ.
Gaṇeśabahādura Pāṇḍe and his wife Jayā Pāṇḍe installed a balustrade of 108 lamps around the temple.
The temple was reconstructed at the leadership of the then-ward chairman Sukharāma Maharjana.
Mādhavaprasāda Aryāla and his wife Urmilā Aryāla installed a bell in front of the temple.

event_name: Construction of separate shrine for various deities
event_description: Jānu Gautama built a separate shrine north of the temple and installed the statues of various deities, including Gaṇeśa (KAT3081-003) and Hanumān (KAT3081-007). These statues were recovered from different parts of Hā̃ḍīgāũ and were initially placed in the sanctum of the Sarasvatī temple.
Nandakumārī Rāṇā, wife of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, commissioned the temple, expressing her devotion to Lord Śiva.
This inscription on the bell hanging from a bell stand to the temple’s south likely records the temple's construction. However, the inscription is no longer legible, so its exact content is unknown.
The temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes but was rebuilt by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

The Sīdhvākhā was one of the two other gates that had retained its original structure Unfortunately, this medieval gate lost its original shape and structure during its reconstruction in VS 2055 (1998 CE) (Ś. ŚreṣṭhaVS 2057, p. 35). The ancient gate was converted into a modern structure arguing that the old gate was not wide enough to allow vehicles like taxis, ambulances, fire brigade, etc. to pass into the city at times of emergency (local knowledge, local resident, Maharjana, male, age 69).
Ānanda Rama Jośī's wife offered a brass canopy (ilā̃) to Gaṇeśa in memory of her husband.

The inscription mentions that Vīra Sāhi Kumhara placed a pinnacle on top of the temple and bestowed it with land to fund the anniversary ritual worship.Pruscha(1975 C/P-279) relies upon this inscription and dates the temple to 1681 CE. However, it is not certain whether Vīra Sāhi actually constructed the temple on this date or merely offered a pinnacle.
Viṣṇulakṣmī Jośī donated a brasspatāḥ(banner) in memory of the late Ānanda Rāma Jośī.
The two brass flags in front of the entrance were donated by the members of Buinā Gaṇeśa Bhajana Guṭhī.

Pruscha(1975, C/P-279) does not provide any source but suggests that the temple was renovated in 1970. There is a heavily damaged inscription attached to the southern wall of the temple; it is possible that was is his evidence.
This temple was renovated in 2003 by Taṅgala Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti.
Vikrama Rāja and his family donated the brasstoraṇawhich is installed above the entrance.
Ānanda Rama Jośī's wife offered a brass parasol to Gaṇeśa in memory of her husband.
Sānukānchā Malla from Taṅgaḥ Ṭola offered a brasstoraṇato Gaṇeśa.

On the western face of the southern pillar (DLK0020-002) is a very eroded inscription composed of four or five lines, in Devanāgarī script.According to D. R.Sharmathe inscription reads: 'tra de wa naṃ śuvamastu'.

On the eastern face of the northern pillar (DLK0020-001) is a very eroded inscription composed of six lines, in Devanāgarī script.According to D. R.Sharmathe inscription reads: 'Oṁ swosti sāke 1331 bhādra badi... kirti'

event_name: Offering of an item to Bhairava
event_description: Nārāyaṇasiṃha Bhāro, Satyarāma Bhāro, Tulasīrāma Bhāro, and other residents of Lubhu made an offering to Luṇḍakoṃḍa Bhairava. The inscription's current state of deterioration precludes the identification of the offered item.

event_name: Installation of lion statues at entrance
event_description: The lion statues flanking the main entrance of the temple were established.
Gagāralakṣimila, Mayathakū, and others offered a brasstoraṇafor Mahālakṣmī and Mahābhairava.

event_name: Marble paving on the sanctum floor
event_description: Śaṅkaralāla Śreṣṭha and his family laid marble slabs in the temple sanctum in memory of his decease wife Harṣamāyā Śreṣṭha.
Pravīṇa Śreṣṭha, grandson of Śaṅkaralāla Śreṣṭha of Lubhu’s Dhasi Ṭola, offered brass seats to Mahālakṣmī, Mahābhairava, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Kumārī.

event_name: Overlaying of windows with brass sheets
event_description: Together with his family, Nandakiśora Śreṣṭha overlaid the wooden windows on the northern façade with brass sheets, wishing for the eternal peace of his deceased parents Śaṅkaralāla and Harṣamāyā Śreṣṭha.

event_name: Overlaying of windows with brass sheets
event_description: Together with his family, Nandakiśora Śreṣṭha overlaid the wooden windows on the northern façade with brass sheets, wishing for the eternal peace of his deceased parents Śaṅkaralāla and Harṣamāyā Śreṣṭha.
Madanagopāla Śreṣṭha, Kamalādevī Śreṣṭha, and their son Vijayagopāla Śreṣṭha installed a steel railing inside the temple.
With donations from locals, silver crowns and other jewelries were offered to Mahālakṣmī, Mahābhairava, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, and Kumārī after their jewelries worn on head and neck were worn out.

Social worker Jagadiśa Vaidya made separate cash donations for various items to be offered to Mahālakṣmī and Mahābhairava like bells, fly whisks, crowns, trident, palanquins, etc. This inscription is a letter of appreciation issued in the name of the donor by the Department of Archaeology for his financial contributions.

monument_name: Kva Hiti (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_description: The Hiti is mentioned in a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 736.

monument_name: Kva Hiti (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_name: Repair of the Hiti and Caitya
event_description: Jayacakra Siṃha, Bhājudhana and other family members jointly repaired the Hiti and the Licchavi Caitya in memory of their deceased family members.

monument_name: Kva Hiti (probably built during the Licchavi period)
event_description: In around 1975 CE, the Hiti had turned into a pond because its drainage system did not work properly. Locals tried to repair the drainage system but were unsuccessful. The pond drained out due course of time, but the Hiti dried up. Thus, locals started digging up the water channel to reach the source of the Hiti. Before they reached the source, the Hiti started to flow again.
सतःमा भएको बुद्धको प्रतिमाको पादमा भने नेसं ८५९ (सन् १७३९) को अभिलेख छ । सतःभन्दा पुरानो उक्त मू्र्ति अन्त कतैबाट सतःमा ल्याई स्थापना गरिएको देखिन्छ ।
बटारबजारको चौकैमा रहेको चौतारामा रहेको यो अभिलेखमा सामुहिक रूपमा स्थानीयले केही कार्य गरेको थाहा हुन्छ । खिइसकेकाले गरिएको कार्य स्पष्ट छैन ।

There is a damaged inscription attached to the western wall of the temple. The inscription records that it was constructed in NS 834. The record mentions that at that time aguṭhīwas also established for the management of the temple.
The temple was renovated during the reign of King Mahendra.
Tuyuṣā Nhasalā and Bhim Latimāyā established this Phalcā in NS 927 (1807 CE).
The Lalitpur Municipality reconstructed the Phalcā.

The Bhaktapur Development Project sponsored the renovation of the roof tower (phucā), roof, walls and windows of the Dyaḥchẽ. The capitals and a few pillars of the rear arcade and the beam of the front arcade were also replaced.

A small mask representing Mahākālī was fixed to the south-eastern pillar of the arcade in the 1980s.  In the present, a metal statue of Mahākālī has been fixed to the same pillar where the mask used to be. It attracts a lot of devotees every morning.
Local youths from Sunaguthi formed a club called Gaṇeśa Bhajana Maṇḍala. This club is responsible for chanting and signing devotional songs and hymns at the Phalcā.

The Phalcā was reconstructed in 1995 thanks to a joint effort by the Village Development Committee (VDC) and local residents. It was inaugurated in the presence of the head of the VDC, Jitamela Maharjan.
Nara Buddhācārya (text: Budhācārjye Bhāju Nara) built thephalcātogether with his wife Thakumati and family members.
Following its collapse, the Bhaktapur Municipality reconstructed thephalcā..
King Bhūpatīndra Malla built the stone temple of Taḥdhaṃ Mahādeva and established other deities adhering to the Śiva Pāñcāyana concept in the octagonal structure.

An inscription is embedded into the eastern wall of the Phalcā, which mentions the locality's name as 'Custhurī' and the installation date. However, the exact purpose or significance of the event on that day is unknown. Notably, the color and texture of the stone inscription match those of the stone toraṇa nearby. This suggests that the inscription might have been created around the same time when the toraṇa was constructed. Shokoohys and Śreṣṭha (2014, p. 282) also associate this inscription with the toraṇa, further supporting the idea that they are contemporaneous.

During the reconstruction project in 2019, a significant discovery was made when a worker uncovered a stone fragment of a metha. Upon examination, it was found that the surface of the metha bore an inscription dating back to the Malla period. This metha is believed to be a part of a hanging bell, suggesting that a hanging bell was once present here, suspended from a stone beam. The inscription on the metha records the installation of this bell, shedding light on the historical significance of this site.

During the rule of King Pṛthvī Śāha, a jyāmadāra named Suravīra's sons, namely Kṛṣṇavīra, Kulamāna, and Budhimāna, were responsible for the installation of stone slabs on a specific section of the main lane within the city of Kirtipur. The approximate length of this paving project is described as extending "from the east of Gaḥchẽ Dhvākhā to the west of Chīthū Dhvākhā." This historical record provides insight into the civic development and infrastructure projects undertaken during that period.

event_name: Addition of lions and paving of stone
event_description: Śemāna, his wife Jīuthakuṃ and other family members facilitated the donation of two lion statues in front of the Gaṇeśa, and also had the front yard paved with stone.
The primary statue of Gaṇeśa (sthāna Gaṇeśa) and the wooden toraṇa above it were stolen during the 1960s to 1970s. Both of these objects were replaced with new ones in the 1980s.
The Phalcā was already in poor condition before the 2015 earthquakes. The tremors further deteriorated its condition. The Department of Archaeology enabled reconstruction in 2021 CE.

Following the completion of the reconstruction project, the Phalcā was officially inaugurated by the Mayor of Kirtipur. As part of this significant event, a mound of samaybaji was exhibited in front of the Phalcā. This exhibition marked a historic occasion, as it was the first time such an event had taken place in the history of the Phalcā.

Various inscriptions from Kirtipur provide historical evidence of the hāthu hayke tradition, where fermented beer (thvã) is discharged from a Bhairava mask's mouth for people to drink. These inscriptions include one from 1694 CE (NS 814) installed at the Khyālidyaḥ Shrine in Kvāḥcva, another from 1698 CE (NS 818) at the Ichẽ Ṭola, another from 1693 CE (NS 813), and a copperplate inscription from 1703 CE (NS 823), all of which mention thehāthu hāyketradition.In more recent times, the Sun Star Club, a youth organization in Kirtipur, aimed to revive this tradition after the reconstruction of the Phalcā and began planning for it in 2019 CE. Krishna Prasad Maharjan and Arjun Prasad Maharjan, the sons of the late Prem Bahadur Maharjan and Ganesh Kumari Maharjan, provided the generous funding of the crafting the Bhairava mask. The responsibility for carving the mask was entrusted to Laxman Maharjan, one of the ost prominent skilled wood craftsmen from Bungamati. However, Laxman Maharjan passed away due to the coronavirus before finalising the mask. His students, namely Rambhakta Maharjan, Amir Shakya, and Jitendra Tuladhar, took over the carving of the Bhairava mask, which stands at over 5 feet tall, and is thus, as of now, the largest Bhairava mask in Kathmandu Valley.On March 1, 2022, the Bhairava mask was transported from the craftsmen's workshop in Bungamati to Kirtipur. event_name: Installation of the Bhairava mask inside the phalcā
event_description: Consecration rituals were performed on the Bhairava mask for two days when it was enshrined inside the Phalcā.

In keeping with the Newar tradition of visiting other major shrines in the city following the installation of a new statue, a grand procession of devotees was organized to pay homage to other significant Bhairava shrines in the Kathmandu Valley. This procession saw the participation of approximately 1,000 devotees. The procession visited a total of 9 major Bhairava shrines, including Pacalī Bhairava, Kāla Bhairava, Ākāśa Bhairava, Ānanda Bhairava, Vaṭuka Bhairava, Tyāṅgā Bhairava, Hayagrīva Bhairava, along with Kirtipur's own Bāgha Bhairava, Aṣṭasiddhi Bhairava, and the newly installed Bhairava mask at the Phalcā. This pilgrimage allowed devotees to offer their reverence and prayers at these sacred sites.

The details of the Caitya’s initial construction are unclear. The inscription on the Caitya’s plinth, which is inscribed in Tibetan and Newari scripts is not related to the Caitya. It records the construction of a guesthouse in the village by a certain Dorje Lāmā, themukhiyāof the village, along with his wife Karmāvatī, son Śerbā Dorje and other relatives, during the reign of King Raṇa Bahādura Śāha. Nothing is known about the guesthouse at present, as no one in the village recalls its existence here.

event_name: Construction of the southern Phalcā and donation of land
event_description: The inscription in the southern Phalcā mentions its construction and the offering of "two ropanis of land called Yantābu" for the building.

The inscription in the western wing states that a group of Prajāpatis/Avāles led by Kṛṣṇamuni Bare (śākya) initiated the construction of a six-bayedPhalcā devoted to Bhīmarāṇeśvara and established a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara (inside the Phalcā). From here, Rām Prajāpati and his family were appointed as the caretakers of thePhalcā. The inscription also mentions the offering of wick lamps, rice and meat on the festivals of Buṃgama Lokeśvara and Indrajātra.

Reconstruction of the Phalcā was carried out by GTZ/udle. Reportedly, there was a marble inscription documenting this event, but today (effective 2019) it is lost. Presumably this happened during the earthquake and the subsequent reconstruction.

Reconstruction of the Phalcā after its collapse folowing the 2015 earthquakes. The reconstruction was financed by photo.circle Kathmandu, UNESCO and local people. Thedhuri pūjāof Nāraṃhiṭi Phalcā was performed by Sānukāji Avāle (52), Kvaylāchi on 9 June 2018. Photo.circle has shared a report about the reconstruction with the NHDP. Photo.circle contributed 12,000 US dollars to the restoration project. Most of these donations came from the PhotoKathmandu festival and UNESCO.

Kumārī Phalcā was renovated from the ground up using new materials. It was shifted to the south in order to make room for the widened road. This renovation saw the addition of new stairs, two lions and a giltgajur.

Rasiṃ, Jitasī, Bhamasi, and others offered the wooden Toraṇa installed on top of the entrance to the Bāhāḥ’s sanctum.
Punasiṃha, Bhuvanasiṃ, Vidurasiṃ, and others established stone statues of a pair of lions at the Bāhāḥ.

On the 6th day of the bright half of Āśvina NS 772, Jyotinarasiṃha Malla (the second son of king Siddhinarasiṃha Malla/younger brother of Śrīnivāsa Malla) died. His wife Chatramatī followed her husband into death and became asatī. The Navarātra of Daśaĩ had been organised to take place that year. Only the royal Upādhyāya priests performed the rituals for ten days. The Taleju was not brought down, and the buffaloes were not sacrificed. Only the deity of Maḍiche (Maṇichẽ) was brought downstairs to the ground floor and placed there according to the tradition. A buffalo was sacrificed at Thaṃchemaṇḍala (Mahālakṣmī) later on. Neither the dance with buffalo-heads was performed nor were the musical instruments played.

Siddhi Bahādura Maharjana, in memory of his parents, offered apatāḥ(ritual banner) to the temple on the occasion of the Chakhaḥ Jātrā.
Rameśvarī, her son Bhīmsena, and Candramāyā, along with others, offered a bell (ghaṇṭa) in front of the temple in memory of their deceased family members.

The Bāhāḥ was renovated.

This inscription is not related to the history of this Bāhāḥ. The stone pedestal (jalahari) dates to Śaka era year 411 (489 CE), the reigning period of Licchavi king Mānadeva. It was found while digging a drain on the road just in front of this Bāhāḥ. At present, it is preserved in the courtyard of the Bāhāḥ. This is the oldest record ever found in Patan. Mālasĩha Bhavo and other Bhavos donated a a lion statue.
Sundara Bahādura and his wife Beljima donated a brasstoraṇa.
Garuḍa Nārāyaṇa Śresṭha, Siddhi Kumārī Śresṭha and other family members offered a copperpatāḥto Caṇḍeśvarī.
Dhanalakṣmī and Bhājudeva Bhāro repaired the temple and donated ajaḥrũhiti.
Govinda Siṃha offered an embossed brass lion throne to Caṇḍeśvarī.

event_name: Covering of upper roof with copper
event_description: Harṣa Narasiṃ, his son Harṣa Nārāsiṃ, and some of his other family members covered the upper roof with copper plates. The embossed copper eaves board was also added at this time.
Nhuchẽlāla and Dhanamāyā from Chābāhāḥṭoladonated a copperpatāḥ.

event_name: Construction of phalcā (to the west of Jora Gaṇeśa)
event_description: During the reign of king Nṛpendra Malla, the sons of Prajāpati Padu, Vāsi, Jevasingh and Herāmani, had constructed a phalcā to the west side of Jora Gaṇeśa.

Heranī Mayī, a resident of the Pasiṃkochẽ Ṭola northeast of Cāpāgāũ, established a religious trust by donating eightropanīs of land to Vajravārāhī. The income from the land was designated for donating various items, including puffed rice, beaten rice, curd, meat, and fermented beer, during the processions in Caitra and Kārtika. Lamps were also to be lit on these occasions. The trust was further obligated to annually feedjogis and make special offerings to them on the new moon day of Bhadra.

event_name: Installation of a stone buffalo statue
event_description: King Yoganarendra Malla installed a stone buffalo statue with a golden parasol at the temple after performing a night-long fire sacrifice with music and offerings.

event_name: Offering of a pair of lions (CHG0110-035, CHG0110-036)
event_description: A pair of stone lion statues (CHG0110-035, CHG0110-036) were installed on either side of the passage to the temple complex. The name of the donor is not mentioned in the inscription.

King Viṣṇu Malla of Lalitpur renovated the Vajravārāhī temple and organized the ‘suvarṇakalaśadhvajārohaṇa’ceremony, involving the installation of a golden finial and the hoisting of a banner. Priests and astrologers like Viśvānanda and Nīlakaṇṭhānanda participated in the ritual. The inscription records the king's donation of land to commemorate the anniversary of the finial installation and mandates annual fire rituals with animal sacrifice. This inscription contradicts the popular belief that the temple has never had a finial.

event_name: Endowment of lands to repair a phalcā
event_description: Gaṃgāsāgara Bābu of the Bhansāra Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ, along with his wife Rājalakṣmī, renovated aphalcaand established a religious trust by donating land. The income from this land was to be used for repairing thephalca's roof and making ancestral offerings in the name of his uncle Mastarāma on the 3rd of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, prior to the worship at the Vajravārāhī temple. It remains unclear which of the threephalcās—west, north, or south of the temple—was renovated.

During the reign of King Surendra, Kāyaṣṭha Akabara Bhāro of the Bhansāra Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ established a religious trust by donating land for cleaning the temple premises daily. He made the donation together with his mother Guṇa Thaku and his sons Mānakāji, Kṛṣṇamehera, Syāmamehera, and Rāmamehera, wishing for the deliverance of his ancestors. He also mandated an annual worship of Vajravārāhī on the 8th of the bright fortnight of Caitra, followed by a feast.
Balabhadra Kāri Kṣitri installed a bell (CHG0110-007) at the temple.
Bahādura Kāki Kṣetṛ renovated and reinstalled the bell (CHG0110-007) offered to the temple by his father Balabhadra Kāri Kṣitri.

Together with his wife Devi Thaku and the family members, Kāyaṣṭha Akabara Bhāro of the Bhansāra Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ installed a brass toraṇa above the entrance to the temple. He also overlaid the entrance with brass sheets on the occasion.
An ascetic named Kāśi Girī established aśivaliṅga(CHG0110-025) north of the temple and named it Kāśī Viśveśvara Mahādeva.

event_name: Offering of silver toraṇa, serpent noose, and parasol
event_description: Kālu Siṃ offered Vajravārāhī a silvertoraṇa(decorative arch), anāgapāśa(serpent noose), and a parasol, with a combined weight of 221tolās of silver. He also presented a 15-tolāsilver garland to the buffalo figure (CHG0110-024), Vajravārāhī's animal mount. These offerings were to be displayed during festivals and on Saturdays. The donor further stipulated that Vajravārāhī be worshipped with an animal sacrifice on the 3rd of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the day his father, Harṣanarasiṃha, passed away. He established a trust with land donation to ensure the continuation of these practices.

event_name: Offering of a pair of flags
event_description: Haribhakta, Caityalakṣmī, and others from Dau Bāhāḥ in Patan installed a pair of brass banners flanking the entrance to the temple.

Together with his sons Kīrtigovinda and Pūrṇagovinda, Jītagovinda Amātya from Dau Bāhāḥ in Patan installed two pairs of stone lion statues in front of the northern (CHG0110-009, CHG0110-010) and southern entrances (CHG0110-011, CHG0110-012) of the temple.

event_name: Repair of the temple and offering of a bell (CHG0110-021)
event_description: Jītagovinda renovated the temple and offered a bell (CHG0110-021). He probably is the same person who installed two pairs of lion statues in front of the northern and southern entrances of the temple.
A stonemaṇḍalawas (CHG0110-022) by the wife of Candramāna from the Ikhā Ṭola in Cāpāgāũ.
King Mahendra renovated the temple and built walls around the temple premises.
Bhairavabahādura Śreṣṭha and Candramehara Kāyaṣṭha jointly renovated and reinstalled the bell (CHG0110-021) previously offered by Jītagovinda.
During the reign of King Virendra, both roofs of the temple were laid with copper sheets.

The upper roof of the Vajravārāhī temple was covered with zinc sheets, while the lower roof was covered with tiles. Due to the deterioration of both roofs, leading to leaks and rotting of the wooden rafters, financial assistance was collected from various sources to replace both roofs with copper sheets. A marble inscription was installed to commemorate this event.
Śānti KC from Jharuvārāsī offered a bell (CHG0110-014) in memory of her decease husband Pūrṇabahādura KC.
Together with their sons, Herālāla and Dāntīmāyā Maharjana of Thecva offered an oblong banner (patāḥ) of copper to the temple.

In memory of her husband, Bhairavabahādura Jośī, Miśrī Jośī and her family members constructed a section of the southern boundary wall of the temple premises, extending from the door on the wall to the southwestern corner.
Residents of Saugal in Patan, Puruṣottamabahādura Śreṣṭha and his wife Maiyā Śreṣṭha installed a metalmaṇḍala(CHG0110-016) in the temple premises.
Kṛṣṇabahādura Sāhī and Tulsīmāyā Sāhī from Jhyālipāṭī in Cāpāgāũ established a Gaṇeśa statue in the temple premises.

Dāna Darśana and his family installed temple bells on the eaves of the upper roof of the temple in the name of his decease parents Śrīnātha and Santamāyā Darśana. He also established statues of his parents.
Amara Rājabhaṇḍārī and his wife Tārādevī Rājabhaṇḍārī installed a woodentoraṇaover the eastern entrance of the temple.

Along with his family, Puruṣottamabahādura Śreṣṭha of Saugal, Patan established new statues of theaṣṭamātṛkādeities inside the sanctum after the previous ones were worn out. He established these statues in the name of his deceased family members Mānabahādura, Gaṇeśakumārī, Śambhūbahādura, and Pūrṇakumārī Śreṣṭha.
Along with his wife Dātīmāyā Maharjana and the family, Harikṛṣṇa Maharjana of Cāpāgāũ offered a silver crown to the goddess.

Jayakṛṣṇa Bhāro, Devidāsa Bhāro, and others jointly offered a woodentoraṇaover the southern entrance of the temple. While the inscription does not contain a date, the donation appears to have taken place in later-medieval period.
Kṛṣṇabahādura Maharjana of Thecva offered an oblong banner (patāḥ) to the temple in the name of his deceased wife Lakṣmīkumārī Maharjana.
An oblong banner (patāḥ) was offered to the temple in the name of the donor’s deceased parents Siddhilāla and Harṣamāyā. The inscription does not mention the name of the donor.
Prime Minister Candra Śamśera commissioned the construction of the temple in his honor.
Prime Minister Candra Śamśera installed a bell at the temple together with his wife and sons that documents the construction of the temple a few months earlier.

event_description: Thecaityain front of the sanctum door was built by Śākyabhikṣu Dharmma, Jujuvirasiṃ, and others, during the reign of King Surendra Vikrama Śāha.

event_name: Installation of the statue of Akṣobhya (object number KAT1060-001)
event_description: Sujabhānasiṃ installed the Akṣobhya statue as the Bāhāḥ's main deity (Kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) inside the sanctum.

Cābāhāḥ Phalcā collapsed completely in the 2015 earthquakes. Musical instruments, books and statues of deities were all buried under the rubble. The traditional drums stored on the upper floor were later recovered by locals and had suffered some damages. However, a local Maharjan resident tells us that the images of Umāmaheśvaraand some other deities remained buried under the rubble, along with an inscription installed in the Phalcā.

The Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was restored on the basis of a plan designed by the Urban Management and Economic Diversification Project (UMEDP), the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust (KVPT) and Jyāpu Samāja, Lalitpur. The final report was written up by Rohit Ranjitkar and Lumanti Joshi in March 2003.Six weeks of research went into the reconstruction process, where researchers tried to work out what the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā may once have looked like (its earlier forms had not been documented). Four different options for the front facade were developed and then shared with the community elders, who were ultimately responsible for the final decision. The window designs were copied from similarphalcādating back to the same period in the Chochhe Gallī area.Emphasis was given to the use of traditional building materials and craftsmanship, something which was uncommon back then.The reconstruction was also an attempt to challenge common views that traditional materials are not sustainable; those who argue this often propose cement be used instead. The process also included training workshops for and by traditional craftsmanship. Two new pillars were recarved on the basis of the historical model. Because it was in such bad shape, a layer of bricks adjacent to the residential house to the west was removed and replaced withma apāusing yellow mud mortar. The niches were installed in line with the photographs taken prior to the dismantling of the rear wall, and the stone statues of the guardian deities Gaṇeśa, Lokeśvara Kumāra, Umāmaheśvara and two others of Cābahā Phalcā were stored there. These statues have been carved anew. Some innovative measures were also introduced, such as putting a waterproof membrane between the planks and the mud bed for the roof tiles.
Donated by Harirāma Bhāvo and his wife Dhavaṃti from thenani(apparently, the courtyard is now known as Lũchẽ Nani) to the east of Jyāthabāhāra Vihāra.

event_name: Renovation of the Phalcā and installation of a statue
event_description: An inscription on thecaityain front of the Phalcā mentions that the Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was renovated and a statue of Umāmaheśvara was installed. The inscription names Harinandana Duvāra Bhāro as the donor of this and other properties in the name of hisīṣṭa devatā. It is likely that he also sponsored the construction of the Caitya and the renovation of the Phalcā, as well as the installation of the statue of Umāmaheśvara.The term 'bhāro'clearly suggests that Harinandana is from the Shrestha community. The extent to which the Phalcā was renovated is not clear. It is worth noting that the renovation was carried out just 12 years after its construction.
Cābāhāḥ Phalcā was finally reconstructed, though it remained a ruin from 2015 until 18 CE. The reconstruction was funded by local donors and the municipality.
Thedyaḥchẽwas reconstructed.
Trailokyarāja and Suvarṇadevī Vajrācārya jointly offered a small wooden chariot to thebāhāḥ. It is used for carrying the statue of Dīpaṅkara and Tārā during theSamyakFestival.
The inscription is hard to decipher. The numerical figure of the date is also illegible.
The last line of the inscription mentions the major task accomplished on that date. Unfortunately, the line is hard to decipher as few letters have been covered with colour.
A Vajrācārya family added a Dharmadhātu in thebāhāḥpremises.
Thetoraṇawas placed over the main entrance.
Thistoraṇawas placed over the main entrance.
Kānchī Vajrācārya and others jointly added the prayer wheesl in front of thedyaḥchẽ.

event_name: Renovation of a royal water channel
event_description: A Licchavi inscription from Samvat 48 (624 CE) which is not related to this monument is in the temple premises.[1]It is not clear why this was moved to this temple. The inscription records the restoration of a water channel by Aṃśu Varman (see the edition and translation of the inscription inVajrācāryaVS 2030, 401-404).^According to Vajrācārya (VS 2030, 401), this inscription is related to Chinnamastā Mandira.

event_name: Pavement of stone and installation of a donor statue
event_description: The inscription records that Maṇirāja Thakālī, a resident of Dathutaḥjhyāḥ Ṭola paved stones on the temple premises and installed his and his wife’s statue there. It further informs us that he made Gaṇeśa happy by reciting the texts dedicated to him and meditating on him.
Tīrthāraja, a resident of Pasala Bāhāḥ offered a gilded banner (patāḥ) to the temple.
A marble plate only containing two names (Dhīrjamāna Sīṃ and Kājimāna Sīṃ) is posted on the northern wall inside the sanctum. It does not explain what these two people did for the temple.
The inscription records that the roof of the temple was gilded during the reign of King Thribhuvana by Kīrtimāya, Śeṣa Narasiṃ, Bekhālāla, Bhekharatna Siṃ, Anantalāla and so forth.
The monument was seriously damaged in the 2015 CE earthquakes.

The inscription in the sanctum suggests that the construction was completed in 1649 CE (NS 769) and a statue of Śākyamuni was consecrated in the sanctum. In consecration ceromony a fire sacrifice calledlakṣyāhutiyajñais performed, followed by dance and traditional music (consisting of five musical instruments) performances. The kings of Patan, Siddhinarasiṃha Malla and Śrīnivāsa Malla, were present during this ceremony.The inscription further records that a person called Hākuju from a Śākya clan constructed this temple. He also constructed Cvay Bāhāḥ (KIR0011), which is located nearby this temple.

The original Śākyamuni statue consecrated in the sanctum in 1649 CE (NS 769) was stolen in 1984 CE. An individual named Kānchī Vajrācarya from the local community installed the contemporary statue on the empty pedestal in the same year.
The temple was demolished and rebuilt by the Department of Archaeology (DoA).

Tharapā(the most senior member of thevihāra) Kantāsura offered atoraṇa,a vajraanda silver banner(kikiṃpā)to Maitreya Bodhisattva anddhakiṃ(curtain), garlands, two lotus flowers, one drum (ḍamaru) and onecāmara(a yak tail used for fanning) to Yogāṃbara, the deity of theāgãchẽ. In addition to this, he offered two stone images of lions, a crown,a vajra, anda pātrakhvālāto Viśvakarmā. He also donatedteliyābricks for the house of the esoteric deity (digī).
Vajrācārya Pṛthimān and family members installed a bell on the right side of the main shrine.
Āśāmadu installed these lions on both sides of the entrance to the main shrine.
Amṛtānanda, his wife Lāni Thakuñ and his son Āśānanda consecrated the lions at the main entrance of the Bāhāḥ.
Buddharāja Vajrācārya donated the Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya.
Deva Vīra Vajrācārya and his family members donated the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala.
Devi Rāja and Budha Rāja Vajrācārya and family installed metal flags on both sides of the main shrine.
Deva Vīr, his son Siddhi Vajra, and his mother Harṣa Thakũ donated atorana,a siṃhāsana, an ilāṅ (metal or coloured cloth kept above the main deity) and a flag made of brass to Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Vaidya Buddha Rāja Vajrācārya laid the stone pavement in the courtyard.
Images of two Lokeśvaras were installed on both sides of the main shrine by Indra Rāj (in memory of Līlākumārī and Munākumārī of Chobhar).

The reconstruction of the Sataḥ was carried out in 2021 CE (2078 VS) by the committee for the Integrated Development of Bagmati Civilization under the Ministry of Urban Development of the Nepal Government, with help by a loan provided by the Asian Development Bank.

The local community initiated the reconstruction of the Pukhū to bring it back to its original size. The Shankharapur Municipality provided NRs. 3.5 million to remove clay deposited in the Pukhū and to build an embankment and walls around it. After the reconstruction of the Pukhū, it is hoped that lotuses will grow again and be used as offerings to Vajrayoginī like in the past.

A Karmācārya’s clan, living in Sundhārā, Patan started performing the daily worship in the temple in 2014 CE. The clan was requested to take over this responsiblity by Sarasvatī Ṭola Development Committee, a local and non-governmental organisation formed to develop and maintain the local area.

event_name: Offering of a Hundred Eight Ghyadevās and a Bell, and Encircling the Temple by Adding a Raised Walkway (Peṭī)
event_description: Arjun and Bāgirathī Suvedī offered a-hundred-eightghyadevāsand a bell to Sarasvatī. They also added the raised walkway (New.phaḥ, Nep.peṭī) running around all four sides to the temple.

This inscription from NS 434 (1314 CE) installed in the temple premise records the installation of a Sarasvatī statue.  Another inscription from NS 567 (1447 CE), installed nearby the this inscription, mentions the same event. Therefore, it remains obscure in which date the present-day statue was installed.

As mentioned in the first historical event, this inscription from NS 567 (1447 CE), too, records the installation of a Sarasvatī statue. However, it can not be identified whether the present-day Sarasvatī statue in the sanctum was installed in the earlier or this date.
Lakṣmīśvara Bhāro, a resident from Khācvachẽ Ṭola, renovated the temple.
The temple suffered serious damages during the 1934 CE earthquakes.
The descendants of Lakṣmīśvara Bhāro who had renovated this temple in NS 899 (1779 CE) restored it after the 1934 CE earthquakes
Govindamāna Śresṭha and his family members donated a bell which is installed in front of the temple. They also fixed modern tiles to the eastern wall of the sanctum.
Purnalala Singh of Tichungalli Tunnani embellished the temple with brass sheets to please Gaṇeśa.
A pair of brass flags (dhvajā) was installed on the left and right sides of the temple. The inscription does not mention the name of the donor family.

The family of Viṣṇulāla offered a bell to their local Sthāna Gaṇeśa. Interestingly, the bell bears a Sanskrit verse dedicated to Gaṇeśa. Compared to other bells from the Rāṇā period, this one shows more elaborate ornamentation, including floral patterns, images of Gaṇeśa, and serpents (nāga) on all sides.
The Bahī complex collapsed in the 1833 (NS 953) earthquake. After the earthquake, the Bahī was reconstructed reestablishing the statues of Vajravārāhī, Prajñāpāramitā and Sarasvatī.

event_name: Donation of a container, mohara and toraṇa
event_description: Brahmācārya Bhikṣus of the Bahī, namely Rāja Vidhi, Lakṣmī Vidhi and other 16 people offered a round-shaped pot (bidola) to Akṣobhya and 10 garlands of coins (mohara mālā) to Matsyendranātha.Images of four donors are sculpted at the bottom of the inscription.
The Bahī complex collapsed in the 1934 earthquake. Theguṭhī-members of the Bahī reconstructed it.
Department of Archaeology, Nepal renovated the Bahī complex.
Due to the 2015 earthquake, some of the parts of the Bahī are damaged.
Dharmasena, Lakudeva and others repaired the Bahī.
Statues of Kranajoti (Karṇajyoti) and his wife were established towards south from the sanctum’s entrance.
Buddhirāja, with the help of his grandson, made adharmadhātujinālaya caityain front of the southern door of the Bahī.
Gaṇeśamān Śākya made adharmadhātujinālaya caityain front of the southern door of the Bahī.

event_name: Copying the regulation of the Bahī
event_description: The regulations of the Bahī according to this inscription, which in earlier times was written in the leaves of a Peepal tree, were copied in the present stone inscription, which regulates to collect money for its reconstruction from the harvest of itsguṭhī-lands located in Nakkhu and Gakhapā. All thebahī-members should participate in the task, otherwise, their sin would be counted as five grave sins or offences (pañcamahāpātaka).  This inscription, placed at the northern corner of the sanctum records three historical events and three different era years.
The inscription mentions that apānejuof the Buṅgmatī temple performed some acts in the Buṅga Bahī. However, the act could not be figured out due to the condition of the inscription.
​ A stone Kīrtimukatoraṇawas placed over the shrine in the name of Biṃma Bhairava.

Individuals from Jholachẽ, including Śyāma Bhābo, Suryya Bhābo, and Gunadeva Bhābo, collectively lit a large lamp (mahādīpa) at the Gaṇeśa temple and offered gilded flags. On the same occasion, aketakīflower was also offered to Āryāvalokiteśvara located in the Haka Ṭola. Two craftsmen, Hāku Bade and Taodhika Bade from the Jyāthā Ṭola, had jointly crafted these items. The flag can no longer be seen at the temple.
Nīlakumārī Dhāinī, the granddaughter of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bārāhī from the Haka Ṭola, offered a bell to the Gaṇeśa temple.
In memory of the late Indrabahādura and Indramāyā Śreṣṭha, the family members offered a metal canopy (ilāṃ) to Gaṇeśa.

As the inscription is not readable, its content cannot be deciphered. Pruscha (1975, P-217) has referred to an inscription that recorded laying of stone slabs in front of the temple in 1877 CE (NS 997). This probably is the same inscription.

The pediment of the temple contains inscribed stone blocks. The inscriptions are very eroded, but it is possible to read the date 1408 of the Śaka era, which corresponds to 1486 CE.The inscription may record the construction of the temple or a later use of it.The inscription was first mentioned by Prayag Raj Sharma (1972).
Thejaḥdhūṃwas renovated by theṭola sudhāra samitiin 2001 CE (VS 2075), restoring its function as a crucial water source and resting place for travelers and locals.
Thephalcā, originally positioned closer to the road, was relocated a few meters away and rebuilt in the mid 2060s (VS) with assistance from the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and theSapājaḥruṃ ṭola.
The family of Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Śreṣṭha installed a stone statue of Gaṇeśa at the center of thephalcā,jaḥdhūṃ, and well.

event_name: Pavement of the courtyard and donation of ornaments
event_description: Harṣajyoti and his wife Bhima Thakũ offered an ornament to Gaṇeśa and Rāto Matsyendranātha and paved the courtyard of this temple with stones.
Thetoraṇafixed above the main door was donated. The name of the donor could not be identified.
Puṇyarāja Tulādhara, Sānumāyā Tulādhara and their family members made an offering of a brass plate engraved with the symbols foraṣṭamaṅgala.

Local residents reconstructed the temple with the help of Bungmati Sāṃskṛtika Adhyayana Kendra, a research center focusing on the cultural history of Bungamti. The reconstruction work started in the 27th of Caitra (VS 2059) and was completed in the 20th of Jyeṣṭha (VS 2060). It was officially inaugurated on the 23rd of Śrāvaṇa (VS 2060).

Harṣarāja and his family established twodharmadhātu maṇḍalasin two different places on the same date. One was established in Cīdhã Bahī and the other was established in the nearby Mū Guita Bahī (LAL1980). The inscription regarding the establishment of themaṇḍalais located in Cīdhã Bahī.

event_name: Repair of statue of Guitaḥ Aji
event_description: The terrecotta statue of Guitaḥ Aji was repaired.
A gilded mask of Mahākāla was consecrated and placed to the north of the outer entrance of the monastic building. The donor's name is not recorded.
Kāsirāma Bhāro of Hatigla established aśikharakūṭa caityain the courtyard and endowed land to perform religious activities of thebahī.
Padmarāya, his wife Dhanavatī and their daughter Pardmalakṣmī established this statue. It shows one male and one female devotee.

Dhammasiṃha Varuḍākāra and his wife Māratimayi, along with Devarāja and his unnamed wife established thecaitya. Additionally, Devarāja donated land parcels, one measuring 1ropanī7 and a halfjavawhile the other measuring 3ropanīs, to fund various rituals at thecaitya, including the lighting of lamps on the full moon day of Āśvina.
Dhammasiṃha Varuḍākāra and Māratimayi donated 3ropanīs of land, a garden measuring 2karṣas, and 140moharas in cash to thecaitya.

event_name: Renovation of the old spouts and construction of a new one
event_description: Prātāpasiṃha Bābu, Vīrasiṃha Bābu, Jayabhadrasiṃha Bābu and Ānandasiṃha Bābu who are the sons of Cakrasiṃha Bābu and Phikunilakṣmī, renovated the Lũ Hiti, added Byā̃cā Hiti and established a golden statue of Lakṣmī in the memory of their mother. Cakrasiṃha Bābu was a son of Bhīmalakṣmī who was a daughter of King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla. King Yoganarendra Malla had performed akoṭyāhūtifire ritual during the inauguration ceremony of the new spout. The event is mentioned also inNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī(19.3.169), however the donor's name is mentioned as Uddhavasiṃha Bābu.

event_name: Consecration of a statue of Viṣṇu ( see object number LAL1860-004)
event_description: This statue of Viṣṇu was installed in NS 965 (1845 CE). The name of its donor is not mentioed.

event_name: Installation of a new Viṣṇu statue (see object number LAL1860-004)
event_description: A new statue was installed by the local residents after the old one got stolen.

The date mentioned in the inscription is rubbed off (see the description above). It records that the Hiti was constructed for the welfare of people.

event_name: Theft of a gilded copper plate and renovation of the Hiti
event_description: The gilded copper plate of the eastern spout (see object number LAL1860-001) of the Hiti got stolen in 2007 CE. Thus, Prabhāta Red Star (Youth) Club renovated the Hiti with the financial support of Lalitpur Metropolitan City and also wrapped the eastern spot with a gilded copper plate.

The inscription records that Lalitpur was attacked by the Ḍoyas (Maithilis of Simraungaḍh) in NS 431 (1311 CE). They occupied the area from Thaṃṭibi (Thati?) to Manigala (Mangal Bazar). Gajurhideva (?) of Luyitī (Lũ Hiti) was upset because of the invasion.

The inscription on a stone stele standing southeast of the shrine appears to be unrelated to Pācāgaṇeśa. It deals with the construction of a road in the Paśupati area by a few persons. The text of the inscription is not fully legible.

In the name of the deceased Harimāyā Śreṣṭha, the large oblong stone (PPK1306-008) set on a wall north of the shrine was renovated by setting bricks around the stone. The stone is revered as Bhairava.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Phalcā at Cvachẽ (built in 1782, rebuilt 2018 CE)
event_description: he Prajāpatis, who are also called Avāle (in Patan) of Bherālivi*, led bythakuBhāgideva and including Silhaṃ Bhāvo, Bhāna Singh Bhāvo, Saṃkha Bhāvo, Rakṣmiṣaṃkha Bhāvo and Mimha Bhāvo from the samecapāḥorganization of the same clan, renovated thedharmmaśālāin 1782 CE. May all be well.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Phalcā at Cvachẽ (built in 1782, rebuilt 2018 CE)
event_description: After the 2015 earthquakes, Lalitpur Municipality spent 41 Lac rupees to renovate the Phalcā. The locals raised money for painting and decoration. The reconstruction was completed in 2018.

During the reign of King Bhāṣkara Malla, Siddhimuni Vajrācārya (text: Vajācājya Siddhimuni) founded the Bāhāḥ and concecrated a statue of Akṣobhya as the main deity (Kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) inside its sanctum. On the same occasion, he endowed land and established aguthito run and maintain the Bāhāḥ. He also erected acaitya. His wife Herulakṣmī, younger brother Padmamuni, second son Beṣādeva, daughters Dhanalakṣmī and Sarvalakṣmī all assisted him in establishing the Bāhāḥ.
Kājī Tulsīmāna renovated the Bāhāḥ.
Jīvaratna, Vimalā, Rāju, Sānu, Ratna, Aśoka, Vinoda, Vinaya, and others constructed the Caitya.

The Bāhāḥ was renovated again in 2007 CE (VS 2064) with financial assistance from Haṃsa Smṛti Samāja, an NGO established in memory of Tulsīmāna’s son Haṃsamānasiṃha. Local donations were also used to fund the renovation.
The floor of the Bāhāḥ premises was paved with stone donated by locals.

event_name: Replacing jhiṅgaṭī roof with brass sheets
event_description: The roof's jhĩgaṭī tiles were replaced with brass sheets. Dīpendra Śreṣṭha, the provincial minister of Bagmati Province, was instrumental in arranging NRs. 860,000.

The devastating earthquakes in 2015 left the building on the verge of collapse. Consequently, the statues of various deities and the sacredśāligrāmastone housed inside theakhaḍāwere relocated to another building intended for ascetics, known as the Bhāgavata Sanyāsa Āśrama. In 2021 CE, the Pashupati Area Development Trust dismantled the hazardous sections of the building.

The Temple completely collapsed during the 1833 CE earthquakes, and was never restored. Its large three-layered plinths suggest that there was a big (at least two-storey pagoda-styled) temple here in the past.

event_name: Theft of the main idol (Viṣṇuvikrāṇta) from the sanctum
event_description: The stone statue of Viṣṇuvikrānta, the main deity of the Temple, was enshrined in a small shrine after the Temple collapsed during the 1833 CE earthquakes. Unfortunately, it was stolen in 1990 CE.

During the joint rule of King Śivasiṃha Malla and Lakṣmīnarasiṃha Malla, Jayalakṣa of Taḥdhaṃ Bāhāḥ (KAT1420) began the construction of Pinchẽ Bāhāḥ. The foundation was laid by performing a fire oblation.
Special worship calledśṛṅkhalāvarohaṇapūjāwas performed in the course of thebāhāḥ’s construction.

event_name: Completion of the construction of the bāhāḥ
event_description: After completing the construction of thebāhāḥ, a stone statue of Akṣobhya was established as the main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ). A gilded statue of Dīpaṅkara, a Mañjuśrī statue, a Halāhala Lokeśvara statue,acaityaand a shrine of Lokeśvara were also established at thebāhāḥpremises.
Jakasiṃha, Jayadhanasiṃha, Cakrasiṃha, Ajayadharmasiṃha, and others offered a woodentoraṇa,which is placed atop thebāhāḥ’s entrance to the sanctum.
Jayadhanasiṃha and Cakrasiṃha offered a few of the struts on the eastern side of the outer part of thebāhāḥ.
Deomuni, Dhamabala, Patāpasiṃha, and others sponsored wings for the door to the sanctum.
Together with his son Mahāmuni, Cintāmani offered a metal sheet with the carvings of thepañcabuddhadeities placed on top of the entrance to thebāhāḥ’s sanctum.
Chinikāji Śākya, Jñānaratna Śākya, Ratnakāji Śākya, and Prema Śākya offered a new pair of lion statues to replace the old ones that flanked the (outer) entrance to thebāhāḥcourtyard.
Nāla Varmā established aguṭhī. It is not clear from the inscription that the guṭhī was for Balabhadra or some other deity.
Some people donated wooden panels to fix on the door of the temple. Only the half portion of the inscription is available.
The statue of Bahabhadra was stolen.

event_name: Installation of new staue of Balabhadra
event_description: Locals installed the new stone statue in 1988 by collecting donations. They are very unhappy that they lost the archaic artistic statue of their deity.
Siṃharatha and his other family members jointly installed the statue of Bhagavatī.

event_name: Formation of guthi for various worships
event_description: Although being constructed in an area densely populated by the Newars, an inscription at the Temple records a non-Newar family of the Khatrī caste forming aguthiin the late 19thcentury in the name of Bhagavatī. According to the inscription, Dhanavīra Khatrī formed the Guthi for the worship of other deities like Nīlakaṇṭha, Nṛtyeśvara, etc. along with Bhagavatī. There is a clear instruction for descendants of Dhanavīra in the inscription: Carry out the activities at this house and the rent from the shop shall be the income of the Guthi. This suggests that the house with a shop was situated near the Temple.Jayalakṣmī formed a trust of 101 rupees in 1816 CE (VS 1873) for feeding seven Brahmins of Paśupati on the full moon days of Vaiśākha and Kārtika along with a donation of 1paisāeach out of the interest received from the amount. Additionally, the income was to be used to light 21 lamps at the Temple on the full moon day of Kārtika.

event_name: Addition of a gilt roof, pinnacle and toraṇa
event_description: Jośī family members, who had been living just north of the Temple, added a golden roof,toraṇaand pinnacles over the Bhagavatī statue.

event_name: Construction of the present Temple structure
event_description: Previously, it used to be a shrine with the statue of Bhagavatī enshrined under an open sky (see, for example the historical photo taken in the early 1970s and published inPursha1975, p. 15). The Maitrī Parivāra Club constructed the present structure keeping the existing shrine at the centre.
Caitya Ratna Vajrācārya (Lāṭā) added a statue of Umāmaheśvara on the facade of the Temple.

event_name: Addition of a pair of flags
event_description: In the name of Narasiṃharāja Jośī and late Nātimaiyā Jośī, the pair of brass flags were added on both sides of the sanctum door.
Rāma Kṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha and his wife Lakṣmī of Thamel jointly offered the brass banner (patāḥ) to Bhagavatī.
The Maitrī Parivāra Club finished the renovation task and the upper surface of the roof was covered by brass sheets.

event_name: Installation of a brass tiger statue
event_description: In the memory of their parents, Sūryabhakta, his wife Campādevī and his son Govindabhakta installed the brass statue of a tiger in front of the Temple.

Apart from constructing the present Temple structure, the Maitrī Parivāra Club also renovated the Bhagavatī Dhvākhā Phalcā (KAT0151) with the financial assistance from the Pacific Asia Travel Association (PATA). Marble tiles were also laid in the courtyard on the occasion.

Śākya and Vaidya(1970, 93-95) refer to an inscription dated NS 723 (1603 CE) which has since been lost but was erected during the joint reign of King Śivasiṃhadeva and Hariharasiṃha. The inscription mentions that a golden urn and a pinnacle were offered to the deity. Relying upon the inscription,Śākya & Vaidyaassume that thetemple was built on the date. However, pinnacles are not only offered upon construction but also traditionally after the restoration or reconstruction of a monument; thus it cannot be ascertained whether or not the temple was indeed built on this date. The text at the end of the inscription mentions that the donor family restored the temple and donated a pinnacle. This phrase also indicates that the temple was not built at that time but was rather restored or reconstructed.
Kīrtimaṅgalā Thakunī, the daughter of Śrīnivāsa Malla, and her husband Amarasiṃha Kumhāraja added a roof in the temple and bestowed land measuring 3.5ropanīsfor the temple.

event_name: Construction of capāḥ in temple premises
event_description: The Bhāro family built acapāḥin the temple premises and donated land for its anniversary worship and maintenance.

Matsyendrasiṃha Bhāro of Aki Bāhāḥ Patan donated acapāḥto please Kvaynā Gaṇeśa and installed idols of Umāmaheśvara and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa in it. He also bestowed fourropanīsand onejabafield to establish aguṭhī. Theguṭhīwas also responsible for repairing minor damages.

event_name: Offering of chariot (khata) for annual varṣavardhana jātrā
event_description: Narayan Bharo of Yaglamadu Ṭola of Patan offered a golden crown, parasol and a garland to Gaṇeśa. He also donated a cot to be used in the anniversary worship, and Rs. 25 as a fixed fund for its maintenance.
An inscription mentions that peopole from Gabāhā in Patan donated a pinnacle in 1849  (Gutschow2011, 458). The inscription could not be found in the temple.

event_name: Renovation of phalcā in temple premises
event_description: Ṭuṃḍirāja and his wife renovated the two-storey Phalcā of the temple complex to please Kvaynā Gaṇeśa and to commemorate the late Bhorāja (Ṭuṃḍirāja's father).
The temple was rebuilt and the arcadedsataḥstructures were added around the temple. Deva Śaṃśera Rāṇā donated funds for this.

event_name: Installation of a brass mouse sculpture
event_description: 16 friends of Haugala Tole in Patan donated the brass mouse installed on a marble pedestal during the reign of King Tribuvhan and Prime Minister Juddha Shamsere Rana.
The inscription has no date. Images of the donor family and their names are engraved on it.
HImāla Cement Factory donated a bell supported by a concrete stand (frame)This undated inscription mentions that the stand was built with the first bag of cement produced by the company.

event_description: In VS 2054, a water supply line was installed from Kirtipur to the Temple.

event_description: Syāmalāla donated the brass eaves board to cover the middle roof.

event_description: The brass door and tympanum were donated to the temple.
