event_description: The colophons of theVasudharādhāraṇīandĀryamaṇibhadrajambhalahṛdayascribed during the joint reign of Ratna Malla and Indra Malla, mention the Bāhāḥ.
Sākebhikṣu Jayadhamma (Śākyabhikṣu Jayadharma), his wife Nugulakṣmī and his other family members erected the above-mentioned three Caityas in front of the Bāhāḥ during the reign of Pratāpa Malla.

event_name: Land endowment and consecration of a Vajravārāhī statue
event_description: Śākyabhikṣu Jayadharma who constructed the above-mentioned three Caityas also made some land endowments to the Bāhāḥ and consecrated a statue of Vajravārāhī.
A damaged inscription is attached to the eastern wall of the Temple. Its contents remain unknown because it is heavily eroded.

The inscription records about the establishment of a Gaṇeśa statue in 1503 CE which is now in the sanctum of this Temple. Since the record shows that the Temple was built only in 1630 CE, it remains obscure where this statue was consecrated before that date.

As mentioned before, the statue of Manavināyaka Gaṇeśa was established in 1503 CE by a certain Hāku Bhāro. After 127 years of the placement of the Gaṇeśa statue, H (?) Bhāro from Vaṃthva Ṭola, Kirtipur built a new temple (probably replacing the one where the statue was consecrated). It is likely that H (?) Bhāro is a decedent of Hāku Bhāro.

An inscription from the time of Yoganarendra Malla records that Keśavarāja Bhāro installed a Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa statue in the month of Āṣāḍha in memory of his deceased wife Śakuntarāmayī.फल्चामा प्राप्त  योगनरेेन्द्र मल्लको शसनकालको अभिलेखमा नेसं ८२० (सन् १७००) मा केशवराज भारो र उनकी दीवंगत पत्नी शकुन्तरामयीको नाममा आषाढ महिनामा लक्ष्मीनारायणको मूर्ति स्थापना गरिएको थियो ।

The inscription notes that two months after the installation of the statue, in the month of Bhādra, a maṇḍapa (a 16-bayed quare phalcā, also called 'sohrakhuṭṭe') was constructed. It also mentions that land was granted to maintain the monument, with the income designated for the worship of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa and Valkhu Gaṇeśa, as well as for hosting a feast for Brahmins following the worship. Furthermore, the inscription instructs that lights should be lit in the Phalcā during the Matsyendranātha festival.मूर्ति स्थापनाको दुई महिना पश्चात् भदौमा मण्डप (फल्चा/सोह्रखुट्टे पटी) को निर्माण सम्पन्न गरिएको कुरा खुलाइएको छ । अभिलेखमा यस कृतिका खातिर जग्गा पनि छुट्याइएको र सोको आम्दानीले लक्ष्मीनारायण र वल्खुको गणेशलाई पूजा गरी ब्राह्मणलाई भोज खुवाउनुपर्ने थितिको उल्लेख छ । बुङ्गद्यः जात्राका दौरान पनि फल्चामा बत्ती बाली पुज्नुपर्ने कुराको उल्लेख छ ।

The Phalcā remained intact as built during the Late Malla period until the 1980s-90s, after which it was transformed into a concrete structure following a mutual agreement by the Jośī guṭhī. A shop now occupies the southeastern columns of the Phalcā, providing income for the guṭhī.उत्तरमध्यकालमा बनेको मन्दःफल्चा विसं २०४० को दशकसम्म सोही अवस्थामा थियो । पछि जोशी गुठीको आपसी सल्लाहमा फल्चालाई भत्काई कंक्रिडको संरचनामा रूपान्तरण गरिएको थियो । फल्चाको उत्तर-पूर्वी कुनामा एक कवलको पसल निकाली गुठीको आम्दानीका रूपमा प्रयोगमा ल्याइएको थियो ।

After falling into a dilapidated state, thedyaḥchẽwas first reconstructed in 1998 CE (VS 2055) through financial support collected from the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna, the then Village Development Committee, and local residents. The reconstruction was completed in 2019 CE (VS 2076).

On the occasion of the completion of the reconstruction of thedyaḥchẽand the adjoiningsataḥ, the inauguration ceremony was conducted under the auspices of literary scholar venerable Satyamohana Jośī. This was made possible through the sustained efforts of Dakṣiṇakālī Municipality and local residents.

As the inscription has already eroded, its content is unclear. However, ‘samvat 9(?)03 jyeṣṭha kṛṣṇa da’ can be deciphered. Both year and lunar day are unclear. But it probably is the 10th of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in 903, i.e., 1783 CE.
The plinths of the temple were renovated when the nearby Triśūla Sataḥ (PPK1216) was rebuilt by the Nepal Army.
According to Pruscha (1975, p. 258), the temple was renovated in 1940 CE (VS 1997), suggesting it may have been damaged in the 1934 earthquakes.

event_name: Addition of a statue and rebuilding of the monument
event_description: Govinda Maharjana, the seniormost member (thakali) of Bulu'sjyāpucommunity, installed a physical Bhairava statue, although, traditionally, such Bhairava temples only featured aniconic stone structures topped with stonetoraṇas. Later, the temple was dismantled and rebuilt on a concrete foundation, resulting in a reduced height.

As of October 2024, the temple is undergoing renovation with the financial support of the Bagmati Provincial Government. The simple columns from the previous construction are being replaced with ornate, carved wooden columns.

Local administrators who took the surname “Duvāra” have been there in Pāṃgā since the Malla period. This inscription at thepīṭhamentions that a certain Beṣārāma Bhāro Duvāla and Devarānimayī erected a Garuḍa pillar. Statues of the two are installed beneath the pillar.
A Viṣṇu statue was established at the temple premises by a Khatrī Kṣetrī family from Chobhar.
A bell was installed at the temple with the joint efforts of the Viṣṇudevī Committee and Khatrī Guṭhī.
A family from the Kaṭuvāla caste from Chobhar added a bell at the temple.

The dilapidated temple was dismantled after performing a worship of absolution (kṣamāpūjā) in 2011 CE (VS 2068). The temple was reconstructed with funds from the Kirtipur Municipality, Department of Archaeology, Guṭhī Saṃsthāna, and local donations in 2014 CE (VS 2071).
Līlā Śamśera constructed the temple in memory of his father Gehendra Śamśera and also offered a bell to Gehendramukteśvara Mahādeva.

Amara Siṃha Kumhara and his wife Kīrttimaṅgalā constructed the water spout (hiti) and aphalcā(public shelter) in memory of their deceased son. They also set up a trust supported by land endowments of 2.5ropanīs in Pāko and 5ropanīs in Aphala for their upkeep. The income from these land parcels was used to clear grass from thehitiandphalcāon the 1st solar day of Vaiśākha and to distributesamaybaji, a Newar food set including beaten rice, puffed rice, roasted meat balls, peas, soybeans, etc. Kīrttimaṅgalā was the second daughter of King Śrīnivāsa Malla. The couple is also known to have built the Kṛṣṇa temple (LAL1450) in the Ko Bāhāḥ Ṭola in 1680 CE (NS 800).
Thehiti’s intra-channel system was repaired, and a stone inscription was installed to commemorate the event.
Locals renovated thehitiand installed an Akṣobhya statue (LAL2421-003).

event_name: Construction of well and installation of biosand filter
event_description: As there was water shortage in the area, a local women’s group built a well south of thehitiand installed a biosand filter for water purification with support from the Urban Environment Management Society (UEMS).

This inscription records the restoration of thephalcāin 1980 which seems unlikely since at this time thephalcāwould not have been older than 7 years. It is possible that the inscription actually refers to the reconstruction of the Samay Phalca (LAL4317) that used to be located just to the south. Could it be that Samay Phalcā was demolished in the late 1970s and subsequently rebuilt in 1980 CE as Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā, about 10 metres further to the north?
Inscriptions on three marble panels (one of which is broken) attest to the restoration of thephalcā.The three marble panels were formerly attached to the outer western wall of thephalcā's extension.

In 2020, the Nāmasaṅgīti Phalcā was undergoing restoration once again. With the financial support of the Lalitpur Metropolitan City office, a new concrete pitched roof, covered withjhĩgaṭītiles, was added to the flat concrete slab roof, giving the structure a more traditional appearance. The concrete pillars were clad with newly madedāci apābricks.

A platform paved with terracotta bricks (teliyā) was constructed to serve as a venue for meetings of the five village elders (pañcasamūha). It can be assumed that such meetings took place in front of thephalcāduring the late Malla period, where elders convened to resolve local disputes.
A woodentoraṇawas added to the Gaṇeśa shrine by Bābu Siṃha Bhāro of Svahanani Ṭola.
Thephalcā'srestoration was commissioned by six individuals: Gopīrāja, Hāku, Vasūdeva, Motirāja, Lakṣmīsiṃha and Suṣuri.

Following its collapse, thephalcāwas restored in VS 1946 by Siddhisudharamātyaya from Bāliphaḥ Ṭola and Ratnakumāra Śreṣṭha from Nabahā Nani. Theguṭhīmembers did not contribute to the restoration. The inscription further stipulates that while any donor may restore thephalcā, no one may claim it as their property.
Parts of thephalcāwere replaced with brick walls and a slab on top. Members of theguṭhirebuilt thephalcāunder the guidance of Ṭākura Māna Śreṣṭha, a senior member of Cauthī Guṭhī.

event_name: Donation of strut (initial construction of the temple?)
event_description: The inscription probably documents the donation of the strut by Viṣṇu Māhāta (text: Viṣṇa Māhāta) in 1668 CE (NS 788), offering it as a dedication to Harisiddhi (text: Harasiddhi). Given that this inscription is the earliest known record associated with the temple, it's plausible that the temple itself might have been built during that same year. However, the precise connection between the temple and Harisiddhi, the deity enshrined in a temple situated approximately 8 kilometers southeast of the capital, remains unclear.

This probably is the record of the installation of the strut in 1685 CE (NS 805). The names of the donor and his father are mentioned in the inscription, but are unclear due to illegibility of the text.
Two struts bear the date NS 805. The name of the donor could not be deciphered. It is likely that the temple was restored in this year.

The names Toyukhvāla, Dhanamayaju and Lakṣmī are engraved on the base of the Kṛṣṇa statue (LAL0820-014). Small donor figures can be seen below the inscription. This undated statue likey belongs to the late-Malla period.
A resident from Taḥnani ̣Tola, Bṛṇathāka and Kṛṣṇalāla offered a bell to theśivaliṅga.
Sundharakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇalāla and Prithi Bahādura offered a brace plate and atoraṇato the deity. These are placed inside the sanctum on the occasion of thebhīmarathārohaṇaritual of Gaṅgālakṣmī.
The Municipality office and the C.D.H.P. (UMN) rebuilt the tank above the historic well and the Jaḥrũhiti near the temple with the help of locals.
Cirīmaĩ Ḍañgola constructed adharmadhātujinālaya caitya.

monument_name: Majāḥdegaḥ (built sometime between seventeenth and eighteenth century)
event_description: The four-layered plinths of Majādegaḥ were renovated by the Kirtipur Municipality.
Vāṇadeva, the son of Yaśodeva, established a Sūrya statue to fulfill his mother’s vow.

Bhājudhana Bhāro of Taṃgaḥ Ṭola renovated the Ādinārāyaṇa and Śiva temples in memory of his late wife, Dhana Thakunī. The Ādinārāyaṇa temple mentioned in the inscription likely refers to the present Hariśaṅkara temple. Similarly, the Śiva temple referred to in the inscription was probably theśikhara-style Śiva temple located south of the Hariśaṅkara temple.
Govindamāna installed a Garuḍa statue at the temple.

event_name: Renovation of the temple and installation of new Sūrya statue
event_description: Following the theft of the Sūrya statue dating back to 1083 CE (NS 203), Īśvaramāna Pradhāna from the Saugaḥ Ṭola established a new statue of Sūrya in memory of his deceased father, Govindamāna Pradhāna, while also renovating the temple on the occasion.
Candrabhakteśvara was constructed by Kṛṣṇa Bahādura Rāṇā, the younger sibling of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.यसको निर्माण जङ्गबहादुर राणाका काइँला भाइ कृष्ण बहादुर राणाले निर्माण गरेको थियो ।

Following the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS), numerous Śivālayas suffered severe damage. The Paśupatī Area Development Trust has undertaken the reconstruction of the dilapidated Śivālayas in 2019 CE (2076 VS).विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्पमा धैरै शिवालयहरूलाई क्षति पुर्याएको थियो । भूकम्पले जीर्ण बनाएको यस शिवालयको पुनर्निर्माण विसं २०७६ (सन् २०१९) मा पशुपति क्षेत्र विकास कोषले गरको थियो ।
A group of Avāles led by Kula Bhāro and Lakṣmīsiṃha Bhāro built thesataḥafter dismantling an oldphalcāat this site in 1751 CE. They also donated 68mohorcoins (mohara-rūpaiyā) to finance its upkeep.
Lalitpur Municipality donated 12,000 Nepalese Rupees and ca. 25,000 Nepalese Rupees were collected from local donors for the restoration of thesataḥ.

Thesataḥwas rebuilt with support from the Bhindyaḥlāchi Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, the Lalitpura Vikāsko Lāgi Samāja, the Indian Embassy, and the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City. The Indian Embassy donated 5,985,000 Nepali Rupees and local donations amounted to about 1,000,000 Nepali Rupees. Thesataḥ wasinaugurated on 2 July 2016 CE by H.E. Shri Ranjit Rae, the Indian ambassador to Nepal.
Indu Gautama reconstructed the water spout, wishing for the salvation for her late husband Rāmacandra Gautama.

event_name: The earliest mention of the Tokhā Taleju
event_description: The incident in which Jayadeva Pvaha of Banepa seized gold kept in the Tokhā fort (Taleju), prompting a rebellion by the Tokhā fort against him, constitutes the earliest historical evidence attesting to the antiquity of Tokhā Taleju.बनेपाका जयदेव प्वहले तोखा किल्ला (तलेजु) मा राखिएको सुन लिएको हुँदा तोखा किल्लाले उनीविरुद्ध विद्रोह गरेको थियो । यो नै तोखा तलेजुको ऐतिहासिकता पुष्टि गर्ने सबभन्दा पुरानो प्रमाण हो ।
The Talejudyaḥchẽunderwent restoration during the tenure of Bhāilāla Śreṣṭha asmūla-nāike.भाइलाल श्रेष्ठ तलेजुको मूलनाइके हुँदा तलेजु द्यःछेँको जीर्णोद्धार गरिएको थियो ।

A major reconstruction of the Taleju Dyaḥchẽ was carried out by the Department of Archaeology at a cost of NPR 6.75 million.पुरातत्त्व विभागले रु. ६७ लाख ५० हजार खर्च गरेर तलेजु द्यःछेँको पुनर्निर्माण गरेको थियो ।

event_name: Offering a jalaharī for the śivaliṅga (object no. NWK0800-006)
event_description: Raṇakumārīdevī offered thejalaharībase for theśivaliṅga(object no. NWK0800-006) established on the southeastern corner of the sanctum.

Kṛṣṇalāla Śreṣṭha offered the copper canopy (ilāṃ) to theśivaliṅgarevered as Candrabhāneśvara Mahādeva. Kṛṣṇalāla originally hailed from Gāḥ Bāhāḥ, Lalitpur, but moved to Triśūlībajāra later and made the offering together with his wife Kṛṣṇamāyā, and sons Kṛṣṇagovinda, Prāṇagovinda, Lālagovinda, and daughter Kṛṣṇamāyā.

event_name: Installation of a new Buddha statue
event_description: When thieves tried to steal the statue of Akṣobhya from the temple, the idol broke down into pieces and the thieves ran away. Later in 2008 CE, locals installed a new statue of the deity.

According to local residents, the temple was built by the ancestors of Śaṅkhalāla Śreṣṭha. As there is no record of the construction of the temple, it is not possible to say on what date this temple was built. Looking at the structure and style of the temple, it can be inferred that it was built during the Rana period.

The eroded inscription on the upper part of pillar three (MUG0030-003) allows a partial reading. The date '1404' has been identified. Since most inscriptions from western Nepal are dated using the Śaka era, this date should correspond to 1482 CE.
The inscription on the temple’s eaves board indicates that the temple was restored in 1881 CE (VS 1938).

Thedharmastambhawas installed at the southeastern corner of the temple by Kavi Prasāda Gautama as part of his wider campaign of Rāma- and Kṛṣṇa-devotion in the Kathmandu Valley and beyond. The inscription instructs that devotional singing (bhajana-kīrtana) should be performed annually on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.

Astone pillar(SAG0010-008) has been erected directly in front of this temple, and alion statueis installed on top of it. Aninscriptionis carved on one side of the pillar. The date carved in the inscription, 'Sambata 2010' (VS 2010), is clear, but the other details are illegible, so the rest of the information mentioned in it is unknown.
Gaṅgā Prasāda Dhaugoḍā of Sā̃gā, along with Arjuna, Acyuta, and Śivaprasāda, offered bells to the goddess.

event_name: Offering of a bell and stone pillar
event_description: In memory of his father Mohanalāla Daṅgola, his mother Aṣṭamāyā, and his wife Nānīmāyā Daṅgola, Gaṇeśa Bahādura Daṅgola of Sā̃gā offered a bell and stone pillar to the temple.

According to the inscribed stone slab (śilāpatra), the temple was constructed in 1838 CE (VS 1895) by Balabhañjana Pāṇḍe, who held the rank ofsardārat the time. The inscription records that Balabhañjana not only built this temple but also established asattal(rest house),phalchā(public shelter),hiti(stone water spout), pond, surrounding wall, gateways, and several other shrines in the area. The motivation behind his extensive building activity at this location remains a subject of interest. His father, Bhotu Pāṇḍe, was likewise an active figure in the construction of religious structures and the establishment ofguthis(religious endowments) across the Kathmandu Valley. The inscription also mentions the arrangements made for the temple’s maintenance, including grass-cutting, cleaning, and the payment of land taxes from the revenues of the endowed lands.

Sixty-eight years after the construction of this temple and its associated structures, the Pāṇḍe family added a new doorway to the Gokarṇeśvara temple and stipulated that its future maintenance should be carried out using the endowment of the Vāṇeśvara estate.
The monument was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.

The east wing was completely dismantled and rebuilt between 2018-2021. Project funding was provided by the Hainan Province Cihang Foundation, China. The project was jointly implemented by the Department of Archaeology and the UNESCO, Kathmandu Office, and executed by the Bjrayogini Chaughera Sattal Nirmaan Upabhoka Samiti.

event_name: Rebuilding of the west and north wing
event_description: In December 2021, the west and north wings were dismantled. Work on new foundations for the western wing is in progress (Dec 2021)

event_name: Repair of the phalcā and establishment of a library
event_description: The descendants of the donor family and other people repaired the Sarāḥ Phalcā and established the Aloka library of Ikhachen.
The building was severely damaged in the 2015 earthquakes. The roof was badly damaged and four corner struts collapsed. Three of them were preserved in the library, while one has been lost.

event_name: Collection of funds for the restoration
event_description: Lalitpur Metropolitan City office provided seven Lakh Rupees for the monument's reconstruction. The descendants of the donor family added fifty thousand Rupees, however, this amount was not sufficiet for the work to begin. The Metropolitan City office has promised to provide an additional three Lakh Rupees.

In the 2022-2024 restoration, the floor plan was expanded to encompass the full width and length of the previously L-shaped building. Additionally, a second floor was added, topped with a flat, steel-reinforced concrete roof. Thus, the style (typology) of the building was transformed from aphalcato asataḥ.
The stone slab inscription likely commemorates the initial construction of thebāhāḥ. However, the inscription remains undecipherable due to heavy erosion.
Due to a thick layer of enamel paint, only the year (NS793) and the name of the donor’s granddaughter, Bhavāṇi (Bhavānī Mayi), remain decipherable.

event_name: Renovation of the Śikharakūṭa Caitya and construction of the Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya
event_description: Caityamāyā and her daughter Dhanamāyā constructed a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (KAT0960-005) and renovated the Śikharakūṭa Caitya (KAT0960-006).
Decedents of thebāhāḥ’s founder carried out minor renovation work in VS 2069 (2012 CE).

During the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla, thephalcāwas facilitated by a person called Anantadhara. A statue of Garuḍanārāyaṇa was established by making a podium (shrine) behind thephalcā. Anantadhara enforced the construction to fulfill the wish that the soul of his deceased father, Viṣṇudhara, would ascend to heaven. The inscription also records the donation of a piece of land to finance the annual rituals (varṣavardhanapūjā).
The Kirtipur Municipality reconstructed the phalcā and the attached shrine in 2020 CE. Only the stone plinth is original.

Kirtipur Municipality reconstructed Gaḥsi Phalcā in 2021 CE. Before the reconstruction, only a rectangular plinth had remained for decades (no other remnants of the Phalcā were found). Even senior members of the locality do not recall whether a completephalcāwas standing here in their lifetime. This suggests that the Phalcā had already ceased to exist before the 1934 earthquakes. It probably collapsed in the previous great earthquakes and was never rebuilt.

The marble inscription mentions that the Hiti was built by the Pradhāna Pañca, Harṣadāsa Amātya and Grāmina Janasahajoga. Even the inscription mentions the building of the Hiti but it was just the act of renovation.
The stone inscription nearby the Gaṇeśa statue records some names, but it is not clear what these people actually did.
Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's wife Putalīdevī built the temple in 1861 CE (VS 1918). However, it is unclear from the inscription who she dedicated the temple to.

This inscription installed inside the Gaṇeśa shrine opposite to the Navadurgā Mandira predates others, but only part of it remains legible, indicating '853caitrakṛṣṇaaṣṭamī'(the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Caitra in NS 853).यो अभिलेख मन्दिर अगाडि रहेको गणेश देवालय (shrine) भित्र रहेको छ । अधिकांश अक्षरहरू नबुझिने भइसके तापनि अभिलेखको तल्लो भागमा '८५३ चैत्र कृष्ण अष्टमी' पढ्न सकिन्छ ।
This inscription records the temple's renovation and the pavement of its premises with bricks.नेसं ८८८ (सन् 1768) मा यस मन्दिरको जीर्णोद्धार गरिनुका साथै मन्दिर परिसरमा इँटा छापिएको थियो ।

The temple underwent restoration led by the community trust named 'Śrī Nātheśvara (Nāṭyeśvara) Guṭhī,' financed by the Ministry of Local Development.लक्ष्मीदास महर्जनको अध्यक्षतामा गठित जीर्णोद्धार समितिले विसं २०४३ मा श्री नाथेश्वर (नाथ्येश्वर) गुठी र स्थानीय विकास मन्त्रालयको आर्थिक सहयोगमा मन्दिरको जीर्णोद्धार सम्पन्न गरिएको थियो ।

A metal bell was offered in memory of Rāma Bahādura Malla of the Guccā Ṭola by his descendants Bābukāji (Nārāyaṇa) Malla, Lilādebī, Nabinā Rājabhaṇḍārī, Kalpanā Vaidya and others.गुच्चा टोलका राम बहादुर मल्लको सम्झनामा उनका सन्तती बाबुकाजि (नारायण) मल्ल लिलादेबी, नबिना राजभण्डारी, कल्पना वैद्य आदिले अजिमालाई धातुको घण्टा चढाएको थियो ।
Minor renovation of the Guthi Chẽ 2 was carried out by the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna after the 2015 earthquakes.
The stonetoraṇawas installed inside the Caithū Vajradhātu Caitya’s eastern niche by Mānasiṃha Bhāro.
Hiraṇyagarbhakumārī, Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā's principal wife, built the temple of Hemagirinandinībhakteśvara in honor of her sister Hemagirinandinī.

event_name: Construction of a sataḥ and installation of a Nārāyaṇa statue
event_description: This inscription is not related to the Chinnamastā Pīṭha. It records that residents of Mvaḥmadugalli, Dathutaḥjhyāḥ called Rāma and Harirāma Bhāro commissioned asataḥand installed a Nārayaṇa statue here along with their family members.

Vaṃśā Rāutta, his father Bābu Narasiṃha, his wife Maijulakṣmī, and his sons Nandalāla, Jujulāla, Kājilāla, Tulasīlāla and Candralāla offered a brasstoraṇato the Pīṭha. All are residents of Mvaḥmadugallī.

The inscription records that the late Matīraja, Bālagopāla, and a son of Mātā Helathakũ and his wife, sons (Vidyālāla and Lakṣmīlāla) and daughters (Gaṅgāmāyā and Gaṇeśamāyā) made offerings of a brasstoraṇa, stone line, silver water vessel and so forth to the Chinnamastā Pīṭha.

Ghanaśyāma Rājakarṇikāra and his wife Bindrā, both residents of Haugala Ṭola, replaced the old bell which was hanging on a Rāṇā-period pillar erected in the Pīṭha's premises with a new one in NS 1131.
The structure covering the Pīṭha was renovated in VS 2058 with the support of a committee (Śrī Chinnamastā Jorṇoddhāra tathā Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti) formed to renovate and protect the Pīṭha.

This inscription, originally set in the wall of the nearby Goḍā Gaṇeśa temple, has been moved to this circular site. Dated 1949 CE (NS 1069), it records that Gaurīlakṣmī Pradhāna, a daughter-in-law from Kathmandu’s Thamel and originally from Pharping, built two "waterholes"—one large and one small—at this location. Having grown up locally, she understood the area’s water scarcity and constructed these "waterholes," while also donating land to a religious trust. The "waterholes" mentioned in the inscription likely refer to the two ponds noted. Elderly locals recall water consistently seeping from the banks, naturally filling the ponds. The term "waterholes" in the inscription seems to reflect this natural replenishment, akin to how waterholes function.

Following its collapse in the 1934 earthquakes, the Temple was rebuilt in its current form. The corrugated metal sheets that were used to cover the ambulatory outside the sanctum and the pillars that supported it have now been removed.
The inscription has eroded beyond readability and does not provide any historical information.
The temple is currently being reconstructed with funding from the Bidur Municipality.

An entry in athyāsaphūmanuscript chronicles Mādheju’s offering of the finial to Tāmraliṃga in Goro, a derivative of Gvala, the vernacular name of Devapattana. Mādheju was the elder brother of Cikuti, an influential courtier during the medieval period.

Due to neglect, the temple had fallen into disrepair but underwent restoration by the Department of Archaeology, in collaboration with the Pashupati Area Development Trust. During this renovation, the traditional roofing tiles were replaced with copper sheets.

event_name: Beginning of the initial construction of the Temple and caugharā sataḥ
event_description: Bhājurāma, who was born on the lineage of the sage Kaśyapa started the construction of this Temple in order to consecrate avāṇaliṅgain the sanctum. He also started the construction thecaugharāḥ sataḥon the same date,which encircles the Temple from all four sides.

event_name: Completion of the Temple and consecration of a Vāṇaliṅga
event_description: The construction of the Temple commissioned by Bhājurāma was completed in three years. The Temple was formally opened after consecrating the Vāṇaliṅga in its sanctum.
Bājurāma, the founder of the Temple offered the trident to the deity, which is erected in front of the northern façade of the Temple.

Upon the completion of the Temple, Bhājurāma had endowed several plots of land to sponsor many religious activities at the Temple such as for performing the daily rituals, organizing its anniversary celebration, making a fire oblation, lighting amahādīpaon the day ofŚivarātrī, caretaking thecaugharāsataḥand offeringpiṇḍa(cooked rice-ball) to him after his death.

event_name: Reconstruction of the Temple and concecration of a new liṅga after the old one was stolen
event_description: The Temple had fallen into disrepair due to lack of proper care and maintenance and had become a latrine. The descendants of Bhājurāma commissioned the reconstruction of the Temple in 2006 CE. The originalśivaliṅgaof crystal was stolen and has now been replaced by a new one.

Dhara Bhāro and his wife Chi Thaṃku, residents of Ikhāchẽ Ṭola, initiated the construction of the Sataḥ in 1836 CE (NS 956). After the construction, the donor couple also established aguṭhīto light butter lamps in the nearby Ālko Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL0991) on the 13thday of the bright fortnight in Bhādra.
The first floor of the Sataḥ was temporarily used by a kindergarten, but this closed down after few years.
The Municipality provided Rupees 16 Lakhs to reconstruct the Sataḥ. The rest was locally fundraised.
A statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa was established inside Ālko Sataḥ.
Nandakumārī, along with her sons Tulsībhakta, Vedabhakta, Ādibhakta, and Haṃsabhakta, had offered the gilt copper finial during the premiership of Vīra Śamśera.
The bell offered by Devanārāyaṇa Nāpita in 1907 CE (NS 1027) broke in 1963 CE (VS 2020). Thus, it was repaired.
Tīrtha Praśād Karmācārya offered thetoraṇaplaced above the aniconic stone in the sanctum.
Bhāṣkara Bodha Miśra and his other family members offered a metalpatāḥto the Temple.
It was completely demolished and rebuilt with the financial support from the Bhaktapur Municipality and donations from local residents.

event_name: Replacing traditional tile-roof with brass sheets
event_description: Āśālāla Śreṣṭha from Cochẽ, Cīnīkājī Śreṣṭha from Bāgbazar and Jñāna Prasāda Karmācārya from Rabibhavan replaced the traditional tile-roof with brass sheets.
Kṛṣṇa Prasāda Pulā̃che offered it to the Temple in memory of his father Jīvana Prasāda Pulā̃che and mother Rāmapyārī Pulā̃che.
Pāhā̃ Bāhāḥ and avajradhātu caityawere constructed by Kanaka, Bhĩsĩ and Śākemuni. Lands were granted to the structures to fund the observance of various religious activities.
A new sanctum was made for thebāhāḥby the owner of a private house.
In 2018, while digging a trench to fix an underground pipeline for the Melamchi drinking water project, the boundary wall of thebāhāḥcollapsed, killing an elderly man.
Jayapāla (text: Jayapāra) offered a strut to be installed on the main building of thebāhāḥ.

event_name: Pavement of the courtyard with floor tiles
event_description: Rāmadeva and Dharmarāja of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ laid floor tiles (cikaṃaḥpā) at thebāhāḥpremises during the reign of King Pārthivendra Malla. Śākyabhikṣu Dharmmasiṃ, Rupādeva, Jayadhanasiṃ, and Daivajña Viśvarāja had also provided financial assistance for it.

event_name: Offering of a pair of lions
event_description: A person named Muni offered a pair of lions.
Mahāratna and his wife Lakṣmī established adharmadhātujinālayacaityaat thebāhāḥpremises wishing for the heavenly abode of Sukhāvatī Bhuvana to his deceased elder brother Caturaratna.
Śākyabhikṣunī Kāle Thakuṃ, along with her son and daughter-in-law installed a balustrade of oil lamps in front of the sanctum.
Śākyabhikṣu Buddharatna of the Kuṃchẽ clan installed gilded cover on the door of the sanctum wishing for the heavenly abode of Sukhāvatī Bhuvana to his deceased parents Jujuvirasiṃ Bhānithakuṃ.
Together with his family, Śākyabhikṣu Dānaratna of the Kuṃchẽ clan of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ established aśikharakūṭacaityaat thebāhāḥpremises.
Together with 26 members of his family, Śākyabhikṣu Dānaratna of the Kuṃchẽ clan of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ installed a gildedtoraṇaon top of the entrance to thebāhāḥ’s sanctum.
Together with 13 members of his family, Jogaratna of the Kuṃchẽ clan of Naḥghaḥ Bāhāḥ installed seven brass windows in the name of his parents Śākyabhikṣu Dānavirasiṃ and Dhīralakṣmī.
The family members of Jogaratna renovated the windows of the Bāhāḥ in the course of its reconstruction.
The monastic building was reconstructed with thebāhāḥ’s funds and financial assistance from the Kathmandu Metropolis.
Maheśa Śākya, Sureśa, Suvāśa, Śrīrāja, and Prajvala offered a new woodentoraṇaafter thetoraṇaon top of the entrance to thebāhāḥcourtyard was stolen.
Due to the poor condition of the Phalcā, it was rebuilt. Traditional architecture of the Phalcā was replaced by modern construction materials in the course of the reconstruction.
The original Bhairava-Viṣṇu statue in the sanctum was stolen.
The Kailāśa Badrīnātha Prabṛti Nijī Guṭhī, a private trust associated with the temple, installed a new statue to replace the stolen one.
The temple was built by Māhilā Dulahī. Although it is unclear who Māhilā Dulahī is, she was likely the wife of Jaṅga Bahādura.
The upper part of the tower fell down during the earthquake of April 2015.

Bhaktapur municipality carried out the reconstruction of the temple damaged in the devastating earthquake of April 2015.  The newly rebuilt temple had been inaugurated by Prema Suvāla, parliamentary member and secretary of the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party. On the occasion, Rāma Kṛṣṇa Tvāynāy, chairperson of the Kedārnātha temple reconstruction consumers committee, which took care of the reconstruction, handed the symbolic key of the temple to mayor Sunila Prajāpati.
Hemamukteśvara was built in honor of Antarī Mahārānī Hemakumārī, who was one of the formal wives of Rāṇā Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura.
Locals of Sunaguthi collected donations to fund the reconstruction of the monument. Mohangopal Dangol donated funds for the copper roof, carved struts, windows and all other wooden materials.

Reconstruction began on the 8th day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa in VS 2067 after residents had performedkṣamāpūjā. The locals formed a committee for the reconstruction work. Technical supervision was provided by the Department of Archaeology in Nepal.

event_name: Covering roof with gilt sheet and installation of finial
event_description: Rāmaprasāda and his brother Lālabahādura Śreṣṭha (bothi residents of Asana) replaced the upper roof of jhĩgaṭī tiles with gilt metal sheets. They also added a gilt finial to the roof's peak.

Dīrghalakṣmī Kũvara, the second wife of Balabhadra's brother Vīrabhadra, established Dīrghabhakteśvara Mahādeva in her and her son Hemamukteśvara Mahādeva's name. She also built this Sataḥ facing the river.

Dīrghalakṣmī Kũvara endowed over 360ropanīs of land parcels and documented the religious trust’s income and responsibilities in an 1881CE inscription. In 1851 CE (VS 1907), Bamabahādura Kũvara, a brother of Jaṅgabahādura, erected a distinctive temple along the banks of the Bāgamatī, known as Tīnadevala (KAT2670). Atāmrapatra(copper-plate) discovered at the site records the simultaneous establishment of the Jagannātha temple (KAT2690). This inscription, installed after the completion of the temple constructions, mentions the surrounding boundary wall and stipulates its repair and maintenance funded throughguṭhīrevenue, indicating the concurrent construction of this gate.

After the 2015 CE earthquake (VS 2072), which inflicted damage upon Tinadevala and various other monuments, the boundary wall also deteriorated significantly. The restoration initiatives for both the wall and gate were led by the Bāgamatī Civilization Integrated Development Committee, functioning under the Ministry of Urban Development, with assistance from the Asian Development Bank. The renovation project reached its completion on October 23rd, 2022 CE.

Pātravaṃśa Hariśaṃkara, along with his mother Rukmanilakṣmī and wife Devīśvarīlakṣmī, from the Tavajhyāra Ṭola, constructed the temple. The inscription, embedded in the northern wall of the temple, further reveals that the donors invited King Yoganarendra Malla of Patan to inspect the temple and other nearby structures. It also documents the installation of statues of other deities, including Bhairava and Halāhala Lokeśvara, as well as the construction of two stone platforms providing shade in the vicinity. The inscription acknowledges the contributions of astrologer Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, and other individuals such as Guruvācārya Govinda and Sūryarāma, in the successful completion of these constructions.
Saṃkrabābu Bhāro, a resident of the Bhansāra Ṭola, built thecaityaduring the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla. He also donated land to set up a trust for carrying out worships at thecaitya.
The stone statue of Ratnasambhava, housed in the southern niche, was stolen on March 1, 2023.

event_description: Dharmarāja Śākya and his wife Lakṣmīmāyā installed statues of Aparamitā and Prajñāpāramitā.

In the early 1990s, the traditionalphalcāwas demolished and replaced with a concrete structure featuring a sloped, tiled roof.
The Godawari Municipality undertook a restoration project, rebuilding thephalcāin its original traditional style.

The inventory published in 1982 CE (VS 2039) records that it was built in 1816–17 (VS 1873) by a person named Jayadutha (Inventory VS 2039, p.165). It is unclear what source this information is based on, as no additional details or surname are provided. As such, it is not possible to determine his lineage or community. A family from Sitapāla visits the Śivālaya next to the sataḥ four times a year to perform a special pūjā. It is believed that Jayadutha may be their ancestor.

After the upper floor collapsed during the 2015 earthquake, a single-storey structure was built, incorporating the two remaining old columns. A family with the Nagarkoti surname, who had been living there for decades, took the initiative to reconstruct the one-storey rectangular room at their own expense.

The Gorakhpur queen, one of Jaṅga Bahādura's many queens, facilitated the construction of the Sataḥ and the Gopāla Mandir (KAT2810) six years after her husband's death. D. Vajrācārya(VS 2030, 596-597) reads the inscription on thejaḥdhuṃ(LAL1360-008) as ‘om saṃvat..... mātā’.R. Jośī(VS 2065, 12-13) reads the last word ‘mātā’as the number ‘eight’ and suggests that thejaḥdhuṃwas constructed in NS 8.S. Parājulī(VS 2068, 157) believes that the inscription is related to the nearby Chinnamastā shrine.हिति परिसरको पेटीमै गाभिएको एक जःधुं हितिमा (LAL1360-008) यो अभिलेख कुँदिएको छ जसमा ‘ऊँ संवत्......, माता........’लेखिएको छ (D. VajrācāryaVS 2030, 596-597) । दुई पंक्तिमा र्दुई शब्दमात्र परेको यो अभिलेखको भाव बुझ्न निकै कठिन छ ।S. Parājulī(VS 2068, 157) ले मङ्गः हिति नजिकै शाक्त सम्प्रदायकी दश मातृका देवीहरूमध्येकी देवी छिन्नमस्ताको मन्दिर रहेकोले यस हिति परिसरमा अवस्थित उक्त जधुं लिच्छविकालको अन्तिमताका सुरुवात भएको ऊँ सवत् को संवत् १० मा छिन्नमस्ता देवीलाई लक्षित गरी स्थापना गरेको हुनुपर्ने अनुमान गरेकी छिन् । त्यसैगरीR. Jośī(VS 2065, 12-13) ले उत्कीर्ण ‘माता’ शब्द लाई अङ्क आठका रूपमा बुझी नेसं आठतिर यो जःधुं निर्माण भएको बताएका छन्  ।

The inscription provides details related to the erection of thestambha. It states that Pratāpa Malla offered six golden pinnacles and a golden umbrella adorned with amālāto his tutelary deity, Taleju Māju. The inscription also mentions his act of lighting 100,000 butter lamps and the creation of statues in gold, representing himself, his consorts, and his sons, with the wish of a favorable rebirth. Additionally, the inscription documents a land endowment of 4ropanīat Dharmasthalī, accompanied by instructions for the pillar's upkeep, including anointing it with 3pāthīof oil sourced from the income generated by the endowed land.
The pillar collapsed in the 1934 earthquake and was subsequently restored, although the precise timeline of its reconstruction is not known.

Śyāmakṛṣṇa Maharjana offered a bell at the temple in the name of his deceased mother Bhuyu Maharjana, who passed away in 1983 CE.
On the occasion of the birthday of Rāmaśaraṇa Maharjana, his father Rāmeśvara Maharjana offered an ornamented arch (toraṇa) of metal on top of the entrance to the sanctum.

Saṃyacā Saṃgata, son of Indramāna and Harimāyā Saṃgata, offered a pair of brass flags installed on either side of the main deity. He also offered a metaltoraṇaon top of the Gaṇeśa statue and established a pair of lions flanking the statue. Likewise, he offered a metal statue to be placed as a cover for the stone statue.
Rekhā Śreṣṭha (Vaidya) set ceramic tiles on the walls inside the sanctum in memory of her deceased father Tārānanda Vaidya.
Guruvācāryya Baktabārasĩ, along with his wife Subhadrā and son Keśava, dedicated the renovation of thephalcāto the deity Triliṅgeśvara Mahādeva (LAL0250).

The dilapidatedphalcāwas renovated for a total amount of Rupees 240,432. The Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided Rs. 2 lakh and the remaining amount was collected through local fundraising. After the renovation, new statues of Sarasvatī and Bhīmsena were installed in the niches.

Above the doorway of thedevalahousing theKvāḥpā Dyaḥthere is a woodentoraṇabearing the inscription “Śrī Ratnapura Mahāvihāra 1981 (VS)” corresponding to 1924–25 CE. Although the inscription itself does not fully express the circumstances of the construction, the descendants of Ratnākara maintain that they possess oral knowledge transmitted from their grandfather regarding the establishment of thebāhāḥ. According to this tradition, their ancestor Ratnākara was a gold merchant who constructed thisbāhāḥbehind his residence and named it after himself.क्वाःपाःद्यः भएको देवलको ढोकामाथि काँठको तोरण छ । यस तोरणमा ‘श्री रत्नपुर महाविहार १९८१’ लेखिएको छ । अभिलेखको अपूर्ण वाक्यले पूर्ण भाव अभिव्यक्ति नगरे तापनि रत्नाकरका पनातिहरू बाहाःको निर्माणबारे ज्ञात भएको बताउछन् । उनीहरूसँग मौखिक रूपमा बाजेबाट सुनाइएको पूर्ण जानकारी भएको दाबी गर्छन् । तिनका जिजुबाजे रत्नाकर सुन व्यापारी भएको र उनले घर पछाडि आफ्नै नाममा यो बाहाः खडा गरेका थिए ।

Outside thedevalahousing the image of Akṣobhya stands a pair of lion sculptures bearing the name “Ratnākara.” The sculptures record only the name of the founder and do not include a date. Since such lion figures typically form an integral architectural component of the shrine, it is likely that they were installed at the same time as the construction of thebāhāḥin 1924–25 (VS 1981).अक्षोभ्यको मूर्ति राखिएको देवल बाहिर एक जोडा सिंहप्रतिमा छन् जसमा ‘रत्नाकर’ लेखिएको छ । यस बाहाःका नर्माताको मात्र नाम परी यसमा मिति उल्लेख भएको छैन । देवलमा एकै अङ्गको रूपमा द्वारपालका प्रतिमा निर्माण हुने भएकाले यो बाहाःसँगै विसं १९८१ (सन् १९२४-२५) मै बनेको बुझिन्छ ।

An inscription is also present on the Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya (KAT2220-004) associated with the shrine of Akṣobhya, although the portion containing the date is no longer legible. The descendants of the founder state that thiscaityawas added only after the construction of the bāhāḥ in 1924–25 CE (VS 1981). On the pedestal of the caitya, small sculpted figures representing members of the founder’s family have been carved, along with their names.अक्षोभ्यको मूर्ति रहेको धर्मधातु जिनालय चैत्य (KAT2220-004) मा अभिलेख छ तर मिति भएको भाग पढ्न सकिएको छैन । यो विसं १९८१ (सन् १९२४-२५) मा बाहाः निर्माणपछि मात्र थपिएको जानकारी निर्माताका सन्तान बताउछन् । चैत्यको वेदीका भागमा निर्माताका परिवार सदस्यहरूको साना प्रतिमा निर्माण गरी तिनको नाम पनि कुँदिएका छन् ।

In 2024 CE (VS 2080), stone paving was laid in the courtyard of thebāhāḥusing funds provided by the Kathmandu Metropolitan City.हालसालै विसं २०८० (सन् २०२४) मा काठमाडौं महानगरको बजेटबाट बाहाः परिसरमा ढुङ्गा विछ्याउने कार्य भएको छ ।

Thejhĩgaṭītile roof of the Phalcā was dismantled and replaced with a concrete slab. The replacement was carried out with financial assistance from the local ward office while the locals contributed with voluntary labor.
As items required for rescue operations during natural disasters are stored at the Phalcā, metal bars were installed on the Phalcā for the security of the items.
Kiṣṇa (Kṛṣṇa) Maharjana and his wife Tuyu (Lakṣmīdevī) living in Lukusi Ṭolaestablished this monastery (vihāra) after performing anahorātrasacrifice.
Kiṣṇa (Kṛṣṇa) Maharjana and his wife Tuyu (Lakṣmīdevī) also donated this Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya.

The inscription, which predates the current building by over two centuries, mentions the installation of a wooden pillar. This suggests a prior structure on the site that likely collapsed over time. Motirāja may have incorporated remnants of this earlier building into the new construction.
This inscription records Motirāja constructing the arcaded platform and consecrating a statue of Bhavāniśaṅkara during the reign of King Jitāmitra Malla.

The temple suffered a collapse during the devastating earthquake of 1934 CE. Subsequently, the gilded statue of Mahāviṣṇu was relocated to Nāsaḥ Cuka, where it remains to this day (as of January 2023 CE).

Following its collapse in the destructive earthquake of 1934 CE, the temple underwent a reconstruction process that resulted in a two-tiered structure. A photograph of the temple in its two-storied form was published by Pruscha (1975, p. 54).

In the early 2000s, plans were initiated to restore the temple to its pre-1934 CE form. The collaborative efforts of the Department of Archaeology and the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust led to the temple's reconstruction in its original three-tiered design. During this process, plain struts were integrated, and wooden components such as columns and windows were meticulously carved. Despite initial intentions to relocate the Mahāviṣṇu statue from Nāsaḥ Cuka to its original sanctum, a decision was made to establish a new statue at the Mahāviṣṇu Mandira instead.
Viṣṇuvilāsa Vajrācārya and Jñānamāyā Vajrācārya of Makhaṃ Bāhāḥ installed the dalū lampstand all around the monastic building.
Viṣṇuvilāsa Vajrācārya (Nātī Gurju) and Jñānamāyā Vajrācārya installed the statue of Mañjuśrī.

event_name: Lãpu Chāygu (refurbishment of the main statue)
event_description: Every twelve years, the clay statue of Dīpaṅkara, who is the main deity of the Bāhāḥ, is refurbished. The family performing daily rituals here used to sponsor the refurbishment locally known as lãpu chāygu . In 2011 CE, a grand ceremony was held to raise funds for the statue's refurbishment.

Yogamatī, the daughter of King Yoganarendra Malla donated this temple in memory of her father. The inscription mentions that the 31 queens of King Yoganarendra Malla performedsatī(self-immolation) after his death.
The temple collapsed completely. The central tower was shortened when it was rebuilt (Korn2014, 49).
The temple suffered severe damage with large cracks showing in the stone masonry. Parts of the first floor balcony level show movement outward.
Two bands of stainless steel collars were installed around the first floor balcony to counteract any outward movement.

The Department of Archaeology (DoA) with financial support from UNESCO and technical guidance from John Sanday and Wolfgang Korn decided to dismantle the northern part of the tower, including the two corner pavilions to uproot apipaltree.The lintel above the arcade was replaced and the tower was rebuilt in cement mortar. In the photo, taken by Rich Pfau, the temple can be seen under the renovation project (psroundsimaging.com/Rich Pfau).
The temple completely collapsed during the 2015 CE earthquake.

The Municipality formed a users’ committee, a Kārya Saṃcālana Samiti, to oversee the reconstruction work in 2016 CE (VS 2073), and released Rs 1, 28, 62,213 (Bhaktapur Municipality). The work was completed in 2020 CE (VS 2077).

The only inscription related to this temple is on the bell's surface which is hung in the bell stand at the lower plinth. It mentions the offering of an initial bell by King Bhūpatindra Malla on the second day of the bright half of Manśira, 1699 CE.[1]He had performedkotyāhutioblation on this occasion.  Generally, kotyahuti oblation is performed in front of the temple after completion of the construction.Exactly on the same day (second day of the bright half of the Manśira), the annual ritual of this temple is observed in the present as well, which is considered as the anniversary of the monument. Thus, it can be assumed that the initial construction of this temple was finished on this date. TheNepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalīalso mentions this date as the finishing date of the temple's construction.Footnotes^MistakenlyGutschow(2014, 33) has converted the date NS 820 Mārgaśira to January 1700.
The bell inscription records that the bell offered earlier by King Bhūpatindra Malla was broken and a new bell was offered again in 1721 CE.
Half of the temple collapsed in the 1934 CE earthquake.
The temple was rebuilt after the 1934 CE earthquake.
The statue of Mahākāla was installed on the northern wall of the Bahī.

event_name: Reference to Bahī as Kāmukanāma Mahāvihāra
event_description: The inscription (attached to thecaitya) refers to this Bahī as Kāmukanāma Mahāvihāra.
The Bahī was renovated after it collapsed during the earthquake of 1934.
The Bahī was renovated using cement and other modern construction materials.

event_name: Inauguration of Lotus Research Centre building in Khvāya Bahī
event_description: The inauguration of the Lotus Research Center building by Minister Buddhirāja Vajrācārya took place on the 27th of Phāguna. Sānukājī Śākya and the family members of thebahīhanded the eastern and southern parts of thebahīover to the centre.

event_name: Establishment of the statues of Vasundharā, Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī
event_description: Harṣamāyā Śākya and her son Sānukājī Śākya established a statue of Vasundharā to the south of the sanctum. They also established the statues of Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī.
The monument was seriously damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.

In 2018, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust, in collaboration with the Department of Archaeology, Government of Nepal rebuilt it with the financial assistance of the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation after it was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
The Phalcā was reconstructed as part of the Bhaktapur Development Project launched in the beginning of 1974 CE with the joint funding of the Nepal and German governments.
First mention of Aki Bāhāḥ asAṭakī Bāhāra.Jaśīrāma Bhāro from Aṭakī Bāhāra donated a begging bowl to the main deity of Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra.
A group of 18 people, including Harṣa Siṃha Bhāro, fixed the bricks on the pavement of the monastery courtyard.

event_name: Establishing of a guṭhī and renovation of the shrine.
event_description: In NS 922, Matsyendra Siṃha Bhāro established aguthiby donating 2ropanīland of Bajaladhenu and another 2ropanīland of Thasi (Siddhipura).In NS 923 (Phāguna, śukla 10), Matsyendra Siṃha Bhāro renovated the shrine.

event_name: Destruction (2015) and rebuilding of the Phalcā (2022)
event_description: Before being rebuilt in neo-traditional style after the 2015 earthquakes in 2021-22, Ipātvāḥ Gaṇeśa Phalcā was made of concrete. The financial support for this has been provided by the Shankharapur Municipality.

event_name: Addition of unknown object and brick paving of courtyard
event_description: An inscription from 1717 CE (NS 837) suggests additions made by two local brothers, but the exact nature of these additions remains unclear due to the illegibility of the inscription. The courtyard's brick paving around this time further confirms thecaitya's pre-inscription existence.

Three brothers—Viśvadeva Bhābo, Bhāgīrāma, and Satyadeva—built Cvaylāchi Chakavaḥ Phalcā in honor of their father, Phachi Bhābo, and installed a deity, likely Sukhāvatī Lokeśvara, currently enshrined in a niche inside the arcaded platform.They also established a religious trust to perpetuate thehāthuhāyketradition.

monument_name: Cakhuṃ Keba Phalcā (originally built in 1857; reconstructed in 2021-22)
event_description: The Phalcā was initially commissioned and built under a person named Dhanathaku from Cakna Kebā ṭola, and in the name of three of his family members: the parents and the younger brother. The donor also made an arrangement to dedicate a regular income (from land) for the conduct of annual rituals. The four family members mentioned in the inscription are said to be respinsible for the ritual conduct. Other details recorded are the position of the planets and a list of objects that must be used in the annual rituals.

monument_name: Cakhuṃ Keba Phalcā (originally built in 1857; reconstructed in 2021-22)
event_description: The monument was badly damaged during in the 2015 earthquakes.

monument_name: Cakhuṃ Keba Phalcā (originally built in 1857; reconstructed in 2021-22)
event_description: Since February 2022, the Phalcā is under reconstruction. The Shankharapur Municipality funds the reconstruction.

monument_name: Cakhuṃ Keba Phalcā (originally built in 1857; reconstructed in 2021-22)
event_description: Since February 2022, the Phalcā is under reconstruction. The Shankharapur Municipality funds the reconstruction.
Minor repairs were carried out by theguṭī-members in 2004 CE. The Caitya was cleaned and its cracks were filled with plaster.

An inscription is embedded on the west-facing facade of the Caitya. The surface is badly damaged and only a few characters are still legible. The text that can be read is not helpful in interpreting the original text.

The Inscription installed in 538 CE (ŚS 460) during the reign of King Vāmanadeva is the earliest dated inscription of Sankhu. The inscription on the pedestal of the statue records King Vāmanadeva installing a statue of the Vāmana incarnation of Lord Viṣṇu and endowed plots of land to establish aguthi. However, the Vāmana Statue is already lost and is replaced by another statue on the Pedestal.

event_name: Addition of Śadāśiva in hiti premises
event_description: A family from Dugāḥ Hiti installed a statue of Sadāśiva, a multi-faced and multi-armed form of Lord Śiva, and formed aguthifor performing yearly rituals. However, there is no statue of Śiva at the Hiti except aśivaliṅga. Probably, the donor family had established this Śivaliṅga as Sadāśiva.

Two Hanuman statues stand in front of the Bāghabhairava shrine.  An inscription has been inscribed on the pedestal of one of these two. The inscription informs about the establishment of these Hanuman statues by a group of Bhāva from Dathu Tvāra (tole), Kirtipur. This inscription does not inform anything about this Hanuman pillar. However, this pillar is erected exactly parallel to the shrine. Thus, it can be assumed that the pillar was also erected at the same time when other two Hanuman statues were established in front of the shrine.
The Kirtipur municipality funded the restoration effort with Rs.14,96,000 in 2019 CE. The reconstruction was completed in December 2020 CE.
On June 29, 2021 the new Phalcā was inaugurated by the Mayor of Kirtipur.

The inscription, though not connected to the Phalcā, has been temporarily placed in front of its northern plinth. The Licchavi inscription dated 616 CE (Mānadeva Era 40) is significant for the study of Sankhu’s history.D. Vajrācārya(VS 2030, p. 508) has published the left side of the broken inscription. The second half of the Inscription was only recovered in 2014 CE, when Gāḥ Hiti (SKH0142), located behind this Phalca, was renovated. The Inscription contains references to a Tṛpura Vihāra and monastic association of the monks of the Mahāsāṅghika (lit. Great Congregation), a Buddhist school of thought.

event_name: Construction of a sataḥ and endowment of land.
event_description: The inscription dated 1558 CE (NS 679) records the construction of asataḥat the Sālkhā Ṭola and endowment of many plots of land, providing income to feed the Jaṅgama ascetics who are said to have come from abroad.This inscription from the Malla period kept next to the eastern plinth is not related to Mandaḥ Phalcā.

An inscription of 1763 CE (NS 883) installed at the Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha (SKH0123) states that the ‘maṇḍapa’ of the Sālkhā Ṭola was renovated and a land endowment was made to manifest and improve the status of Piunārāyaṇa and his family from Kathmandu. As this is the onlymaṇḍapain Sālkhā Ṭola, it is clear that the renovation refers to it. The Inscription was probably shifted to the nearby Brahmāyaṇī Pīṭha later.
The southern plinth and wall of the monument were badly damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.
The Phalca was demolished and rebuilt by the Department of Archaeology after the 2015 earthquakes.
On the occasion of completion of the restoration, atulasī maṭhawas added in the name of late Vīra Kumāra Śreṣṭha.
Harṣaṇārāyaṇa and his family members renovated it wishing for the liberation of their ancestors’ souls.
According to Pruscha (1975, 189), it was renovated also after the 1934 earthquakes.
On the back of the watercolour Oldfield produced in 1853 CE, without referring to any source, he had dated the temple to 1586 CE.
A copper plate nailed to the eastern portal mentions land donated for the daily rituals by Rajajita Malla in 1757 CE.Gutschow(2011, 424) has mistakenly read the king's name as Jayakrakāśa Malla.

The temple was dismantled in 1976 CE and rebuilt in cement mortar, introducing reinforced concrete ring beams, replacing the threshold of the western portal and replacing most of the vertical members of the outer frame.
Govinda Siṃha and his wife Vidyā Lakṣmī established thispañcāvaliyukta caityain memory of their son Jitamāna.
This shrine was constructed in memory of Govinda Siṃha and Vidyā Thakũ by their grandson Harṣarāja and his wife Harṣa Thakũ.

This inscription embedded in thejaḥdhuṃ’s upper section records its inauguration on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, the 3rd of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha in 1659 CE (NS 779). It was built by Kālirāma Bhāro and his wife Vimalāmayi Bhari of Khalachẽ, with land allocated for maintenance under Vāvusiṃ Bhavo’s care.
The Amātya and Maharjana families plastered thejaḥdhuṃand made niches to house new statues. Sānulāla Maharjana and his wife Rādhādevī Maharjana established a new statue in the niche.
The Amātya and Maharjana families plastered thejaḥdhuṃand made niches to house new statues. Suvarṇalakṣmī Amātya established a new statue in the niche.

event_name: Renovation of the Phalcā, establishment of a Bhavānīśaṅkara statue and a land grant
event_description: The inscription from 1716 CE records its renovation and establishment of a Bhavānīśaṅkara statue by Vaṃśīdharadeva Śarmā and his wife Lāvatī Brāhmaṇī, the descendants of its founder Jayasiṃhadeva. The Bhavānīśaṅkara statue mentioned in the inscription does not exist in or around the Phalcā at present. The inscription also records a land grant by them for celebrating the Phalcā’s anniversary rituals.

Puncali Phalcā was completely dismantled and reconstructed in 2003 CE (cf.Bāsukala & Gutschow2018). During the reconstruction, it was moved a few cubic feet back from its original location because it allegedly narrowed down the street too much.
Puncali Phalcā was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.
After it was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes, Puncali Phalcā was reconstructed in 2019 CE with the financial support (of 23,58,759 rupees) from the Lalitpur Metropolitan City Office.
Bhājumāna and Siramāya donated a small bell. This hangs in front of the entrance to the sanctum.

event_name: Establishment of gold gilded icon of Bodhisattva
event_description: A gilded icon of Bodhisattva was established as a Gandhurī Tathagata in the Vihāra.
Lakṣāhuti Yajña (a one hundred thousand oblation sacrifice) was performed.
A new bell was donated to the main deity of the Vihāra as the old one was damaged. The donors were Jayanarasiṃha, Kitiju, Sidhsiṃju, Basudeva and Ānanda.

A staircase was installed to connect the ground floor to the first floor (second storey). The staircase was constructed by Takṣakāra Mela and its donors were Laṇhasiju and Viśeśvaju from Haḥkha, as well as Halisaṃṣara (Hariśaṃkara) from Tulāchẽ.

Those involved in laying the foundations of the Vihāra were as follows:1. Śrī Dakṣina Vihāra kulumbaja Mahāpātra Rājasiṃha Malla Varmā, who calls himself a devotee of Lokeśvara,2. Pradhāna Mahāpātra Śrī Udayasiṃha Malla Varmā3. Pradhāna Mahāpātra Śrī Jayadharmasiṃha Malla Varmā4. Pradhāna Mahāpātra Śrī Rudrasiṃha Malla Varmā5. Pradhāna Mahāpātra Śrī Jayabhīma Malla Varmā(Vajrācārya2011, 277-278)

A copperplate inscription details the consecration of the monastic building. The Vihāra was consecrated in the presence of King Jayajyotira Malla. An offering of three golden kalaśa was made and a play namedVīrabāhuand written by Rām Bhāro was performed. The chief of Vajrācārya played Śrī Panḍuju of Bubāhā and Karma Vajrācārya was played by Śrī Lokarāmaju from Taḥbāhā. It is written that Jyantarāma Mulmi worked hard to complete the monastic building. This copper plate inscription was made by Udaya Rāut.
The Vihāra was renovated: this saw the brickwork on the external walls of the first and second floor replaced.

event_name: Construction of the main entrance of the Vihāra
event_description: The main entrance of the Vihāra was erected.

The restoration was completed in two phases. The first phase (1990-1993) saw restoration carried out on sections of the eastern and northern buildings. During this phase, technical assistance was offered by the Agency for Cultural Affairs of Japan, and the cost of restoration was borne jointly by the government of Nepal and the Nippon Institute of Technology. During the second phase (1993-1995) restoration work was carried out on the southern and western buildings. The cost of restoration for the second phase was borne solely by the Nippon Institute of Technology.

An inscription found in this place records that a resident of Nakabahī ṭola named Bhājumuni constructed the dharmaśālā, possibly a sataḥ or a phalcā in CE 1822 (NS 942). This inscriptions on the roadside wall leads to confusion when trying to identify the specific phalcā/sataḥ mentioned.यहाँ प्राप्त नेसं ९४२ (सन् 1822) को एक अभिलेखमा नकबही टोलका भाजुमुनि नामक दाताले धर्मशाला (सतः/फल्चा) बनाएको करा उल्लेख छ । तर अभिलेख बाटोको पर्खालमा राखिएकाले बनाइएको सतः- फल्चा कुन हो भन्ने कुरा अन्यौलपूर्ण छ ।

event_name: Buddha statues were fixed on top of the Stūpa
event_description: According toPruscha(1975, 131), these four cardinal Buddha statues were consecrated in 1878 CE with a religious feast attended by King Surendra Śāha. Pruscha does provide any references for his knowledge of this event.
This is the oldestdharmadhātu maṇḍalaof the surrounding monuments; it was commissioned by Mañjuvajra and his family in 1881 CE.
Pruscha(1975, 131) mentions that a worship was organised in the Stūpa in 1881, though he does not mention any sources.
Pruscha(1975, 131) mentions that a worship took place in the Stupa in 1899, though he does not mention any sources.
Pruscha(1975, 131) makes mention of a worship organised in the Stūpa in 1927, though he does not mention any sources.
Acaityawas constructed in front of the Stūpa.
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityawas commissioned by Mānavīra, Mānakāji, Śrīmāyā and other family members.
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityawas commissioned by Buddha Ratna Mānandhara from Vijeśvarī, Kathmandu.
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityawas commissioned by Bābukāji Maharjana, Aṣṭalakṣmī and other members of their family.
Adharmadhātujinālaya caityawas commissioned by Sidulāla Maharjan and his wife Kayo.
Herākājī Śākya constructed adharmadhātujinālaya caityain commemoration of the late Vajrarāja Śākya.
A bell was offered to Akṣobhya by Candra Bhāi Śākya from Okubāhāḥ, Patan

Two stone lions flank the modern gate of the Caitya. Gaṇeśarāja, his wife Indirā and some of their other family members commissioned the construction of these lion statues in memory of their parents Keśavarāja (Pvāḥ Syāḥ) and Surjamāyā Tāmrākāra.
Hirāmāyā and other family members commissioned adharmadhātu maṇḍalain memory of Bābukājī Maharjana.
Nāmasaṅgīti Khalaḥ of Lagankhel commissioned this Phalcā and had the Vairocana Statue placed inside it.

An inscription on the phalcā, dating to 1758 CE (NS 878), documents the construction of a brick wall in the Dharmaśālā (phalcā) by Pūrṇatāja Vajrācāryā and his family members. Although this inscription does not offer specific details about the initial construction of the phalcā, it confirms that the structure existed during the Malla period.

The phalcā, which had fallen into disrepair, was reconstructed in 2012 CE (2069 VS) with the support of Bhaktapur Municipality, both financially and technically. Consequently, the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS) did not cause any damage to the building.

event_name: Covering the shrine with gilt copper sheets and addition of toraṇa
event_description: Residents of Dhālāchẽ, namely administrative clerk Indralāla, Sukalāla, Sundarlāla, Purṇalāla, Śyāmlāla, Saṅkharalāla, Kedaralāla, Keśavalāla, Īśvaralāla, Maheśvaralāla, and others, contributed to the embellishment of the wooden frame above thegavākṣahousing the Gaṇeśa image by cladding it with brass sheets. Members of the same Pradhāna lineage, including Īśvaralāla, Maheśvaralāla, Bekhalāla, and others, who were responsible for the brass-sheet embellishment of the wooden elements surrounding the Gaṇeśa image, also installed a bell (ghaṇṭā) in front of the temple.गणेश मूर्ति वरिपरिका काष्ठ सामग्रीमा पित्तलको पाताले मोडी सजाउने उही प्रधान खलकका इश्वरलाल, महेश्वरलाल, बेखालाल आदिले मन्दिर अगाडि एक घण्ट स्थापना गरे ।

The Inventory published by the Department of Housing and Physical Infrastructure in VS 2036 mentions that thesataḥwas built by Dayā Śaṃkara Bhaṭṭa. "Due to the lack of inscriptive evidence, it is difficult to determine its date. The Sivalaya to the east retains its original carved wooden door. The arched style of this door only appeared after the Malla period. Such doors were built from the early Śāha period through the Rāṇā period. If the sataḥ was built at the same time as the Śivālaya, then it must belong to the Śāha-Rāṇa period. Dayā Śaṃkara’s son, Hariśaṃkara Bhaṭṭa, was employed in the court of a Rāṇā (family member, Bhaṭṭa, male, age 40). This information further confirms that Dayā Śaṃkara lived during the Rāṇā era.विसं २०३६ सालमा प्रकाशित एक इन्भेन्टोरी (VS 2039, p.166) मा  यस सतःको निर्माण दया शंकर भट्टले गरेको भनिएको छ । दयाशंकर भट्ट कुन समयका हुन् भनी तिथिमिति स्पष्ट छैन । सतः र मन्दिरमा अभिलेख नपाइनाले यसको ऐतिहासिकता तय गर्न कठिन छ । मन्दिरमा प्रारम्भिक निर्माणताकाको बुट्टेदार काष्ठढोका बचेको स्तिथिमा छ । आर्च (arch) शैलीका यस्ता ढोका मल्लकाल पछि नेपाल भित्रिएको हो । प्रारम्भिक शाहकालदेखि राणाकालसम्म यस प्रकृतिका ढोकाहरू बनेका थिए । यदि यस शिवालय संगसंगै सतः बनेको थियो भने यसलाई शाह-राणाकालीन मान्नुपर्ने हुन्छ । दयाशंकरका छोरा हरिशंकर भट्ट कुनै राणा शासकको दरबारमा कर्यरत थिए (one of the family members, Bhaṭṭa, male, age 40) । यस विवरणबाट पनि दयाशंकर राणाकालतिरकै ठहर्छ ।

थिमि, दथुटोल निवासी रषराम भारोले लोकेश्वरलाई दुई रोपनी जग्गा गुठी राखिदिएका थिए । उक्त जग्गाको आयस्ताले प्रत्येक वर्ष आश्विन शुक्ल पूर्णिमाको दिनमा लोकेश्वरलाई समय्‌बजि सहित पूजा गर्नुपर्ने नियम बनाइएको थियो । केसव भा र किति मयिलाई गुठीयारको रूपमा नियुक्त गरिएको थियो ।
आशा बहादुर प्याथ र जिन बहादुर प्याथले मिलेर लोकेश्वर मन्दिरमा घण्टा चढाएका थिए ।

During the reign of King Bhūpatīndra Malla, Bīradeva Vajrācārya, along with his wife Pūrṇa and other family members established the Jīsvāṃ Bāhā. They adorned thebāhāḥwith a goldencaityaand parasol (chatra) as its finial. To ensure the monastery’s sustainability, Bīradeva endowed eightropanīs of land as a religious trust, dedicated to the perpetual worship of Akṣobhya and Dīpaṅkara and the recitation of thePrajñāpāramitā, a revered Buddhist scripture.

On the birthday of King Mahendra, the pond was renovated and the temple premises was laid with stone slabs. He also constructed a new cement pathway with stone steps leading up to the temple. Given that both pillars in the temple compound are inscribed with the letter 'M', it is likely that they were also renovated around the same time.

On the eastern edge of the pond stands a Śivālaya named Jagatamukteśvara. In front of it, there is a statue of Lieutenant Jagata Siṃha, who died in the Nepal–Tibet war of 1912 B.S.
