Dhīra Śamśera had a large inscription installed, incorporating the contents of previous inscriptions that were separately installed for each of the temples established next to Dhīrabhakteśvara in honor of his wives. This combined inscription instructs various rituals to be performed at each of the temples on designated days and lists land parcels donated to the trust.

event_name: Replacement of the old bell with new one
event_description: Candra Śamśera, one of the sons of Dhīra Śamśera, installed a new bell at the temple after the original bell that his father had installed was broken. The inscription on the new bell only mentions “Śrī 3 Mahārāja” as the donor without specifying the name. Given that Candra Śamśera was the prime minister at that time, it appears he donated the new bell to the temple his father had built.
During the reign of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha, the family members of the deceased Viṣṇusiṃ Mānandhara installed a gilded roof in his memory.
A figure of a shrew, the animal mount of Gaṇeśa, was installed in front of the shrine by Kularatna, Sibaratna, Herānānī, and others.
Due to the poor state of the shrine, it was rebuilt by a local trust named the Aśoka Vināyaka Guthi.
The metal lampstand was offered to the deity by Śrī Aśoka Vināyaka Guthi Mūla Kamiti, the trust of locals formed for the conservation of the shrine.
Only a small section of the inscription is legible.
Consecration of Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in front of the main shrine by Harṣa Bir, Rāj Bir, Nhukṣhe Bir, Dharma Bir, Hela Thakũ and family members in memory of the Dhirja Bir Company
Harṣa Bir, Rāj Bir, Nhukṣhe Bir, Dharma Bir, Hela Thakũ and family members donated this lion in memory of the Dhirja Bir Company.
Harṣa Bir, Rāj Bir, Nhukṣhe Bir, Dharma Bir, Hela Thakũ and other family members donated funds for the restoration of the main shrine in memory of the Dhirja Bir Company.
The Maṅkaḥ Khalaḥ, a Newar community organization from Hā̃ḍīgāũ’s Dathu Ṭola, installed a balustrade of 108 lamps around the Dhanagaṇeśa temple.

event_name: Installation of iron grill for protection
event_description: Kṛṣṇalāla Prajāpatī, Aṣṭabahādura Prajāpatī, and their friends put up an iron grill to protect the temple. They also installed a lock for extra security.
Viveka Siṃha Prajāpatī of Jyāsaḥ Nani area of Hā̃ḍīgāũ donated 108 lamps to surround the temple and a special ritual cup (pātra) as an offering to the Gaṇeśa statue.
In memory of their late father Ratnalāla Maharjana, his son Aṣṭalāla Maharjana and daughter-in-law Hirākumārī Maharjana offered an elongated banner (patāḥ) to the temple.
Rameśanātha Pāṇḍe, a former minister, oversaw the temple's renovation, including the installation of a copper roof, a copper finial, a bell (KAT3100-009), and marble flooring.
Together with his son and grandsons, Jayarāma Śreṣṭha, a resident of Viśālanagara, offered a bell (KAT3100-010) to the temple.

event_name: Offering of a pair of flags
event_description: Viṣṇuprasāda Koirālā offered a pair of flags in memory of his late grandfather Śaśidhara Koirālā, late father Vinodaprasāda Koirālā, and late mother Śāntā Koirālā.

event_name: Erection of a stone pillar with statue of shrew
event_description: In memory of his deceased father Kṛṣṇa Prajāpatī and mothers Purṇamāyā and Jñānamāyā, Tīrtha Prajāpatī, along with his family members, installed a stone pillar with a cast metal figure of a shrew, the animal mount of Gaṇeśa.

event_name: Offering of toraṇa and gilded pinnacle to Nāsaḥdyaḥ
event_description: Mukundasiṃ, Rudrasiṃ, and other members of the Dāphā group jointly offered a toraṇa and a gilded finial to Nāsaḥdyaḥ. At that time, the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple had not yet been built, it existed only as a shrine.मुकुन्दसिं, रुद्रसिं लगायतका दाफा खलकका सदस्यहरूले मिलेर नासःद्यःलाई तोरण र सुनको मोलम्बा लगाइएको गजूर चढाएका थिए । त्यस बेलासम्म नासःद्यःको मन्दिर बनेको थिएन, देवस्थलको रूपमा मात्र स्थापना गरिएको थियो ।

During the reign of King Raṇajita Malla, Dhanabilasiṃ (Dhanavīrasiṃ), Bhāgivantasiṃ, and other Dāphā group members built a proper temple for Nāsaḥdyaḥ where Hāku Bande served as the priest.राजा रणजित मल्लको राज्यकालमा धनबिलसिं (धनवीरसिं), भागिवन्तसिं लगायतका दाफा खलकका सदस्यहरूले मिलेर नासःद्यःको लागि मन्दिर निर्माण गरेका थिए । उक्त काममा हाकु बन्देले पुरोहितको काम गरेका थिए ।

As the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple became dilapidated over time, the locals contributed donations to rebuild it in 1853 CE (NS 973).नासःद्यःको मन्दिर जीर्ण भएकोले टोलबासीसँग चन्दा उठाएर जीर्णोद्धार गरिएको थियो ।

event_name: Reconstruction of the Nāsaḥdyaḥ Bhajana Phalcā
event_description: As the Nāsaḥdyaḥ temple became dilapidated, it was completely torn down and reconstructed with the donation of local. Subbā Rāma Basi, his son Kirtimāsī Basi (Kirtimānasiṃha Basi), and Madhausiṃha (Madhava Siṃha) played key roles in this project.नासःद्यः भजन फल्चा जीर्ण भएकोले टोलबासीहरूसँग चन्दा उठाएर जगैदेखि भत्काएर पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको थियो । उक्त पुनर्निर्माण कार्यमा सुब्बा राम बसि, उनका छोरा किर्तिमासी बसि (कीर्तिमानसिंह बसि), माधौसिंह (माधवसिंह) लगायतका व्यक्तिहरूले प्रमुख भूमिका खेलेका थिए ।

When the phalcā became damaged again, it was reconstructe with funding from the Madhyapur Thimi. Municipality. Before this, it only had one floor. There was a house belonging to the Kapilā family attached to the north side of the phalcā, where two Kapilā families lived. During the reconstruction, the south side of the phalcā was expanded, and the Kapilā house in the north was demolished. After the renovation, the Kapilā families were no longer allowed to live there.फल्चा जीर्ण भएकोले मध्यपुर थिमि नगरपालिकाको आर्थिक सहयोगमा फल्चाको पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको थियो । पुनर्निर्माण हुनुभन्दा अघि फल्चा एक तलाको मात्र थियो । फल्चासँगै जोडिएर उत्तरपट्टि कपालीहरूको घर बनाइएको थियो जहाँ कपालीहरूका दुई परिवार बसोबास गर्थे । पुनर्निर्माण गर्दा दक्षिणपट्टि फल्चाको क्षेत्रफल बढाइएको थियो र उत्तरपट्टि कपालीहरूको घर भत्काएर फल्चा विस्तार गरिएको थियो । पुनर्निर्माणपछि कपालीहरूलाई फल्चामा बस्न दिइएन ।
Napati, Vidyāpati, and Jñāneśvarī offered a woodentoraṇaon top of the entrance to the sanctum of the temple.
Icchaharṣa Vajrācārya and his family established adharmadhātujinālayacaityaat the Bāhāḥ premises in the name of his deceased parents Vajraharṣa and Ratnakumārī.
The main building of the Bāhāḥ was rebuilt with funds from the Kathmandu Metropolis. Concrete was used in the course of the reconstruction without adopting the traditionalbāhāḥarchitecture.
Queen Lalitatripurasundarī laid the foundation stone for the construction of the bridge, praying for the eternal peace of her husband Raṇabahādura Śāha.
A land grant of 150ropanīs was made in the name of Hanumantasiṃha Amātya for the expansion of settlements in Kupondole and the maintenance of the bridge.

The bridge was inaugurated by Queen Lalitatripurasundarī after 15 months of the laying of the foundation stone. A stone inscription marks this achievement, noting the bridge's 1253-cubit length and the involvement of a government officer named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.

The king added an additional 25ropanīs of land grant to Hanumantasiṃha Amātya, who previously received 150ropanīs of land grant, and mandated that anyone settling on this land must contribute to the upkeep of the bridge. The inscription can be found at the Hanumān Devala (LAL2851) in Kupondole.
The foundation stone was laid for the reconstruction of the bridge using iron girders from Britain, after the bridge suffered damage in the 1902 floods 94 years after its initial construction.

Candra Śamśera installed an inscription recording the construction of the bridge that was completed in only 131 days. This is the longest inscription with embossed text. This iron bridge was known as "Red Bridge" due to its color.
The bridge became congested due to urbanization and was eventually replaced with a two-lane concrete motor bridge built with Indian iron beams.
This is the sign board mentioning the name of the bridge. It states the year of its installation as 1969 CE (VS 2026).
Two more lanes were added to the bridge with Japanese assistance.

event_name: Addition of pillars with miniature replicas of important monuments
event_description: The Patan side of the bridge was beautified with miniature replicas of famous temples during Mayor Buddhirāja Vajrācārya's term.
Raghuvīra Amatya and his family from Lalitpur Daubahāla renovated thecaityas
At the reigning period of King Śivasiṃha Malla, Minister Luṃguḍo Bhāro and his wife Jayamayi renovated thesecaityas. They also performed fire ritual worship and installed the statues of Five Buddhas.

event_name: Paving the courtyard and establishment deities
event_description: The reconstruction committee installed the statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara. At the same time, the committee paved stones on the courtyard and made a compound wall with praying wheels. The committee also installed statues of 16 gods which are placed inside the tiny rooms made at the southern corner of the courtyard.

Gaṇeśadāsa and Ratnadāśa, grandsons of Dharmanārāyaṇa Mānandhara, built thesataḥto enable their clan members to rest and store materials at the time of cremating their deceased family members. It was also built for travelers to stay for the night.
The descendants of the Mānandhara brothers renovated thesataḥand added a restroom.
The inner and outer walls of thesataḥwere renovated by members of the same Mānandhara family.
The decendants of thesataḥ's original donor restored the inner and outer walls in 2014 CE.

After the 2015 earthquakes damaged thesataḥ, the High-Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization rebuilt it with loan assistance from the Asian Development Bank. The reconstruction was completed in November 2021.
The Shankharapur Municipality renovated it in 2018 CE at the initiation of the locals. During the renovation, the Hiti was thoroughly cleaned and walls were built around its three sides.
The main deity was established in theāgãchẽby Jujumāna, a son of Lasalāni of Bhelupāta, Kathmandu.
Donation of prayer wheels and oil lamps by Āśāmadu and his wife Jivo Lāni.
Inscription by Devajati (Devajyoti)
The courtyard was paved in stone and a surrounding platform was built by Siramān, his wife Viṣṇu Māyā, son Bābu Lāl and Bābu Lāl's wife Dhana Māyā.
The inscription on the north-western side of the Bāhāḥ premises records five historical events including theSamyakMahādānaheld in 1660 CE.
In 1665 CE, lamps were offered around the Dharmadhatu Caitya.
The inscription (see above) records the installation of two Dīpaṅkara statues in 1666 CE.
Theāgãdyaḥand Tārā were installed in memory of Jinipāra in 1669 CE.
Jinadeva and his family members installed the Vajradhātu Caitya in NS 790 (1670 CE).
The wooden door which is the entrance door of the Bāhāḥ has been renovated.
The son of Motiratna Vajrācārya, Caiteratna Vajrācāryā, and the family had offered the brass bell to the Kvāpā Dyaḥ of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ.
The group of Teja Narasiṃha, Tejānaṃda, Javaratna, Lāla Bahādura, etc people jointly installed the door to the house and repousse with copper plate.
Mānakāji, Herākāji, and the other 13 people jointly installed the door and repousse with brass.
The resident of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ Śrī Jogapāla Vajrācārya had installed the statue of Lokeśvara (Karuṇāmaya).

The three sons of Honavisiṃ Vajrācārya of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, Harṣavirsiṃ, Rāmavirasiṃ, and Paṃcavirasiṃ, offered the copper plated door to the Kvāḥpā Dyaḥ, on the occasion of the 32nd birthday of the third son, Paṃcavirasiṃ.

event_name: Installation of a pair of brass lion
event_description: In memory of father Jñāna Ratna Vajrācārya, Mother Sānu Māyā, step mother Sajikaharṣa Māyā, their sons Vahi Ratna, Keśaratna, Guhyaratna and family installed the pair of brass lion in front of Kvāḥpāḥ Dyaḥ.

event_name: Installation of Lokeśvara, Sāriputra and Maudagalyāyana
event_description: The main Gurū Jogendra Ratna and the Śrīnātha Gurū Samuha had installed the statue of Lokeśvara, Sāriputra and Maudagalyāyana.
The Mañjuśrī Pādukā was installed by Jogendra Ratna Vajrācārya and the family.
The Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya has been installed by the Jogendra Ratna and his family,
In the name of father Veṣāratna and mother Puṇya Śobhā, Pannāratna and Hirāratna had offered and installed the brass bell.
In 1996, Motikāji Vajrācārya and his family jointly installed the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalā on the premises of Kwā Bāhāḥ.

The copper plate, which sits on a pedestal of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalā and dates back to VS 2056 (2000 CE), only mentions the establishment of Śrī Vāka Vajra Cacā Khalaḥ, and does not provide any additional information.

event_name: Replacement of the old Lions statue and installation of the new one
event_description: The two statues of the lions on the entrance gate of the Bāhaḥ deteriorated, thus the old statues of the lions were replaced, and installed the new pair of lions at the same place.

The inscription has been covered with cement as a result of painting and plastering on the wall. Additionally, the woods and other materials have been placed in front of the wall, making it difficult to clean and read the inscription.

The stone inscription records a renovation of the Nāsadyaḥ’sphalcāby Dharmanārāyaṇa (text: Dhamanārā), Raśmi, Jñānalakṣmī (text: Gyāṃlakṣmi), Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (text: Lakṣminārāṃ), and Dhanalakṣmī (text: Dhanalakṣmi).
The brass bell was offered in 1926 CE. However, the name of the person(s) who offered it is not mentioned.
Ratna Bahādura Mānandhara, living at the Thãhiti Ṭola installed the statue.
The resident of Thãhiti ṭola Sitārām and their sons offered the metal flag to the deity.
The sons of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Bhakta Kṛṣṇa, Pratāpa, and others installed the brass bell to the deity.

event_name: Rebuilt of the temple and the library
event_description: According to the marble inscription from NS 1125 (CE 2004), the Thãhiti Upabhoktā Samiti had rebuilt the Nṛtyeśvara Mandira and the library (attached to the western part of the Mandira).
Rājendra Dāsa Śreṣṭha offered the patāḥ to the Temple in 2005 CE.

A copper-plate inscription is nailed against the bottom of one of the struts of the southern façade of the Temple. Since it records only names of two persons: Nitā Khaḍkā from Svayambhū and Niraṇa Mānandhara from theThãhiti, it remains obscure whether these persons sponsored the strut or did something else.

A copper-plate inscription is nailed against the bottom of one of the struts of the southern façade of the Temple. Since it records only names of two persons: Śāntimāyā Mānandhar from the Thãhiti Ṭola and … Khaḍkā (this name is covered due to the bulb fixed just below the inscription), it remains obscure whether these persons sponsored the strut or did something else.

event_name: Donation of bricks for the courtyard

event_description: The land of Luchẽnani (to the eastern side of the Bahī) belonged to that monastic building. It contained some houses with roofs made of straw. The roof of theākhāchẽ(a cultural house where musical instruments, masks and dresses are stored) was tiled by a group of volunteers led by Narami Bhāvo.
The entrance of thekvāpādyaḥshrine is clad in brass. Kājīlāl and his wife Sānu donated funds for this work to be carried out in memory of their deceased father Jitamā.
Consecration of thecaturvyūha caityaoutside the Bahī during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla. This was conducted by Harinandan Duwāra Bhāro and Binatā Mayi.

event_name: Consecration of tower over the roof and donation of a pinnacle

event_description: Consecration ofdharmadhātu maṇḍalaby Vajrācārya Lakṣmī Joti

monument_name: Subāhāḥ Hiti Phalcā (c. late 18th cent. CE)
event_description: The stone inscription on the Phalcā records that five elders (Lakṣmidhaṃ, Siṃgha, Kulamānasi, Lakṣmījoti and Bekhā) and other members of thesaṅghacompleted the renovation of the Phalcā on a Wednesday during the dark fortnight of Āśvina in NS 1025 (1905 CE).

monument_name: Subāhāḥ Hiti Phalcā (c. late 18th cent. CE)
event_description: Reconstruction of the Phalcā with the help of GTZ/udle.

monument_name: Subāhāḥ Hiti Phalcā (c. late 18th cent. CE)
event_description: GTZ/udle helped during the reconstruction of the Phalcā.
Paduma(!) Bhāro constructed the hiti.

King Jitāmītra Malla, after composing the dance-drama version of theAdhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, built the Vatsalā temple for the performance of thesiddhipūjā. The inscription installed during the temple’s construction refers to the deity as Karma-Vatsalā.राजा जितामित्र मल्लले अध्यात्म रामायणको नृत्य रचेपछि सिद्धिपूजा गर्नको लागि वत्सला मन्दिर निर्माण गरेका थिए । मन्दिर निर्माण गर्दा राखिएको अभिलेखमा उक्त वत्सलालाई 'कर्म-वत्सला' भनिएको छ ।

event_name: Offering a stone lamp to Nāsaḥdhaḥ
event_description: King Bhūpatīndra Malla, on the occasion of performing theghāgharasiddhi-pūjā—the consecration of the dance costume used in the playKolāsuravodhopākhyānabased on theMahālakṣmī-māhātmya—offered a stone lamp (pānasa) before theNāsaḥdyaḥshrine.राजा भूपतीन्द्र मल्लले महालक्ष्मी माहात्म्यमा आधारित 'कोलासुरवोधोपाख्यान' नाटकको घाघरसिद्धि पूजा (नाटकमा देखाइने नाचमा प्रयोग गरिने घंगलाको पूजा) गरेको अवसरमा नासःद्यःको देवस्थलअगाडि ढुङ्गाको पानस चढाएका थिए ।

King Bhūpatīndra Malla also offered a bell, made from the proceeds of staging the playGaurīvivaḥain Lalitpur. The inscription engraved on the bell is addressed toNṛtyanātha, indicating that although dedicated toNāsaḥdyaḥ, the bell was installed in front of the Maṅgaleśvara temple.राजा भूपतीन्द्र मल्लले ललितपुरमा 'गौरीविवाह' नामको नाटक देखाएर उठेको पैसाले घण्टा चढाएका थिए । घण्टामा कुँदिएको अभिलेखमा नृत्यनाथलाई सम्बोधन गरिएकोले भूपतीन्द्र मल्लले उक्त घण्टा नासःद्यःलाई चढाएको देखिन्छ । तर उक्त घण्टा मङ्गलेश्वर मन्दिरअगाडि स्थापना गरिएको छ ।

The Bhaktapur Municipality reconstructed the Vatsalā temple, which had been severely damaged in the 2015 CE (VS 2072) earthquake.भक्तपुर नगरपालिकाले विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्पले क्षति पुगेको वत्सला मन्दिरको पुनर्निर्माण गरेको थियो ।
Theśivaliṅgawas under the open sky until the present Temple structure was constructed in 1960 CE with the financial help from Dāmodara Śamśera Rāṇā.

Jñana Bahādura Maharjana, the caretaker of the Temple, took initiative to renovate it in 1997 CE (VS 2054). During that renovation, the lower part of theśivaliṅga, which is called Brahmā section, was brought above the ground. Usually, as mentioned before, the Brahmā section of aśivaliṅgaremains underneath the ground.

Two statues of Nandī (one made of brass and the other one made of stone) were installed inside the sanctum on the same day. The brass statue was offered by Rāju Rājopādhyāya, the priest of the Temple, and the stone one was offered by a police officer.
The temple was severely damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes.
The Government of Nepal and the Asian Development Bank jointly reconstructed the temple at a cost of two million rupees. After the reconstruction, a newśivaliṅgawas consecrated inside the sanctum.
Ratna Vajrācārya constructed the Vihāra during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla. At that time, Nārāyaṇa Dāsa wascautāra(minister). Matirāja and Mañjurāja helped to finish the construction.
Rājrakarṇikāra Mānavīra and others donated a pair of metal flags.

event_name: Construction of a pair of Yamadūta statues
event_description: Śākyavaṃśa Nhukṣarāja and family made a pair of stone statues of Yamadūta and placed them on either side of Siṃhanāda Lokeśvara...

event_name: Fixing tiles on the temple wall
event_description: Maṅgal Kṛṣṇa and Mohan Kṛṣṇa donated funds to fix tiles on the wall of the temple.

event_name: Donation of finial, flag and umbrella
event_description: This inscription from the time of Yakṣa Malla (reignedc.1429–c.1482) states that a golden finial, flag and umbrella were donated. It mentions the names of Bhāskaradevasaṃskarita Srivihāra, Māṇigalya, Saptakūṭumbaja tribhaya pradhānaśrīpātra, Bhuvanākara Śrivihāra, Ruparāja, Lakṣarāja, Cintāmaṇi vajra and Līlā Vajrāchārya. The inscription is very old and damaged, and the writing is in part difficult to read.
Mīnānātha's seat was clad with silver. The donor's name is not mentioned.

event_name: Replacing the jhĩgaṭī roof with copper roof
event_description: Āśāratna Dhākhvā replaced the lowerjhĩgaṭīroof with a copper one.

event_name: Repair of bathing platform and Aśoka Caitya

event_description: Omkārāsa Maharjan and his wife Rāmadevī donated the metalvajrawhich is placed in front of theaśoka caitya.
Aṣṭakoṇākāra Caitya was constructed to the north of Mīnanātha Temple by Jayakṛṣṇa Bhāro. He also donated land to conduct religious activities.
Pannālāla Śākya and Gaṅgā Śākya established adharmadhātu jinālaya caityato the east of Mīnanātha Temple.

A stonetoraṇawas donated to Mahākāla at the Yamadvāra Shrine during the reign of King Viṣṇu Malla. The aniconic stone placed in the Yamadvāra is referred to as Mahākāla in the inscription, however, local call it Yamarāja.
Ratnarāja donated funds for the gilding of the upper roof of the Mīnanātha temple.
Gangālakṣmī and her son Mānasiṃha donated threemandaḥpāḥsto be placed on the threshold of the entrance to sanctum.
Śīdhīlakṣmi donated funds for the gold cladding of the entrance door of the sanctum.
Aśoka Caitya was repaired by Caityarāja of Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra.

event_name: Donation of pillar and beam to hang a bell
event_description: Kṛṣṇavīra Bhālo (Bhāro) and family donated stone pillars and a beam upon which to hang a bell. This is placed to the north of Siṃhanāda Lokeśvara.
Virasĩna and family donated praying wheels to Jaṭādhārī Lokeśvara.

Vyakhārāja, his wife Nanda Kumārī and family made donations for the bathing platform (nhavã dabū) for Mīnānātha to be repaired. A stone lotus flower was fixed in the middle of the stage. White stone tiles were paved behind the temple and black stone tiles were paved on the courtyard to the east, south and north of the temple.
Rājamāna Siṃha donated the Simhanāda Lokeśvara images that are placed on both sides of the entrance to the sanctum.

event_name: Donation of golden amulet and necklace
event_description: Lāni Thakũ donated a golden amulet and a silver necklace to Jaṭādhārī Lokeśvara.
A modern addition to the shrine's surroundings is the installation of a Śani statue (KAT1551-007) situated behind the shrine. For further details, refer to the description and objects above.
Munirāja, the founder of thebāhāḥ, established the statue of Cakrasaṃvara as theāgamadeity.
Pruscha(1975, 208) mentions that thecaityawas made by Dhanavantasiṃha Vajrācārya. However, the name of the donor could not be read from the inscription and so is unconfirmed.
Munirāja (son of Dhanavantasiṃha), his wife Puṇi Thakũ and their sons Nhukṣarāja and Harṣamuni made a Buddha shrine in the courtyard. Thereafter, it became known as abāhāḥcā.
Mādhasiṅa and Sivarāma established their own tutelary deities (KIR0083-001 and KIR0083-002) in the form of plain stones adorned with a Garuḍa-toraṇaat the same site.

Viśvasiṃha (also spelled as Visvasiṃha) Bhāro of the Bāghabhairava temple area erected the stone shrine of Bhājaṅgāla Degudyaḥ by installing a Gaṇeśa statue. This construction was undertaken to appease his tutelary deity Bhavānī, who was already present at the location.

The earthquakes of 2015 CE resulted in numerous cracks on the shrine, which was already in a deteriorated condition. The process of reconstruction was initiated by the Kirtipur Municipality in early 2023 CE and is still ongoing as of February 2023.
Raṇadhvaja Thāpā, the founder of the temple donated plots of land and established asadāvartaguthifor the temple's maintenance.

event_name: Installation of a statue of Raṇadhvaja Thāpā
event_description: Raṇadhvaja Thāpā had his family tree inscribed on the pillar and installed his own statue atop of it.

event_name: Endowment of land for Narmadeśvara  and Umāmaheśvara
event_description: Land measuring 15ropanīswere endowed to maintain the Narmadeśvara and Umāmaheśvara temples, located around the Jayeśvara Mahādeva Mandira.
Several plots of land measuring 95ropanīswere endowed for the operation and maintenance of the Jayeśvara Mahādeva Mandira including other temples around it.

event_name: Endowment of lands by King Rājendra
event_description: King Rājendra donated plots of land measuring 76murīsof crop yields to Jayeśvara Mahādeva.
Raṇadhvaj, the founder of the temple, purchasedt several plots of land in different places to endow theguthifor the temple.
All above mentioned events were inscribed on the Raṇadhvaja Thāpā pillar in VS 1900.
The Nepalese Department of Archaeology renovated the temple.

During King Pratāpa Malla's reign, Suṣurī Bhāro, an assistant (bhaṇḍārī) at the Paśupatinātha Mandira, renovated thephalcācontaining the Matsyendragaṇeśa statue, dedicating it to his deceased son. After the renovation, he reestablished the statue in thephalcāthrough a fire oblation. This inscription reveals that Matsyendragaṇeśa was initially established in aphalcāand a temple was built for him only later.
Rāmakumāra Śreṣṭha and his wife Sītā Śreṣṭha offered a door with a cover of metal sheets to the temple in the course of its reconstruction.
Renukā Vaidya offered a metal banner (patāḥ) to the temple in the name of her deceased parents-in-law Dirgānanda Vaidya and Candabahada Vaidya along with her late husband Sūryānanda Vaidya.
The temple underwent reconstruction with donors contributing financially.

event_name: Installation of an inscription with names of donors
event_description: An inscription was installed listing the names of the committee formed for the reconstruction of the temple and of the donors.
The Phalcā building was further damaged by the earthquakes of 2015. There are structural cracks visible throughout the brick masonry.

event_name: Offering of Bronze Patāḥ on the Temple
event_description: The resident of Dhobicaura Śrī Rāmdāsa Mānandhara and his wife Devī Mānandhara offered a patāḥ (an ornament of the temple) to Bodhika Gaṇeśa Temple.
In 1996 CE, Purṇamāna Nakarmī and his family members offered two bronze flags in front of the main entrance of the temple, in the name of his late parents, Rājamāna Nakarmī and Nānī Nakarmī.

In 1997 CE, the temple was renovated under the leadership of Vijaya Bahādura Mālī. The Kathmandu Municipality Ward Number 17 funded 380,000 rupess, and other necessary expenses were covered by collecting offerings from the devotees. This temple did not suffer any damages in the 2015 CE earthquakes.
A pillar was installed in front of the temple. Avāhana(vehicle) of the lord Gaṇeśa, the mouse, was placed atop of the pillar which was built by Rāma Dāsa Mānandhara and his family members in 2003 CE.

event_name: Built Rām Sītā Laksmaṇ and Rādhā Kriṣṇa Temple
event_description: The resident of Dhobīcaur, Rāmdās Mānandhara, financed and built the Rāma-Sītā-Laksmaṇa Temple, Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa Temple, and installed a statue of Hanumān at the back of Bhuḍe Gaṇeśa in 2010 CE.
The devotees offered the bells and the stone standing in front of the temple. Due to the thick layer of oil, the inscription is illegible, and thus the name of the donor remains unknown.

In the year 2019 CE, the entrance to the premises of this Gaṇeśa temple was built by the Kathmandu Municipality Ward Number 17. The construction of the entrance has almost finished, however the inauguration programme is yet to be held.
Linage deity shrine of Jyāpu caste which is situated to the west of this temple was renovated in 2008 CE by a group called Ṭengha Śrī Aṣṭamī Pyūjā Khalaḥ.

event_name: Construction of Rāma-Lakṣmaṇa-Sītā and Rādhā Kṛṣṇa Temple
event_description: The resident of Dhovīcaur, Rāmdāsa Mānandhara, built the Rāma-Lakṣmaṇa-Sītā and Rādhā Kṛṣṇa temples. Moreover, he installed a statue of Hanumān behind Bhodikha Gaṇeśa temple. The Mānandhara family also covered the roof of the newly built temple with brass plates.
The temple was renovated after the earthquakes of 1934 CE.

An inscription on a strut supporting the lower story on the western side of the temple records that Hākurāma donated the strut on the mentioned date. It may have been that he donated the strut during the reconstruction of the temple.
Nine members of the Dāphā Khalaḥdonated thetoraṇa.
Gumiṃ Siṃha, Bhāvo Abhi Siṃha, Panu Siṃha and Herāma Ralakesa reconstructed the temple.
Viṣṇu Maharjan, grandson of Bekhāsĩ and son of Bekhālāla, donated the brasstoraṇawhich is fixed on top of the image of Gaṇeśa with his wife Nānī and son Āśisa.
Paridhara Jyāpu, Kīsalakṣmī, Dhimāsī, Pasīmuni and Kṛṣṇalāla donated the bell that hangs in front of the temple.

event_name: Installation of a stone toraṇa and formation of a group of devotees
event_description: Vijarāja Vajrācārya (of Guru Bāhāla) formed theGaṇeśaSevā(probablyKhalaḥ, which means a group of devotees). Gvamirāja was thethakāli,and the other group members were: Vijasiña, Jagarāma, Yandrarā, Gumisiña, Asiña, Jñokita, Tethā, Manisiña, Gumirāma, Hākusiña, Suṣudeva,  Suṣucā,  Silāma, Mālasiña, Madhasiña Kihima(Kimhi)siña and Amirāja, among others. The inscription also records that a group was formed to acceptYināya Mataor the Gaṇeśa flame (probably butter lamps), with the people named in the inscription as its members. The team installed a stonetoraṇaover the entrance of the Gaṇeśa shrine in the temple. A special worship calleddahrūwas performed on the same day one year later.

event_name: The lower and middle copper roofs were fixed

event_description: Lalitapur Sub-Metropolitan City, Sanāḥ Guthi and Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti renovated the temple.
Pāṇḍva, Dīpaka and Lakṣmī donated a bronzepatāḥto Gaṇeśa.

event_name: An institution of devotees (Sakebāra Sevā) was formed and two images of lions were installed
event_description: The inscription records two events: one is the formation of thesakebāra sevā,a group performing certain activities in honor of Gaṇeśa, and the other is the installation of two images of lions in the Bāhāḥ or Dupātṭola. Fortunately, the date is very clear.Thesakebāra sevāconsisted of ten people; this was agroup of devotees that performed certain activities on Tuesdays in honor of the localGaṇeśaand installed two images ofsiṃbāhāna(likely two lion statues). Some of the names mentioned are Mādhava Siṃha Bhāvo, Māla Siṃha Bhāvo, Hari (Siṃha??) Bhāvo and Bābu Deva Bhāvo. The leader of these ten men appears to be Biṣṇu Siṃha Bhāvo. It is clear that ten people of the Bhāvo (Jyāpu) community were involved in the event.

monument_name: Maṇḍapa Phalcā at Pimbahal (first half 17th cent. CE)
event_description: Reconstruction by the Department of Archaeology.

A pair of stone lions were offered to Mahākāla in 1663 CE (NS 783). Members of the Caturdaśī Sevā Guthi, a religious service performed on the 14thof the dark fortnight of every lunar month, including Śiva, Candrasiṃ, Rāmadeva had made the offering (D. Sharma and T. Shrestha2016, p. 413).
An ascetic stole a golden umbrella (chatra) offered to Mahākāla. He was punished later.

event_name: Performance of rituals for auspiciousness after a sharp discuss (cakra) installed at the Vajrayoginī temple premises fell off
event_description: There are records of Mahākāla receiving animal sacrifices at times of any impediment at and around the Vajrayoginī temple. A sharp discuss (cakra) installed at the Vajrayoginī temple premises fell off in 1683 CE (NS 803). Special rituals for auspiciousness were performed along with a sacrifice of a buffalo to Mahākāla following the incident (T. Siṃha1136, p. 12, folio 17B-18A).

event_name: Performance of rituals for auspiciousness after Caughrā Sataḥ caught fire
event_description: Caugharā Sataḥ (SKH0560) caught fire in 1795 CE (NS 915). Following the incident, King Raṇa Bahādura Śāha performed special rituals for auspiciousness by sacrificing a buffalo, two goats, and five ducks to Mahākāla.
The inscription is illegible. Therefore, what it has recorded remains obscure.

event_name: Installation of iron grille and roof
event_description: Bālakumārī Śreṣṭha, proprietor of Hotel Blue Diamond of Thamel in Kathmandu, sponsored the installation of a roof and metal grille on all four sides of the Shrine.

The construction date of the original Guru Nānaka Ghara is not documented. According to the Maharaja of the Akhaḍā (male, age 65), Guru Nānaka (1469–1539) visited Kathmandu and stayed at this place and a temple to Guru Nānaka must have existed here for hundreds of years. Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā built the surroundingsataḥ(KAT2831 Udāsī Akhadā) in the late 1870s.

According to the inscription, the building was built by the Shri Guru Nanak Dev Sewa Society International, based in El Sobrante, California.However, according the the Mahārāja of the Guru Nānaka Ghara, the building was only repaired rather than built new in early 2015 CE.

The entire Capāḥ was dismantled and rebuilt in 1995 with the support of the German Technical Cooperation (GTZ-udle).According to locals from the neighbourhood, the wood that was used for restoration came from a large tree that stood in front of Thalbuṃ Phalcā (LAL4150). Vegetable vendors used to sit underneath the tree: there is a myth is that everyone who touched the tree with a vegetable would then be able to sell it immediately.
The stone inscription embedded into the northern side of the plinth is severely damaged and its writing is no longer legible.

On the thirty-first day of Aṣāḍha, 2018 CE (VS 2074), the Department of Archaeology and thesaṅghamembers of Cilancva Bāhāḥ signed an agreement to restore the caitya,dyaḥchẽand thisPhalcā. The project was successfully completed in 2019.
The temple was built in 1847 CE. Although the name of the donor is unclear, it was possibly commissioned by Badrīnarasiṃha Kũvara, the younger brother of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.

King Surendra, through alālamoharaissued in the name of Badrīnarasiṃha Kũvara, endorses the donation of land parcels in favor of Jyotirbhakteśvara, along with two adjacentśivālayas, Līlābhakteśvara and Badrībhakteśvara in Mṛgasthalī.

Queen Siddhimaṅgalādevī Thakunī (wife of King Śrīnivāsa Malla) initiated the construction of this Phalcā in 1686 CE. She endowed the site with four different areas of land so that aguṭhīmight be organised to look after the construction and take care of the monument. The inscription placed in the Phalcā mentions that the Queen commissioned the monument in memory of the King, and an image of Umāmaheśvara was installed in the Phalcā in his name.
Locals reconstructed the Phalcā by collecting donations.
The Phalcā was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes (see photographs in 'Monuments after 2015').

The Dathu Nani courtyard was laid with bricks with the joint efforts from Cāka Bāhāra’s Devamuni Bhāro, who was the local administrative officer (pramāna), along with Punarāma, Bāsurāma, Sivaharī, Madhurāma, Harigovinda, and Manhahosiṃ. The inscription also enforced rules that prohibited bringing cows and bulls in the courtyard, along with other acts like urination and defecation, grinding of wheat, and driving nails on to the ground.
Thedyaḥchẽ, which had already deteriorated before the 2015 earthquakes, was rendered uninhabitable due to the earthquakes.

After the reconstruction of the ground floor of thedyaḥchẽ, Nirakumārī Vajrācārya, a resident of the Naudvã Ṭola, Lalitpur, along with her husband Mānavira Śākya and family members, donated a statue of Amitābha (BDG0030-001) to be enshrined in the sanctum. She also donated statues of Śākyamuni Buddha, Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara, and Āryatārā for the establishment in the sanctum.

An inventory published in 1982 CE (VS 2039) refers to an inscription stating that akājīfrom Chāgaḍola, Kathmandu, built thesataḥaround 1915–16 CE (VS 1972), although the individual's name is not recorded. The current residents are unaware of the existence or content of this inscription. In the vicinity, Dirghalakṣmī—wife of Vīrabhadra Kũvara and sister-in-law of Balabhadra—constructed anothersataḥalong with a Śivālaya, suggesting that the Teku Sataḥ may also have been built by akājīfrom the same Kũvara lineage. However, due to the loss of the inscription, further details remain unavailable.
Thesataḥunderwent renovation in 1971-72 CE (VS 2028) (Inventory VS 2039, p. 165).

The historicsataḥwas badly damaged in the 2015 earthquake, consequently demolished, and rebuilt as a simple brick and mortar shack, covered with a corrugated metal roof.Only one historic carved window was reused in the new building. All other historic materials, such as carved windows, doors, columns etc., were lost.

According to later chronicles, particularly theBhāṣāVaṃśāvalī, this statue was established by Amara Malla during his reign from 1529 to 1560 CE. The year of its construction is unknown due to the lack of an inscription.
The Chaudhary Foundation, in collaboration with the Pashupati Area Development Trust, undertook the renovation of the shrine after it had fallen into disrepair.

event_name: Initial Construction of the Temple and Land Endowment to GAuṭhī
event_description: Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī constructed this temple in the memory of his deceased father Siddhinārāyaṇa Rājabhaṇḍārī and endowed some plots of land to aguṭhīto sustain the performance of the daily rituals. He also constructed Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (KAT2636) and Dhaneśvara Mandira (KAT2638) on the same date.

The earliest historical record of Kirāteśvara dates back to 1728 CE (NS 848), when King Jagajjaya Malla (r. 1722-1734 CE) of Kathmandu granted land for the establishment of a trust responsible for conducting daily and periodic rituals at various deities in the Paśupati area, including Kirāteśvara Mahādeva.

event_name: Renovation of the temple and offering of bells
event_description: The inscription records that the temple was renovated by Mukhiyā Māna Bahādura Karmācārya with the help of Dhīrjā Mādhāva Jyāpu from Dupāṭa Ṭola. It further mentions that Māna Bahādura was instructed to renovate it by his mother from her death bed. He also offered the bells that are hanging on the eaves.

event_name: Regulations laid down for organising the anniversary celebration of the temple
event_description: This inscription records the regulations laid down for organising the anniversary celebration of the temple.
The inscription is hard to decipher. Also, the last numerical figure of the date is not clearly readable. It looks like the number ‘6’.

The Licchavi inscription kept at the northeast corner of the temple does not belong to the temple itself. According toVajrācārya(VS 2030, 391), it seem to be issued during the reign of Aṃśuvarman (VajrācāryaVS 2030, 391). TheJaḥdhuṃhiti(see the object number LAL2120-006 above), too, bears a Licchavi inscription.
The Phalcā suffered structural damages due to the 2015 earthquakes. Later, it was dismantled for reconstruction.

The Phalcā was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. Therefore, Uttama Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha-the grandson of Candra Nārāyaṇa Śreṣṭha, got the Phalcā dismantled and rebuilt in 2016 CE. According to local oral tradition, Candra Nārāyaṇa had sponsored the construction of the Phalcā during the partyless Pañcāyata rule.

According to C. Nepālī (VS 2020, p.26), Raṇabahādura Śāha built the Temple and also established abhairavīcakrain the month of Phālguna in 1797 CE (VS 1853). Similarly, Hasrat (1970, p.156) mentions the establishment date as the month of Māgha in 1797 CE (NS 917). Gutschow (2011, p. 891), on the other hand, believes it was built around 1794 CE by Raṇa Bahādura.
The Temple was destroyed in the 1833 CE earthquake. Under the debris, twenty-two people were killed and thirty others were injured.

The original Temple structure did not survive even three decades, collapsing in the 1833 CE earthquakes. The Temple was most likely rebuilt, with the earlier multi-tiered temple being replaced by a much simpler copy of  Bhīmabhakteśvara temple. Gutschow (2011, p.874) writes: "… Jagannātha temple collapsed in the earthquake of 1833, killing 22 persons. It must have been at this time that an earlier multi-tiered temple was replaced by a hybrid mixture of an outer ambulatory around a core which rises to support a bulbous dome. The finishing of the plaster and the details of the ambulatory’s pillars are devoid of details, as if restricted resources resulted in a much simplified copy of the Bhīmabhakteśvara temple. Its annual proportion support the assertion that it is a replacement: From the centre of a comparatively low ground floor without pilasters but with an ambulatory, a pilastered first floor complete with bottom mouldings rises up as if this was to be the actual temple”.
The 2015 earthquakes caused numerous cracks in the Temple.

In July 2022, a procession of Jagannātha was organized following the deity's grand worship. The president of the country also attended the event, which was organized by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness of Nepal (ISKCON-Nepal).
Virapati Jogi and his wife Madhari Jogini renovated the shrine.

event_name: Stone statues of devotees, made on a single stone was attached to the northern wall of the Gorakhanāta Shrine
event_description: The images of Punāvatī, Saṅṣadāsa, Punasvarī and Acikitī's have been installed.

The inscription mentions that Darśandhāri Rāmdāsa Jogīhad established an image but it is not clear which image it is. Inside the Gorakhanātha shrine beside the inscription there are images of stone devotees. It is possible that these images were installed by him.
Kisalāla Maharjan, Nānimāyā, Nhuccheñmāyā and their family reconstructed the Sūryavināyaka shrine.

event_name: Coral studded golden feet (pādukā) was offered to the Gorakhanātha
event_description: Darśandhāri Pvaṁca Jugi donated coral-studded golden feet (pādukā) to Gorakhanātha.
Jayañta Maharjan and Bāla Kṛṣṇa Maharjan, sons of the late Śuṣālāla Maharjan, donated thetoraṇa.
The entrance was reconstructed in the name of late Herākāji, most probably by his family members.
Thekuladevatāshrine was restored by the Kuladevatā Mandira Jīrṇoddhāra Samiti.

event_name: A patāḥ made of brass was hanged on the Gaṇeśa temple
event_description: Silāl, Matimāyā and the Maharjan family hung a brasspatāḥon the Gaṇeśa temple.

event_name: Construction of a pāṭī/sattal behind the Gaṇeśa temple
event_description: Thepāṭī/sattalwas constructed by the local community.

event_name: Construction of a pātī/sattal behind the Gaṇeśa temple
event_description: Dhanamāyā Maharjan, Kṛṣṇa Maharjan and their family constructed apātī/sattalbehind the Gaṇeśa temple.

event_name: Construction of a shrine of a family deity
event_description: Jagata Siñ Bhāvo, Jugi Rāma Bhāvo and other Bhāvos constructed a shrine. Relying upon the inscription (LAL1490_I_20181203_06.JPG),Pruscha(1975,170) assumes that the Gaṇeśa temple was constructed in 1681. However, the inscription suggests that some other shrine was constructed at the date. Regarding the object, only the last letter of the word ( ‘ri’ ) is retained in the inscription; the first two letters of the word are effaced. With this in mind,Siṃha(2018, XX) postulates that the rubbed word is‘gajuri’(i.e. pinnacle), but that it could also be read as‘deguri’(a temple of family deity) because there are several such shrines in this temple area.
On the south-west corner of the temple and above the wooden pillar, a lintel is embossed with the numbers '1997'. This suggests that the temple was reconstructed on this date.

event_name: Temple like small structure was covered by brass
event_description: Kṛṣṇa Lāla Maharjana Dhana Māyā Maharjana and their family covered a small, temple-like structure with brass. This was placed inside the Gaṇeśa temple on the New Year of NS 1113.
Two lion statues were donated by Darśanadhāri Rāma Jogī and Darśanadhāri Ramnātha Jogī. The location in which the statues were placed is not mentioned in the inscription.
Rājeśa Kapālī installed an oil-lamp balustrade in the Gorakhanātha shrine in memorandum of his late mother Dānamāyā Kapālī.

The inscription of NS 977 mentions that there was no temple for the deity at that time. The statue of Gaṇeśa was simply covered with a small roof. In NS 977, Raghuvaṃśa Rāotta (Rāvuta) and Bhavā[nīrā]ma Babu from Ikhāchẽ Dvaka dismantled the old, dilapidated roof and built a new temple in its place.

Ajay Bajaj and Mukta Bajaj from India offered brasspatāḥ(metal banners) to the deity. Local resident Yogendra Tandukar assisted them with this, and so the name of his mother (Ganga Devi) has also been engraved on the banner.
The temple had aged and become damaged, and so locals Bhajumani Tandukar (Vajracharya), Dyaḥpāḥlāḥ and others carried out maintanence work.
The temple was slightly damaged by the earthquake of 2015. Initiatives are being taken to rebuild the temple.
Gokula Khatrī and his wife Kṛṣṇapyārī Khatrī installed a bell in front of the temple.

A pair of lion statues were installed in the temple. The inscription is covered with ghee and oil and parts of it are diificult to decipher. The text at the bottom refers to political events between the kingdoms of Kantipur, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur. The names of King Śrīnivāsa Malla and Pratāpa Malla are mentioned.
The eroded inscription cannot be deciphered.
The owner of the house rebuilt this Phalcā in concrete, inccreasing its height and changing from three to four bays (supported by round concrete pillars).

King Rājendra issued alālamohara(K_0008_0040B) approving land parcels donated in the name of Mālikeśvara and Kapileśvara Mandira for performing daily and other rituals of the deities using the rent from the land. Given that thelālamoharaaddressed to Dalakeśara Pā̃ḍe is related to the temple built by his wife, it is evident that the temple already existed in 1846 CE.

Nine years after the issuance of thelālamohara, its contents were inscribed in a stone inscription placed next to the temple. The inscription also outlines the activities to be carried out from the income of the donated land parcels.
A Vajrācārya called Abhaya of the Paśupati Mahāvihāra (Pasu Bāhāḥ) is mentioned in a palm-leaf deed written during the reign of King Jayadharma Malla.
After completing the Aṣṭamīvrata in the bāhāḥ, Hākudeva, Jivajrāja, Mahāpāla and other people offered atoraṇato theāgaṃdyaḥ.

event_name: Erection of a pillar with a caitya on top
event_description: Vajrācārya Khāni Thakuṃ and his son Khāniharṣa erected a pillar with acaityaat the bāhāḥ courtyard.
Varjācāje Punacandra (Vajrācārya Pūrṇacandra) and other family members established the Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya at the bāhāḥ courtyard by spending his wealth earned from his business in Tibet.

event_name: Offering of a gilded gate and window
event_description: The name of the donor(s) who offered the gilded gate and window cannot be deciphered from the inscription recording this event.
Kājimāna Buddhācārya constructed the Yajñakuṇḍa in the bāhāḥ courtyard.

event_name: Establishment of statues of Sāriputra and Maudagalyāyana
event_description: Aṣṭa Buddha Śākya established the statues of Sāriputra and Maudagalyāyana inside the sanctum.
The badly eroded/damaged inscription cannot be deciphered.
Dharmmapāṇi, his son Ratnākara, Dharmmacandra and other family members jointly constructed it.

event_name: Collapse of the āgaṃchẽ in the earthquake.
event_description: The westāgaṃchẽcollapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.

In 2023, theāgaṃchẽwest was reconstructed from ground-up. None of the original doors, windows and carved pillars were reused and their whereabouts are not know. A photograph by John Huntington from 1970 shows threetoraṇaabove the first floor windows. In Hugh Down's photo from 1980 thetoraṇaabove the windows on the left and right are missing.All threetoraṇawere likely lost or stolen over time.

Śākyas from the Cola Nani constructed the Śikharakūṭacaitya(BUN0023-003) and established aguṭhīfor its management. The names of the main donors could not be deciphered due to the poor condition of the inscription. However, it appears that Namo Siṃju, Ranhāvatī, Dhanasiṃ Jyoti, Śrī Bhāgi Siṃja and others made thecaitya.
Locals made a house for the deity around 1973. They used wood from the nearby forest to construct it.
Many of the houses in the Cola Nani area collapsed in the 2015 earthquake. Thephalcā,naniand other monuments were also affected by the earthquake. People built huts in thenani.
The prayer wheels to the west of thecaityawere donated in memory of Viṣṇu Māyā Śākya in NS 1112. The donation was made  by her family.
The oil-lamp balustrade surrounding thecaityawas donated in memory of Viṣṇu Māyā Śākya in NS 1117. The donation was made by her family.
Guṇasiṃhadeva sought permission from King Nareśa Malla and built Nī Bāhāḥ.
Mahantamuni offered a bell to thecaityain thebāhāḥpremises.
Budhacāryye Nānimāyā and her family installed a pair of bronze lions.

event_name: Paving of courtyard with floor tiles
event_description: Ratnamāna, with community support, paved the courtyard with floor tiles.
Ratnamāna, together with his wife Dānamāyā and family members, restored the shrine housing thebāhāḥ’s main deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) in memory of his deceased grandparents Mānabīrasiṃ and Devalāni.
Sīdhīnarsi, Rājindramuni, and others jointly renovated a bell following its deterioration.
Commemorating the laying of floor tiles in thebāhāḥpremises and renovation of the main shrine, Ratnamāna installed a copperplate inscription north of the main deity.

event_name: Installation of copperplate inscription recording ancestors' contributions
event_description: The members of Nī Bāhāḥ installed a copper plaque to honor their ancestors' contributions to art. The inscription mentions Guṇasiṃhadeva’s death in 1646 CE (NS 766) and records that his grandsons—Sabhākara, Guṇākara, and Ratikara—constructed the famous Lũ Dhvākhā (Golden Gate, BKT0080) in Bhaktapur’s palace area in 1753 CE (NS 874). The plaque also states that the three brothers jointly offered a diamond-studded necklace (herāphvaḥ) to Viśvakarmā in 1751 CE (NS 871). However, this date appears to be an error, as other inscriptions confirm that the offering was made in 1755 CE (NS 875), shortly after the Lũ Dhvākhā’s completion (S. Śākya NS 1141, p. 28).

event_name: Formation of organization for Guṃlā Bājā
event_description: To ensure the continuity of the Guṃlā Bājā (a traditional musical procession held during the holy month Guṃlā), a non-expendable fund (akṣayakoṣa) was established through collective donations while also forming an organization to oversee the musical performances.

A marble inscription commemorates the formation of an organization by setting up a non-expendable trust by the locals, highlighting the community’s efforts to institutionalize the tradition of performing the Guṃlā Bājā ensemble of drums and cymbals.
Nī Bāhāḥ marked the 100th anniversary of its Guṃlā Bājā with a grand celebration, reflecting the enduring cultural significance of this musical tradition.
With contributions from thebāhāḥmembers, the courtyard was paved with stone slabs.
The Temple collapsed completely in 1961 CE (see the description above for more information).
The Temple which collapsed completely in 1961 CE was rebuilt from the ground up in 2018 CE.

event_name: Initial construction of the Temple and land endowment
event_description: Bhavānīśaṇkara Bhār living in west of Yachu Ṭoola built this Temple in the memory of his parents. He had also endowed five and a halfropanīsof land to run the Temple and sponsor its annual rituals.

Along with his family members, Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Bhāro constructed the two-tiered temple with a gilded finial and enshrined a statue of Lokeśvara. He also established agūṭhīof NRs 201 to fund daily and annual rituals at the temple.

event_name: Offering of a bell (object no. NWK0600-006)
event_description: Together with his family, Devidāsa Amātya of Kvālkhu, Patan installed the bell at the temple.

event_name: Offering of a pair of lions
event_description: Subedāra Rāḍhākṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha of Kathmandu's Makhana Ṭola installed the pair of stone lions at the temple.

event_name: Offering of a bell (object no. NWK0600-005)
event_description: Nityalakṣmi and her son Kulamāna installed the bell at the temple.

event_name: Covering of toraṇa and entrance with brass plates
event_description: Kālīdāsa Śreṣṭha, who had moved to Triśūlī from Ikhāchẽ, Patan, covered the entrance andtoraṇaof the temple with gilded sheets.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. NWK0600-007)
event_description: Vṛṣabahādura constructed it to the west of the temple.
Gauridāsa from the Triśulībajāra offered the gilded narrow oblong banner (patāḥ) to the temple in memory of his deceased family member Visvalachimi.

The Saṃlhu Gūṭhī carried out the renovation of the temple roof, which had fallen off, using its own funds and donations from the locals, probably replacing the traditionaljhĩgaṭītiles with copper sheets.

event_name: Repairing of brass cover of threshold
event_description: The brass sheet with embossed designs that clads the threshold of the main entrance was renovated. It was originally installed by Bhājumuni, his wife Devi Thakuṃ and Punerāja in memory of their deceased family member Gajaratna Śākya. The name of the person to renovate it is not mentioned in the inscription.
Rośanī Dhaubanjāra, a resident of the Sūryavināyaka bus park in Bhaktapur, installed the metal flag erected east of the temple.
Dipaka Mānandhara from Kuleśvara in Kathmandu installed the metal flag erected west of the temple.
Captain Amulya Ratna Śākya offered thekuṃpatāḥshanging on the four corners of the temple's upper tier.

event_name: Covering the temple with brass sheets
event_description: The Trishuli Savings and Credit Cooperatives covered the outer walls of the temple with brass sheets.
The renovation of the Gāḥ Hiti in 2009 CE was completed with an active participation of local residents and the fund provided by the Seva Network Foundation and Nepal Samaj Netherlands.

The contents of this inscription are similar to the previous one. The inscription is written in Newari and English language. It records the renovation of the Hiti in 2009 CE under the initiation of Dr. Bāla Gopāla Śreṣṭha.
Queen Bhuvanalakṣmī built the temple.

Based on extant historical photographs, it becomes evident that the upper section of the temple experienced considerable damage due to seismic activity, prompting subsequent reconstruction efforts. The documented images portray the aftermath of the earthquakes and the subsequent renewal endeavors undertaken to reinstate the temple's architectural integrity.

In a collaborative initiative, the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust carried out the restoration of the temple during the period of 2004-2005 CE, in collaboration with the Department of Archaeology and the Kathmandu Metropolis. This endeavor was made possible through financial support generously provided by the US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation.
The temple'sśikharacollapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.

The Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust rebuilt the temple after the collapse of theśikharain the 2015 CE earthquakes. The project was carried out in cooperation with the Department of Archaeology and the Kathmandu Metropolis. The US Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation provided the funds for the reconstruction.

बज्राचार्य पुरोहितले लाउने एक मुकुटमा भएको नेसं ७९७ (सन् १६७६-७७) को अभिलेखमा ‘खालछेँ चैत्य बाहार’का ल्हासा व्यापारी रत्नदेवले उक्त मुकुट चढाएको प्रसंग छ । यस उल्लेखनबाट यो बाहाः उत्तरमल्लकालमै अस्तित्वमा आइसकेको थाहा हुन्छ ।
बाहाःको द्यःछेँको मोहोडालाई सन् १९८० को दशकमा मर्मत गरिएको थियो ।
द्यःछेँ अगाडि ननिको भूमि र पेटीमा पनि नयाँ टायल बिच्छाउने कार्य हालसालैमात्र (सन् २०२५) काठमाडौं महानगरबाट सम्पन्न भएको हो ।
A bell was offered to Vajrayoginī. The name of the donor is obscured by a coat of enamel paint on the bell.

event_name: Installation of tiles on sanctum walls and floor
event_description: SubbāTulasīdāsa Rājabhaṇḍārī,KharadāraMohanadāsa Rājabhaṇḍārī, and others had marble installed on the walls and floor of the sanctum.

Heramba Bahādura Rājabhaṇḍārī and his family renovated the Vajrayoginī shrine, adding a new door, in memory of his parents, Dhīrja Bahādura and mother Cinīyālakṣmī Rājabhaṇḍārī. He also had the shrine's courtyard paved with marble.

The oldtoraṇaabove the sanctum entrance was stolen and replaced by Acyutānanda Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī and Keśava Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī in honor of their father, Kṛṣṇa Rājabhaṇḍārī, mother Satyamāyā Rājabhaṇḍārī, and elder brother Dāmodara Prasāda Rājabhaṇḍārī.

Together with his family, Bhūpendra Bahādura Rājabhaṇḍārī installed a lamp balustrade containing 108dalūlamps at the shrine in memory of his decease parents Bhairava Bahādura Rājabhaṇḍārī and Gaṇeśa Kumārī Rājabhaṇḍārī.
Rakṣa Rājabhaṇḍārī offered a brasstoraṇato Vajrayoginī in the sanctum.
Acyuta Bahādura Rājabhaṇḍārī and his wife Rubekā Rājabhaṇḍārī from Pulcoka, Lalitpur, offered a brass oblong banner (patāḥ) to Vajrayoginī.

The bell that initially belonged to the nearby Indrabhakteśvara temple (KAT2650) has been relocated and installed on the plinth of this temple. This was likely intended as a temporary measure, given the collapsed stone bell support at the Indrabhakteśvara temple. However, it has remained in its current location since then.

event_name: Covering the Shrine with a tin-roof
event_description: Previously, this Shrine was under an open sky. Its present structure was made by collecting donations from devotes.
Gaṇeśamāyā and her family members jointly offered the oil lamps surrounding the rectangular platform in memory of their mother Aṣṭamāyā Śreṣṭha.
The Shankharapur Municipality has allocated a preliminary budget of NRs. 200,000 for the Bāhāḥ’s reconstruction. However, the reconstruction process is yet to commence (as of February 2022 CE).
As mentioned above (see the description), the stone palm contains an inscription, but it is heavily damaged, thus cannot be deciphered.

This inscription does not belong to the Phalcā. It records a certain land endowment (probably to the above-mentionedcaitya) by a person named Hari Nārāyaṇa and his wife, both living at the Mañjuśrī Ṭola, Patan. The inscription also mentions the position of the stars and a list of items that is to be used for the annual rituals (probably) of thecaitya. Since the upper part of the inscription is badly damaged, its actual contents remain obscure.

This inscription embedded into the wall of the Phalcā does not belong to the Phalcā itself, but it records the construction of a stonecaityaaround the Svayambhūnātha area by Kāji Vaṃdhu Rāṇā and his wife Kājinī Jayakumār. However, thecaityacould not be identified at present.

The Svayambhū Vyavasthāpana ra Saṃrakṣaṇa Mahāsamiti began reconstructing the dilapidated Phalcā right before the 2015 earthquakes. By the time of the 2015 earthquakes, the brick walls were already completed. The walls built with newdāciaḥpāandmāaḥpābricks laid in cement mortar suffered no damages. After a break of about a year due to the earthquakes, the reconstruction concluded in around October 2016 CE.
In memory of his father, Mohanavīrasiṃha Tulādhara, a resident of the Asana Ṭola in Kathmandu, constructed the Phalcā together with other family members.

Construction of Mahabuddha Temple was completed by Abhayarāja Śākya's grandson Jīvarāja and great grandson Jayamuni, following a model that Abhayarāja allegedly brought with him from Bodh Gaya (Gutschow2011, 516). King Shivasiṃha Malla was invited to participate in the worship ritual that was organised upon completion of the work. Siddhidevaju was the chiefācāryaon this occasion.

Paṇḍita Jīvarāja and Jayamuni went to Sikkim and offered a plate ofprasādafrom the Mahabuddha enshrined in thisvihārato the King of Sikkim. Grateful for this offering, the king filled the plate with gold. When Jayamuni returned with the gold, he called a meeting of the members of thesaṅghato determine what to do with it. They decided to make fixtures (side panels for the four sides, thetoraṇas, and the decorations above thetoraṇasfor the chariot) of the Red Matsyendranātha. These fixtures were placed upon the chariot for the first time in NS 774 upon its arrival to Gāḥ Bāhāḥ. Aguṭhīwas then set up to ensure the safekeeping and maintenance of the fixtures. The lintel of the main temple's door is a repurposed stone memorial pillar. The pillar's typology dates it to the mid-14th century. Astūpais carved on the top of the pillar and a heavily eroded inscription written in Nāgarī script can be seen beneath thestūpa. Posterior to this original inscription are other more recent inscriptions and carvings, such as the central arch with round decorative patterns. To the right is a more legible inscription with the date 1976 (on the image). This date corresponds to 1919 CE when expressed in the Vikram era.

event_name: Donation (possibly the building of the sataḥ)
event_description: Hailing from Prasannaśīla Mahāvihāra, Siṃhanarasiṃha Buddhācārya (text: Siṃghanarasiṃ Buddhācāryye), together with his wife Thakuṃlāni, sons Narasiṃha and Naramāna, as well as his daughter-in-law Mohanamāyā, made a charitable offering in honor of Nāmasaṅgīti, a revered figure within the Buddhist pantheon. While the specifics of the donation are not expounded upon, it is plausible that he was involved in the construction of thesataḥ, which was likely presented in dedication to the aforementioned deity. The inscription further documents Siṃharanasiṃha Buddhācārya's directive to commission a statue of Nāmasaṅgīti within thesataḥ, with the necessary funds originating from the rental income of his ancestral residence in the Bikumāḥchẽ Ṭola.

event_description: The exteriors of thesataḥwere adorned with depictions of diverse deities and also featured an image of Candra Śamśera Rāṇā.

On the upper level of thesataḥ, a ritual known as "Lakha Caitya Pūjā" was conducted. This unique worship practice involves crafting one hundred thousandcaityas out of black clay. Similar ceremonies are periodically arranged by Buddhist monasteries across the Kathmandu Valley.

Despite surviving the 2015 earthquakes, thesataḥsustained significant structural damage from the tremors. Presently, a substantial tarpaulin has been employed to shield the roof from rainwater. According to local accounts, the ownership of thesataḥlies in private hands and the renovation of thesataḥremains in a state of uncertainty due to an ongoing family dispute.

A copper-plate inscription listing the names of Rājamāna Siṃha, Dinanātha, Nandalāla, Juju Ratna, Kāji Bahādura, and others is mounted on the upper storey of the temple. Although undated, the inscription appears, upon close observation, to be composed of fragments of a much larger inscription originally from another location, later brought here and reassembled on the temple wall.

This inscription records Hṛdayaratna Gvaṃgaḥ and his wife, Manitha[kuṃ], establishing Hṛdayeśvara Mahādeva in the temple. While the inscription has been somewhat damaged, obscuring the year of its construction, Pruscha (1975, p. 230) reports the existence of an inscription from 1865 CE, which corresponds to VS 1922. The temple's architecture and the artifacts found here seem to originate around the same period, suggesting that Pruscha likely read the date from this inscription. Hṛdayaratna additionally established various other deities, including Hṛdayavināyaka, Hṛdayeśvarī, Hṛdayanārāyaṇa, Garuḍeśvara, Trailokeśvara, Umāmaheśvara, Viśveśvara, Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, Kāmadeva, Durlabheśvara, Umeśvara, Maṇikeśvara, Vaṭuka, Joginī, Kṣetrapāla, Brahmāyaṇī, Mohinī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī. He also built anāgaṃchẽdirectly in front of the temple, along with the Nārāyaṇa temple accompanied by a Garuḍa pillar. Ample land parcels were endowed for their worship and upkeep.
The 2015 earthquakes inflicted substantial damage on the temple, leaving cracks throughout its structure. Despite the extensive cracking, the temple initially withstood the seismic forces.
The temple succumbed to the damage caused by the 2015 earthquakes and collapsed completely on the day ofŚivarātrī.

The Department of Archeology reconstructed the temple. A photograph published by Pruscha (1975, p. 230) reveals that the temple's upper section featured a bell-shaped design, and its finial was notably tall. The recent reconstruction, however, replaced the bell-shaped dome with a dome and reduced the finial's height.

The Shankharapur Municipality renovated the Jaḥdhuṃhiti. In the process, the position of the Licchavi Caityas was changed and the stone ceremonial mirror (jvalānhāykaṃ) and a broken piece of a finial were installed as the finial of the Caityas (see the description above for more information).

Statues of Śiva, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Lokeśvara, Gaṇeśa, and others were established at theghāṭa. Although Topabahādura Khatrī oversaw their installation, his name is not mentioned in the inscription recording the event. However, his contribution is documented in another inscription he installed in 1978 CE.

Thisghāṭaand itssataḥwere established by the ancestors of Topabahādura Khatrī, a local Panchyat-era zonal commissioner. He contributed various statues to theghāṭaand organized its religious functions by setting up a religious trust. An inscription by Khatrī details his religious devotion, the religious structures he founded, and his development initiatives, aiming to document his life's achievements. It mentions his installation of deities, the novel concept of apitṛ guṭhī, a religious trust dedicated to his ancestors, with donated properties intended for lineal descendants (including daughters in the absence of sons), and the income from this land being designated for weekly worship of deities in Sanepa and at theghāṭa. The inscription also mandates monthly full-moon worship and devotional singing at theghāṭa, and a Rāma Navamī exhibition of historical books and related images at thesataḥ. Furthermore, it outlines the deposit of principal in a bank for managing daily worship and annual tree planting through the interest. Interestingly, Khatrī even made provisions for his post-mortem devotional singing. As the head of the local construction improvement committee, a list of his accomplishments is included in the inscription. Following damage to thesataḥfrom a recent earthquake, the resident Girī family undertook partial repairs.
A square-base Licchavi-eraśivaliṅgawas recovered at the Bagmati-Vishnumati confluence.
The Licchavi-eraśivaliṅgawas recovered at the Bagmati-Vishnumati confluence.

event_name: Establishment of pillar with Śiva statue
event_description: This inscription is undated. It documents the installation of a stone pillar topped with a statue of Śiva, positioned between two bridges connecting Kathmandu and Lalitpur. However, a nearby foot relief indicates that it was emplaced in 1993 CE (VS 2050).
This inscription carries a single message: “In the end, there is no one but the Lord for all beings.” The words are engraved on the relief (pādukā) of the Lord’s feet.
The family of Kṛṣṇalāla offered a bell inside the temple.
The temple was renovated by the municipality and local contributions after the temple was damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.

event_name: Initial Construction of the Temple, Establishment of a Guṭhī, and Land Endowment
event_description: The temple was built by Siddhirāma Bharo and his wife Gaṅgāmayi. They endowed fiveropanīsof land and established aguṭhīfor the operation and maintenance of the temple.
Since the inscription is broken, its content remains obscure. Perhaps, the inscription might have been brought here from somewhere else.

event_name: Thievery of the Original Statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara and Installation of Replica
event_description: The original statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara consecrated inside the sanctum during the initial construction of the temple was stolen. Thus, a replica of the stolen statue was installed.
The Department of Archaeology carried out a minor renovation of the stone joints with waterproof chemicals.

event_name: Land grant and installation of a sculpture
event_description: The only inscription at the site is found on the broken base of a stone sculpture (BTD0030-013). The inscription is written indevanāgarīscript and contains six lines.D. R. Sharma read the inscription as follows (Sharma 2012: 349):Oṁ śri bahatari ra na ka sri karlla māhā maṇdalika rāni śri yaṃ debi putra śri Garbha deva sutra dhāra ha ra de be na pyādina nena pyādinala deva kāyana pradattam bhumiand translated it as:In Bahatadi (Baitadi), consecration of... mahāmandalika sri... queen's son, Garbha deva, and Hara Deva the architect... has offered land... as for religious merits.

event_name: Gilding the Akṣobhya Statue and Land Endowment
event_description: Brahmacārī Bhikṣu Saṃvaraju, his wife Raca, and son Guṇarāja gilded the Akṣobhya statue and endowed land to aguṭhīto worship the Buddha.
Nalaharī Bhara (Bhāro) donated atoraṇato the Gandhurīdevata of thebahī. Thetoraṇawas fixed above the main entrance on the Śrīpañcamī day, fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha.

event_name: Donation of an Umbrella and Kadamba Tree
event_description: Harṣavīra and his wife Asalakṣmi, Aṣṭalakṣmī, donated an umbrella made of brass,dhaloṭa,and akadambatree.
Brahmacārī Bhikṣu Saṃvaraju and his son Guṇarāja jointly offered a gold finial, performing a day and night sacrifice,ahorātrayajña.
Brahmacarya Bhikṣu Harṣavīra and his wife Aṣṭalakṣmī consecrated the Gandhurīdevatā.

event_name: Construction of a Monastery for the Sthavīra Monks
event_description: A monastery for the monks, who follow thesthavīradoctrine of the Buddhism, was built by the monk Jñānapūrṇika to the north of thebahī’s courtyard in VS 2028 (1971 CE), which was used as a public toilet before.
Bhikṣu Jñānapūrṇika Mahāsthavira renovated thedhyaḥchẽby collecting donations form the devotees.
Sureśa Śākya and Puṣpa Śākya offered a metal vajra to thebahīin the memory of their deceased parents.

event_name: Renovation of the Bahī and Establishment of Stone Statue
event_description: Jalaga, Bhorī, and his son Jayacandra renovated thebahīby changing its door wings, father, and the main staircase. They also established a stone statue of a couple.

The Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala was constructed by Śivadhana Bhāvo, his wife Pārvatī, and sons Bābusĩ, Bhāicā and Lĩbucā. The consecration ritual was performed by Caityarāja Vajrācārya from Dhum Bāhāḥ and Vajrarāja Vajrācārya from Cuka Bāhāḥ.

Caityarāja Śākya from Cikã Bahī constructed this Śikharakūṭa Caitya at the centre of the Om Bāhāḥ Nani. Since the stone inscription recording the information about the Caitya is completely rubbed off, the date of this event is unknown.
Dilakumārī, the wife of Bhīma Śamśera, offered a bell (PPK0426-003) together with her daughter Divyalakṣmī.
Divyalakṣmī, the daughter of Dilakumārī and Bhīma Śamśera, offered a bell (PPK0426-004) to Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
The brick gate in front of the temple sustained minor damages in the 2015 earthquakes.

Information referring to the installation of Gaṇeśa's vehicle is legible.यस अभिलेखमा मिति पढ्न सकिएको छैन । दाताका रूपमा कीर्तिमान सिंहको नाम पढ्न सकिन्छ । काठमाडौं उपत्यका नगर विकास योजनाद्वारा विसं २०३९ (सन् १९८२) मा प्रकाशित एकइन्भेनटोरीमा यसै अभिलेखका आधारमा कीर्तिमान सिंहले नेसं १०२४ मा यो सतः बनाएको भनिएको छ (Inventory VS 2039, p.163) । अभिलेख पढ्न कठिन भएकाले उनैले यो सतः बनाएको हो-हैन भन्ने तथ्यको तुलना गर्न सकिएको छैन । उनले पहिलेनै स्थापना गरिएको गणेशलाई वाहन थपेको वाक्य पढ्न सकिन्छ ।

Despite surviving the Gorkha earthquakes of 2015 (VS 2072), the Sataḥ's extensive wall cracks necessitated its reconstruction. The Ministry of Urban Development's Bagmati Civilization Integrated Development Committee, with support from the Asian Development Bank, completed the reconstruction on November 29, 2021. The exterior wall now features white cement plaster.विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्पमा सतः नढले तापनि गारोहरू चर्की पूर्णक्षतिको स्थितिमा पुगेकाले भत्कालई पुनर्निर्माण गरिएको हो । शहरी विकास मन्त्रलाय अन्तर्गत रहेको अधिकार सम्पन्न वागमती सभ्यता एकीकृत विकास समितिद्वारा एशियाली विकास बैंकको ऋण सहयोगमा यो सतःको पुनर्निमाण कार्यलाई पूर्णता दिइएको थियो । विसं २०७८ साल मंसिर १३ गते (November 29th, 2021) का दिन सतःको निर्माणकार्य सम्पन्न भएको थियो । पुनःनिर्माण पश्चात् सतःको वाह्य भित्तामा आधुनिक प्रकृतिको सेताम्य सिमेन्टको लेप (plaster paris) लगाइएको छ ।
Babara Śamśera commissioned the temple in memory of his deceased son Bāla Śamśera and also installed a bell on the occasion that documents the event.

Historical photos of the Phalcā (taken by Niels Gutschow in 1992) show adhaḥmā(beam of the chariot used for religious processions) in front of the structure. The olddhaḥmāplaced at the Taḥ Bāhāḥ (LAL0050) was carried here by the locals of Kutisaugaḥṭola. Locals stated that the olddhaḥmāburned down some years back on the evening of Śivarātri.
The Phalcā collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.

From the GTZudle report/Patan conservation and Development Programme:"Repair of the Kuti Saugal Pati. At the request of the local community and Chandra Pustakalaya of Kuti Saugal Tole, Patan Programme undertook in May 1993 to renovate this resthouse (pati). Construction was finished in October 1993.Existing condition:The main damage to the structure was in the roof, the Achilles tendon of the local architecture. Because all the existing timber was pine, roof damage had quickly led to complete deterioration of this less durable wood. As the floor of the resthouse was finished only in clay, most people chose to sit on the wall across the pokhari (pond) across the lane rather than in this pati.Repair work:  The timber floor structure was replaced with all new sal timber: new sal floor planking was also provided. The timber beam above the columns was replaced with sal timber wood to match the historical size and shape. All columns were in good condition and only cleaned. The brick wall below the floor level, the front wall above the timber beam, and a few brick layers at the back wall were repaired using traditional mud mortar and oldma-apa. The roof was repaired using almost all new sal timbers and planks, incorporating a waterproofing membrane of tarfelt.Summary:Project dates May 1993-October 1993, Total costs including construction, design, implementation, supervision: Rs 178,582 "

The Phalcā is now (in October 2019) under reconstruction. Lalitpur Metropolitan Office has provided Rs 28,00,000 to fund this. According to the president of the Sthānīya Upabhoktā Samiti (Local Consumer’s Committee), the committee collecting these donations added 10% to this amount.
