event_name: Establishment of the Sataḥ and Rādhākṛṣṇa Temple (KAT2710)
event_description: The foundation of the Sataḥ and Rādhākṛṣṇa Temple was laid in honor of Bhāgavatabhakta Māthemā's commitment. Sardāra Haribhakta Māthemā, a poet who expressed his literary prowess in Nepalbhasa, was the father of Bhāgavatabhakta Māthemā. Among the four martyrs, Dharmabhakta Māthemā was Bhāgavatabhakta Māthemā's grandson (L. Śākya NS 1122, p.17). Kājī Bhāgavatbhakta, driven by his dedication, pledged to establish the Rādhākṛṣṇa temple (KAT2710) along with this Sataḥ. Despite his passing, he designated 20murīsof paddy and 1murī10pāṭhī(9ropanī-s, 12ānā) of land for the annual rituals of the Sataḥ and temple. He couldn't fulfill his commitment during his lifetime. In fulfillment of his wish, Bhāgavatbhakta Māthemā's five sons, named Subbā Vedabhakta, Subbā Ādībhakta, Subbā Lilābhakta, Kharidāra Haṃśabhakta, and Kharidāra Ratnabhakta, undertook the construction of both the Sataḥ and the Rādhakṛṣṇa temple (KAT2710).

In 1951 CE (2008 VS), an inscription was affixed to the Sataḥ's wall, outlining allocated lands for the Sataḥ. This measure was taken to prevent the loss of these lands. Following the Sataḥ's completion in the early 20th century, provisions were established for daily rituals and an annual observance on Kṛṣṇaṣṭamī. This inscription bears testament that any descendant of Sardāra Haribhakta Māthema carries the responsibility of its future restoration.

In the aftermath of the 2015 CE earthquake, the Sataḥ encountered extensive damage, necessitating the evacuation of its inhabitants and eventual reconstruction, which concluded by 2022 CE. This revival of the Sataḥ was facilitated through the collaborative efforts of the Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilization project, an initiative under Nepal Government's Ministry of Urban Development, along with financial support from the Asian Development Bank. The Sataḥ's refurbishment was successfully accomplished, culminating in its inauguration in October 2022 CE (2079 VS).
A stone name plate positioned above the main entrance, although lacking a specific installation date, serves as an identifier for the location.
A metal name plate, denoting the alternative name "Māthemā Sattala" for Bhagvateśvara Ghāta Sataḥ, has been attached. However, no record of the installation date is present.

Lack of care and renovations for a long period had developed the Hiti into bushes. In 2019 CE, the Kirtipur Municipality reconstructed the monument. At the same time, the statues of Viṣṇu, Nāga and Bhagīratha were added in the hiti premises.

The Sataḥ was constructed in the name of Kṛṣṇasaṃkala, Viṣṇusaṃkala and Maheśvarī Mayī by Jayasaṃkara and other family members. The donor family also made arrangements for regular income for annual rituals to be performed. Other details recorded in the inscription are the position of the planets and list of things required for the annual rituals.
The latest renovation of the Sataḥ was carried out by 'Friends of Sankhu', a local non-profit organization.

monument_name: Jāvalākhela Phalcā 2 (ca. 19th cent., rebuilt in 2020 CE)
event_description: The Phalcā collapsed completely in the 2015 earthquake.

Viṣṇurāja Bhāro, a resident of Cāpāgāũ Bhansāra Ṭola, renovated the temple along with his wives Maṃgarārakṣmī and Caṇḍikārakṣmī. A statue of Vaṃśagopāla (Kṛṣṇa) was also established in the nearby Kṛṣṇa temple on the same occasion.
Kaviprasāda Gautama and his followers Komalaprasāda and Jyotiprasāda Gautama came to Cāpāgāũ and erected a stone pillar to promote Vaishnavism.

Vārtta Pratihāra Dhruvasaṅgha established the Bhadreśvara Śivaliṅga along with four otherśivaliṅgas revered as Nātheśvara, Sthiteśvara, Ravīśvara, and Śubheśvara. He also endowed plots of land to fund regular worship of theseśivaliṅgas.
The inscription records the establishment of thephalcāand consecration of Halāhala Lokeśvara.

This inscription on the pedestal of the Mahākāla statue is erroneously dated "Saṃvat7009," which can be accurately dated to NS 709 (1589 CE) based on the mention of King Śivasiṃhadeva (r. 1578-1619 CE) and his brother, Raṇajitasiṃha. While some names like Hāku, Lavasiṃha, and Gunasiṃha are legible, the inscription remains largely indecipherable. It is plausible that these individuals collectively commissioned the establishment of this Mahākāla statue, along with the accompanying sculpture of Sarasvatī.
The temple suffered severe cracks in the 2015 earthquake but did not collapse.
The inscription mentions that Dhanasimāna, Rājamāna and others from the Jaladyaḥ lineage renovated a certain structure. However, the specifics of this could not be figured out.

Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided 10 Lakh rupees for the reconstruction of the temple. Locals worked on the reconstruction. Thejhĩgaṭī-tiled roof was replaced with a copper plate. The struts,toraṇasand other woodworks were made by locals. The Gaṇesa statue of the sanctum was also cleaned by removing the cement plaster that had fallen in.
The content of the inscription is unclear, as it is no longer readable due to erosion.
Kṛṣṇaprasāda offered the bell to Bhīmasena.
The water spout was renovated by Rāṇā Prime Minister Candra Śamśera.

King Virendra renovated the water spout and Queen Aiśvaryā inaugurated it. The intra-canal system that brought water to the spout was searched in the course of the renovation to ensure the continuous flow of water.
The recent renovation of the spout was carried out by the Pashupati Area Development Trust in 2002 CE (VS 2059).
The inscription posted on the western wall of the Temple records its initial construction by Kṛṣṇalāla Śreṣṭha from the Gaḥchẽ Ṭola.
In VS 2039 (1982 CE), Santalāla Śreṣṭha, son of the founder of the Temple Kṛṣṇalāla installed a statue of Sītārāma on its plinth.
Again, in VS 2061 (2004 CE), the Śreṣṭha family added a statue of Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa.
Thebāhāḥ, which sustained damage in the earthquake of 1934, was repaired in the aftermath of that disaster.सन् १९३४ को भूकम्पमा क्षति पुगेको बाहाःलाई भूकम्प पश्चात् मर्मतकार्य गरिएको थियो ।

Thedevalahousing the Aśoka Caitya (KAT2360-005), which suffered severe structural damage and was on the verge of collapse during the most recent major earthquake, was reconstructed with funds from the Constituency Development Programme of the Bagmatī Provincial Government and through public donations. The reconstructed structure was inaugurated by Provincial Assembly Member Ajaykrānti Śākya.पछिल्लो महाभूकम्पमा भत्किने अवस्थामा पुग्ने गरी पूर्ण क्षति भएको अशोक चैत्यको देवल (KAT2360-005) लाई वागमती प्रदेश सरकारको निर्वाचन क्षेत्र विकास कार्यक्रम अन्तर्गतको बजेट र चन्दाबाट पुनर्निर्माण गरियो । यसको उत्घाटन प्रदेशसभा सदस्य अजयक्रान्ति शाक्यले गरे ।

Traditional terracotta tiles were laid across the courtyard of thebāhāḥ. This work, financed by the provincial government, was inaugurated upon completion by Provincial Assembly Members Suraja Bajrācārya and Samitā Khaḍgī.बाहाः परिसरमा टेराकोटाको परम्परागत टायल बिच्छाउने कार्य भयो । प्रदेश सरकारको बजेटबाट भएको यस कार्य समापन पश्चात प्रदेशसभा सदस्य द्वय सुरज बज्राचार्य र समिता खड्गीले उत्घाटन गरे ।

event_name: Construction of a phalcā at Pacalī Bhairava
event_description: An inscription, currently located within the premises of the Purohita Ghāṭa Śivālaya, documents the construction of a newphalcā(resting place or pavilion) in front of the Svacchanda Bhairava temple (Pacalī Bhairava, KAT2580). This construction involved the dismantling of the oldphalcāthat previously stood in the same location. Notably, the inscription is not directly associated with any of the temples in the vicinity.

Kāśīrāja Panḍita Satyāla, along with his wife Bhavānīdevī and son Śivarāja Paṇḍita Satyāla, made an offering by presenting a bell (object no. KAT2730-013) to the Dvārikānātha Mandira. This temple was constructed by Kāśīrāja Panḍita Satyāla, where a statue of Viṣṇu (KAT2730-012) was enshrined. This offering possibly coincided with the time of the construction of the shrines.

Kāśīrāja Panḍita Satyāla, along with his wife Bhavānīdevī, son Śivarāja Paṇḍita Satyāla, and daughter-in-law, made endowments of land. These endowments established a trust aimed at facilitating the observance of daily and anniversary rituals for the temples, the provision of musical instruments during the daily rituals, and the offering of alms to mendicants on the occasion of Śivarātrī, the 14th day of the dark fortnight of the month Phālguna
In the course of restoring a school building behind the Indrāyaṇī Dyaḥchẽ, a German project renovated thehitias well.

event_name: Installation of inscription with verses praising Brahmeśvara
event_description: Pārthivendra Malla, having sincere devotion to Śiva, visited the Brahmeśvara Śivaliṅga, the 27th among the 64śivaliṅgas located in the valley of the Kabilāsa hill. He probably went up the hill and visited Kapileśvara Mahādeva as well. This inscription with verses dedicated to Brahmeśvara Mahādeva that he composed himself was probably installed during this visit.

The inscription on thejalaharībase of theśivaliṅgainside the sanctum cannot be fully understood due to chips coming off it. While its content appears to deal with the establishment of aśivaliṅga, the name of the donor is unclear but the term "rājendra," meaning "the king of kings," is legible. Possibly, Pārthivendra Malla also established theśivaliṅgarevered as Kapileśvara while also installing the inscription (NWK0650_I_001) with verses dedicated to Brahmeśvara Mahādeva.
Motīmāna Nyāsi Śreṣṭha, son of Lakṣmīdevī of Dhuṃllā Ṭola in Sankhu, offered a narrow oblong banner (patāḥ) of silver to Kapileśvara.
Together with his family, Colonel Yajña Śamśera, grandson of Dhīra Śamśera and son of Bhīma Śamśera, offered a bell to Sarasvatī, the goddess of wisdom, enshrined near Kabilāsa Nāsaḥdyaḥ.

event_name: Establishment of Gaṇeśa , Nandī and Hanumān
event_description: Bālakṛṣṇa Mānandhara, Lakṣmī Mānandhara, and Kubera Mānandhara, residents of Banepa, established statues of Gaṇeśa (NWK0650-008), Nandī (NWK0650-009), and Hanumān (NWK0650-010) south of the Kapileśvara Mandira in memory of their deceased parents Herābahādura and Santuku Mānandhara. They also installed a trident on the occasion.
The temple collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes, injuring some people.

It was rebuilt with funds from the National Reconstruction Authority and the cooperation of local people. Before the earthquake, the temple had a stone roof, but after reconstruction, it was replaced with a copper roof.

A statue of Guru Padmasambhava, brought from New Delhi, India, was established west of the Kapileśvara Mandira. Followers of Tibetan Buddhism believe that Guru Padmasambhava meditated on the Kabilāsa hill before heading to Tibet.
With the financial assistance from the Bagmati Provincial Government and donations from devotees, stone slabs were laid along with the construction of a rest house inside the temple premises.
The Phalcā was renovated. It was plastered with cement and the roof was replaced with corrugated metal sheets.
Around VS 2040-2045 local youths established a library in the upper floor of the Phalcā. However, the library has been closed for many years as it was seldom used.

In June 2019, the Phalcāwas dismantled and all building materials were discarded. The reconstruction started in July 2019 and incorporated traditional design features. The painting of the snake was preserved and covered with a protective layer of foam. The foundations were rebuilt with reinforced cement concrete beams and the floor was recast as a 4-inch-thick steel reinforced concrete pad. The walls were constructed using modern brick withdāci āpāfacing. Six newly carved hard wood columns and highly decorated capitals and beams replaced the earlier plain timber frames. The first floor received a projecting central window and two flanking windows, all carved in great detail and vaguely resembling a late 19th century style.According to a local informant, the design for the Phalcā was provided by Rohit Ranjitkar from the KVPT. Working drawings were made by Anil Basukala.The project was conceptualised by Śobhā Śākya and funded through the Parliamentary Development Fund (Sāṃsada Vikāsa Koṣa/ सांसद विकास कोष).

The Sataḥwas built by Nārāyaṇa Jośī. The inscription mentions that he built the Sataḥwith the help of Kājī Śamśera Jaṅga Pāṇḍe. However, it not clear whether Kāji Śamśera provided him with money, land or something else in helping him to construct the Sataḥ.The inscription begins with the name of Lord Gaṇeśa and also mentions a special worship (pūjā) to him on the day of Indrajātrā, thus clearly connecting the Sataḥ to a shrine of Gaṇeśa.
The Sataḥ was dismantled in June 2019 and replaced by a three-storey concrete building with a roof terrace.

event_name: Installation of a pair of lions
event_description: Jakṣa and Siṃha, sons of one of the elders of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ, erected the pair of stone lions in front of the entrance of thedyaḥchẽ.

event_name: Construction of a dyaḥchẽ for lineage deity
event_description: According to the stone inscription from NS 774 (1654 CE) affixed to the backside of thedyaḥchẽ, three people, including Narasiṃhadeva, built a god house (dyaḥchẽ) fordigudyaḥ. This suggests thatdigudyaḥwas initially an open shrine, and thedyaḥchẽwas constructed only in 1654 CE.

event_name: Renovation of the Vajradhātu Caitya (object no. KAT1200-010)
event_description: During the reign of King Pratāpa Malla, the elders of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ renovated the Caitya in front of the entrance to the courtyard of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ.

event_name: Construction of Pañcāvaliyukta Caitya (object no. KAT1200-015)
event_description: During the reign of King Rājendra Vikrama Śāha, Bhājuvīra Śākyabhikṣu (text: Sākebhikṣu Bhājubila) constructed the Caitya in memory of his father Bekhāsiṃhadeva (text: Bekhāsiṃdeo). He also endowed some plots of land to make periodic offerings (śrāddha) to six of his ancestors and perform the anniversary ritual of the Caitya.

event_name: Construction of Jalaharyoparijinālaṅkṛta Caitya (object no. KAT1200-014)
event_description: Together with his family, Dharmasiṃha (text: Dharmmasiṃha) constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani.

event_name: Construction of Jalaharyoparijinālaṅkṛta Caitya (object no. KAT1200-011)
event_description: Śākyabhikṣu Jujuvirasiṃ constructed the Caitya in memory of his father Dhirjavīrasiṃ.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-008)
event_description: Devalakṣmī Maharjana, Hela Thakuṃ, and Pune Thakuṃ of the Yatkhā Ṭola constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani. They also endowed some plots of land to observe the anniversary ritual of the Caitya.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-017)
event_description: Jīvaratna constructed the Caitya (KAT1200-017) at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani in memory of Dhirjamāna of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-007)
event_description: During the reign of King Vīrendra Śāha, Jogaratna (an elder 'āḥju'of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ) constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-016)
event_description: Dharmasiṃha constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani in memory of his father Dhanavīra (text: Dhanabi).

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-006)
event_description: Jogaratna Śākya (an elder 'āḥju'of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ) constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-013)
event_description: Najaramāna and his family constructed the Caitya at the Ituṃ Bāhāḥ Nani in memory of Caturamāna.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-018)
event_description: Members of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ constructed the Caitya.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (object no. KAT1200-019)
event_description: Cinīkumārī Śākya and her family constructed the Caitya in memory of Sānu Śākya, an elder 'āḥju' of Ituṃ Bāhāḥ.
Thedyaḥchẽwas reconstructed with funds provided by the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office's Hanumandhoka Palace Area Conservation Program.

monument_name: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Kālikā Devī Mandira (built in the second half of the 20th cent.)
event_description: The exact date of construction of the Kālikā Devī Mandira is unknown but it can be situtated in the second half of the 20th century CE. This is indicated by the monument's absence from Marc Gaborieau's 1968 photos. On the other hand, one can make out the temple in a photo published in Dilli Raj Sharma's 2012Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture(Sharma 2012, p. 226, Pl. 60b.).
Puṇyarāja and his wife Buddhimāyā Śākya offered the bell to the Bāhāḥ.

event_name: Construction of Dharmadhātujinālaṅkṛta Caitya and pavement of  the courtyard
event_description: The Bāhāḥ’s courtyard was paved withteliyabricks and the Dharmadhātujinālaṅkṛta Caitya was constructed there.

Siṅgarāja and his family members (wife Aṣṭamāyā, sons Śrīrāja and Bhimarāja, and daughter Punamāyā) constructed the Dharmadhātu Maṇdala in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard. They also donated a crown andlhegāto thekvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.
Puṇyarāj Śākya also offered three praying wheels to the Bāhāḥ.

event_name: Mention of Sum Bāhāḥ in a copy of a document
event_description: A copy of the document reporting a dispute from NS 656 (1536 CE) between the members of Sum Bāhāḥ and their neighbour Phyāku Mulmī suggest that the Bāhāḥ was built before this date.

event_name: Returning of the Bahāḥ’s guṭhī land
event_description: Twentyropanīsof land belonging to the Bāhāḥ was returned to the Bāhāḥ’sguṭhīin 1862, which was confiscated during the reign of King Raṇa Bahādura.

event_name: Consecration of the statues of Nāmasaṅgīti and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara
event_description: Śukrarāja Śākya and family members consecrated the Nāmasaṅgīti and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara statues.
The Bāhāḥ suffered heavy damages during the 2015 earthquakes.

event_name: Damages to the Phalcā due to the 2015 earthquakes
event_description: The 2015 earthquakes incurred severe damages to the Phalcā. Previously, a three-story building, the Phalcā was later reduced to two floors due to the damages.

Within a year of the 2015 earthquakes, the Phalcā was renovated. The second floor that was dismantled owing to the damages caused by the earthquakes was covered with corrugated tin sheets that allowed the use of its first floor.
The Hiti was constructed by King Jagata Prākāśa Malla (cf.S. KhanālaVS 2068, 254).
It was repaired during the reign of King Mahendra.
The 2015 earthquake severely damaged the temple. The Department of Archeology has provided wooden columns for extra support.
The temple was in a dilapidated state, and so it was restored by the Department of Archeology with the help of the German government.
After the statue of Hariśaṇkara was stolen from the temple, Shobhā Doṅgola, wife of Buddhi Lāla Doṅgola, installed a new statue.

Visarāma Bhābo, his wife Lakṣmī (text: Rakṣmī), and his family members commissioned the Mandaḥ Phalcā (text:maṇḍapa), along with ajaḥdhuṃwater tank. The inscription is primarily a stonedalūlampstand with a small statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara atop it, along with what appear to be two standing figures of donors. Thephalcāwas consecrated on the 1st of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the same day the statue of Buṅgadyaḥ is placed on the chariot in Pulcoka.

Bhikṣu Indraśvari, Manasiṅa Bhābo, Punasiṅa Bhābo, Majurāma Bhābo, and Bhaginī Mayi made cash donations for the worship of Buṅgadyaḥ and the main deity of a nearbybahī, and for the distribution ofsamaybaji. The formation of the trust came five years after the inception of thephalcā.

A concrete square building of two floors was erected in place of the Mandaḥ Phalcā, with a portion of the ground floor left open while the upper floor utilized for the operation of a public library named “Pūcva Pustakālaya.” Meanwhile, thejaḥdhuṃmentioned in the inscription no longer exists, as it was never restored after this reconstruction of thephalcā. The stone water container of thejaḥdhuṃwas relocated to the nearby Lāchi Ṭola, while the stone blocks in excellent condition were repurposed for renovating the nearby Pulcoka Lohãhiti (LAL0570).

The concrete structure that replaced the traditional Mandaḥ Phalcā sustained damage in the 2015 earthquakes. It was once again dismantled and rebuilt as a concrete structure in 2020 CE (VS 2077) by the donor family with financial assistance from an NGO named Prārambha. The donor family provided a finial that now crowns thephalcā, while the Lalitpur Metropolis supplied veneer bricks. The library, Pūcva Pustakālaya, continues to operate from thephalcā’s upper floor onwards. Notably, an inscription installed after the recent reconstruction erroneously mentions that thephalcāwas originally built in 1709 CE (NS 829), the year the donor family set up a trust in the name of thephalcābuilt five years previously.
Following the Court Building's partial collapse in the Great Earthquake 1934 it was restored with one floor less; e.g., in a two-story configuration rather than the original three stories.
Śaṅkarasiṃha restored thehitiduṃ(a wooden structure with functions such as underground pipes to channel water from the source to the Hiti).
During the reign of King Mahendra Śāha, the Hiti was restored by collecting donations.
Āloka Hiti Saṃrakṣaṇa Tathā Khānepānī Vikāsa Upasamiti (Ālok Hiti Conservation and Water Supply Users’ Committee) renovated the Hiti premises, including the surrounding walls and the water source.

Together with his wives Indralakṣmī and Jayalakṣmī, his son Phyakudeva and his daughter Śuṃdaralakṣmī, Tuhūdeva Vajrācārya had this Hiti constructed on Thursday 8thof the bright fortnight of NS 535 (1415 CE). Since it was dry at the time, a Tantric ritual was performed in advance of its construction. He also bestowed nineropanīsof land upon the Hiti to fund its continued maintenance. The copperplate regulates that the stone which was placed after the Tantric ritual should never be uncovered. In addition to this, honey, dirts, soap and leather shoes should not be taken into the Hiti area.The copperplate mentions that there is a stone inscription attached to the Caitya, and that this provides more information about the construction of the Hiti. However, this inscription is missing.
An inscription dated 1413 CE was erected in the area before the construction of the spouts. It could not be figured out what Ajay Bharo did on this date.

After the bone factory closed in VS 2057, locals became more conscious of the need to conserve and protect the monument. The stakeholders formed a committee named Ālko Hiti Saṃrakṣaṇa Tathā Khānepānī Vikāsa Upasamiti (Ālko Hiti Conservation and Water Supply Users’ Committee). The committee has now managed to collect the water in a big tank so that it can be distributed to locals via pipes. The committee collected Rs. 2,000 from every household to raise funds for the construction of this system.

A factory producing manure from buffalo bones was established to the east of the Hiti. After heavy rains, the water from the bones collected in the factory mixed with the water for the Hiti, and bloody water started to flow from the spouts. The administration closed the bone factory after locals protested.
In the memory of the late Utsava Ḍuṅgānā, his family members installed a stone statue of Sarasvatī inside the Phalcā.
This inscription is embedded above the Sarasvatī statue, only mentioning the name of the goddess.
The inscription on the eaves fascia (mhuraḥpau) records the renovation of the roof by replacing the traditional tiles with copper sheets by Gopāladhvaja, Lakṣmī, Devendradhvaja, and others.

The inscription on the eaves fascia (mhuraḥpau) reveals that theāgaṃchẽwas renovated in 2006 CE (VS 2063). There is another inscription from 2007 CE (VS 2064) set on the back of theāgaṃchẽ. This inscription does not mention the event but lists the names of donors, who probably contributed to the renovation the previous year.

event_name: Rebuilding of the southern house of the Āgaṃchẽ
event_description: The southern building attached to the tiered structure collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes, leaving the main building of theāgaṃchẽpartially damaged. The collapsed portion was rebuilt in 2019 CE (VS 2076) while the main building was also renovated. Wooden supports were later added to the main building.

The Vaiṣṇava reformer Kaviprasāda conductedbhajana-kīrtana, charitable donations, and a continuousahorātra yajñain front of the Varāha image, erecting a stone pillar (dharma-stambha) to commemorate the event. The inscription on this pillar instructs that such observances should continue annually on the same day. Since the Newar community traditionally performed goat sacrifices duringdegu-pūjās near the image, the inscription explicitly declares this site to be aViṣṇu-kṣetra, forbidding all acts of violence (hiṃsā).
Astamāna and Mīsarī jointly constructed a raised platform (sataḥ) in dedication to Varāha.
Two devotees, Gaṇeś and Candra, together offered a bell (ghaṇṭa) to the Varāha temple.

event_name: Construction of a building for bhajana
event_description: Rukmiṇī Lāmichāne built a hall in memory of her late husband and founded abhajana maṇḍalī(devotional singing group).

event_name: Construction of pillars and beam for a bell
event_description: Before offering a bell to the deity, the family of Bhaktalāla Siṃha constructed a necessary support frame (thāmo) for hanging it.
The family of Bhaktalāla Siṃha from Cāpāgāũ offered a bell (ghaṇṭa) in front of the Varāha temple.
Śyāma Bahādura Maharjana, in memory of his father and grandfather, dedicated a brass oil lamp encircling the temple.

The inscription on the base of the main deity of the temple records that the image of Mañjunātha was installed. Although the date on the inscription is eroded, Regmi (1966, p. 2) has dated it to around 10th century.
Bhājumāṃ and other family members jointly offered a bell in the name of Mañjeśvarī (Mañjuśrī).

A partially damaged stone oil lamp is kept within the sanctum. An inscription is engraved on its surface, though nearly half of it has weathered away. The stand bears carved figures of the donor family, with their names inscribed in the lower  part of the images. The donors of this object were Ganasiṃ and Cikuti. It remains uncertain whether the oil lamp stand was originally dedicated to this temple or brought here from elsewhere, where it might have been simply lying around.

The temple is flanked by a pair of stone lion statues. An inscription carved on the lower part (pedestal) of the statues records that they were installed in front of the temple by Bisamā and twelve other individuals.

During the reign of King Surendra, the temple’s previous tile roof was replaced with gilt copper sheets. Similar gilt eave boards, inscribed with embossed letters, were also installed on all sides of the upper roof.

In the northwestern corner of the temple is a small courtyard containing two caitya and a historic well. One of the caitya bears an inscription on the lower part of its eastern surface. According to the inscription, a Persian resident of the same courtyard, named Kehemāna, along with his family members, constructed this caitya.

Bhājumāna Ranjitakāra, along with his family members who resided near the temple, installed a brass banner inside the sanctum. The walls of the temple’s ground floor were decorated with imported tiles. Furthermore, they also installed sixty oil lamps surrounding the temple.
In VS 2040 (1983–84), the temple was jointly rebuilt by all concerned bodies. Local residents, the elected ward committee, and the priestly clan collectively contributed to its reconstruction.
Following the theft of the original image in the 1980s, Guṇanidhi Rañjita undertook the reinstallation of a replacement statue of Durgā on the left pedestal.

The restoration work of the temple was carried out in the presence of the then Member of Parliament Dhyan Govinda Ranjit, representatives from the Department of Archaeology, other concerned authorities, and local residents.
The Sataḥ was completely dismantled and rebuilt withmāaḥpā(bricks of relatively large size) and new columns.
The roof of the Sataḥ was seriously damaged during the 2015 earthquakes.

A historical Jadhuṃhiti was placed on the western side of the Sataḥ. Previously, this water diviner was attached to Nāsaḥ Capāḥ. But when the Phalcā was dismantled in 2013 CE and incorporated in a large four-storied concrete structure, the Jadhuṃhiti was kept there depreciatingly until its shift. This activity was undertaken by the joint effort of Lalitpur Metropolitan City, Hakatvāḥ Mankāḥ Khalaḥ and Śaharī Garibaharūko Lāgi Samāja.
As of October 2020, the roof of the Sataḥ is under reconstruction. A local committee is managing the project with funding from the Lalitpur Metropolitan City.

event_name: Renovation of the Caitya (B) (the object number LAL4066-007)
event_description: Punasiṃ, Āsācā, Dhanarā, Tavadhika and others jointly commission the renovation of the Caitya.

Probably, this inscription does not belong to this Sataḥ, despite being embedded in its facade. It says that in the name of late Raghunātha Ujhā, Sundarī Brāhmaṇī 6ropanīsof land were granted from an area calledNhulakvāṭha. It also records the regulations for organising different religious events forthe Patan Kumārī.
Dedicated to the Buddha, tiles have been paved in front of the Sataḥ by Lalita Bhāva and Najani Mayi.

event_name: Renovation of the Caitya (A) (the object number LAL4066-007)
event_description: The Caitya was renovated. At the same time, Nārāyaṇī Mayī and Jagata Rāma added four Dhyānī Buddhas facing the four cardinal directions.
Bhairavasiṃha Vajrācārya and his family established thisbāhāḥtogether with thedharmadhātu maṇḍala.
Mañjuśrīnaka Mahāvihāra Sudhāra Samiti offered aprabhāmaṇḍalaat the back of Akṣobhya.

event_name: Offering a golden image of Akṣobhya
event_description: During the reign of king Yakṣa Malla, jayateja Pāla and his brother Anantateja Pāla had offered a golden image of Akṣobhya in memory of their father Rajyadā Pāla.
The Bāhāḥ was renovated by raising donations from its saṅghamembers.

event_name: Offering golden kalaśa and five flags
event_description: Śākyabhikṣu Rūpateja Pāla, his wife Rūpālakṣmī, their eldest son Abhayajyoti Pāla, his wife Padūmayī together offered golden kalaśa and five flags on the roof of the bāhāḥ.

During the reign of King Śivasiṃha Malla, eight people, including Śākyabhikṣu Samalasiṃha and Tāmrākāla Abhayasiṃha Bhāro, who returned to Nepal after earning money by trading in Tibet, had organized Samyaka Mahādāna. Vajrācārya Ravicandra of Sikomaguḍi Bāhāḥ had acted as a priest in that mahādāna.
Śākyabhikṣu Sūryyajyoti wished for the salvation of his brother Candrajyoti and offered umbrella, flag,patāḥ, yak tail fan, conch and bell to Akṣobhya.

Jayadhana had organized Samyaka Bhojana and invited King Nṛpendra Malla on that occasion. The donor had offered a golden throne with a golden umbrella surrounded by goldenprabhāmaṇḍala. Pārthivendra Malla and Mahīpatīndra Malla were also present on the occasion.
A Wooden toraṇa was offered over the entrance to the sanctum.
General Lalita Śamśera Rāṇā commissioned the temple in his honor. He was the son of Dhīra Śamśera, the younger brother of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust renovated the temple after it was badly damaged in the 2015 earthquakes.
Around 2005 CE, the Phalcā was rebuilt by the Bhaktapur Municipality.

This inscription is engraved on the southwest, south and southeast sides of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalā. The main actor's name is not legible, but other family names can be read: the donor's grandfather Siddhiju, elder uncle Nhuccheju, father Cidhiju, mother Amit Lakṣmī, elder sister Thakũmati, younger sister Bhīma Thakũ, daughter Rāni Thakũ, younger brother Dhija(bī)ra, youngest brother Bhājupati.
The monastic building collapsed during the earthquake.

Thetoraṇaover the main entrance to Kvāpādyaḥ was donated. However, it was buried under rubble after the building was destroyed in the 2015 earthquake. Thetoraṇabroke into pieces when it was extracted from the rubble.
In 2002 CE, it was renovated at the initiation of the locals and local government, as it was on the verge of collapse.
In the course of constructing a new building of Bhāstipura Jñānamālā Bhajana, a local group of hymnists, in 2018 CE, this Temple also received minor renovations and coats of paint.
Prime Minister Vīra Śamśera offered a bell to Jagadmukteśvara.

विसं १९६४ बाट जलविद्युत आयोजनाको निर्माण कार्य थालिएको आयोजना समापन भई विसं १९६८ (सन् १९११) जेष्ठ ९ गते सोमवारका दिन तत्कालीन राजाको उपस्थितिमा टुँडिखेलमा बत्ती बाली उद्‌घाटन गरियो । यसै आयोजनाको मुख्य अङ्गका रूपमा बनेका संरचनामध्ये यो पोखरी पनि थियो ।
Lokapati and Hirāmāyā Vajrācārya installed the statue in memory of their daughter Someśvarī.
Lokapati and Hirāmāyā Vajrācārya established the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in memory of their son, Cakrapati Vajrācārya.
Vācaspati Vajrācārya, a member of Mūladuvā clan of Bu Bāhāḥ, built adyaḥchẽand installed a stone statue of Akṣobhya in thephalcāhe was residing in.
Lokapati Vajrācārya and his wife Hirāmāyā installed this statue in memory of their late daughter Śaundarīśvarī.
Lokapati Vajrācārya and his wife Hirāmāyā constructed this Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalain memory of their late son.

Bhagīratha Bhaiyā, a trusted minister of King Śrīnivāsa Malla, dedicated a Garuḍa image to Śikharanārāyaṇa (also known as Śeṣanārāyaṇa). The responsibility for its preservation was entrusted to Amātya Naraharī Bhāro, a resident of the Ikhālakhu quarter in Patan. Today, this Garuḍa image is no longer placed in front of Śeṣanārāyaṇa but instead stands before the Kṛṣṇa Temple (PRN0080-001). It appears that at some point in time, likely out of ignorance, the image was relocated to its current position.
A person named Padmānanda installed a stone image of Hanumāna at the Śikharanārāyaṇa shrine. At present, this image is placed facing toward the Kṛṣṇa Temple (PRN0080-001).

On the occasion of his birthday, King Mahendra installed stone slabs in the temple courtyard. He also commissioned the construction of a new cemented path with steps leading to the Śikharanārāyaṇa temple. During this renovation, the ponds in the area were also restored.
Thedyaḥchẽwas reconstructed into a modern building after it fell into poor state of repair, without adopting its traditional architecture.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
event_name: Initial construction of the capāḥ (Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā)
event_description: The Phalcā was constructed on the plots of land endowed by three persons from the Su Bāhāḥ Ṭola—Jivarāma Bhābo, Hṛdāma Bhābo, and Jayarāma Bhābo.  Its initial construction took place when a person named Jyoti was thethakāliof a group that used to conductaṣṭamīvrata, a ritual fast observed on the 8thlunar day. Although it is aphalcāat present, its inscription refers to the building as acapāḥ.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
event_name: Renovation of the capāḥ (Phalcā) and land endowment
event_description: Śivarāma Bhāro renovated thecapāḥand endowed some plots of land to sponsor the regular offering of oil lamps to Gaṇeśa.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
event_description: Harisiṅ Bhāvo, Bhāgīsiṅ Bhāvo and others jointly renovated Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
event_name: Construction of two wells and pavement of road
event_description: Sidikisana, Pāhā̃siṃ and others jointly constructed two wells at the Su Bāhāh Ṭola and also paved the road.

monument_name: Gaṇeśa Bhajana Phalcā (originally built in 1505 CE)
event_description: The Subāhāḥ Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti renovated the Phalcā with the help of the then Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, UDL and local residents of the Subāhāḥ Ṭola. Old wood and bricks were used for restoration as much as possible.

Atāḥ Phalcā was part of the first PhotoKathmandu festival, which included an exhibition and curated walk entitled 'Patis in Patan'. It was curated by Sujan Chitrakar (Kathmandu University, Centre for Art & Design), Rajendra Shakya (South Asia Institute branch office, Heidelberg) and Christiane Brosius (Heidelberg Centre for Transcultural Studies, HCTS) in November 2015 following the 2015 earthquakes. The project focused on the everyday lives of people in public spaces such as the arcaded rest houses. Photographs were taken of elderly women using the Phalcā, who also spoke with interviewees about their lives and the role of the Phalcā in them. A selection of these photographs was exhibited on the walls inside the building and next to it.The Phalcā has been used as an exhibition space to tell the stories of the women who sit in it every day, and to create awareness of and interest in the site as a social space.

The Phalcā was reconstructed almost entirely without using older materials. It is an important site for the community, but had been in a badly damaged state due to water leakage and the earthquakes of 2015.

Before its reconstruction in 2019, a metal plate dated NS 842 could be seen on the beam of the Phalcā.However, it did not state what happened on that date. The metal plate was removed during the reconstruction.

As mentioned before, there was a small shrine in this place before it was replaced by a proper temple structure. The inscription records about a renovation of the shrine carried out by Jakerāma, Nugurāja, Dharamakesa and others.
The inscription cannot be deciphered because it is heavily eroded, thus its content remains obscure.

Before Halisaṅkhara (Hariśaṅkara), Satyāra, Abhayakesa Māhāna and other people jointly constructed a proper Temple during the joint rule of King Siddhinarasiṃha and Śrīnivāsa Malla, there was a small shrine in this place.

event_name: Offering of a golden pinnacle and umbrella
event_description: Śivarāma Bhāro, Devarāma Bhāro, Jitalasiṃha Bhāvo and others jointly offered the pinnacle and umbrella to the Temple.
Bekvadala Bhāro and his wife Sivadevī offered the golden crown to Gaṇeśa.

event_name: Repair of Temple with teliā bricks
event_description: Madhanasimha Bhāvo repaired the Temple usingteliābricks.
Lakṣmisĩ Bhāvo and others constructed thecapāḥat Pinchẽ Ṭola.
Punasi, Sighavīra, Jogīlāla and Kṛsamā jointly covered thetoraṇawith brass sheets.
A group of twenty-four people including Dhijavigula and Jigidhaṃ offered the brasstoraṇakept atop of the door to the sanctum.
Saṅkharvi (Śaṅkaravīra) covered the door to the sanctum with brass sheets.
The Shrew Pillar (see the monument objects and site plan above) was installed in front of the Temple by Āsāmāna and Aṣṭamāyā. Statues of Āsāmāna and Aṣṭamāyā can be seen on the bottom of the Pillar.
Bhājumāna offered the new bell after the one offered in 1957 CE (NS 1077) was broken.

event_name: Offering a pair of metal flags
event_description: Nhuche Bāhādura and Machimāyā's sons and grandsons Gaṇeśa Bāhādura, Dineśa and Śrīgeśa jointed offered the pair of metal flags to Gaṇeśa.
The Temple was jointly reconstructed from the then Lalitpur Metropolitan City Office, Patan Conservation and Development Program (PCDP) and local residents.
Sānukājī Maharjan together with his family members offered the brasspatāḥto Gaṇeśa .
There is no trace of inscription on the stone tablet due to a heavy erosion and coverage by oily substances.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
event_description: This inscription was installed in the sanctum of the temple by an astrologer called Śivanārāyaṇa. It records the names of his predecessors.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
event_name: Addition of a Garuḍa pillar, a bell and an oil-lamp balustrade
event_description: Lalitpur sub-metropolitan city, Cakravarti Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti and local people installed the Garuda pillar in front of the temple as well as an oil-lamp balustrade, a bell, and a wind vane together with icons of Viṣṇu's weapons.

monument_name: Nārāyaṇa Mandira at Cāka Bāhāḥ (ca. 1699 CE)
event_description: This event is not related to this temple. Aphalcāsomewhere in theṭolawas renovated in NS 764 by Rāmabhadra. It seems that this inscription was brought from somewhere else and preserved here.

King Mānadeva established the statue of Viṣṇuvikrānta by building a grand temple for it here in the Paśupati area in memory of his mother Rājyavatī. He established a similar statue in Lazimpat, Kathmandu on the same day with a similar inscription on their pedestal. Although the inscription of the statue mentions the construction of a grand temple, it no longer survives in the vicinity.
The Ward No. 8 office of the Kathmandu Metropolis renovated the shrine where the statue currently is.

event_name: Roofing of the Bhairava shrine with tiles
event_description: A group led by Budha Baṃde and Kṛṣṇa Siṃha Bhāro laid traditional tiles on the roof of the Bhairava shrine. Other individuals like Jivarāja Bhābo, Jikisiṃṅa, Rūparāma, Budhacanda, and others also assisted the work. One-fourth of the tiles required for the roof was sponsored by a person named Rūpa, while the rest were contributed by other members of the group. This record suggests that the open shrine was covered with a tiled roof.
A group led by Guṇarāja Bhābo built a proper temple for Bhairava and offered a pair of flags as well. Individuals like Jogideva, Mahāmuṇi, and Suṣurideva were also involved in the group.

During the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla, Suṣudeva Bhābo, Karirāma Bhābo, Jagadeva Bhābo, and others jointly offered a pair of stone lions to the temple. Two local administrators, Karyāsiṃha and Jayakṛṣṇa, were appointed aspramāṇaof Sānāgāũ at the time of this event.

event_name: Offering metal utensils and farming tools
event_description: Indralachami, along with her sons Dhanabṛdhi, Vīramuni, and Dharmmavīra, offered utensils and agricultural tools to the temple.
Together with his wife Dhijalakṣmī, son Byakhā, and other family members, Munirāja Bhāro offered a brasstoraṇato the temple.
Kuṃbha Bhāro and his family from Sānāgāũ offered two brasstoraṇas to Bhairava.
A community group with Muni Thākuli as the most senior member installed a bell at the temple.
Kavi Prasāda erected a stone pillar in Sānāgāũ after organizing devotional singing dedicated to Viṣṇu and hosting a feast for brahmins.
Tulsībahādura Maharjana offered an oblong banner (patāḥ) to the temple.

event_name: Offering of trident to Siddheśvara Mahādeva
event_description: Kṛṣṇagopāla Maharjana, Nāti Maharjana, Ajaya Maharjana, Lakṣmī Maharjana, and family members offered a trident to Siddheśvara Mahādeva.
After the oldtoraṇawas stolen from the temple, a new one was installed by Hareśa Maharjana and Tīrthamāyā Maharjana.

event_name: Offering of a garland of bells
event_description: A group led by Siṃghavīra offered a garland of small bells to the temple.
Byakhāsiṃ, Rāmanārāṃ, Harṣamāna, and others installed a bell at the temple. After the bell was stolen, a new bell (SAN0010-006) was installed in 1889 CE (NS 1009).

The Phalcā was constructed by the ‘Māheśvarī Pīṭha Saṃrakṣaṇa tathā Vikāsa Samiti’, a committee of locals formed in 2000 CE (VS 2057) for the conservation of the Pīṭha premises. According to senior citizens from the area, there used to be a three-bayedphalcāsouth of the Māheśvarī Pīṭha. It was destroyed in the early 1960s due to the lack of timely maintenance and was never rebuilt. In 2004 CE, a new Phalcā was built a few meters northeast of the spot where the lost Phalcā once stood.

The family of Jita Govinda Amātya from Daubāhāḥ Ṭol offered a brass throne (siṃhāsana) to Kwayna Gaṇeśa, inviting the deity’s presence into their neighborhood through the consecration of the mask (mukhākṛti).

The construction of the presentdyaḥcheṃwas completed with financial support from Prince Dhirendra Śāha, on the occasion of King Virendra’s 39th birthday. The project was carried out under the supervision of the then Minister Jogmeyara Śreṣṭha, with additional material and financial contributions from the local community. A detailed record documenting the nature and extent of local donations was inscribed and preserved at the site.
The concrete roof (ḍhalān) of the second floor of the adjoiningsattalawas laid with the collective physical, financial, and voluntary labor (śramadāna) of the local residents.
Within thedyaḥcheṃcomplex, a new toilet facility was constructed, and the interior and exterior walls of the compound were plastered through local community support.

As the oldkhaṭa(palanquin) used in the annual procession of Kwayna Gaṇeśa had become dilapidated, a new one was built through community contributions, and the festival was celebrated with the participation of various musical ensembles (bājā).
The smaller mask of Gaṇeśa (LAL2970-002), which had deteriorated over time, was replicated and restored by the family of Hari Maharjana, preserving the original design.
In memory of Nhucchelāla Maharjana, his sons Surya and Devendra Maharjana decorated the roof above the main entrance of thedyaḥcheṃcomplex with brass plating.
The descendants of the lateāḥjuBulāla Maharjana offered anāgaornament made of 98.84tolaof silver to adorn the image of Gaṇeśa.
Omlāla Śreṣṭha and his family members collectively dedicated a silverkikipā(forehead ornament) to embellish the mask of Kavyna Gaṇeśa.
The roof of thevihārawas repaired by Lalitpur Metropolitan City.

event_name: Consecration of image of wooden Vajrasattva
event_description: During the reign of King Yakṣa Malla, the Mahāpātras of the Piṃ Bāhāla area of Patan performed a great fire worship (yajña) and established a wooden image of Vajrasattva Tathāgata. On the same occasion they offered a bronze image of the moon, two bells and abhṛṅgāra. However, the image of the Vajrasattva kept inside the sanctum of the Bāhāḥ has since been stolen.

With the permission of the Vajrayoginī Sevā Samiti-a local organization formed for the conservation of the area, the family of Kṛṣṇa Kumārī Śreṣṭha belonging to a clan named Baḥsimākva Khalaḥ had commissioned the reconstruction of the Hiti. Concrete was used on the wall from which the spouts protrude and marble slabs with line carvings of the figures of the moon deity (Candra) and the sun deity (Sūrya) were also posted on the Wall.

The tip of thejalaharīfaces north while an inscription from the era of King Rāmadeva is found on its western side. According to the inscription, in 546 CE (Śaka Era 467), a woman named Mānamatī donated land to establish a trust in the name of Nātheśvara. However, it remains unclear from the inscription whether she solely founded the trust or also established the Nātheśvara Śivaliṅga. It also records the donation of land for a sage named Khuḍu Svāmī. This inscription holds significant historical value, as it not only introduced King Rāmadeva into the Licchavi lineage but also illuminated the rising influence of a courtier named Kramalīna during that period.

Following the earthquake of 2015 CE (2072 VS), the Paśupatī Development Fund issued an appeal for assistance, allowing those individuals who were willing to privately reconstruct the damaged heritage to do so. Based on this appeal, the Phalcā was reconstructed with the financial support from Ratna Stephenson (Maske), an person based in the United States of America.विसं २०७२ (सन् २०१५) को भूकम्प लगत्तै पशुपति विकास कोषले क्षति भएका सम्पदाहरूको निजी तवरमा पुनर्निर्मान गर्न इच्छुक भएमा गर्न सकिने प्रावधानका साथ सहयोगको आह्वान गरेको थियो । यसै आह्वानको आधारमा अमेरिका बस्दै आएकी रत्ना स्टेपहेन्सन (मास्के)को आर्थिक सहयोगमा यो फल्चा पुननिर्मान गरिएको थियो ।
The originaljhĩgaṭītiled Phalcāwas dismantled and replaced by a concrete slab supported by three RCC columns.

राजा प्रताप मल्लको राज्यकालमा भिक्षु रामचन्द्र, भिक्षु देवचन्द्र, भिक्षु पुनदेव लगायतका व्यक्तिहरूलाई बाहा:को क्वा:पा:छेँ निर्माण गरेर हस्तान्तरण गरिएको थियो । बाहा: निर्माण गर्ने दाताको नाम पढ्न सकिँदैन ।
काशिराज र उनकी श्रीमती सुमंगरिले छोराहरू सिवराज (शिवराज), दन्दपानि (दण्डपानि) र मनोहोरसँग मिलेर बाहा: प्राङ्गणमा शिखरकूट चैत्य निर्माण गरेका थिए ।
राजा राजेन्द्रविक्रम शाहको राज्यकालमा दिवंगत बुबा जगबासिंह र आमा पुण्यलक्ष्मीको नाममा छोराहरू लक्ष्मीनारां र जयन्तिसंहले बाहा: प्राङ्गणमा चैत्य (KAT0390-008) निर्माण गरेका थिए ।
राजा राजेन्द्रविक्रम शाहको राज्यकालमा भाजुधन, भिमनसिं (भीमनरसिंह) लगायतका व्यक्तिहरूले मिलेर बाहा: प्राङ्गणमा पञ्चावलियुक्त चैत्य (KAT0390-007) निर्माण गरेका थिए ।

राजा राजेन्द्रविक्रम शाहको राज्यकालमा आफ्नो बुबा रक्ष्मिनारां (लक्ष्मीनारायण) को नाममा छोराहरू रत्नसिंह, भाइ जयन्तसिंह लगायत परिवारका सदस्यहरूले मिलेर बाहा: प्राङ्गणमा पञ्चावलियुक्त चैत्य (KAT0390-009) निर्माण गरेका थिए ।

event_name: Offering of statues of Sarasvatī, Tārā and lions
event_description: तुलाधर मानकाजीले श्रीमती जोगमाया लगायत छोरा, बुहारीहरूसँग मिलेर सरस्वती, तारा र एकजोडी ढुङ्गाको सिंहको मूर्ति चढाएका थिए ।
Toraṇadivyeśvarīdevī consecrated the mainśivaliṅgain honor of her husband Narendra Bahādura Śāha.

Post the temple's completion, Toraṇadivyeśvarīdevī, in the same year, generously donated land for the perpetual observance of rituals at this temple, as well as at the Gorakhanātha and Dhīramukteśvara temples.
Salyānī Mahārānī Toraṇadivyeśvarīdevī installed a bell at the temple.
Anotherśivaliṅga(PPK1953-006) is established to the southwest of the temple, marking the site where the ascetic Viṣṇunātha Yogī was entombed.
The Pashupati Area Development Trust restored the temple following the damage inflicted upon it by the earthquakes of 2015.

Taking into account the discernible letters, the faded inscription located west of the temple implies an age predating the temple's construction. Despite the unclear content of the inscription, it appears that its installation may not be directly associated with the temple.

This stone inscription by King Vasanta Deva (r. 506-532) stands against the plinth on the northwest corner of the temple.In the 1970s when Dhanavajra Vajracharya documented the inscription (Vajracharya(VS 2030,112), he found the upper part severely damaged with most of the letters rubbed off and the lower section buried.
Offering of thetoraṇawhich is installed above the main entrance to the temple.
Amara Girī Gusāyī established aguṭhīfor the daily and casual worship at the temple.
Jitgovinda Amātya and his family supported the renovation of the temple.
Endowment of areas of land to the trust of the deity. This document appoints Lakṣmī Girī Gosāi as priest and allows him to use the trust.

Built in honor of the king’s tutelary deity, the inscription decrees its preservation and mandates royal restoration if damaged. It further notes that the administrative rules of the Bhaktapur palace—covering courtyards, gardens, pavilions, andhitis—also applied here, naming Ugra Malla and Bhūpatīndra Malla, and designating the palace as “Thaṇthu Rājakula” with its outer courtyard “Siddhicuka.”

The donor offered 5ropanisof land (called Thacheṣelakṣetra) to finance the renovation of the Phalcā. The descendants of the donors were allowed to use any surplus money.Donation of land, 5ropanīs
The Lalitpur sub-metropolitan city office donated funds (reportedly 1,40 thousand rupees) and land (totalling 5ropanis)for the reconstruction of the Phalcā.

Anuparama Gupta, a powerful figure during the Licchavi period, erected a Garuḍa column in front of the temple and inscribed verses dedicated to Dvaipāyana Vyāsa. Anuparama Gupta's wife was Ābhirī Gominī, and his son was Bhauma Gupta, who later became a powerful figure in the Licchavi administration. This inscription, with its mature writing style and philosophical content, is considered of high quality. While the inscription lacks a specific date or the name of the reigning king, based on its script, it is attributed to the reign of Vasantadeva, who succeeded Mānadeva. A human-like Garuḍa statues are customarily erected in front of Viṣṇu statues in Nepal. These statues often resemble the face of the devotee sponsoring the statue (G. Vajrācārya VS 2033, p. 127). Possibly, Anuparama Gupta established this statue to reflect his own likeness. As Anuparama Gupta's wife, Ābhirī Gominī, installed the Anuparameśvara Śivaliṅga at Paśupati in 540 CE (ŚS 462) (D. Vajrācārya VS 2030, pp. 170-171), it can be inferred that Anuparama Gupta died around that time. Therefore, the Garuḍa column in front of the Satyanārāyaṇa temple must predate 540 CE (cp. Acharya 2007, pp. 30-32).

event_name: Initial construction of the Dhāmī Ghara
event_description: An inscription at the Bhairavī temple (NWK0040) suggests its initial construction. The inscription records the "construction of a house" by the then Bhelu (Dhāmī) Kṛṣṇa and Bhulu (Dhaminī) Sūryalakṣmī, and it further instructs their eldest son and daughter-in-law, who are the inheritors of the Bhelu and Bhulu titles, to "reside in this house and maintain it." It is most likely that the house discussed in the inscription is the Dhāmī Ghara.

The building was reconstructed from the ground up with new bricks while reusing the historic doors and windows. The construction work was carried out under the supervision of the Department of Archaeology.
The central roof tower (phucā) collapsed in the 2015 CE earthquakes. Falling debris damaged the main roof.

event_name: Reconstruction of the roof tower and renewal of the roof
event_description: The roof tower, which collapsed in the 2015 CE earthquakes, was rebuilt by the Department of Archaeology using new materials. Additionally, thejhĩgaṭī(traditional Nepalese roof tiles) cover of the entire roof was renewed.

The temple, initially constructed by the royal astrologer Bhānu Aryāla, was established with significant endowments to ensure the sustainability of its rituals. Bhānu Aryāla dedicated various land parcels to fund both the daily rituals and special periodic ceremonies at the temple.
This damaged inscription is not clearly readable and the event(s) recorded remain obscure.
Only fragments of this damaged inscription remain legible. It documents astuti(eulogy) dedicated to a deity, with no specified date.
Haridāsa Śreṣṭha and his wife seem to have offered something to Dhũllā Gaṇeśa. However, it is unclear what they had offered.
The above-mentioned Mehera family offered the bell in memory of the chief donor's deceased elder sister Kamalādevī Śreṣṭha.

event_name: Installation of brass roof and laying of tiles
event_description: Gopāladāsa, the grandson of Tusīṃ Bhāṣkara and son of Janakalāla, commissioned the installation of the brass roof at Dhũllā Gaṇeśa and laying of tiles at the Shrine. Locals say that Gopāladāsa had won a lottery he had bought in the name of Dhũllā Gaṇeśa, therefore he donated some parts of his lottery to Gaṇeśa.
Gopāladāsa commissioned the pavement of the tiles in the Shrine premises.

A Buddhist verse was inscribed on this inscription without recording any historical event. AlthoughD. Vajrācārya(VS 2030, p.587) has mentioned that the verse was inscribed on a smallcaityaat Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ, locals say that it was inscribed on the Caturvyūha Caitya (KAT0250-010). The inscription is no longer at the site.

event_name: The earliest mention of the Bāhāḥ
event_description: As discussed in ‘description’ above, a palm-leaf document mentions the name of Guṇavajra of Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ (text: Dhvākhā Bahāra). This is so far the earliest record that mentions the name Dhvākhā Bāhāḥ.

Jñānajoti of Henākara Mahāvihāra organized theSamyakMahādānaceremony together with his son Guṇajoti, grandson Dhanasiṃha, and great-grandson Parikhadeva. King Pratāpa Malla, too, was invited to the ceremony. A total of 7,500 Śākyas and the Dīpaṅkaras statues received various items in alms.​

event_name: Consecration of statue of Vajrasattva and construction of tiered tower
event_description: Vajrācārya Palikhadeva installed a statue of Vajrasattva and constructed a tiered tower (pula) on the roof of the Bāhāḥ. The tower no longer exists at present.

event_name: Installing a new pinnacle to a caitya
event_description: Palikhadeva offered a new finial after the old finial of a goldencaityainstalled by his grandfather Guṇajoti was in poor condition. He also installed a stonecaityain front of the statue of Akṣobhya inside the sanctum.
Vajrācārya Dhijamuni, the eldest son of Vajrācārya Samantabhadra, renovated the statue of Buddha’s closest disciples Sāriputra that was in poor condition.
The Caitya was installed in the name of a deceased member of the family. Due to the poor state of the inscription, the names of the donor and the deceased person are unclear.​
Jvagalānī Vajrācāryye repaired the Caitya.

event_name: Reconstruction of the Kāḥpāḥchẽ of the Bāhāḥ
event_description: The main building (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) of the Bāhāḥ was reconstructed with the funds from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Office. The office provided sixty percent of the cost while the Bāhāḥ contributed the remaining fourty percent.

event_name: Construction of a dharmadhātu maṇḍala and pañcāvalīyukta caitya (KAT0250-013)
event_description: Thedharmadhātumaṇḍalaand apañcāvalīyuktacaityawere installed west of the Bāhāḥ on the completion of the Bāhāḥ’s reconstruction.
In the name of her deceased father Yādiratna Vajrācārya, Rūpaśobhā offered a leaf like ornament adorned on the main deity’s crown (kikiṃpā) together with her husband Sugata Śākya and the children.
The Jalavināyaka temple was rebuilt and the arcadedsataḥstructures were constructed around the temple. Deva Śaṃśera Rāṇā donated funds for this.
Construction of Kṛṣṇa temple and Garuḍa pillar by Śyāma Lāla, Lakṣmī Lāla, Hṛdaya Ratna and Hari Lāla
Donation of thecaityaby Kṛṣṇabhīra Bhāro and Nīranārāyaṇa Bhāro. The main priest during the ritual was Nandamuni Vajrācārya of Taḥ Bāhāḥ.
This inscription is from the pedestal of the Nārāyaṇa statue inside the temple in front of the entrance to the Taleju courtyard, though most of the text is now illegible.
The palace building collapsed in the 1833 earthquakes.
A family from the Pradhāna caste offered a bell to Taleju.
The school originally established as the “Thimi Adult Coaching Class” in Siddhikālī Dyaḥchẽ, the god-house dedicated to Siddhikālī, was relocated to the palace complex.
The “Janapremi Secondary School”—previously operating from a private residence in Nigū Pukhū—was moved to the Taleju courtyard.
The deteriorating main structure of the Taleju temple was reconstructed through the efforts of the school’s teachers and with support from the Department of Archaeology.
Jñānaśrī, Dharmamuni, Dhanasiṃha Jayasiṃ, Pariṣadeva, Kutusiṃha, Mahīndra, Maṇirāja and others renovated the temple.

Samvarasiṃ and Maṇirāja offered flags, a golden pinnacle and garlands in memory of their father Dharmasiṃha. They also established a statue of Prajñāpāramitā in memory of their mothers Lakṣmī and Lakṣavatī. Rakṣasiṃ, Guṇākarasiṃ, Jñānīkarasiṃ, Lakṣavatī, Vasundharā, Apsarā, Sūryavatī and other family members are also mentioned.

Most of the letters on the inscription are effaced. The writing appears to mention a land donation and offers regulations as to how to use its income to organise worship rituals. However, it is not clear whether this concerns thecaityaor the temple.
Harṣamāna and Lakṣmīmāyā donated the oil lamp balustrade that surrounds the Śikharakūṭacaitya(LAL0108-002).
Yajñaratna donated the oil lamp balustrade that surrounds the Śikharakūṭacaitya(LAL0108-004).
Members of Yākaḥ Chẽ Khalaḥ collected donations and renovated the temple. The flags, banners and eaves board were renewed as well.
A member of the Citrakāra (painter) community made and installed an image of Garuḍa (LAL2711-001).

event_name: Covering of the dome with brass sheets
event_description: The upper part of this caitya’s harmikā is decorated with a copper sheet covering. On that sheet is inscribed: “In 1899 CE (VS 1956), thecaityawas established by the family of Kulanārāṃ (Kula Nārāyaṇa) Citrakāra.” From this statement, it is difficult to determine whether the entirecaityawas constructed in that year, or only the upper caitya portion was covered with the sheet; the inscriptional language does not make this clear.

The work of covering the upper part of the caitya—from the harmikā upward—with gilded brass was done by Kṛṣṇabahādura Citrakāra in 1935 CE (NS 1055). Judging by the style of the images and the stone carvings used in thecaitya, it appears to have been built in the early Śāha period; however, in the absence of an inscription, this cannot be stated with certainty.
Prajāpati Thakura Kṛṣṇavīra and his two sons Jagatavīra and Rudravīra donated a bell in 1902 CE (NS 1022). The inscription on the bell refers to Hona Bāhāḥ as Kṛṣṇavīra Vihāra.
Prajāpati Thakura Kṛṣṇavīra constructed the Pañcāvaliyukta Caitya.
Thebāhāḥwas damaged in the 2015 earthquake and reconstructed in 2018. The Lalitpur Metropolitan City contributed 12,36,324 rupees and additional funds came from the local community.

A Licchavi inscription stands at the south-western corner of the courtyard. The subject matter of the inscription is not related to this courtyard. The inscription mentions that King Narendradeva transferred some of the rights to people.

At the main entrance to the courtyard, a golden gate was offered by Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā. The inscription mentions that the golden gate costmoha rū3,212. Some of the money was raised from selling an old gilt pinnacle, a bell and copper pots.

On the occasion of the coronation of King Mahendra, a beautification programme resulted in the corrugated sheet iron roofing being replaced by large sized British style roof tiles. The masonry surface of the coka was covered with cement plaster. The work was supported by His Majesty's Government of Nepal.

The north wing as restored with funding from the Austrian Development Agency; the Federal Ministry, Republic of Austria; Federal Chancellery of Austria; The University of Applied Arts, Vienna; and the Nepal Reconstruction Authority, Government of Nepal.
Following the 2015 earthquakes the galleries in the north, west and south wings were relocated to the north-east wing in order to allow the restoration of the damaged sections of the building.
The west wing was restored with funding from the Nepal Reconstruction Authority.
The Patan Museum was inaugurated by King Vīrendra Śāha. The inscription is embedded in a wall of the east-wingdalan.

event_name: Restoration and establishment of the Patan Museum
event_description: Between 1982 and 2000 the Keśavanārāyaṇa Coka was restored and converted into the Patan Museum.
The Phalcā had been in a poor condition. Due to the lack of repair, the roof collapsed during the heavy monsoon of 1987 CE. It remained in a ruinuous condition for 32 years.

There is an inscription on the base of a niche embedded in the back wall of the Phalcā. The inscription documents the renovation work in 1743 CE by a person named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Amātya. Most likely, we can assume that a Phalcā stood there before this date.

event_name: Reconstruction and inauguration of the Phalcā
event_description: Lalitpur Metropolitan City, ward number 17, funded the rebuilding of Ilachen Phalcā with 1 million NRS. Local residents had also been actively involved in this project by voluntarily contributing their time and human resources support. After the rebuilding was completed in August 2020, a formal inauguration worship (pūjā) was performed.

There is another inscription from 1779 CE on the base of a niche which is embedded into the back wall of the Phalcā. The incomplete inscription reads "......has been placed.........." and doesn't mention what exactly was placed. It has been inscribed on the base of niche and statue of Viṣṇu can be seen at the centre of atoraṇainstalled over the niche. Most probably, it refers to the act of installing a statue of Viṣnu in the niche.

This inscription from NS 785 is attached to the eastern wall of the Phalcā. According to the inscription, the Phalcā was constructed with three bays by a group of Bhāvos. This inscription indicates that there used to be two bays previously, thus allowing for the addition of a third one. Above of the inscription one can see a statue of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara standing intribaṅga āsanawith two hands. The statue is holding a flower of lotus in its left hand and holding its right hand in a gesture ofvarad.Candraandsūryahave also been inscribed on Lokeśvara's left and right sides respectively.This is a fine example of inscription worship. On the top of the inscription, there is an icon of Bungadyaḥ. Worshipping of the inscription equals worshipping the deity. Some say that itt is not allowed there to sit in thephalcāin front of the inscription showing the back of the body. It is considered as an insult like to a king.
The Phalcāwas renovated by GTZ/Udle and Lalitpur Metropolitan City.

The Phalcā was completely dismantled and reconstructed in a 'traditional style' again. New carved pillars were used and the platform was raised in height. The inscription is still there, but the candle stand has been lost.
Rāmeśvara, a resident of Panauti’s Kvāchẽ Ṭola, installed the images of his parents (PNT0050-008) in front of the temple.

event_name: Construction of the temple and endowment of lands
event_description: The queen of King Bhūpatīndra Malla of Bhaktapur and Viśvalakṣmīdevī, the mother of King Rañajita Malla, built the Brahmāyaṇī temple with a gilded finial (molamba). She endowed twentyropanīof agricultural land asguṭhīfor the temple’s maintenance, with provisions for ritual worship at both Brahmāyaṇī and Indreśvara temples on nineth of bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha. The meat of the sacrificial goat offered during the worship was to be distributed to the king, the prince, and the queen-mother as consecrated food (prasāda). She also arranged for an annual state offering of twotolasof silver to Brahmāyaṇī and donated various utensils.
Viśvalakṣmīdevī, together with her son King Rañajita Malla, endowed an additional fourteenropanīof land asguṭhīfor the temple.
Five brothers—Dhana, Hāku, Kṛṣṇa, Siri, and Sukula, the sons of a man named Mani—jointly offered threetoraṇainside the temple.
In memory of his late parents Devalāla Bhuju and Chandrakumārī, Gaṇeśalāla Bhuju of Panauti’s Balākṣe Ṭola donated a bell (PNT0050-006).
In memory of his late father Rāmakṛṣṇa Ghulu and late mother Īśvarīlakṣmī Ghulu, Śyāmakṛṣṇa Ghulu, together with his wife Bālakumārī Ghulū, donated a bell (PNT0050-007).

Because many of the characters of the inscription (śilāpatra) are broken, the date and most details cannot be deciphered. Names such asAnanta Bhari,Lele Bhari, andRāma Bhārocan be read. Judging from the script, the inscription appears to belong to the early medieval period. Thus, it likely predates the conversion of the open Brahmāyaṇīpīṭhainto the present temple.

event_name: Initial Construction of the Bāhāḥ and Donations Made by Dhanasiṃ
event_description: Dhanasiṃ Tāmrākāra constructed thisbāhāḥinside his private house after he returned from Tibet. He offered this house to the Svayambhū Caitya and Vajrayogīnī.He also donated some cash to aguṭhīassociated withtheSvayambhū Caitya and contributed to the renovation of the large clay image at Buddhabārī.

This copper plate inscription documents Jitāja Bhāro, a Tulādhara from Asana, Kathmandu, inviting the Dipaṅkara Buddha statue of thebāhāḥto take part in theSamyak Mahādāna, a grand alms-giving ceremony hosted during the reign of King Sadāśiva Malla. The invitation requested the participation of thebāhāḥ’sthapāḥju(seniormost member) and other members, along with the ornaments, parasol (chatra), and flag (dhvaja) of the Dipaṅkara statue. However, the inscription does not clarify whether both of thebāhāḥ’s two Dipaṅkara statues were invited or just one.

During the reign of King Jitāmitra Malla, Daṇḍapāṇi Vajrācārya undertook renovation of the Bāhāḥ'skvāḥpāḥchẽ. His contributions included installing a gilded parasol on the finial and erecting a pillar bearing his own statue. His wife Ratnamaṇi, son Manamohanasiṃ Vajrācārya, and other family members also supported the renovation efforts.
Rachamāvati—along with her son Tadhika, daughter-in-law Ranhāvati, and other family members—donated a woodentoraṇato adorn the entrance of the sanctum.
Ratnamuni Vajrācārya and his family members established a statue of Vasundharā in thebāhāḥ, following a month-long religious sermon delivery program conducted by Pundit Badrīratna Vajrācārya.
Thebāhāḥis undergoing reconstruction with financial support from the Madhyapur Thimi Municipality, allocating Rs. 5 million in the first phase of funding.

Most of the letters on the inscription installed at the Phalcā are unreadable. Therefore, it is unclear when the Phalcā was first constructed. The script and language of the inscription suggest that the Phalcā was constructed during the Śāha period. The term ‘divaṃgata’, which means ‘the late’, is legible in the inscription. Probably, Putalināni, Bhājudeva, Jayalachimi, Lādhāmuni, and Gyānavira–the names featured in the inscription–constructed the Phalcā in memory of a deceased member of their family.

The Covid-19 pandemic disrupted the chariot festival of Buṅgadyaḥ in 2020 CE. The statue of Buṅgadyaḥ was supposed to be accessioned to the chariot on the 1stof the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha but the chariot was not constructed due to the pandemic. Therefore, the statue was placed here on Dabū Phalcā until it was accessioned to the chariot on July 25, 2020.
A signboard of Śrī Karuṇāmaya Misā Pucaḥ was installed on top of the central bay of the Phalcā.

event_name: Installation of the statue of Nāmasaṅgīti
event_description: Śrī Karuṇāmaya Misā Pucaḥ, a women’s group, installed a Nāmasaṅgīti statue made of an alloy of copper and zinc at the Phalcā.

During the reign of Śrīnivāsa Malla,PramānaViśvambhara Bhāro of Cākra Bāhāra, Lalitpur, donated one and a halfropanīs of land to set up a trust for performing daily worship at the Bāḍegāũ Caitya. Of the income from this land, 20pāthīs of the harvest were allocated for the priest and 10pāthīs for the deity's worship.
Jayadeva Vajrācārya, Dharaṃsiṅa Vajrācārya, Gopirāma Bhābo, and other members of the “Purṇimā Sevā Guthi” jointly established a pair of stone lions on either side of Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara.

Devamuni of Bāḍegāũ donated one-third of a plot of land located in Dhvapagāma to set up a trust to fund a fire oblation in front of thecaityaon the full moon day of Māgha, along with a sacrifice of a duck to Gaṇeśa, and to perform asinhaḥpūjā(a worship involving vermillion powder) at the shrine of the esoteric deity. A balconied tower (phucā) was also added to the esoteric shrine on the same occasion. Viśvambhara Bhāro of Cākra Bāhāra was thepramānaof the area when these works were carried out.

A certain religious trust operated by Ranajita Kārki and Kavirāja Kārki was subsequently reorganized and brought back into operation. The income from the trust was to be used for conducting worships and hosting feasts. Individuals such as Siṃhamāna Kārki, Citradhoja Kārki, and Jagabira Kārki were involved in the management of the trust. Due to the erosion of text, the content of the inscription cannot be fully understood.
Upīndradhoja Kārki of Thaiba offered a bell (BDG0040-003) to Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara.

event_name: Covering dharmadhātu maṇḍala with copper sheets
event_description: Together with his sons Nīramuni and Tejamuni, Jujumuni established adharmadhātumaṇḍalain front of the Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara statue. With the permission of Jujumuni’s grandsons Kabiramuni, Kānchāmuni, and Maṃgalamuni, Bhimarāja Daṃgu of Dhvākhā Nani, Bāḍegāũ covered thedharmadhātumaṇḍalawith copper sheets.
Jagadīśa Vaidya and his wife Mirā Vaidya, residents of Devanani, Lubhu, offered a bell (BDG0040-002) to Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara.

As most of the letters in the inscription have eroded, the content of the inscription is unclear. However, the name of King Surendra can be deciphered, suggesting that a certain activity was carried out at thecaityaduring his reign (1847-1881 CE).
In 2002 CE, the standing Gaṇeśa statue was stolen. The stolen statue is depicted in a photograph from 1999 CE published in Shokoohy and others (2014, p.270).

event_name: Installation of a new standing Gaṇeśa statue
event_description: The original standing Gaṇeśa statue, as previously stated, was stolen in 2002 CE. As a result, a new Gaṇeśa statue (see object number KIR4031-002) was installed in the same wall niche in 2006 CE.

event_name: Replacement of traditional roof with concrete
event_description: The Phalcā's traditionaljhĩgaṭītiled roof was replaced with concrete around 2006 CE (VS 2063), with the financial assistance from the local government body, Ward Office.
Traditional bricks and stones were used to enhance the Phalcā's exterior wall. On that occasion, the concrete roof was also tiled withjhĩgaṭīto give it a more traditional appearance.
Balabhadra Bhāro of the Solaṅkī (text: Suraṃki) dynasty built the stone spout south of his hometown.
Jita Lāla (grand son of Sundara Rāja Bhaṇḍārī/son of Suvānanda Lāla) and his wife Nānī donated a copperpatāḥto Gaṇeśa.

In 2009, a house attached to the temple was dismantled to be reconstructed. During this process, the temple was damaged. Śrī Kvālkhu Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti therefore began renovations of the temple in 2009. This was completed in 2010 CE.

event_name: Donation of brass flags on either side of the main image of Gaṇeśa
event_description: Two brass flags were donated and fixed on either side of Gaṇeśa.
Suvānanda replaced the tiled roofs of the temple with copper plates.

Purṇasiṃha Bhāro, Basundharā Mayī, and Dhanadeva Bhāro from the Jelā ṭola were instrumental in the renovation of one of the phalcās within the premises of the pīṭha. Additionally, Basundharā endowed land at a location known as Ithari to observe the anniversary ritual (varṣavarddhana) of the phalcā. However, it is currently unclear whether the inscription found in the Maheśvarī Mandira (BKT0300) is directly related to these activities or if it pertains to another aspect of the site's history.

The inscription from 1746 CE (NS 866) documents the offering of a golden pinnacle to the temple at the premises and the construction of the five-bay arcade during the reign of King Raṇajita Malla. It is not clear whether the inscription found at the Maheśvarī Mandira (BKT0300) is related to the Sataḥ.

The Sataḥ underwent a significant transformation, as it was dismantled and reconstructed into its current form. In the 1970s, its previous structure featured jhĩgaṭī tiles on the roof and a bay window on the first floor. A photograph published by Pruscha in 1974 (p. 224) provides a visual record of this earlier appearance.

As mentioned in the 'description,' an inscription that used to be at the temple but has since been relocated to an unknown location** mentions a certain Siddheśvara Brāhmaṇa erecting a statue of Kṛṣṇa at his own residence. The Kṛṣṇa statue appears to have been installed on the ground floor of the donor's house before being relocated to where the temple now stands (November 2022 CE). The donor, Siddheśvara, was most likely a member of the clan of the renowned tantric Lambakarṇa Bhaṭṭa.** The inscription was published by S. Rājavaṃśī (VS 2027, p.114).
The signboard states the year 1636 as the original time of the monastery's establishment.

event_name: Renovation of the monastery's courtyard building
event_description: The courtyard building was rebuilt from ground-up as a concrete-frame structure. All doors and windows were made new - no historic building components were preserved.

event_name: Inauguration of the renovated Deryang (courtyard building)
event_description: The brass plaque records the foundation laying by His Holiness the Dzarong Trulshik Shatrul Rinpoche in 2006 and the inauguration of the building by His Holiness the Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche Yangsi in May 2011.The main donors to the project are listed. It is interesting to see how many of the area's former residents have emmigrated to foreign countries.

पाटीको क्षेत्र छुट्याउन चारैतिर केही फिट उचाइको इँटाको पर्खाल निर्माण गरिएको छ र यसको मध्यभागमा ढुङ्गाको शिवलिङ्ग स्थापना गरिएको देखिन्छ । साप्कोटा समुदायको पहलमा पाटीको मध्यभागमा ढुङ्गाको मूर्ति स्थापना गरिएको थियो ।
The phalchā on the northern side of the hiti was constructed by Kanhasiṃ Jāma Śreṣṭha and his wife Nānīthakum, both members of the Jāmanaḥ lineage.

In VS 2078 (2022 CE), Madhyapur Thimi Municipality allocated a budget for the simultaneous reconstruction of thephalchās, hiti, pond, and surrounding structures. At the same time, the ground was upgraded with stone paving.

Funds were raised for the reconstruction of the building in 2017. The Lalitpur Metropolitan City provided 12lākhrupees (ca. 9,000 Euros), the descendants of the founder donated some additional money and locals contributed through charity works. The reconstruction work was completed in early 2020, but as of summer 2020 the formal inauguration had taken place.
The phalcā was already in need of repair before it was further damaged in the 2015 earthquakes. A tree in front of the Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL0840) fell on the building  and damaged its roof.

King Jitamitra Malla, during the tenure of Prime Minister Bhāgirāma, constructedHiticuka—a hiti (stone water spout) with a fine flow of water, along with a beautiful pond—to please his tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā). He also built an arched gateway with a door for the Hiti. Above the arch, atoraṇa(decorative tympanum) was placed, and inside the gateway golden images were installed. Around the same time, Tuthacuka (a square with a well), Lakṣmīvilāsa Chowk, Dumāju Chowk, and Kisigara (an elephant stable) were also built.

A few months after the construction of the Hiti, King Jitamitra Malla endowed 10ropaniof land as aguthifor the upkeep of the Hitiand for the worship of Taleju. The inscription records that the revenue from this land was to be used every year on the 3rd day of bright fortnight of Vaiśākha (Akṣaya Tṛtīyā) to perform theVarṣavardhana Pūjā(annual ritual) of the Hiti, as well as for various other ritual observances dedicated to Taleju. For this purpose, one Rājopādhyāya Brahmin, along with Candraśekhara Rāya and Bhāyarāma Karmācārya of the Vidyāpīṭha, were appointed as theguṭhī-members. As witnesses to this deed, the king’s brother Ugra Malla, his son Bhūpatindra Malla, and Prime Minister Bhāgirama Pradhānāṅga were named.
Jaṅga Bahādura offered a bell to the temple after its establishment. The bell inscription refers to the main deity as Kāmakāmeśvarī instead of Viśvarūpa.

The 2015 earthquakes badly damaged the temple. Half of its dome collapsed while the temple only barely managed to remain standing with cracks all around. About three months later, overnight rain on August 20, 2015, made the temple collapse on the morning of August 21st.

The reconstruction of the temple began after the minister for Culture, Tourism, and Civil Aviation laid the foundation stone in early June 2022 CE (VS 2079) years after its collapse in 2015 CE. The government has allocated a budget of NRs. 450 thousand for the reconstruction of the temple as well as the rest houses at the premises.
