Under the supervision of Viśva, a family of Vyanjankars of Cheri Yantāgṛha of Ombahāl renovated Kisi Phalcā. They were appointed as the monument's caretakers.Transliteration of the stone inscription of thePhalcā (provisionally by N. Sharma)(svasti sign) śreyostu || samvat 826 āṣāḍha śukla pa-n͂camyāntithau uttarā phālguṇī nakṣatre parighayoge bṛhaspati vāsare thva kunhu vaṃbāhāra cheriyantāgṛha byan͂janakāla viśva thaṃkādi pramukha-mi thava bhochi samuhasana kṣaca dasyaṃ coṃgva capāḍa dādvāpva mokasa thva bhochi samuhasana jīrṇo-ddhāra yāṅa dayakaṃ pratisthā yāṅā juro thva ca-pāḍasaṃ chagu julasanāṃ mālako thva bhochi sa-muhasa odhina jura || meva sunānuṃ kaciṃga-la thanan͂asāṃ  mado juro chetrisa ju-ko bhālana pāli choyake do  talesa joko-yā thva bhochiyā ādhina juro || bhālana ma-ko palatra thva bhochina lhoṅā juro sunānuṃkacigala thaṅasā gobrāhmaṇādi paṃca tra-hā pātaka lākahu juro bhinakalasā u-trotra kuro sāki(kṣi) rāmakṛṣṇa bhāro dṛṣṭa||  yathāśāyukta phalamastu śubha ||Rough Translation of the stone inscription of the Phalcā (by N. Sharma):[Svasti sign].  On the 5th day of the bright half of the Lunar month of Āṣāḍha in NS 826 (1706 CE) in the constellation of Uttarā Phālgunī, in the combination of Parigha, on Thursday, on this day, the whole family of Vyanjankars of Cheri Yantāgṛha of Ombahāl led by Viśva, thethakāli(senior person and guthi member) renovated thecapāḥwhich was here from earlier times.  Whatever is necessary for thecapāḥ, the responsibility [to fulfill this] goes to the family. Nobody else is allowed to create trouble. The upper part of thecapāḥshall be under the control of the family. If anybody else creates problems, s/he shall get five kinds of great sins such as killing a cow or a Brahman etc. If anybody else does better s/he shall get prosperity.  Witness is Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhāro. May all be well.

Ripu Malla offered the lamp to his tutelary deity Nārāyaṇa. He is addressed only as 'Candravaṃśī' without being described as a king. Two craftsmen, Jayatarāja and Devarāja, residing in the Vaṃtu Vihāra, had crafted the lamp.The inscription edited in D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha VS 2032, second part, pp. 4-5 reads as follows:L1 श्रीयोस्तु सम्वत् ५६१ भाद्रपदमासे शुक्लपक्षे सप्तम्यां तीथौ अनुराढनक्षत्रे वुधवासरे दीपिकाकृतदिवशे ॥ स्वस्ति ।L2 श्रीउत्तरगिरिकविलासनवकोष्ठपत्तनेषु श्रीश्रीगण्डकीदेवा ॥ भट्टारिक परिसंष्ठान महास्थानेषु तत्र सर्व्वजनपूजितस्वे-L3 ष्टदेवताश्रीश्रीनारायणाय ॥ समस्त विद्युत्जनमनोरञ्जनैकपटुतरेण श्रीमत्सोमवंशार्णवजतिलकायमानगरुडनारायनL4 श्रीरिपुमल्लदेवेन । सद्भक्त्या दीपिका निर्द्यातयामि ॥ प्रदत्ता पुण्यभावेन कुशलानि हि मे सदा राजलक्ष्मीष्ठिराश्चैव प्रतापसिद्धिL5 सर्व्वदा ॥ सुखिनः सन्तु ते पुत्रपौत्रादिसंयुता ॥ श्रीवंतुविहाराधिवासिन जयतराज देवराज तदुभयशिल्पिकृतं शुभं ॥

event_name: Offering of a bell (object no. NWK0170-007)
event_description: Dharmaśīlavantīdevī (text: Dharmasīlavaṃtidevī), the senior queen of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha, offered the bell in the name of Lord Kṛṣṇa. The name of Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama's senior queen was Ratnadivyeśvarī, who hailed from Punjab, India. She married King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha in 1887 CE (VS 1943) (see P. Rāja VS 2071, p. 13). On the bell installed after the king's death, her name was inscribed as Dharmaśīlavantīdevī, not Ratnadivyeśvarī, raising uncertainty about why the name was changed. As the bell is offered to Kṛṣṇa, it could have been brought from somewhere else and installed in this temple.

A significant portion of the temple was damaged by the devastating 2015 CE earthquakes. The Department of Archaeology, acting on behalf of the Nepal Government, engaged the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage (CACH) of the Chinese Government to oversee the restoration of the temple along with other adjacent monuments. Scaffoldings were erected around these structures, and the roofs were shielded with corrugated metal sheets to safeguard against rain. However, as of March 2024 CE, restoration work is yet to commence.
Rana Prime Minister Juddha Śamśera reconstructed the temple.
The temple collapsed in the earthquakes of 1934, causing the death of a man who had been sitting on the plinth.

The temple was slightly damaged in the earthquakes of 2015. Navin Mangal Joshi, the chairman of the Kobāhāla Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti, is an engineer himself; he and his friends renovated the temple free of charge.

The day after the statue of Vaṃśagopāla was installed in the sanctum, 13 pinnacles were fixed on top of the temple. Kīrtimaṅgalā and her husband also bestowed 30ropanīof land on the temple and established theguṭhī.

This 614 CE Licchavi inscription is not directly related to the caitya, but it records that King Aṃśuvarmā remitted themalla kara(a form of state tax) that had been levied upon the inhabitants of Ahiduṃkoṭṭa-grāma—present-day Bālūvagā̃—where theRājavihārawas located.

The local residents of Bālūvagāṃ hold a long-standing belief that the ancient image of Mahākāla once enshrined at this site was transferred to Tundikhel by King Pratāpa Malla. On the basis of this local tradition, the aniconic stone formerly worshipped as Mahākāla was replaced in 2016 CE by a new anthropomorphic image, and a two-storied temple was constructed over it.

With the support from the local community and Kirtipur Municipality, thephalcāunderwent restoration decades later a structure was erected on the platform of thephalcā. Theinscriptionthat records the construction of thephalcāis presently located in the nearby Nārāyaṇa Mandira (KIR0005). As part of this reconstruction effort, a statue of Tārā was installed in thephalcā.

In 1861 (NS 981), Biṃnasiṃ (Bīranarasiṃha), a resident living on the northern side of the road in the Jamala Bāhāḥ quarter of Kathmandu, together with his wife Dhirjalakṣmī and other family members, donated twelve copper images for the purpose of conducting the procession. Fourdhāraṇīof copper were used in casting these images. The donor also offeredpatāḥand a banner (dhvajā) for Pāsikva Ajimā, and aguṭhimemberwas appointed for the maintenance and care of all these endowments.काठमाडौंको जमल बाहा: टोलमा रहेको बाटोको उत्तरपट्टि बस्ने बिंनसिं (बीरनरसिंह) ले श्रीमती धिर्जलक्ष्मी लगायत परिवारका सदस्यहरूसँग मिलेर जात्रा गर्नको लागि १२ वटा तामाका मूर्तिहरू बनाएर चढाएका थिए । ती मूर्तिहरू बनाउनको लागि चार धार्नी तामा खर्च भएको थियो । दाताले पासिक्व अजिमाको लागि पता: र ध्वजा पनि चढाएका थिए । ती सबैको हेरचाहको लागि गुठीयार पनि नियुक्त गरिएको थियो ।

As Pāsikva Ajimā was originally apīṭha, no temple structure existed initially. Only an aniconic stone was installed in an open space beneath a pear tree. Since thepīṭhalay below the level of the road, worshippers had to descend seven steps to perform rituals, and during rainfall the site would become completely submerged. Consequently, funds were collected from devotees to raise thepīṭhaup to the level of the road. Thereafter, a small temple was constructed over the site, to which members of the royal family also contributed donations.पासिक्व अजिमा पीठ भएकोले कुनै मन्दिर निर्माण गरिएको थियो । नासपातीको रूखमुनि खुल्ला ठाउँमा आकृतिविहीन ढुङ्गा मात्र स्थापना गरिएको थियो । बाटोको सतहभन्दा पीठ तलपट्टि रहेकोले पूजा गर्नको लागि सातवटा खुड्किला झर्नुपर्थ्यो । पानी पर्दा पीठ पूरै डुब्ने गर्थ्यो । त्यसैले भक्तजनसँग चन्दा उठाएर पीठलाई बाटोको सतहसम्म उठाइएर स्थापना गरिएको थियो । त्यसपछि पीठको लागि सानो मन्दिर बनाइएको थियो । मन्दिर बनाउन राजपरिवारका सदस्यहरूले पनि चन्दा दिएका थिए ।

पाकशालाभित्र विसं १९८२ (सन् १९२५) मा राखिएको वृहत ताम्रपत्र अभिलेख छ । उक्त अभिलेखमा विसं १९४३ वैशाख शुदी तृतीयादेखि शासकबाट गुठी प्रणालीको व्यवस्था भएको कुरा उल्लेख छ । यसै उल्लेखनलाई आधार मानी हाल प्रशासनले पाकशालाको शुभारम्भ मिति मान्ने गरेको छ । अभिलेखमा पाकशालासंगै मन्दिर बने-नबनेको कुरा स्पष्ट खुल्दैन । तर पाकशाला संगसंगै वीरनारायणका नामले मन्दिर पनि उठाइएको अनुमान सहजै गर्न सकिन्छ । विसं १९४५ (सन् १८८८) को गुठी सम्बन्धि लिखित सामग्रीमा पाकशालासंगै यस मन्दिरको पनि प्रसंग परेकाले दुबै एकैसाथ निर्माण भएको कुरालाई थप बल मिल्दछ (K_0037_0019F) ।
वीर शम्शेरका नाममा स्थापना भएको वीरनारायण मन्दिरमा उनकी कान्छी महारानीबाट एक घण्ट चढाइयो ।

पाकशाला र वीरनारायण मन्दिरको वार्षिक कार्यका खातिर आय र खर्च व्यवस्थाको विस्तृत ताम्रपत्र अभिलेख लेखी पाकशालामा टाँसियो । यो अभिलेखीकरण कार्य श्री पूर्वतर्फका कमाण्डर जनरल धर्म शमशेर राणाका मर्जी मार्फत् नारामान भक्तले गरेका हुन् ।
वीर शम्शेरका नाममा स्थापना भएको वीरनारायण मन्दिरमा उनकी कान्छी महारानीबाट विसं १९४४ (सन् १८८७) चढाइएको घण्ट बिग्रेकाले जीर्णोद्धार गरियो ।
विसं २०४७ (सन् १९९०) सालमा तत्कालीन प्रधानमन्त्री कृष्णप्रसाद भट्टराईबाट यस पाकशालाको सतवार्षिकी मनाइएको थियो ।

After the Hiti’s water source failed and remained dry for about twenty to twenty-five years, Queen Gambhīrakumārīdevī, the youngest wife of Rana Prime Minister Juddha Śamaśera, funded its restoration. The work involved repairing the structure, restoring the water source and supply channel, and embedding marker stones along the route to trace future blockages. One marker was placed on the main road from Guita ṭola’s Guita Bahi to Bh̃uḍe Gaṇeśasthana, another twenty-five feet north, and additional drainage channels (maṃgāla) were installed at one-hundred-foot intervals to reestablish both the source and outlet.
The renovation of the Hiti was carried out collectively by the local community.
The Shrī Bālakumārī Temple Conservation and Improvement Committee raised funds to repair the Hiti, focusing on its external appearance rather than restoring the water source.

This stone inscription from MS 39, affixed to the wall in front of the Jaḥdhuṃ near the main outer gate of Paśupati (but unrelated to the present monument, the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Jaḥdhuṃ), records a royal decree issued by King Aṃśuvarmā. The inscription states that the king entrusted the administrative authority over three temples—Śūrabhogeśvara, founded by his sister Bhogadevī; Laḍitamaheśvara, founded by his niece Bhāgya Devī; and Dakṣiṇeśvara, founded by the ancestor of his niece’s lineage—to the Pāñcālikas.

Dated to 1317 CE (NS 437), the inscription attests to the joint rule (saṃyuktaśāsana) of Ānandadeva and Rudra Malla, distinguished by the use of threeśrīsfor Ānandadeva and two for Rudra Malla. It records that the Jaḥdhuṃ was commissioned by a royal physician (rājavaidya) on behalf of a patron for the spiritual benefit of his ancestors. The text concludes by proclaiming the merit of both offering and drinking water.
During the reign of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha, Lālabahādur, his wife Sīrāmāyā and son Puṇamāna had jointly paved the bāhāḥ courtyard in memory of the late father Dhanarāja.

event_name: Renovation of the Śikharakūṭa Caitya and establishment of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla
event_description: Śikharakūṭa Caitya was renovated and statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla were established. At that time Gyānapāra (Jñānapāla) was the thapāḥju of the bāhāḥ. The name of the donor could not be ascertained as the inscription is heavily damaged.

Bāhaḥ was damaged by an earthquake in VS 2072 (2015).Kvāḥpāḥchẽof the bāhāḥ have been rebuilt at a cost of Rs 90 lakhs received from the Kathmandu Metropolitan City and Rs 19 lakhs collected from raising funds. Although the reconstruction work has been completed, it has not been inaugurated yet.
In memory of his late father Jyāna Bahadur Śākya, his son Padma Bahadur Śākya had erected an iron railing for the protection of bāhāḥ.
According to the inscription in the temple, thecaityain the sanctum is referred to as Vajradhātu Caitya and was renovated in 1853 CE.
BothPruscha(1975, 44) andLocke(1985, 290) have mentioned that thiscaityawas renovated in 1853 CE. They might have taken the inscription of the temple as their source.
The temple's structure was changed during the renovation in 1987 CE. The work was carried out without any coordinatation with the local community. The temple was rebuilt by the Pañcāyata Government.

The information board installed by PURPP/LMC records the initial construction of thehitiand itsguthi. It reads: “Thishitiwas built in Nepal Sambat 870. The Makara headed Hiti faces north (sic). There is aguthiassociate with thehiti. The source of water of thishitiis Emudon, a hillock on the backside of thehiti.”There is no evidence to verify the information recorded on this board.

The ID plaque was placed by the Heritage Conservation Centre, Lalitpur Metropolitan City, and the Centre for Integrated Urban Development (CUID) as part of an project inventorising heritage sites inLalitpur.
Thehitiwas repaired by the Lalitpur Metropolitan City with funding from the World Bank.

The bell, positioned in front of thesataḥ, bears a votive inscription documenting its dedication to Goddess Gaurī by Mukhyānī Viṣṇubhakta Kumārī, the senior wife of Colonel Dalabhajana Thāpā, in 1888 CE (VS 1944). This clearly suggests that thesataḥwas constructed before this date.

The waterspout, located in front of thesataḥand right on the river bank, was constructed by the Vāgamatī Kṣetra Ḍhala Nirmāṇa Sudhāra Āyojanā Kāryanvayana tathā Anugamana Samiti, a government body dedicated to drainage management in the Vāgamatī area.

Bāghanasiṃha (Bāghanarasiṃha Śākya) of the Gautamagotra, a member of the Śākya lineage residing in the southwest corner of Hiranyavarṇa Mahāvihāra, Kwāḥ Bahāḥ, undertook the renovation of the dilapidated Lokākīrti Mahāvihāra at Naḥ Bahī (LAL0880). As part of this project, he constructed a three-tiered stone staircase in front of thebahī, built the Bhvaneśvara shrine, and performed asahasrāhuti yajña(fire offering with a thousand oblations). He was assisted in these activities by his wife Hel Thakuṃ, his sons Bāhadursiṃha and Lakṣmīnārasiṃha, his nephew Kubersiṃha, and his grandsons Harṣanārasiṃha, Byasanārasiṃha, Harṣamānasiṃha, Ratnanārasiṃha, and Samyakanārasiṃha, as well as other family members.

The worship of the tenMahāvidyāgoddesses, which had been initiated at Bagalāmukhī in VS 2025 (1968 CE), was later discontinued for various reasons. In VS 2074 (2017 CE), a rotational system was introduced in which the ten neighborhoods (ṭola) housing theMahāvidyāshrines would take turns organizing the annual worship. That year, Pūlchok’s Tārā/Khadvayoginī (LAL0630) shrine hosted the festival, followed the next year by Naḥ Bahī Ṭola, where Bhuvaneśvarī is located.

event_name: Offering of a pair of metal flags
event_description: At the entrance of the Bhuvaneśvara shrine, a pair of metal flags was installed on either side of the doorway through the joint efforts of Sidhīrāja (Siddhirāja), Lakṣmījoti, and Muni Thakuṃ.

The stone slab inscription above the spout records that the Fountain was built during the reign of King Mahendra (who reigned from 1955 CE to his death in 1972 CE) and named ‘Fivefold Venerable Mahendra Dhārā”.The inscription reads:Śrī(written on top margin)Line1:śrī 5 mahendra dhārāḥ(!)Line2:a. ma. bhai. bināyakaLine3:grāma pañcāyataLine4:pra. paṃ. rana bahādura kaḍāyataLine5:kṣetrīLine6:samba(!)ta 2020 sāla bhādraLine7:2 gate roja 1 māḥ(!) ||
Amātya Rāma Bhāro, Govindarāja Bhāro and others jointly commissioned and engaged in the construction of thephalcā. The first digit of the date recorded in the inscription is not clearly readable.
Amātya Kṛṣṇagovinda, his wife Mānakumārī and two sons commissioned the repairing of thephalcā.

In 2009 CE (VS 2065), local community members and the Department of Lalitpur Sub-metropolitan City jointly engaged in the reconstruction of thephalcā. The Sub-metroplitian City contributed 4,35,742 Rupees to this endeavor.

The temple was damaged in the 2015 earthquake. It was restored in 2016. The inscription that was installed after this work was completed mentions that the woodentoraṇaplaced above the northern entrance was constructed by Gunnā Śilpakāra.

event_name: Formation of guṭhī and donation of land
event_description: Aguṭhīwas formed and land was also donated to fund the daily worship and annual rituals of the temple.

During the reign of King Trailokya Malla, a group of people including Vajrācārya Mahāpāla and Hāku Bande installed a door carved with figures of a lion on the entrance to the main sanctum of the Dīpaṅkara.
During the reign of King Jagajjyoti Malla, donors Vajrācārya Sāja, Mahābuddha, Silipāra, Gyānasiṃ Bade, and others established acaityaat the Bāhāḥ premises.
The god-house (dyaḥchẽ) was renovated while Mañjudeva was serving as the seniormost elder (thapāḥju). The rafters were also replaced during the renovation.

Harihara (text: Halihara), resident of the Yachẽ Ṭola, offered atoraṇawith the carvings of the scene ofMāraVijaya, i.e., the victory over Māra, a malignant celestial king who is known for his failed attempt to disrupt the meditation of Prince Siddhartha while he was on the verge of attaining the enlightenment to become the Buddha. He also offered a window on the same occasion. However, it is unclear which window it was.
Thapāḥju Sūryajyoti Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāryya Sūryajoti) and his wives Sitarā and Locanī (text: Rocani) installed a stone lion (BKT0210-021) west of the entrance.

Thapāḥju Sūryajyoti Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāryya Sūryajoti) and his sons Sūryamuni (text: Surjamuni), Jayamuni, and Siddhimuni (text: Sidhimuni) installed a stone lion (BKT0210-022) east of the entrance.
Ten persons including Jayamuni and Padmajyoti offered a bell.
Tejanarasiṃha (text: Tejanarasiṃ) installed a statue at thephalcāin the name of his father Tejarāja (text: Tejalāja) and mother Maithakuṃ. However, it is unclear whichphalcāit was.
Rājamānasiṃha Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāryya Rājamānsī) together with his wife Lānikutu and the family members establishedcaityas at the Bāhāḥ premises. It is unclear whichcaityas they were.
Dhirja Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāyya Dhija), Guṇasāgara Vajrācārya (text: Vajrācāyya Gunasāgara), and others renovated a previously-installed bell.
Locals reconstructed the Dyaḥchẽ after it was in a poor state of repair. After the reconstruction, the Dīpaṅkara statue was shifted from the first floor to the ground floor.
The government of West Germany sponsored the renovation of the Bāhāḥ’s Dyaḥchẽ.

event_name: Offering a statue of a female
event_description: Ratnakājī Buddhācārya (text: Ratnakājī Budhācārje) offered a statue of a woman.
A large prayer wheel was installed on the ground floor of the Bāhāḥ. Although the inscription does not mention the name of the donor, locals say that it was installed by monk Caityarāja.

Ajuvarasiṃha Buddhācārya (text: Ajuvarasiṃ Buddhācāryya), Thakulāni, Kuberamāna Buddhācārya (text: Kuberamāṃ Buddhācāryya), and others offered a certain object to the Dyaḥchẽ. As the inscription is from the golden widow, it probably was the golden widow that they offered.
The content of the inscription is unclear, as the letters have eroded.
Kājī Ḍillīsiṃha Basneta built the temple and installed a bell to commemorate the event.

Kājī Ḍillisiṃha Basneta donated land parcels to establish a trust for the performance of daily and periodic rituals at the temple. King Surendra issued a copperplate inscription detailing the land parcels Ḍillīsiṃha donated in the name of the temple.
The Department of Archaeology carried out a minor renovation in the stone joints with waterproof chemicals.

event_name: Initial Construction of the Temple and the Land Endowment
event_description: The temple was constructed by two brothers - Śivarāma and Hari Bhāro. They also endowed eightropanīsof land to secure its operation and maintenance.

स्थानीय, वडा र पाण्डे परिवारको त्रिपक्षीय समझदारीमा ऐतिहासिक बहीको अवशेषका रूपमा बचेको परिसर खुला छाड्ने, बाहाःपुजाका खातिर साँघुरै भए तापनि सार्वजनिक बाटो छाड्ने आदि सल्लाह भएको थियो । यसै अनुरूप बाटो पनि कायम गरी वडाले यस परिसरमा गारो र टायल बिच्छाई स्तरोन्नति गर्ने कार्य हालैमात्र (सन् २०२५) भएको छ (local resident, Tulādhara, male, age 67) ।
A now lost inscription states that during the reign of Śivasiṃhadeva, acaityalocated near Yampistūpawas renovated. The text of the inscription is published inVajācāryaVS 2056, 55-56.
The inscription names Mevarāma, Hākudeva and Vinhu Simha, disciples of Karmapaṇi Bhikṣu, as donors of the lion statues.

event_name: Construction of the Priukhā temple at Aśoka Stūpa
event_description: Brahmacarya Bhikṣu Cintāmaṇi of Yampi Vihāra, Rām Bhāro of Konimha and otherguṭhīmembers made the Priukhā temple at the Aśoka Stūpaduring the reign of King Yoganarendra Malla. It is possible that, at that time, the Buddha statues were enshrined in the niches of thestūpa,and that those niches are addressed as the Stūpa temple in the inscription.

event_name: Repairs of the stūpa, repair of six caityas and the courtyard paving.
event_description: Siṃhavīr Bhāvo, resident of Gaḥchẽ, during the reign of King Rajendra Vikarama Śāhadeva, repaired thestūpaby applyingvajralepaand changing the central pole. He alsorepaired sixcaityasin the courtyard (three at the north-east corner, two at the south-east corner and one at the north-west corner) and paved thestūpacourtyardwithteliyābricks.

Harṣapuṇya Jyoti, resident of Itilhane (Nāga Bāhāḥ), repaired thecaityasituated at the north-east corner (LAL1480-033) and seven additionalcaityasin courtyard. He also constructed a wall surrounding thestūpacourtyard.

event_name: Application of cement plaster to the stūpa
event_description: Thestūpawas covered with cement plaster. Land was endowed by Lakṣmī Narasiḥma Śākya, resident of Nyākhācuka, for thestūpa'sannual whitewashing.
Consecration of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in front of Akṣobhya shrine.The inscription mentions the donors as Vajrācārya Siddhivajra and family, from Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra.
Dhanamāya Maharjan and Kṛṣṇamāya Maharjan donated oil lamps in memory of their ancestors Bābulāl and Hāku Maharjan.
A group led by Kulasiṃha constructed a dance platform in Thecva. Other individuals like Doya Gvāra, Luṃgurāma, Jitalasiṃha, and Keśavacā were also involved in the construction.
Bhārasiṃha Bhābo and Sūrya Bhābo, seniors of Thecva, established a Gaṇeśa statue (THC0030-002).

A guild dedicated to chanting Buddhist hymns in Thecva paved the open space in front of the Brahmāyaṇī temple and the area around the Kvaylāchicaityawith floor tiles. The guild was led by Kṛṣṇadeva at the time with Viśvahari, Sūrjjarāma, Raghu, Siddhirāma, and others involved as members. The inscription recording this event bears a carving of acaityaon its upper portion. Thecaityamentioned in the inscription is Kvaylāchi Cībhāḥ (THC0130).
Gumīsiṃha Bhābo, Dātemha Bhābo, Indrasiṃ Bhābo, and others collectively donated three woodentoraṇas for Brahmāyaṇī.
Hākorāma Bhābo, Satyasiṃha Bhābo, Mohona Bhābo, and others jointly offered atoraṇato Brahmāyaṇī.

event_name: Offering of a statue of shrew
event_description: Suja Bhābo, Bābusiṃha Bhābo, Rāma Bhābo, and others made a collective offering of a stone statue of shrew, the animal mount of Gaṇeśa, for the Gaṇeśa enshrined in the Brahmāyaṇī temple.

event_name: Replacing wooden pillar with stone pillar
event_description: Hākusiṃ Bhābo of Nhesaḥ Guthi, Nekusiṃ Bhābo of Mū Guthi, Kṛṣṇasundara Mālī of Kvanā Guthi, and others jointly replaced the old wooden pillar in front of the Brahmāyaṇī temple with a stone pillar.

As the previous Gaṇeśa statue was in poor state, Jitāsiṃ Bhābo, Tulsī Bhābo, Nasiṃ Bhābo, Kīrtimāna Bhābo, and others offered a new statue. They also established a religious trust by donating land for the worship of Gaṇeśa on the 8th of the dark fortnight of Phālguna. Rājamāna Śākya was the artist who crafted the new statue.

The temple damaged by the 2015 earthquakes was reconstructed and the Brahmāyaṇī statue temporarily relocated to a nearbysataḥwas re-enshrined back to her usual seat in the temple after the installation of finial. The reconstruction was carried out by the Department of Archaeology.
The temple was constructed in honor of Yajñeśvarīdevī, the wife of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, and thus, it acquired the name Yajñeśvara.

Some elderly locals recall that thephalcāwas in a dismal state of disrepair, deemed as visual pollution in 1972 CE, just as King Vīrendra was scheduled to pass through with a foreign dignitary en route to Godāvarī, a town in southeastern Lalitpur. Consequently, it was dismantled.

event_name: Decision taken to rebuild the phalcā
event_description: In 2020 CE, a reconstruction committee was established; however, the commencement of work was impeded by a protracted legal battle to obtain official permission.

The first elected local body following the promulgation of Nepal's new constitution allocated a budget for the reconstruction. Nearly 5 decades after thephalcā’s dismantling, reconstruction commenced in September 2021.
Following the completion of the reconstruction, Samay Phalcā was inaugurated by the mayor of Lalitpur. It was rebuilt at a total cost of NRs. 3.5 million.

An inscription on a stone slab placed on the right side of the door provides information about the monument's construction. The document is dated of  ŚS 1741 and VS 1876, which correspond to 1819 AD. It starts by naming the queen and king of Nepal (Rājendra Śāha, r. 1816-1846). The queen is mentioned as 'lakṣmīnārāyaṇadevatā'. It is probably Queen Samrajya Lakshmi Devi (c. 1814-1841), who was then five years old.Bishwo K. C. Pokharel (Pokharel 2011 [VS 2068], pp. 146)) read the inscription as follows:श्री ५ लक्ष्मीनारायणदेवता २ श्री ५ महाराजा राजेन्द्रविक्रम साह १श्रीगणेशाय नमः ॥ राधिकानयनकंजहारको माधवो विजयतेतरां गुणैवत्सलो ह्नलय्यतितरां सुसेवके येन रक्षितमितीरितं जगत्‌ ॥॥॥ गोरघाचलमणीयदानृपो राजविक्रमपदान्तरेन्द्रकः ॥ यस्य दिग्गजनूपा हि विक्रमात्सत्रदानकुशला हयाभवन्बै ॥२॥ देवदत्त इति तत्र नायकों राजनीतिकुशलो (हि) भुभूजाम्‌ । यस्य नाम समुदारणाहिशापालका अपि नृपा बितत्रसु: ॥३॥ तस्य सदगुणयुताबलां सती तत्र तंत्रनितुणोजनि भाव: ॥ मानदों हि यशपावनामक: शंकरों व जगतामहिं: क्षितौ ॥४॥ बीरबीरबन्दितों गुडाकेशवत्पृथुरिवातिधार्मिक: ॥ ज्ञानदानकुशलेषु चाग्रणीर्जान्हवीसुतशिवीव सम्मतः ॥५॥ चन्द्रवेदनगचन्द्रनामके शाकके भृगुजतुल्यनामके ॥ मासि वै दशहरातिथौ गुरौ वासरेग्निवसतौ हि क्षेत्रके ॥६॥ तेन पान्थजनतापनुत्तये निर्मिता हि सुखदा खलु प्रपा ॥ भुक्तिमुक्तिफलदोहरिमयाराधितो भवतु तत्फलस्थ वै ॥॥स्वस्ति श्रीशाके १७४१ सम्वत्‌ १८७६ साल मिति ज्येष्ठसुदि १० रोज ५ तस दिनमा ...१...का रजाईमा श्रीकाजि event_name: Establishment of the Nyakū Jātrā Matayāḥ Central Management Committee's office
event_description: The Nyakūjātrā Matayāḥ Central Management Committee, the organization that manages the annualMatayāḥprocession in Patan, has established its office here at the Sataḥ. A contract was signed between the representatives of the Building Department of the Ministry of Urban Development and the committee that allowed the use of the Sataḥ by the latter. Senior culture expert Satyamohana Jośī inaugurated the office.
During the reign of Candraśamśera, the local merchant Pṛthvīvilāsa Sāpakoṭā constructed this Śivālaya along with a sataḥ nearby, and endowed ample land asguṭhīto sustain the annual rituals.
Kaṃpālidāsa and his wife Māneśvarī constructed the temple. They also endowed land to sustain the daily, annual, occasional, and other worships, and to light up butter lamps on various occasions.
Phini Nānī Pradhāna and her son Keśava Māna Pradhāna established this Gaṇeśa Shrine in the memory of Badrimāna Pradhāna.
Members of the local community had offered a copperbhujāpātrawhich was established on the southern staircase. It was recently stolen.
The construction of the temple was commissioned by King Rājendra with the intention of seeking salvation for the consorts of King Raṇabahādura.

Following its destruction in the earthquake of 1934 CE (VS 1990), the temple underwent reconstruction eleven years later and was built in its current form, mirroring the architectural style of the Vaṃśeśvara Temple (KAT1330) and Naudegaḥ (KAT1280).

Jāminī Mayī, a resident of Tupulāchi, not only commissioned the water fountain but also installed the sacred images of Umāmaheśvara and Viśveśvara Mahādeva. An inscription from the time of thehiti’s construction issues a warning that any act of desecration or damage would invite the wrath of Umāmaheśvara, Viśveśvara, and Cāmuṇḍādevī.

Bhājunarasiṃha, a member of the Śākya lineage of Dyaḥnanī (LAL2650), established acaityaat Taḥdhananī. With achepuon itsharmikā, thiscaityafeatures a unique form, style, and craftsmanship. Unlike the more commoncaityas found in the Valley, this one (object no. LAL2651-006) exhibits a distinct appearance. The design reflects an experimental approach by the artist of that period.

Bhājunarasiṃha of the Śākya lineage from Dyaḥnanī (LAL2650), together with his family members, dedicated a bell in the name of the Mahālakṣmīpīṭha. The same individual also built the stonecaitya(object no. LAL2651-006) at Taḥdhananī.

Siṃharāja of the Śākya lineage and his wife Aṣṭamāyā offered a bell with a stone pedestal on the northern side of thepīṭha. The chain of this bell is adorned with a distinctive leaf-vine design that is rarely seen elsewhere. During the Rāṇā period, various innovations in metalwork emerged in Patan—such as rows of stylized leaves added totoraṇas of courtyards, altered lion figures, and the uniquedalūof the Kṛṣṇa Mandira. Similar innovation can also be observed on the upper part of this bell.

The rectangular superstructure erected above thepīṭhabears "19 Mahālakṣmī 97" on its façade. This indicates that the structure was built in 1940–41 CE (NS 1097). It may have been reconstructed in this year, possibly following damage from the great earthquake of 1934 CE.
The temple was renovated by the Kathmandu Valley Preservation Trust.
Story of Śivaśarman inscribed on struts

The temple was constructed by King Siddhinarasiṁha Malla. He performedhomaand installed Viśveśvara (Śivaliṅga) in the temple. He also made asunadhāraon the west side of the temple and organised a feast forjogīs.
The temple was badly damaged during the earthquake of 2015.
The temple was renovated with UNESCO's emergency fund.

event_name: Pavement of the Street with Stone Slates
event_description: The inscription (from 1821 CE, i.e. NS 942) found in thehitipremises is not related to thehitiitself. It records the pavement of a street, from Lāchi Ṭola to the Bhimasena Mandira, with stone slates.
During the time of Prime Minister Candra Śamśera, Colonel Madanamānasiṃha Basneta renovated these spouts.
The Jabara Jaṃga Gaṇa of the Nepalese Army and the local body jointly renovated the spouts.

As discussed in 'description', thissattalawas erected by Kājī Phaudavīra Rānā. After its construction, he installed a statue and established agūṭhīfor daily ritual worship. The lower part of the inscription lists the names Karavīra Rānā, Jvālā, Nanda, Trivinā, Buddhimatā, Ṣaḍgavīra (Khaḍgavīra) Rānā, Hematā, Saravarasiṃha Rānā, Lachimā, Raṇavīra Rānā, and Buddhilakṣmī, along with their figures. Karavīra Rānā and Khaḍgavīra Rānā are noted as siblings of Kājī Phaudavīra Rānā.
Thesattalacollapsed due to lack of timely renovation, resulting in the loss of its elements.
Hastamāyā donated money for the Bhajana Maṇḍala Phalcā's renovation. The lower structure was left as it is but the first floor and the roof were replaced with concrete walls and slabs.

event_name: Consecration of Buddha statue (Construction of Bāhāḥ)
event_description: As mentioned above in ‘description’ both Pruscha (1975, 32 [K-80]) and Locke (1985, p. 348) mention, by referring to a now-missing inscription on the pedestal of the buddha statue in the sanctum, that the statue was consecrated by a Śākya monk Cakrapati Deva. However, the former mentions the year as 1754 CE and latter NS 865 (i.e., 1745 CE). Though Locke may have misread the date or Pruscha may have converted the year given in the Nepal Samvat to Common Era incorrectly, we use Locke’s dating for documentation because he has mentioned the date in the local era (Nepal Samvat).

event_name: Renovation and transformation: rebuilding the temple
event_description: The Gaṇeśa Mandira, once aśikhara-style temple, underwent a significant makeover. Its evolution took place during the broader restoration efforts that preceded the SAARC summit in Kathmandu in 1987 CE (VS 2044). Divya Pradhāna, associated with the Kulu Cuka at Makhana Ṭola, played an important role by offering financial support for the temple's reconstruction. The exact reconstruction date may have faded from memory, but locals recall the earlier temple as a simpleśikhara-style structure.

Bhuvanesa Pradhāna undertook the refurbishment of the palanquin that holds significance in the yearly procession of the Gaṇeśa Mandira. This palanquin, a gift from his forebears, received the renovation under his care.

The gate was rebuilt in a traditional style with the financial help of 5,00,000 from the Kirtipur Municipality. This rebuilding project was managed from the Bāghabhairava Mandira Guṭhī Vyavasthāpana Samiti.

This inscription records about the establishment of thejaḥduṃhiti(KIR0060-002) near to the Gaḥ Dhvākhā. Originally, thisjaḥdhuṃhitiwas placed at the Lāykū ṭola (Malla palace of Kirtipur). The United Club (a local organization) shifted it from its original place to its present location.
Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā’s wife Bhaktakumārī established the temple.
Jaṅga Bahādura donated land parcels measuring 12khetas for performing various rituals at the Pandhra Śivālaya ensemble.

event_description: During the reign of King Surendra Vikrama Śāha, Harṣanarasiṃha and his older brother Jīvanarasiṃha constructed this Bāhāḥ. On that occasion, Harṣanarasiṃha also established an esoteric deity (āgamadevatā) in the Bāhāḥ’skvāḥpāḥechẽ,and constructed a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya in the courtyard.
Jīvadhanasiṃha installed the metal Vajra in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.
Harṣanarasiṃha, his wife Dhana Thakunī, and other family members constructed the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.
Harṣarāja and his family members offered three prayer wheels to the Bāhāḥ.
The members of the Bāhāḥ’ssaṅgharenovated thekvāḥpāḥchẽwith the financial aid received from the local residents.
Thephalcāwas rebuilt in 1982 CE (NS 1102) replacing an earlier traditional timber and brick structure.

In 2020, the Lalitpur Municipality sponsered the restoration of thephalcā. Rather than reconstructing itfrom ground-up, the existing concrete structure was covered with traditional bricks, and a new pitched concrete roof, adorned with terracotta tiles reminiscent of historicjhĩgaṭīroof tiles, was added.

Rādhākṛṣṇa Mandira was finally reconstructed in early 2022, after many failed attempts to do so.

The inscription records the names of donors such as Junā Mahārānī, Indra Bahādura Siṃha, and Kaviratna Narendranātha.
Viśvajīta Kirātī installed railings and lighting around the temple.

event_description: With financial assistance from the Kathmandu Municipality, the temple was clad with gold-plated brass sheets in 2022 CE (VS 2079).
Thebāhāḥand thecaityawere commissioned by Bekhārāja Vajrācārya during the reign of King Pṛthvī Vīra Vikrama Śāha Deva.
The renovation was commissioned by Gaṇeśarāja Vajrācārya in 1970 CE.

At end of 2015 CE, the Phalcā was dismantled and the reconstruction work was started at beginning of 2016 CE. The project was conceptualised by Rajana KC and funded RS 7,00,000/- (seven lakh) through the Parliamentary Development Fund (Sāṃsada Vikāsa Koṣa).
Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City renovated this Hiṭī.

Attached to the western plinth of the Hiṭī is an inscription of Licchavi King Jayadeva II (r.713-733).Vajrācārya(2030, 539-42) has read this inscription. The inscription mentions Narāyaṇa as a lineage deity. It is possible that the image of Narāyaṇa was also established close to the inscription. The Hiṭī, thus named Nārāyaṇahiṭī, lated called as Nāya Hiṭī (Khanal2068, 225). It is 131cm tall and has 50cm breadth.

event_name: Foundation of the Vihāra and consecration of Caitya
event_description: Śrī Thakuṃju founded the Vihāra and consecrated a Caitya during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla.
Bekhā, Lāl, Punajoti, Jitamāna Siṃha and Kulabīra donated alhegā(brass made cloth) and a necklace to the main deity of the Vihāra.

The Vihāra completely collapsed in the 1934 earthquake. The Saṅgha members and the surrounding Jyāpu community renovated it. Due to the 2015 earthquake, the back side of the monastic building also collapsed, and the front facade was severely cracked. The local residents therefore decided to demolish it.

The facade of the Sataḥ was spray-painted by Seb Toussaint, an Anglo-French artist. The monument caught the attention of artists and cultural actors and caused an agitated public debate surrounding the definition of ownership of endangered cultural heritage. Seb Toussaint and his Outsiders Krew were accused of abusing religious sites and local people for the ‘wrong’ purposes; i.e. harming sites through sacrilege and 'insulting' their 'authentic' purposes instead of working to beautify underprivileged sites. The art group travels around the world and visits impoverished and neglected urban settlements, where they invite local inhabitants to ‘participate’ in the beautification of their area by selecting meaningful words that the artists then, sometimes with the help of local artists or laymen, paint on the walls of residential houses. The Sataḥ at Purohitaghāṭa was the first example of a religious compound being used in the art project, which is why it enraged some groups even a few weeks after the wall had been already painted and sprayed. The question of ‘Whose heritage’ was raised, and ranged between accusations of iconoclasm against a Hindu temple (though the Shiva temple lied behind the Sataḥ at Purohitaghāṭa) to damaging heritage structures (such as spraying unremovable paint onto a rare window design from 1883). One critic argued that, “the Shiva Temple, though not on the World Heritage Site List, has something to contribute to the remarkable cultural heritage and legacy of Nepal. Any kind of intruding and defacing it would be overlooking history of the place and hurting sentiments of my people.” (inThapa 2014)The case is also interesting because it draws attention to the fact that the Satah had long been in a dilapidated state and sidelined by public attention. Some Nepalis questioned why this had been the case for so long, and why it took foreign artwork to notice this. As such, these voices found the accusations ambivalent, claiming that had the site been recognised as heritage, people would have cared about its neglected state beforehand. The fact that it was left uncared for for so long was seen as a sign of ignorance on behalf of the Nepalese people vis-à-vis their own heritage.Thapa (2014)refers to Niels Gutschow’s mention of the site in his third volume of Architecture of Newars: “The sattal at Purohitghat was one of the smaller endowments, but probably the most fascinating one. The baluster columns and the cusped arches of the arcade follow early 19th century prototypes, but the first floor windows went beyond the scope of carved window frames … The frames of the side openings add to the stunning design, contributing to a move that culminates in the flower motifs that crown the central opening. In a playful manner, curled appendages frame the entire window, flush with the wall“ (see primary image).Mahaju (2015)connects cultural heritage to the idea of national progress and development for which it has often been sacrificed, showing that cultural heritage has been dramatically endangered in times of urban transformation: “in 1993/4, during the construction of the Bagmati Bridge in Thapathali, the government tore down a historic temple and a pati. What remains of the complex is cramped away in one corner. The government had assured the public that those structures will be relocated with due honour as it merits a place of worship. Twenty one years hence, the promise still hangs in the air. The recent road widening also has upset conservationists and heritage practitioners, common people notwithstanding, at how the government has treated places of utmost importance.”

event_name: Collapse of the roof and upper floor
event_description: The roof and upper floor of the Sataḥ collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes.
The Sataḥ was constructed by a Satyāla family from Kathmandu.

event_name: Theft of Hanumān and Garuḍa statues
event_description: The statues of Hanumān and Garuḍa were stolen. Some days later, the statue of Hanumān was found on the banks of the Bagmati close to Kālamocana.

The ruins of the upper floor were left uncovered for about a month after the earthquake. It took about a week for the French Army rescue team of seventy members to remove the ruins. During the removal of the debris, the windows of the Sataḥ were safely collected by the Department of Archaeology in the presence of the local residents.
Southern Commanding General Mohana Śamśera commissioned the Ḍillīrājamukteśvara Temple's construction and donated the bell together with his family.

event_name: Installation of the inscription by recording the construction of Temple and land endowment
event_description: The stone inscription (see description above) erected by Udaya Bahādura Pā̃ḍe and his wife Lalitā Devī mentions the installation of the inscription by recording the construction of the Temple by his grandparents, parents and uncles on their private land and land endowment by them for the maintenance of the Temple. However, it does not mention the date of the Temple’s construction.

event_description: The bell was installed by General Jaya Bahādura Kuvara Rāṇā in VS 1907 (1850 CE).

Pūrṇa Māyā constructed thedharmadhātuin memory of her late husband Pūrṇa Bahādura Nāpit.
Construction of thedharmadhātucaityaby the Lucidyaḥ Guthi from Thyaka Tol.
Restoration of the central shrine building with funds provided by the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City.The restoration was completed on Śrāvaṇa 19, VS 2064.
Restoration of the base of the Nīla Mahāvriṣaratna and addition of a roof by the Shree Nīl Mahā Vriṣa Ratna Boddhisattva Degaḥ Punaḥ Nirmāna Samiti.

event_name: The earliest mention of Taḥ Bāhāḥ
event_description: A copperplate inscription at Ibāḥ Bahī mentions Taḥ Bāhāḥ as Śrīṭavabahāra. The inscription records the building of the esoteric shrine of Ibāḥ Bahī (LAL2730) in NS 547 (CE 1427) and that Lokarāma of Taḥ Bāhāḥ played a vital role as avajrācāryaduring the accomplishment ritual.The orifginal copperplate inscription could not be found at Ibāḥ Bahī.
Amṛtasiṃha, the grandson of Rājsiṃha and son of Gyānsiṃha, organised asamyak mahādānain Taḥ Bāhāḥ.
A pair of lions was offered to Kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ by Kāśirāma Bhāro together with his wife Gaṅgā and their three sons Viśeśvara Bhāro, Dhaneśvara Bhāro and Maheśvara Bhāro and a daugher Gauri.
Taḥ Bāhāḥ Dyaḥchẽ was renovated.
Sundaralāla Khaḍgī renovated the esoteric shrine of the Bāhāḥ in memory of his family members.

Dhana Mānāndhara and his wife Tuyudhari and their other family members jointly constructed the Caitya and made arrangements for a regular income to sponsor the annual rituals here. A group of five Mānandharas (Tavadhika, Bhāgivṃta, Rachimi Nārā and Dharma Nārā) are mentioned as ‘caretakers’ of the Catiya. For the inscription seeKIR4027(KIR4027_I_001).

event_name: Installation of a Gilt Gaṇeśa Statue and Land Grant
event_description: This inscription records that a person named ?? Kṛṣṇa Bhāro gilded the Gaṇeśa statue and offered a golden pinnacle to the temple. During the late medieval period, it was a common practice to offer golden pinnacles following the construction or the renovation of the temples. It is not clear, however, that the pinnacle offered by ?? Kṛṣṇa Bhāro was after the construction or the renovation of the temple.
Cirīmaiṃ Maharjan and family members added a metal channel gate to the façade of the temple's ground floor.
Punasiṃ Bhāro (text: Bhāvo), Dhaṃchimi, Dhanavirasiṃ, and Mānithakuṃ jointly offered the bell to the temple.

?? Kṛṣṇa Bhāro[1](text: Bhāvo), Laṃsiha Bhāro, Mālasika Bhāro, Kutu Bhāro, and other Bhāros jointly installed this stone statue of Nandī in front of the Cvaḥpvaḥ Gaṇeśa temple.Footnotes^Two characters of this name are illegible in the inscription.

event_name: Inscription Issued by Licchavi King Aṃśu Varman
event_description: This inscription issued by King Aṃśu Varman is not related to Cvaḥpvaḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira. Previously, it was attached to the temple’s plinth. Around 2000 CE, the Department of Archaeology and residents of the area jointly shifted it slightly to the east of the temple. The inscription records the regulations which prohibit to encroach or damage the public heritage, such as statues and temples.

The Kaṅgaḥdyaḥ Shrine (see object number LAL1790-009 above) is under reconstruction (as of December 2020) by the joint efforts of Caḥpata Sampadā Saṃrakṣaṇa Samiti (a non-government organisation formed to develop the local heritage) and Caḥpata Ṭola Reform Committee (also a non-government organisation formed to develop Caḥpata Ṭola). A person called Mukeśa Maharjana drafted a roadmap and a design for its reconstruction.

According to the now-lost inscription found on the site (refer to D. Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha, VS 2032, second part, p. 9), a Brahmin constructed the Maṭha and allocated lands for its upkeep during the reign of Pratāpa Malla. When Vajrācārya and Ṭ. Śreṣṭha read the inscription, it was already eroded, with only the number seven visible.The inscription in their edition reads as follows:[L1.] शुभ ॥ सम्वत् ७ …. वैशाख … राजराजेन्द्र कवीन्द्र जयप्रतापमल्ल प्रभु ठाकुरस विजयराज्ये[L2.] श्रीनिवक्वाठया व्राह्मन …. तुलसिया मठ दयका …. वु ….[L3.] पिक दुंता थो वुया ओलसानन, गुथि …. (म)न्दिर दयके माल । थो सेनकुम्हया महापातक
Vīṇā, Vinoda and Suvīna installed a Viṣṇu statue (LAL4245-011) in memory of the late Sūryakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha.
Vinoda Kṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha and his wife installed a statue of Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī (LAL4245-014) in memory of their late nephew Savina Kṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha and his wife.
A statue of Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī (LAL4245-015) was installed in memory of Nārāyaṇakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha (VS 1978-2071) and Kadamalatā Śreṣṭha (VS 1982-2071).
Sūryakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha and Vinodakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha installed a statue of Viṣṇu-Lakṣmī in memory of their late father Candrakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha and mother Kuntīdevī Śreṣṭha.
A Viṣṇu statue was installed in memory of Rojakṛṣṇa Śreṣṭha (VS 2009-2075).
A Viṣṇu statue (LAL4245-020) was installed in memory of Cainakṛṣṇa.

Between 2019 and 2021, Ikhālakhu Phalcā, then built in cement, has been rebuilt using wood and brick, no historic materials have been used. The niches with deities have been removed, in March 2022, the statues made from stone have been placed on wooden shelves.

Thishitiwas established in 1168 CE (NS 288) during the reign of King Rudradeva. Water spouts were installed in memory of the sponsor's deceased mother, father, and son. Unfortunately, the sponsor's name is unclear due to the breakage of the inscription that records this event.
Seven family members, including Samundaya and Vāsiṃha, installed the Buddha statue in memory of a deceased family member.
Together with his wife Bhuvaneśvarī and son Raṇavīrasiṃha, a donor offered a beam support for a bell. The name of the main donor and the bell for which the support was installed are both unclear.

event_name: Construction of a rest house and installation of a Gaṇeśa statue
event_description: Aphalcā, featuring a statue of Gaṇeśa, was constructed with the wish for the emancipation of Saṃgrāma Siṃha and Mayaju Thakuṃ of Kathmandu.
The Akṣobhya statue was erected by the family in memory of the late Rājeśa Vajrācārya.

Jñānabhakta, the president of the Bungmati branch of the Kṛṣṇa Praṇāmī sect of the Vaiṣṇava denomination collected donations from the locals to construct the Phalcā. Herā Jyāpunī gave snacks to the workers during the construction period.
The Nijānanda Bhajana Maṇḍala group was formed and began to organise chanting sessions on the ground floor of the building.
The Phalcā was severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes.

The Centre for Integrated Urban Development (CIUD) rebuilt the Phalcā from the ground up using entirely new materials. After the reconstruction, the Gaṇeśa Mandira (BUN0021) and this Phalcā were both inaugurated simultaneously.

The last king of Kathmandu, Jaya Prakāśa Malla, originally constructed 21 water spouts. No inscriptional record has been found regarding the construction of thishiti(water spout complex). However, it is known that it was built during his reign (1750–1768 CE).काठमाडौको अन्तिम राजा जयप्रकाश मल्लले प्रारम्भमा २१ वटा धाराको निर्माण  गरेका थिए । यस क्षेत्रमा हिति निर्माण सम्बन्धी कुनै अभिलेख प्राप्त छैन । उनको शासनकाल (सन् १७५०- १७६८) मा यो हितिको निर्माण भएको थाहा हुन्छ ।

Later, by adding one more spout to the existing twenty-one, Raṇabahādura Śāha expanded it into a set of twenty-two spouts. From that time onwards, the site came to be known as Balaju Bāisadhara (Balaju Twenty-Two Spouts).एक्काईवटा हिति भएको ठाउँमा थप एकवटा हितिको निर्माण गरी रण बहादुर शाहले बाइसधारा बनाएको थियो । त्यस बेलादेखि यस धारालाई 'बालाजु बाइसधारा" भन्न थालेको हो ।

In 1961 CE (2018 VS), Minister of Agriculture Suryabahādura Thāpā laid the foundation stone for a garden in the area. From this, it is understood that the Balaju Park was initially named Mahendra Udyāna (Mahendra Park).कृषि मन्त्री सूर्य बहादुर थापाबाट विसं २०१८ (सन् १९६१)मा बगैचा बनाउनको लागि शिलान्यास गरेको थियो । यसबाट केथाहा हुन्छ भने बालाजु पार्कलाई पहिला महेन्द्र उद्यानको नाम दिइएको थियो ।

The Bāisadhārā Udyāna (Twenty-Two Spouts Garden), constructed through the Valley Development Committee and public cooperation, was formally inaugurated by Dr. Tulśī Giri, the Chairman of the Cabinet.उपत्यका निर्माण समिति र जनसहयोजद्वारा निर्मित 'बाइसधारा उद्यान' को उद्घाटन मन्त्री परिषदका अध्धक्ष डा. तुल्शी गिरिले गरेका थिए ।
The 2015 earthquakes badly damaged the houses of this Courtyard. Some of the houses are on the verge of collapse and some of them are yet to be renovated.

An inscription posted on the plinth of the statue of Nandī deals with the donation of money by some devotees to form aguthifor worshipping Sumeśvara Mahādeva on Śivarātrī and offering animal sacrifice to the Gaṇeśa enshrined nearby. The donation took place on the 13th of the dark fortnight of Māgha but the year is illegible due to the erosion of the text. The donor’s name is also unreadable due to the same reason.

As the Sataḥ was in a poor state of repair, it was dismantled and rebuilt from the ground up at the initiation of local residents. As modern bricks and cement were used during the reconstruction, the traditional architecture of the Sataḥ was lost.

A marble inscription posted on the western side of the plinth of the statue of Nandī records the renovation of Sumeśvara Mahādeva Shrine by Lakṣmībhakta Śreṣṭha and his family in memory of his deceased parents Haribhakta Śhreṣṭha and Ṭikāmāyā Śhreṣṭha.
The 2015 earthquakes damaged the Sataḥ internally. It was dismantled in 2022 CE after remaining in poor condition for almost seven years. The Department of Archaeology is funding the reconstruction.

To the left of the sanctum door, below the Gaṇeśa statue, one can find a stone inscription. In 2014,Śākya(1134, 118) read four lines of the inscription. These lines recorded the anniversary ritual worship of thebāhāḥand some names of thesaṅghamembers. Tthe inscription is now far too damaged to be legible.
A palm-leaf manuscript dated NS 688 (1548 CE) mentions a monastic building named Naka Bāhāra.
Theguṭhīof the Bāhāḥ renovated it.
Images of seven Tathāgatas, Nāmasaṅgīti and Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara were painted on the wall.
Naḥ Bāhāḥ Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti paved stones on thebāhāḥcācourtyard.
Jagajyoti Malla's reign saw the initiation of stonework for a certain purpose.
During Jagajyoti Malla's reign, stone carvers like Manajurāma and Rāyarāma began stonework for a specific purpose not clarified in the inscription.
Stones were selected for a certain purpose.
Stonework was initiated for the construction of a certain pond.
Jitāmitra Malla initiated stonework for a grand fire oblation.

Bhupatindra Malla, in the name of his father, selected stones and marked it for the construction of a stone temple. A similar inscription with the same date and details is found on the Nālāchāpa rock formation (BKT0660).
Statues of the four Dhyānī Buddhas were installed in niches facing the cardinal directions.
An inscription dated to 1561 CE (NS 681) mentions the renovation of thestūpa(D. VajracharyaVS 2056, 21), yet this inscription is now lost.
Pruscha has cited an inscription from 1759 CE (Pruscha1975, 144). It is probable that he is referring to this particular inscription

This Dharmadhātu rising in front of the Stūpa. The date could not be figured out from the inscription. However, the name of the donors Govinda Devi, Bābumāna, Sāhilā are clear. As the inscription in Devanagarī script, it can be assumed that it is not so old.
In the name of late Āsāmadu, Candrarāja Śākya offered a bell in front of the stūpa.

event_name: Addition of māne (Prayer wheel) around the stūpa
event_description: In the memory of Keśab Bahadura Śreṣṭha, who passed away on Caitra 22, 2057 BS, a prayer wheel was added around the Stūpa by his family members.

event_name: Donation of butter lamps and a metal darmadhātu
event_description: Devaratna Śākya and family members presented 16 metal butter lamps along with a metalvajrawhich was installed on thedharmadhātu(LAL0610-007).

During the reign of King Tribhuvana, Rājamānasiṃha (text: Lājamāṃsī) and his wife Āsāthakuṃ of Koṣāchẽ Nani in Thecva undertook restoration work on thecaitya. The donor couple also laid the surrounding area with stones on the occasion. Additionally, they established a land endowment and a non-expendable fund of Rs. 200 to support its upkeep. The income generated from the land endowment and interest from the fund was designated for the regular maintenance of thecaitya. It was also stipulated that lamps should be lit at thecaityaon the full moon day of Āśvina. Ten trustees were appointed to oversee these arrangements and were provided with meals on the full moon day of Āśvina and the following day.
Dyaḥchẽ of Lokeśvara was renovated.
The statue of Lokeśvara was repaired.

event_name: Rebuilding the Dyaḥchẽ and installation of new statue of Nīlakaṇṭha Lokeśvara
event_description: After the dilapidation of Dyaḥchẽ of Lokeśvara, it was completely demolished and rebuilt with the financial support of Lalitpur Metropolitan City.
Jujubhāi Śākya, Sarītā Śākya and Amararāja Śākya jointly offered a metal patāḥ to the dyaḥchẽ.
Caityarāja Vajrācārya donated the security grills for the dyaḥchẽ.

An inscription on the upper part of the well tells us about its builders. It says that the well was built in 1928 CE (VS 1985) during the reign of King Tribhuvan and Candra Śamśera. The builders were Viṣṇulāl Mākaḥju, his wife Vālamāyā, and his brother Kṛṣṇalāl. Viṣṇulāl was the grandson of Cakanārāye (Cakranārāyaṇa) and the son of Mahādyau (Mahādeva), and he was a wealthy resident living near Ganeśasthān in the Oṭola area of Dhulikhel (local resident: Mākaḥju, male, age 61). The inscription also expresses the family’s wishes for their sons’ and grandsons’ success, prosperity for future generations, and for their family name to continue. For many years, the family followed the tradition of cleaning the well every year onSithi Nakha, a festival for cleaning water sources. This practice stopped around the 1990s (VS 2050), but the well still flows and continues to serve the community.
The stone inscription, installed on the south plinth of thecaitya, is illegible. It is not known if the inscription is related to the initial construction of thecaitya.

Viṣṇu Māyā and Herā Māyā established this Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in the memory of Lakṣmī Nārā̃, his wife Gaṇeśa Māyā, his brothers Śeṣa Nārā̃, Gaṇeśa Lāla, Satyanārā̃, Jaga Nārā̃, Harṣa Nārā̃ and other family members.

event_name: Offering of a lion (siṃha) and a banner (dhvaja)
event_description: According to an inscription from the reign of King Nṛpendra Malla, son of King Pratāpa Malla, a certain Vīrabhadrafrom Kāntipura (Kathmandu) had offered a lion (siṃha) and a banner (dhvaja) to the goddess. However, as part of the inscription is damaged and the letters are worn, the exact date inscribed cannot be determined.
At the main site where theamūrta(aniconic) stone representing Bhadrakālī was established, Bama Bahādura Kuvara Rāṇā offered a bronze toraṇa adorned with images ofMātṛkās.
Dhīrtavīra from Kathmandu offered two bronze banners to the goddess.

Harṣa Nārāyaṇa Taṇḍukāra, son of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and Bhāgyalakṣmī Taṇḍukāra of Kathmandu, together with his wife Dharmalakṣmī and other family members, undertook the renovation of thehiti, stone platform (sataḥ), and bell (ghaṇṭa) situated at thispīṭha(sanctuary).
According to the inscription on the bell, the original one installed in 1827 CE (NS 947) had been damaged, and a new bell (KAT3380-021) was offered in 1882 CE (NS 1002).
Narasiṃ of Kathmandu, together with his wife Lānibeti (Rānībeṭī) Sāhu Haribinda, Mānasiṃha, and other family members, offered a bronzeīlā(ritual object) to the goddess.
Gopāla Kṛṣṇa, Gopī Kṛṣṇa, and other members of their family dedicated a bell to Bhadrakālī Devī.

On the eastern wall of thepīṭha, a marble inscription is affixed bearing the donor’s name Bhairava Bahādura and the date 1942 CE (VS 1999). No further details are provided in the inscription, making it difficult to ascertain additional information.
Keśara Jaṅga Parākrama Śāha and his descendants restored and reinstalled the bell that had been originally offered to Bhadrakālī by their ancestors.

The bell donated by Śarata Śamaśera Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā in 1919 CE (VS 1976) was later repaired and reinstalled by the Śrī Bhadrakālī Bhajana Maṇḍala after restoration.शरत शमसेर जङ्ग बहादुर राणाले विसं १९७६ (सन् १९१९) मा चढाएको घण्ट जीर्णोद्धार गरी श्री भद्रकाली भजन मण्डलले जीर्णोद्धार गरी भद्रकालीलाई चढाएको थियो ।

Indra Bahādur Taṇḍukāra, a resident of Putalisadak, Kathmandu, transferred ownership of his house to the individuals named in an inscription with the condition that, after his death, they must annually perform his death ritual in his name.
Gopālamāna, Pūrṇamāna, Jyotilakṣmī, Jayantikṣmī, Suśīlalakṣmī, and others made and offered a bell to Bhadrakālī.

event_name: Copper plate repousse on the Navagraha (KAT3380-009)
event_description: Ratna Dyaḥpālā, his wife Tuyū Mai Dyaḥpālā, their son Bāburatna, Banadēvī, and the entire Dyaḥpālā family gilded thenavagrahashrine located in front of the Bhadrakālī Pīṭha with copper sheets.

event_name: Brass plate repposse on the Vetāla satatue
event_description: Keśava Bahādura Gaḍtaulā and his late wife Umā Gaḍtaulā covered the Vetāla image in front of the Bhadrakālī Pīṭha with a bronze sheet.

event_name: Rebuilding the entrance gate to pīṭha
event_description: As the original wooden entrance door to the pīṭha had decayed and broken, it was reconstructed in cement with the support of Indra Bahādura, Caṅkha Māyā, and their associates. Since the inscription lacks a date, the precise year of reconstruction cannot be determined.

Nārja Māyā, wife of Harimāna, along with Nārāyaṇa of Putalisadak, his wife, and other donors, contributed funds to the Taḥdhaṃ Guṭhī of Khićā Pokharī, assigning the responsibility to Harimāna Taṇḍukāra and other members to perform annual ancestral rites after their deaths. However, no date is inscribed on this record.
The terrace on the second floor of the Chẽ was covered to add an additional floor to the building.
The Phalcā was rebuilt in 2010 CE. As the building was old and on the verge of collapse, the owner had rebuilt the house along with the Phalcā using the old columns and capitals.
Kaviprasāda organized devotional singing dedicated to Nārāyaṇa and erected the stone pillar at the Bhujinda Ṭola.

The Department of Archaeology reconstructed the temple after it was damaged by the 2015 CE earthquakes. While digging the foundation for reconstruction, old coins were recovered. These coins were taken away by the Department of Archaeology.
The temple was built in memory of Viṣṇukumārī, the wife of Prime Minister Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā, and was hence named Viṣṇumukteśvara.
Restoration of the monastic building in 1933
The building suffered immense damage in the 2015 earthquake, rendering it no longer inhabitable. The family who lived there demolished it and reconstructed it as a more modern structure.

event_name: Construction of a phalcā and establishment of statues of Umā-Maheśvara and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa
event_description: Vidyānanda Śarmā established aphalcāalong with images of Umā-Maheśvara and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa at Corcā Hiti. The pavilion and the Umā-Maheśvara sculpture no longer survive, but the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa image mentioned in the inscription may correspond to the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa (BKT0820-007) still visible on the northern wall of the Hiti.

event_name: Establishment of a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya and a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala
event_description: Thapāju Dhīrjamuni of Śrīvatsa Vihāra established thisdharmadhātu maṇḍala.Sundari Vajrācārya, wife of Uṣṇisa Vajrācārya donated money for thedharmadhātu jinālaya caitya.

Thedharmadhātu jinālaya caityawas constructed in NS 1128. The inscription on the plinth of thecaityarecording the date of its construction and donor is covered at present. The date could be identified from a photo taken by Bruce Owens in 2014 (see the photo below)

event_name: Addition of a brass plate to the Dharmadhātu
event_description: The upper part of the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (LAL0390-015) was coverd with a brass plate by Harṣarāj and Ratnarāj Vajrācārya.
The temple of the Bāhāḥ collapsed in the great earthquake of 1934.
Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala was added inside the courtyard by Jñānavīra and his wife Harṣamāyā Vajrācārya.
Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala was added inside the courtyard by Muniratna and Harṣaratna Vajrācārya .
Inside the bāhāḥ, Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (LAL0390-11) was constructed by Dayāmuni and family members.
The courtyard of the Bāhāḥ was paved withcikã apā.
Renovation of the temple (Kvaḥpāḥchẽ) by the Saãgha members

Between NS 1000 and 1081 several renovations and restd donations took place, e.g.NS 1000: The roof of the temple (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) was renovated by Cakreśvara and other Saṅgha members.NS 1000: Roofs of the temple (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) were covered with gilded copper by Yoga Vīra Siṃha and Byakhārā Vajrācārya.NS 1000: In front of the main entrance of the temple (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) a brass Yajñasālā was installed by Harṣa Vīra.NS 1013: The main deity (kvaḥpāḥdyaḥ) was temporarily shifted by Cakreśvara and other Saṅgha members.NS 1025: Rebuiling of a house by Cakreśvara and other Saṅgha members with funding from the BāhāḥNS 1030: Addition oftoraṇasba DanakutũNS 1030: Donation of Bhikku statues by Tataḥ Guṭhī members of Haka BāhāḥNS 1034: Installation of a Prajñāpāramitā statue by Dharma rāj and Ratna VajrācāryaNS 1046: Donation of a Vajra by TrailokyamuniNS 1054: Donation of an oil-lamp balustradeNS 1055: Renovation work started by Cakreśvara and other Saṅgha membersNS 1056: Donation of lions and Lokeśvara by Pūrṇa Bahādura VajrācāryaNS 1059: Donation of a gate with oil-lamps by Dharmarāj VajrācāryaNS 1060: Donation of stone elephants by TrailokyamuniNS 1060: Donation of a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala by Cidhimāya
Above the main entrane of Kumārichẽ, a woodentoraṇawas added by Yoga Vīra Siṃha and his family members.

The Vajrasatva shrine was constructed. Three stone statuse (Vajrasatva, Vasundharā and Mañjusrī) were installed inside the shrine. A Guṭhī was formed and lands were donated as a source for annual rituals.
Although is no historical source to date the shrine’s initial construction, the statue of Hanumān is said to have been established by King Raṇajīta Malla (r. 1722-1769 CE).

With the aim of shielding the statue from unceasing sun and rain, devotees joined forces to install a tin roof over the revered figure. They diligently replaced the small parasol that had adorned it before, ensuring that the elements would no longer impinge upon its sacred presence.
कविप्रसाद गौतमले तुलानारायण मन्दिरमा पूजाआजा गरी शिलास्तम्भ स्थापना गरेका थिए ।

Pañcamāyā Khaḍge of Mahārājagañja commissioned the construction of aphalcāon the northern side of the Porpā Ajimā Pīṭha in memory of her late father-in-law Śeramāna Khaḍge, mother-in-law Ratnamāyā, husband Surjamāna Khaḍge, son Rāmeśvara, and other deceased members of her family.महाराजगञ्ज निवासी पञ्चमाया खड्गेले दिवंगत ससुरा सेरमान खड्गे, दिवंगत सासु रत्नमाया, दिवंगत पति सुर्जमान खड्गे, दिवंगत छोरा रामेश्वर लगायत दिवंगत भएका परिवारका अन्य सदस्यहरूको नाममा पोर्पा अजिमा पीठको उत्तरपट्टि फल्चा निर्माण गरिदिएकी थिइन् ।

event_name: Establishment of the statue of Sarasvatī
event_description: Dasamāyā Maharjana installed an image of Sarasvatī.दसमाया महर्जनले सरस्वतीको मूर्ति स्थापना गरेकी थिइन् ।
Minādevī Rājabaṃśī of Jhāpā laid marble flooring on the ground surface within the shrine precinct.झापा निवासी मिनादेवी राजवंशीले देवस्थलभित्रको भुइँमा मार्बल बिछ्याएकी थिइन् ।

event_name: Establishment of the statue of Rādhākṛṣṇa
event_description: In memory of her deceased son Rājindra Basneta, his mother Sumitrā Basneta installed an image of Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa.दिवंगत छोरा राजिन्द्र बस्नेतको नाममा आमा सुमित्रा बस्नेतले राधाकृष्णको मूर्ति स्थापना गरेकी थिइन् ।

event_name: Establishment of the statue of Gaṇeśa
event_description: In remembrance of their deceased son Rāju Śreṣṭha, his father Bālakumāra Śreṣṭha and mother Bimalā Śreṣṭha installed an image of Gaṇeśa.दिवंगत छोरा राजु श्रेष्ठको सम्झनामा बुबा बालकुमार श्रेष्ठ र आमा बिमला श्रेष्ठले गणेशको मूर्ति स्थापना गरेका थिए ।

In memory of their deceased grandfather Kulaṃ, father Kulabīra, mother Bāṃlā, and elder brother Pañca, family members jointly installed acaitya(KAT3400-008).दिवंगत बाजे कुलं, दिवंगत बुबा कुलबीर, दिवंगत आमा बांला, दिवंगत दाजु पञ्चको स्मृतिमा परिवारका सदस्यहरूले मिलेर चैत्य (KAT3400-008) स्थापना गरेका थिए ।

Triratna of Asan, Dharmadhvaja Tāmāṅa of Udayapur, and other individuals jointly installed anothercaitya(KAT3400-007) within the Porpā Ajimā Pīṭha precinct.असनका त्रिरत्न, उदयपुरका धर्मध्वज तामाङ लगायत अन्य व्यक्तिहरूले मिलेर पोर्पा अजिमा पीठ परिसरमा चैत्य (KAT3400-007) स्थापना गरेका थिए ।

Ś. Śreṣṭha(VS 2057, 45), without refereeing to any sources, mentions that this Temple was constructed by Hastikā (one of the nannies of King Raṇabahādura Śāha) in 1803 CE during the renovation of the Bāghabhairava Temple (KIR0004).
Jītavīra (who was supposedly a government employee), a resident of the Tuṃjhvaḥ Ṭola (Kirtipur) renovated the Temple in 1932 CE (VS 1988).

event_name: Minor renovation and formation of a guṭhī
event_description: The exterior of the Temple was coated with lime plaster and was given its present shape. Aguṭhīwas also established for the religious observances and the upkeep of the Temple.
King Pratāpa Malla constructed the pond in memory of his son Cakravartendra Malla.
In the northern section of the pond, Pratāpa Malla also established an image of Nārāyaṇa facing west, in honor of his deceased son, Cakravartīndra Malla.
Theśikhara-style temple built by Pratāpa Malla was badly damaged in the 1934 CE (1990 VS) earthquake and was subsequently reconstructed by Juddha Śamaśera Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā.

The National Reconstruction Authority completed the reconstruction of both Rānīpokharī and the Bālagopāleśvara temple, strictly following Malla-period style, techniques, and materials. The rebuilt Rānīpokharī and Bālagopāleśvara temple were then inaugurated by President Vidyā Devi Bhandari.

शाक्यभिक्षु मानविर सिंले श्रीमती भनि थकु, जेठा छोरा भाजुरत्न, बुहारी बेतिमाया लगायत परिवारका सदस्यहरूसँग मिलेर बाहाःमा जीर्णोद्धारको काम गरेका थिए । उनले बाहाःको क्वाःपाःछेँ जीर्णोद्धार गरेका थिए वा अमिताभ ‍बिराजमान भएको गर्भगृहको मात्र जीर्णोद्धार गरेका थिए भन्ने कुरा स्पष्ट छैन ।

दिवंगत शाक्यभिक्षु मानविर सिंको नाममा उनकी श्रीमती भनि थकुले जेठा छोरा भाजुरत्न, बुहारी श्रीमती बेतिमाया लगायत परिवारका सदस्यहरूसँग मिलेर गर्भगृहभित्र प्रवेश गर्ने ढोकामाथि राखिएको तोरणलाई मर्मत गरेर चढाएकी थिइन् ।
ओम्बाहाः टोल निवासी गुह्यहर्ष वज्राचार्यले त्वाःक्यब बाहाः प्राङ्गणमा रहेको पुरानो चैत्य जीर्ण भएकोले उक्त जीर्ण चैत्यलाई गर्भमा राखेर त्यसमाथि नयाँ चैत्य निर्माण गरेका थिए ।
The traditional structure was dismantled and a new building was made.
A youth club named Unique Club utilized two rooms of the ground floor, one for the office and another as a store. The club engaged in social welfare.

With devotion to their tutelary deity, two brothers, Śivakṛṣṇa Bhāro and Bhima Bhāro, living in Khaṇḍachuka within Yaṃparācha ṭola in Bhaktapur, built theJaḥdhuṃtogether. Local Pañcas were given the responsibility for its maintenance. In this inscription, theJaḥdhuṃis referred to asJaradhārā, meaning a water source or spout. The inscription records the address of those who established the Jaḥdhuṃ as Yaṃparācha ṭola. Over time, the pronunciation of Yaṃparācha ṭolā gradually changed, leading to the current name Jelā̃ ṭolā.

event_name: Offering of a pair of lions
event_description: A group of persons led by Dharmasiṃha Bhābo installed a pair of lion statues in front of the temple.
Jītabahādura Kusle (text: Jitabahādura Kusala), the grandson of Bakhabira and the son of Māhilā, donated a bell for Candrabhairava.
Harimāna Jośī (text: Harīmāna Josī) of the Bhansāra Ṭola, Cāpāgāũ installed a metaltoraṇaon top of the entrance to the sanctum.
Saroja Karmācārya, the grandson of Kṛṣṇa Karmācārya and son of Sanukājī Karmācārya, offered an oblong banner (patāḥ) to the temple.

As the temple is located adjacent to a busy road, vehicles passing by would often collide with its eastern roof. Once, a large vehicle collided and completely destroyed the eastern roof. The locals collectively managed the finances and reconstructed the temple. The temple was reconstructed into a two-tiered structure, conforming to its original appearance prior to the 1934 earthquakes. However, the eastern and western sides of the temple were open in the previous construction, but were walled in the reconstruction.

event_name: Donation of a pair of lion
event_description: Nhukṣamāyā and his family from Bāliphala area offered a pair of lion’s statues to the Bāhāḥ.
Śāntaratna Vajrācārya, Dharmakumārī and Lakṣmīkumārī had jointly established adharmadhātujinālayacaityain the Bāhāḥ-courtyard.

With the financial support of Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and donations from locals, the Bāhāḥ building was reconstructed. After the reconstruction, Constituent Assembly member Pampha Bhusal inaugurated it.

As mentioned above in the description, a vehicle, while clearing away the debris of the buildings that collapsed in the 2015 earthquakes, knocked the Shrine down. As the locals threatened to keep the vehicle in their possession until the Shrine was rebuilt, the vehicle owner got the Shrine reconstructed soon after the incident.

event_name: Construction of a chaitya (near to the phalcā)
event_description: A stone inscription from NS 931 does not belong to this Phalcā even though has been embedded into the eastern wall. However, it belongs to the nearby stone caitya (KIR0073) and informs about its construction.  The full text and ink impression of this inscription has published by Shokoohy and others (VS 2014, 289-290).

The Kirtipur municipality planned to rebuilt a phalcā at the same place and funded Rs. 23, 64,000 to built a new phalcā in 2020 CE. The construction task was completed in 2020 September and inaugurated by the Mayor of the municipality on the 30th day of November 2020.

There was a ruined phalcā exactly at the place where the new phalcā stands today. From the previous phalcā, only a square plinth had remained until the end of 1980. The plinth was then replaced by a one-storied concrete structure in around 1980. That building was used by a social neighborhood development organization - Kirtipur Vācanālaya - for decades.
A dispute regarding the ownership of the land belonging to the deity was resolved and a set of rules were enforced upon the concerned people.

Locals of Asana (text: Aśvaka Maṇḍapa) renovated thenipathapuli(?) of Annapūrṇā (text: Asaṃmaru Ajimā) temple. Harṣabhadra Vajrācārya of Taḥchẽ Bāhāḥ was the priest who officiated various rituals involved in the course of the renovation.

A bell was installed on the southwestern corner of the temple. Due to the metal bars installed for security reasons, it is not possible to read the inscription in full. The name of the donor is, therefore, unclear.
Eighteen members of the Cākaḥmata Guthi offered a golden roof to the uppermost tier of the temple.

A royal decree set aside the rent obtained from certain shops at the Asana square to be used for observing various socio-cultural activities in the area including the annual procession of Annapūrṇā. The content of the decree issued through a document was also ordered to be placed at the temple in the form of an inscription. Besides the enforcement of the decree, the inscription also records Hākyā Kaṭuvāla pledging to offer 1dhārnīof vermillion powder to the deity during her annual procession while submitting Rs. 100 to the government.
Residents of the Asana Ṭola offered a goldentoraṇaon top of the main entrance to the Annapūrṇā temple.

Jayanarasiṃhalakṣmī (text: Jayanarasiṃlakṣmi), his wife, and other family members laid the second tier of the temple with gilded sheets, fulfilling the pledge of his deceased elder brother Manorathasiṃha (text: Manorathasiṃ).

event_name: Replacement of lower roof with gilt sheet
event_description: Cakravīra, Jñānathaku, Puṇyalakṣmī, and the family members installed gilded sheets on the lower tier of the temple and placed the inscription recording the event on the eaves fascia (mhuraḥpau) of the same tier.

event_name: Beautification of many objects with metal
event_description: A certain item in the sanctum was gilded. Mohanavīrasiṃha (text: Mohanavīrasiṃ) and his wife Bekhālāni installed brass covers for the temple’s door leaves and pillars.

event_name: Covering of struts with gilt metal
event_description: Kularatna and Siddhirāja, who hailed from Itilanhe in Patan, installed gilded covers on the statues of the wooden struts.

Mohanavīrasiṃha (text: Mohanavīrasiṃ) and his wife Bekhālāni installed a goldentoraṇaon top of the northern entrance of the temple. His father Cakravīrasiṃha (text: Cakravirasiṃ) had wished to make the offering that was fulfilled by his son and daughter-in-law.

A donor from the Tulādhara community offered a goldentoraṇaon top of the southern entrance of the temple. The name of the donor, a resident of Ontāchẽ (lit. eastern house) at Bākunani in Asana, is unclear as the name is covered in the inscription.
A bell was installed on the northwestern corner of the temple. The name of the donor could not be read due to the placement of metal bars around the bell.

A donor of the Tulādhara caste from Asana offers two statues to the temple and gilds the quarter-round design (nāḥgvaḥ) and frill pattern designs of the temple during the reign of King Prithvī Vikrama Śāha (r. 1881-1911 CE). The full name of the donor and the year of the donation cannot be traced, as a portion of the inscription is covered by the temple’storaṇa. Only the first two digits of the year are visible. The event took place between 1881-1911 CE.

The members of theguthiformed to observe certain rituals at the temple performed certain activities here at the temple. As a portion of this eroded inscription is under the ground, it is unclear what was accomplished on this occasion.

event_name: Covering of wooden frame with silver plate
event_description: Residents of Bhoṭāhiṭī, Balarāma Śreṣṭha, his younger brother Kṛṣṇalāla Śreṣṭha, and the family installed a silver cover on the wooden frame of the front entrance to the sanctum.
Posted below the lower roof of the temple, the content of this brass-plate inscription is not clear, as the presence of metal bars in front obstructs reading it.

event_name: Covering of objects with brass plate
event_description: Mohanavīrasiṃha (text: Mohanavirasiṃ), his wife Bekhālāni, and the family installed covers of brass sheets on the statues ofaṣṭamātṛkā, Siṃhinī, Vyāghrinī, the five Tārās, along with the beams, capitals, cornices, etc. of the temple.
Tejaharṣa Tulādhara, his wife Herādevī, and the family members installed a brass statue ofkhyāḥ, a humanoid goblin, andkavaṃ, a skeletal being, outside the temple.
Local devotional singers formed Śrī Annapūrṇa Jñānamālā Bhajana Khalaḥ for the continuation of singing hymns at the temple.
Buddhist nun Sumati Padmā of Maitri Vihāra in Svayambhū offered a brassmaṇḍalato Goddess Annapūrṇā.
Cinīdevī Śreṣṭha of the Asana alley offered a fire oblation pit (yajñakuṇḍa) to Goddess Annapūrṇā.
A local organization named Asana Pāsā Pucaḥ organized a fire oblation to appease the planetary deities following the massive loss of lives and property in the 2015 earthquakes.

event_name: Addition of many objects and beautification of the monument
event_description: Asana Sevā Samiti, another local organization, collected donations to improve the temple aesthetically. Silver statues of theaṣṭamātṛkādeities were installed inside the sanctum along with the addition of theaṣṭamaṅgalaemblems together with silverkalaśas on either side. The statue of the serpent in the sanctum was gilded. Two largekalaśas were established in front of the temple with a smallerkalaśaeach on the other three sides. Brass sheets were set on the steps by the main entrance. The Patāḥ hanging from the finial was also cleaned and regilded on the occasion.
Various parts of the temple received a cover of brass and silver sheets besides the offering of various new items to the deity.

event_name: Renovation and addition  of a statue
event_description: In CE 2005 (NS 1125), the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City restored the temple. During this restoration, local Dharma Maharjana installed a new statue of Hariśaṅkara in place of the one that had been lost (local resident, Maharjana, male, age 64).

event_name: Covering the roof with cooper sheet
event_description: The aforementioned family of Rāmaprasāda from Asana covered the Temple's roof with cooper sheet and topped it with a gilded finial.
Kānchā Sarāphī, Ratnalāla, and other family members renovated the Temple. They also marble-paved its plinth and tiled the walls.

The construction of Bhelāchẽ Phalcā was funded by a Khusaḥ (Taṇḍukār) family, the descendents of Mangal Tandukar. However, Mr. Tandukar could not remember the name of his ancestor who actually commissioned the Phalcā. According to the house owner, the Phalcā was rebuilt some 20 years ago (around 1995/2000 CE). Niels Gutschow estimates 1980 to be the date of reconstruction, but this could not be confirmed.

The Phalcā was in a bad condition and on the verge of collapse. Mr Tandukar had it dismantled and rebuilt in its present structure in the late 1990s. The Bhelāchẽ Phalcā was converted into a concrete Phalcā with a terrace on top.
The statue was consecrated in the sanctum by Abhayasiṃha Duvāla Bhāro.

event_name: Building the stone plinth of the Temple
event_description: Juti Bharo, a grandson of Abhayasiṃha Duvāla Bhāro who consecrated the above-mentioned statue in the sanctum built the stone plinth around the Temple.

event_name: Installation of statues in the Lāchi Hiti
event_description: The inscription kept inside the sanctum from NS 853 is not related to the Temple itself, but belongs to a nearbyhiti(THK0021). It records the installation of statues of Nārāyaṇa, Umāmaheśvara, and Sarasvatī at thehitiby Kṛṣṇānandana and his wife, residents of Thankot.
The Temple was rebuilt at the initiation of a local organization called Simrika Thakvāḥ Pucaḥ. Most of the woodworks were reused during the reconstruction.
Kṛṣṇabahādura Śreṣṭha, a resident of the Pakanājola Ṭola, renovated it.
